*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

On Benefits to Brutus, seven books.
On Anger, to Novatus, three books.
On Providence, one book.
On the Happy Life, to Gallio, one book.
On Consolation, to Marcia, one book.
On Consolation, to his mother, one book.
On Tranquillity of Life, one book.
That Injury Does Not Befall the Wise Man, four books.
On the Brevity of Life, one book.
On Moral Studies, one book.
On Natural Questions, seven books.
Of Suasory Sentences, one book.
Of Controversies, five books.
On Poverty, one book.
To Polybius, of Consolation, one book.
On the Games of Seneca, one book.
On Abundance of Words, one book.
On Marriage, one book.
Of Tragedies, ten books.
On the Death of Claudius, one book.
Of Letters to St. Paul, one book. “I believe you, Paul, now.”
Of Letters to Lucilius, twenty-two books. “Therefore do this, my Lucilius.”

These are the works of Seneca’s writings that I have been able to find at present. He is also said to have written some other little works, which have not yet come into our hands. He was certainly a most ardent lover of wisdom, and a zealous seeker of it, and of so retentive a memory that, when two thousand names had been read before him, he soon recited them from memory. Moreover, when a certain poet had composed two hundred verses and, after putting them onto a sheet, was reciting them in order before Nero, Seneca at once, using his memory instead of the volume, repeated the same verses one by one, beginning from the last and proceeding in reverse order as far as the first. He is read to have held in memory the names of all his fellow citizens. He flourished at Rome in the times of the apostle Paul, under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

Marcellus, son of Marcus, prefect of the city of Rome, once a disciple of Simon Magus, sufficiently instructed in secular letters, converted to the faith of Jesus Christ by the preaching of the blessed apostle Peter, composed many things for the benefit of the Church of God. For, at the request of Christians, he wrote: On the Conflict of St. Peter and Simon Magus, one book.
To the saints Nereus and Achilleus, one book.
On the Acts of Peter and Paul, one book.
On the Arts of Simon, one book.
On the Death of Saint Petronilla, one book.
On the Passion of Saint Felicula, one book.
On the Passion of Saint Nicomedes, one book.

He also published other things concerning the deeds of the saints, which have not come to our knowledge. He flourished at Rome in the times of St. Peter the apostle, in the year of the Lord 50.

Linus, the first bishop of the city of Rome after blessed Peter, a Tuscan by nation, a man of most holy conduct, held the pontificate for eleven years, three months, and twelve days. Since he was a very learned man, beloved by God, he wrote in the Greek language concerning the holy apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered on one day: The Martyrdom, one book.
And certain letters.

At length, by Saturninus the prefect, whose daughter he had freed from a demon, he was punished by a capital sentence and became a martyr on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Galba, in the year of the Lord 70.

Philo the Jew, an Alexandrian by nation, of the race of priests, is placed by blessed Jerome among ecclesiastical writers for this reason: because in his little works he is very often engaged in praise of Christians. When he had been sent to Rome as envoy of his people, he is remembered as having had the friendship of the blessed apostle Peter; for this reason also he adorned with his praises the followers at Alexandria of Saint Mark, Peter’s disciple. He was a man most learned in every respect, regarded as another Plato, so that it was commonly said: either Plato imitates Philo, or Philo imitates Plato. For so great a likeness of thought and expression between them is reported. He wrote very elegant books, of which the following are given below: On the Life of the Wise Man, one book.
On the Conduct of Life, one book.
On the Confusion of Languages, one book.
On the Nature of Quadrupeds, one book.
On Those Things Which We Attest by Sense, one book.
On Education, one book.
On the Succession of [generation?], one book.
On the Change of Names, one book.
On the Heir of Divine Things, one book.
On the Division of Unequal Things, one book.
On the Three Virtues, one book.
On the Nature of Invention, one book.
On Covenants, one book.
Adam Begot Three Sons, one book.
On [unclear]
On

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

On Giants, book 1. On Victims and Promises, book 1.
On the Five Books of Moses, books 5. On Providence, books 5.
On Dreams, book 1. On Ideas, book 1.
On the Tabernacle, books 4. On Alexander, book 1.
On the Contemplative Life, book 1. On the Reason of Animals, book 1.
On Agriculture, books 2. That Every Fool Becomes a Slave, book 1.
He is read to have written many other things as well, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

Josephus the Jew, by nation a Jerusalemite, by religion a priest, son of the priest Mattathias, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished writer of the times, whom I would not place in our catalogue unless the Church read his writings and Blessed Jerome had done so before: after the destruction of Jerusalem he was captured by the emperors Vespasian and Titus and brought to Rome; because of the excellence of his talent he was magnificently honored by the senate and people of Rome. Although he remained a Jew, nevertheless he often praised the race of Christians, and in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities he set down a notable testimony concerning our Lord Jesus Christ. His volumes were held in such authority among the Romans, while he was still alive, that they were handed over to the public libraries; and after his death he was granted a bronze statue by the senate and people. Of his little works I have seen only the following: The Jewish War, books 7.
Antiquities of the World, books 24. To write the history
Against Apion, book 1. sufficiently, as I think
On the Power of Speaking, book 1.

He flourished at Rome under the emperors Vespasian and Titus, and remained among men down to the times of the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 100.

He described the contest of the sufferings of the seven sons of one mother, with their mother.

Ignatius, the third bishop of the church of Antioch after Blessed Peter, a man of outstanding holiness and a most singularly fervent lover of our Lord Jesus Christ, was accustomed to say, as Dionysius bears witness: “My love has been crucified.” This most blessed prelate, since he was a learned and zealous preacher of the divine word, wrote several elegant letters full of fervor, in which he showed himself to have been a lover of holy martyrdom. Among these the following are considered the more important: To the Church of the Ephesians, one letter.
To the Magnesians, letter 1.
To the Trojans, letter 1. To the Ro-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

To the Romans, letter 1.
To Saint John, letters 2. To the holy elder John
To the Blessed Virgin, letter 1. To Mary, bearer of Christ, her
To the Philadelphians, letter 1.
To Polycarp, letter 1.

He suffered at Rome under the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 111.

Papias, hearer and disciple of Saint John, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, a most steadfast propagator and defender of the Christian faith, disciple and zealous imitator of the holy apostles, wrote little works of authority not to be despised. Among these there exists a distinguished work, divided into five volumes, which he titled thus: Explanation of the Sayings of the Lord, books 5. Other things which he wrote we have not seen. He first invented the novelty of the thousand years, after which he dreamed that Christ would reign again in the flesh with the elect upon the earth; those who afterwards spread this error were called Chiliasts, from the thousand.

He flourished in the times of Caesar Trajan, in the year of the Lord 100 and thereabout.

Hegesippus, a Jew by nation, converted to the faith of Christ, shone forth as admirable in teaching and holiness in the Church of God; his feast has a place in the martyrology with the other saints. He wrote several little works of excellent talent, of which I have found only this: from the time of the Lord’s Passion down to his own age, a distinguished work, History of Ecclesiastical Acts, books 5. In the Parthian war, which between
I have seen no other work of his.

He flourished near the apostolic times, under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 160.

Justin, converted from being a philosopher to the catholic faith, a distinguished lover and worshipper of Christ, when in the city of Rome he rebuked Crescens the Cynic, who was blaspheming Christians, as gluttonous and afraid of death, and as a follower of luxury and lusts, was accused before the senate through that man’s plots, because he was a Christian, and was crowned with martyrdom for Christ. He wrote many distinguished little works in defense of our faith, of which these are reported: Against the Gentiles, to Antoninus, book 1. On the Soul, book 1.
To Aurelius, Against the Gentiles, book 1. The Pre-noted Psalter, book 1.
Likewise Against the Gentiles, book 1. Against Trypho the Jew, book 1.
Corrections Against the Gentiles, book 1. Against Marcion, book 1.
On the Monarchy of God, book 1. Against All Heresies, book 1. Others

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

He composed, besides, many other works which have not come to our knowledge. He flourished under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 150.

Quadratus, an Athenian, bishop after the martyr Publius, once a hearer and disciple of the holy apostles, a man steadfast and of incomparable learning, labored much for the usefulness of the Christian faith, made much progress, and gathered into the unity of the faith the church dispersed by fear of persecution. Since he was an eminent teacher, he wrote, among other things, on behalf of the Christians to the emperor Hadrian, an Apologeticum full of instruction, 1 book. And other works unknown to us. At last he suffered for the defense of the catholic faith on the seventh day before the Kalends of June. He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Aristides, an Athenian philosopher, a man most learned in secular letters and very studious in the divine scriptures, shone forth distinguished by such eloquence that he offered the nations a marvel of himself; under the garb of a philosopher he bore both Christian faith and Christian conduct, and shone forth renowned by reputation, not without holiness. He wrote an Apologeticum on behalf of the Christians to the emperor Hadrian, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Melito the Asian, bishop of Sardis, a man learned in the divine scriptures and venerable no less for holiness than for doctrine, shone forth renowned among catholic preachers. For the usefulness of the church of the faithful he wrote many distinguished volumes, of which these are reported: On Easter, 2 books.
On the Life of the Prophets, 4 books. On the Church, 1 book.
On the Fallen, 1 book. On the Lord’s Day, 1 book.
On the Body and the Soul, 1 book. On the Senses, 1 book.
On Baptism, 1 book. On Faith, 1 book.
On Truth, 1 book. On Hospitality, 1 book.
On the Generation of Christ, 1 book. The book entitled Key, 1.
On the Prophet, 1 book. On the Devil, 1 book.
Of Selections, 6 books. On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book.
On the Passing of Saint Mary, 1 book. Melito, servant of Christ, He also published other small works, which age has not permitted to come down to our memory. Tertullian, mentioning in a certain passage this man’s elegant and declamatory talent, says that he was regarded by our people as a prophet. It should indeed be noted that the book On the Passing of Saint Mary ascribed to him is reckoned among the apocrypha, in distinction 15, Sancta Romana. He flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 160.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

Theophilus, sixth bishop of the church of Antioch, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in talent and speech, and an excellent declaimer, wrote many volumes for the benefit of the faithful, and shone forth as an excellent expounder of the Lord’s discourses. Of his little works the following are reported:

*Against Marcion*, one book. *Commentaries on the Gospels*, four books.

*To Autolycus*, three books. *On the Proverbs of Solomon*, one book.

He also composed several other short treatises pertaining to the edification of the Catholic Church, which among the Latins are rarely found together. He was ordained bishop in the year of the Lord 173, indiction II.

Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, a learned man and distinguished defender of the Christian faith, eminent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote little works of reading not to be despised, in which he showed himself a man not so much learned as zealous. Among them these are reported:

*Apologetic for the Christians*, two books. *On Truth*, three books.

*Against the Cataphrygians*, five books.

But he also published some other works, knowledge of which antiquity has taken from us. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 165.

Dionysius, bishop of the church of the Corinthians, a most eloquent man and very learned in the divine Scriptures, a most vigilant shepherd of Christ’s flock, was of such concern and diligence that he instructed not only the people of his own city with salutary teachings, but also, by letters, summoned the peoples of foreign cities to constancy in the faith. These letters are indeed reported to be so useful and lengthy that they may not improperly be called books; of them the following are listed:

*To the Lacedaemonians*, one letter. *To the Athenians*, one letter.

*To the Nicomedians*, one letter. *To the Cretans*, one letter.

*To the Gnosians*, one letter. *To the Pope and the Romans*, one letter.

*To the Amastrians*, one letter. *To Chrysophora, a woman*, one letter.

He flourished under the rulers Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 170, not without a reputation for sanctity, and wrote various works.

Tatian, heresiarch, hearer and follower of Justin Martyr, did not depart from his side for as long as [unclear]. But afterward, when Saint Justin had been crowned, puffed up with swelling eloquence, he founded a new heresy, which is called that of the Encratites, which Severus later enlarged; from him those of the same party

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

[unclear] heretics were called Severians. They abominate flesh, do not drink wine, do not accept the Old Testament, and do not believe in the resurrection. Tatian, however, wrote almost countless volumes, though they have not come to my knowledge. For because of the teacher's error, even his writings, despised, perished. There survives, with Jerome as witness, a distinguished volume of his, which he entitled *Against the Gentiles*, book 1. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 170.

Philip, bishop of Crete, that is, of the city of [Gortyna?], whom Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, placed above, mentions in his letter which he had written to the church of that same city, a noble and learned man, published for the benefit of believers volumes sufficiently instructive, as they say, which have by no means come into our hands. There survives one book of his, *Against Marcion*. He also wrote certain letters to various persons and various treatises, which have still by no means come into our hands. He flourished in the year of the Lord 170, in the times of the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus.

Modestus, a man indeed of flourishing talent, although it is unknown to us what dignity or rank he held, wrote, as blessed Jerome witnesses, little works not contemptible in their reading, in which the abundant vein of his talent is seen. Of these there survives a distinguished volume, *Against Marcion*, book 1. The rest are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 175.

Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon in Gaul after the triumph of blessed Photinus the martyr, formerly a hearer of Polycarp the martyr, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and very learned, sent as legate to Rome under Pope Eleutherius, was approved as most illustrious no less in holiness than in doctrine. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which these are reported: *Against the Gentiles*, one book. *On the Monarchy of God*, book 1. *On Discipline*, book 1. *On the Ogdoad*, book 1. *To Blastus on Schism*, book 1. *On Easter, to Pope Victor*, book 1. *Against Heresies*, book 1, *Insofar as the truth re[unclear]*. *On Apostolic Preaching*, one book. *Of Various Treatises*, one book. He also wrote many other things, which have still by no means come to my knowledge. At last, when persecution was raging against the Christians, with all fer[unclear] Arq

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear] with the people of his city he was crowned with martyrdom for the Catholic faith on the fourth calends of July. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus, in the year of the Lord 175.

Theodotion, by origin an Ephesian, once a pupil of Tatian the philosopher while he was still faithful, a man certainly most learned from every source, and the third interpreter of the divine Scriptures, besides the translation of the Scriptures which he made Latin from the Hebrew, also wrote certain other little works, which however have not yet come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Commodus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Rhodon, an Asian by race, once a hearer and pupil of Tatian, most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, is said to have written many works in the Greek language, copies of which are rarely found among our people. Of these, however, the more important are reported to be those which we have set down: Against Marcion, 3 books. To Callition, 1 book.
Against the Cataphrygians, 1 book. On the Hexameron, 6 books.

He flourished under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Clement, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, hearer and pupil of Pantaenus the Stoic, once a Christian philosopher, who after him held the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria for many years, was a devout, learned, and most eloquent man. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which these are reported: Stromata, that is, Varieties, 1 book. On Disputation, 1 book.
Against the Nations, [unclear] books. On the Salvation of a Rich Man, 1 book.
The Pedagogue, 3 books. On Detraction, 1 book.
On Easter, [unclear] book. Against Those Judaizing, [unclear] books.
On Fasting, 1 book. On Ecclesiastical Canons, 1 book.

He also published many letters and various treatises, whose titles we do not know. He flourished in the times of the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Melciades, whom Rhodon remembered in his work which he composed against the Cataphrygians, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, the mad prophets, a man most learned in secular letters and exercised by constant study in the divine Scriptures, wrote not a few little works for the edification of the faithful, of which the following are reported: Against the Nations, 1 book. Against the Jews, 1 book.
Against the Nations, 1 book. An Apologetic for Our Faith, 1 book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Marcus Antoninus Commodus, in the year of the Lord 170. Apol-

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Apollonius, a certain learned and most eloquent man, distinguished no less in life than in eloquence, a most valiant overthrower of heretical depravity, composed many things for our faith, and often refuted the madness of Montanus in words and writings, as is clear to those reading that notable volume which he is said to have composed with the greatest charms of eloquence: Against Montanus, 1 book.

But he published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Serapion, formerly an anchorite and the eighth bishop of the church of Antioch, a man of keen intellect, very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge, is reported to have fashioned several little works for the [unclear] of believers, in which he shows himself a learned man and a most vigorous defender of the Christian faith. Of their number there are: To Domnon Judaizing, one book.
To Carinus on Montanus, 1 book.
On the Gospel under the Name of Peter, 1 book.
Of brief but numerous letters, one book.

He was ordained bishop of the aforesaid city under Commodus, ruler of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 193, in the first indiction.

Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, venerable no less for sanctity than for knowledge, when before the senate he had been denounced as a Christian and refused to deny Christ, received sentence of death, since an old law among them prevailed that Christians were not to be released without denial, once they had been brought before their judgment. Among other things he wrote: An Apologetic for Our Faith, 1 book.

When he had recited this in order before the senate, he was beheaded. He flourished at Rome under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 190.

Tertullian, presbyter, by origin a Carthaginian of the African province, his father being a centurion, a proconsular man, a man of keen and vehement intellect, most learned both in the divine and in secular writings, since indeed at Carthage he gloriously taught rhetoric for many years, wrote almost countless little works in the Latin language, in which he strongly crushed the errors of the heretics. The most blessed martyr Cyprian held this man’s writings in such veneration that he let no day pass without reading them; for he was accustomed to say to his secretary, “Give me the master,” meaning Tertullian. At last he slipped into the error of Montanus

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He is called apocryphal, because his little works are counted among the apocrypha, Distinction XV, *Sancta Romana*. And although he erred in some matters, nevertheless he wrote well on many, as his volumes attest. Of these I have seen: *On the Patience of God*, one book, “I confess to the Lord God”; *Against Praxeas*, one book; *Against Marcion*, five books; *Against the Jews*, [unclear]; *Against All Heresies*, one book; *On the Prescriptions of Heretics*, one book; *Against Hermogenes*, one book; *Against the Valentinians*, one book; *On the Flesh of Christ*, one book; *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, one book; *On the Soldier’s Crown*, one book; *To the Martyrs*, one book; *On Repentance*, one book; *On the Veiling of Virgins*, one book; *On Women’s Dress*, one book; *On the Adornment of Women*, one book; *To His Wife*, two books; *On Persecution, to Fabius*, one book; *To Scapula*, one book; an *Exhortation to Chastity*, one book; *On Monogamy*, one book; *On the Pallium*, one book; *On Spectacles*, one book; *On Fasts*, one book; *On Ecstasy*, one book; *Against Apollonius*, one book; *On Modesty*, one book.

He also wrote many other things and various treatises, which have not yet come into our hands at all; and he lived studiously even to old age and senescence. He flourished in the times of the emperor Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Origen, who is also Adamantius, a priest, Alexandrian by nation, son of the martyr Leonides, once a disciple of Clement of Alexandria, was a man of great and excellent talent, so that in zeal and learning he never had his equal. In the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, when a persecution was set in motion against the Christians and his father Leonides was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, he was left poor with his widowed mother and six brothers, being about seventeen years old.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

For the treasury had seized all their substance because of their confession of Christ, so that they no longer had anything from which they might live. And although the number of years was reckoned slight in the young man, nevertheless his learning was already wonderful, and his constancy in the Christian faith admirable. For he had resolved to die bravely with his father, the faithful Leonides, for the faith of Christ, had it not happened that, by his mother’s stratagem, he was preserved for the usefulness of the Church, since he was to become a great teacher. For when, early in the morning, he had resolved to run to his father at the place of contest on the preceding day, his garments were taken away by his mother during the night, and the doors of the chamber were locked, and he was forced to remain at home.

When, however, he had grown into a man, he resolved to lead the apostolic life, and, proclaiming the word of God in the region around him, he went about barefoot for many years. Finally, he never slept on a bed stuffed with feathers; he abstained completely from wine and meat, except in illness; he was intent on serving God devotedly with fasts, vigils, prayers, and continual studies and expositions of the divine Scriptures. Also, according to Christ’s counsel, he was accustomed to wear only one tunic, and, having become a despiser of all worldly things, he took no thought for the morrow. Out of love of chastity, so that he might dare to preach safely to women, he had himself castrated, although in this deed zeal remained without knowledge.

Because of his learning, eloquence, and apostolic life, Mammaea, the most Christian mother of the emperor Alexander, when she was seized with a desire to hear him, came from Alexandria to Antioch, and heard his honey-sweet doctrine with great admiration. He was so intent upon the study of the divine Scriptures that he never took either food or sleep unless one [unclear] of the brothers had first delivered a reading of the Scriptures while all listened. He knew the New and Old Testament by heart like another Ezra, and when already an old man, contrary to his age, he learned the Hebrew language; and with wonderful zeal he brought together into one all the editions of the interpreters, besides the Septuagint.

In dictating editions of the Scriptures he had so admirable a memory and subtlety that, with incredible speed of utterance, he wore out seven notaries and the same number of girls, very swift in writing, besides other young men, all at the same time writing different things from his mouth. And although he was held, and was, so great and distinguished a teacher among all ecclesiastical men, nevertheless he is marked by great errors, by which either he himself was foolish, or he was corrupted by others inserting false things into his writings. The opinion of learned men about Origen was always varied, some asserting that he was a heretic, others affirming that a fraud had been imposed upon him. It is not to be wondered

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

... it is not [unclear], if he erred as the first man without an example, who expounded so many volumes without a preceding teacher. Yet it is our part, not only concerning Origen, but concerning any writers whatsoever, to think with the holy Roman Church and to despise superfluous opinions. He published, moreover, almost infinite volumes, of which I have seen only the following translated into Latin: On Genesis, 16 homilies. “In the beginning God made...” “It seems to me one...”

On Exodus, 15 homilies. “As on the last day...” “As on the last days...”

On Numbers, 28 homilies. “In Numbers not all...” “The Lord gave a name...”

On Joshua, 26 homilies. “God for doing good...”

On Judges, 9 homilies. “As long as King Uzziah...”

On the beginning of [Idida?], 2 homilies. “Not from the beginning only...”

On Isaiah the prophet, 9 homilies.

On Jeremiah the prophet, 4 books.

On Ezekiel, 14 homilies.

Likewise on the Gospel of Matthew, 26 homilies.

On the Song of Songs, 4 books. “As formerly among the people...” “Concerning the Song of Songs...”

On the number 150. “Blessed is the man,” this psalm.

Against Heretics, 5 books. “Adamantius said, who...”

Against Celsus the philosopher, 8 books.

Periarchon, 4 books. “All who believe...”

On the Epistle to the Romans, 15 books. “Because the rest of the Apostle Paul...”

On the beginning of John, 1 book.

He also composed many other works, which have not come into our hands. There are those who write that they have read six thousand treatises of Origen, a number both large and unknown to the Latins. Nor is there any doubt that many little works of his have lately been translated, which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He died an old man and poor, buried at Tyre, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 261, the ninth indiction, in the seventieth year of his age.

Ammonius of Alexandria, the most celebrated of all men of his time, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek language certain distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity; of their number the following are extant: On the Harmony of Jesus and Moses, 1 book.

Of the Evangelical Canons, 1 book. “In the first canon four...”

One from Four, 1 book. “Since indeed many...”

And certain other things. The most impious Porphyry, a pagan philosopher and the bitterest enemy of Christians, falsely accuses him of having denied the faith and become a heathen, though it is established that he remained a devoted Christian until death. He flourished under Alexander, son of Mammaea, in the year of the Lord 230.

Ambrose, a hearer of Origen, first a Marcionite and afterward corrected by Origen himself, an outstanding confessor of the Christian faith, also deserved to be promoted to the office of deacon. He was certainly a most learned man and a zealous lover of books; with him furnishing the expenses, notaries, and copyists, our Adamantius composed almost infinite volumes. He was so great an admirer of his studies that day and night he urged him on, in words and in writings, to write something new, so that in a certain familiar letter he is named by Origen as the taskmaster of the work. He used to say that he never went to bed in Origen’s presence, nor took food, unless first one of the brethren who was always present had sounded forth in the letters of the sacred offering. He wrote, concerning his conversion, giving thanks, to Origen: Epistles, 1 book.

And certain other things. He flourished with Origen in the year of the Lord 230.

Tryphon, a hearer and disciple of Origen, to whom some of Origen’s letters are extant, a man most learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek language certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are extant: On the Red Heifer in Deuteronomy, 1 book.

On the Quality of Sacrifices, 1 book.

On the Dove and the Turtle-Dove, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 230.

Minucius Felix, an advocate, Roman by nationality, a man most learned in secular letters and zealous in divine readings, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Latin language certain distinguished little works, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there is extant a dialogue between a Christian and a heretic, which Octa-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

The eighth is entitled, one book. *On Fate, against the Astrologers*, one book. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 230.

Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular letters, after he had governed the church gloriously for some time, at last fell into the heresy of the Paulianists, who denied that Christ existed before Mary; but, corrected by Origen, he wrote many things, of which there survives a *Dialogue* held among them, one book; *Letters to Various Persons*, one book; and certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 254.

Hippolytus, bishop of a certain city whose name Jerome did not specify, certainly a man both studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, wrote many and almost incredible volumes, so that Ambrose, of whom we have already made mention above, used to urge Origen to imitate him, and strongly encouraged him to expound the divine Scriptures, providing him, as we have said, with seven copyists, the same number of very swift girls for writing, and a considerable number of book-copyists, with their costs and expenses. You would have seen a beautiful and delightful contest, in which each of the two greatly desired to surpass the other in the publication of books. The following are reported among the works of Hippolytus: *On the Hexameron*, six books; *On the Apocalypse*, one book; *On Genesis*, one book; *On the Proverbs of Solomon*, one book; *On Exodus*, one book; *On Ecclesiastes*, one book; *On the Song of Songs*, one book; *On the Antichrist*, one book; *On the Prophet Zechariah*, one book; *Against Marcion*, one book; *On Daniel*, one book; *Against All Heresies*, three books. He also published many and varied treatises on the Psalms, as well as homilies and sermons almost innumerable, and many other works still unknown to us. He flourished under the prince Alexander, in the year of the Lord 220.

Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, when out of desire for the holy places he was traveling to Jerusalem, was there, by divine revelation, ordained bishop after Saint Narcissus. Illustrious for much holiness and learning, he shone forth, and at last, for the faith of Christ, under Decius, a most impious tyrant, completed his martyrdom. He wrote many elegant letters to various persons, among which the following are chiefly reported: *On the Peace of the Church, to the Aaronites*, one letter; *For Origen against Demetrius*, one letter; *To the Antiochenes*, a letter; *To Origen*, several letters. Pas-

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

He suffered at Caesarea under Decius, in the year of the Lord 253, in the first indiction.

Julius Africanus, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, historiographer, and distinguished theologian, and a most ardent lover of divine Scripture and of books, founded by his own efforts and at his own expense a notable library at Caesarea in Palestine, in which he gathered many volumes both of secular and of divine writings. He also wrote several very useful little works, of which the following are reported: Five books of *Chronicles*. One book *On Easter*.

One book *On the Holy Trinity*. One book *On the Sabbath*.

One book *On Circumcision*. One book *To Origen on Susanna*.

One book *On Attalus*. One book *To Aristides the Philosopher*.

And he is said to have composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Marcus Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 220.

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a hearer and disciple of Origen, a learned and holy man, both wrote many things and, while living, shone forth with miracles. While still a young man, seeking the study of secular philosophy with his brother Athenodorus, he placed himself under the school of Origen; by him, together with his brother, he was gradually, as if imperceptibly, converted to the faith of Christ, and became a most learned and most holy man. Of his writings there survives: One book, a *Panegyric* addressed to Origen. One book of *Interpretations on Ecclesiastes*.

And several letters. He flourished under the emperor Gordian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Cornelius, the twenty-second bishop of the city of Rome after Peter, a Roman by birth, his father being Castinus, was made pope after the glorious martyrdom of Fabian and sat in the chair of Peter for two years, a learned and most holy man, until at last he too, crowned with martyrdom, passed, released from the flesh, to those above. He wrote several letters for the benefit of the Church; of these I have found only the following: To Fabius, bishop of Antioch: One letter *On Synods*. One letter *On Novatian*.

To the same, one book *On the Novatians*. One letter *On the Acts of the Synod*.

He wrote several letters to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, and others to other persons. He flourished under the tyrant emperor Decius, in the year of the Lord 255.

Cyprian, bishop of the church of Carthage in Africa, a learned and most holy man, taught rhetoric gloriously for many years, and was a magnificent teacher in all secular literature. Then, at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius, from whom he obtained his surname, he was converted to the faith of Christ, [unclear] all his substance to the poor

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

...he distributed. And not long afterward, having been chosen priest, he was also ordained bishop. Since he was zealous in the divine Scriptures, he usefully published many things for the edification of the faithful, and composed the following volumes in the Latin language, namely: On the Grace of God, to Donatus, one book: “You admonish well, Donatus...”
Against Demetrianus, one book: “You, barking at and against...”
[unclear], one book: “Many and great are...”
On Piety and Almsgiving, one book: “You desired, Fortunatus...”
On the Praise of Martyrdom, one book: “Be zealous for what is good...”
On Zeal and Envy, one book: “Let us speak of patience...”
On the Good of Patience, one book: “And if among very many...”
On Mortality, one book: “The evangelical precepts...”
On Virginity, one book: “Discipline, guardian of hope...”
On the Lapsed, one book: “Peace, behold, most beloved...”
On the Sacrament of the Cup, one book: “Cyprian to his brother Caecilius...”
On the Unity of the Church, one book: “Since the Lord warns and...”
On the Lord’s Prayer, one book: “The chief evangelical...”
On the Vanity of Idols, one book: “That idols are not gods...”
On the Life of Clerics, one book: “I had indeed promised you...”
On the Two Mountains, one book: “The proof of the chapters...”
To Antonianus concerning Novatus, one book: “We have received the first letters...”
On the Jews, to Quirinus, two books: “The Jews into offense...”
To Pope Cornelius, eight letters: “We have learned, dear brother...”
On Gamblers, one book.
To Julianus his friend, one book.

He is said to have composed letters to various people and also many other works, which have not come into our hands. The little book On the Twelve Abuses of the Age, ascribed by many to Cyprian, does not have the flavor of his style. At length he suffered martyrdom under Valerian, on the same day as Cornelius at Rome, but not in the same year, namely in the year of the Lord 249, in the twelfth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

Pontius the priest, hearer and disciple of blessed Cyprian, a learned and holy man and an outstanding declaimer, after the glorious triumph of his master came into Gaul and at the city of Cymerla won the palm of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. This Pontius, by his honey-flowing preaching and industry, converted the two emperors Philips to Christ, and persuaded them, the first of the Roman rulers, to renounce idols. He also wrote, in an elegant style, a notable volume, which contains: The Life of Saint Cyprian, one book: “Cla[unclear]...”

*Abbot of Sponheim*

He flourished under the emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 240.

Dionysius, the thirteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, once a hearer and disciple of Origen, while he was still a priest held the public school under Heraclas, and gained great glory for his learning. For he was a man most learned in every science of doctrines, a distinguished philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian. Agreeing with the doctrine of Cyprian and of the African synod concerning the rebaptizing of heretics, he wrote very many letters on that matter to various people, of which the following are reported among the number: On Penance, to Flavianus, one letter.
To the Romans, one letter.
To Saint Pope Sixtus, two letters.
To the priests Philemon and Dionysius, two letters.
Against Nepos the Chiliast, one book.
To Pope Dionysius, one letter composed.
Against Sabellius, four books.
To Novatian the heretic, one letter: “Dionysius to Novatian...”
To Ammon, bishop of Berenice, one letter.
To Pope Dionysius, four books.
To Telephorus, one letter.
To Dionysius and Didymus, one letter.
To the Laodiceans, on Penance, one letter.
To Euphranor, one letter.
To the Armenians, on Penance, one book.
To Origen, on Martyrdom, one letter.
On the Order of Sins, one letter.
To the Alexandrians, on Exile, one letter.
A Canon on Penance, one book.
On Easter.
On Nature, to Timothy, one book.
To Heraclas, bishop in Egypt, one book.
On Temptations, one book.
Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, one book.
To Basilides also several letters of his are reported.

An outstanding letter of his against Paul of Samosata is extant, which he had written a few days before his death. He also composed many other works for ecclesiastical utility, which are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Gallus and Volusianus, in the year of the Lord 255.

Novatian, priest of the Roman church, attempted to seize the episcopal chair against Cornelius; when he could not do so, he stirred up the first schism in the Roman Church and established the heresy of the Novatians, refusing to receive penitent apostates and rebaptizing those duly baptized. The author of this error was Novatus, Cyprian’s priest. Now Novatian wrote: On Easter, one book.
On Jewish Foods, one book.
On the Sabbath, one book.
On Urgency, one book.
On [unclear]...

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On Circumcision, one book. On Attalus, one book. On the Priest, one book. On the Holy Trinity, one book. On Prayer, one book. Several letters to various persons. He is said, moreover, to have written some other works, which have not come to my notice. He flourished in the times of the emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 250.

Malchion, presbyter of the church of Antioch, a learned and very eloquent man, since indeed he taught rhetoric in that same city for many years with the greatest success, published some distinguished little works, which in his own time seemed greatly useful for the defense of the Christian faith against heretics. Of these there survives an excellent work of dialogues: Against Paul of Samosata, one book.

To Pope Dionysius, from the synod, one epistle.

He flourished under the rulers Claudius and Aurelian, in the year of the Lord 270.

Victorinus, bishop of [Pictavium?], a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, furnished with Greek and Latin eloquence, wrote many distinguished little works, in which he magnificently exercised his talent. He was an eminent preacher of the divine word, and at last is read to have been crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ. Of his writings the following are reported: On Genesis, one book. On Habakkuk, one book.
On Exodus, one book. On Ecclesiastes, one book.
On Leviticus, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book.
On the prophet Isaiah, one book. On the Apocalypse, one book.
On Ezekiel, one book. Against All Heresies, one book.

And many others. He flourished in the times of the rulers Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 270.

Pamphilus, presbyter of Eusebius of Caesarea, gathered so many books at Caesarea out of love for the Scriptures that in all the world at that time no library was more celebrated. Indeed he copied out a large part of Origen’s books with his own hand and placed them in that same Caesarean library. From him Eusebius obtained the surname Pamphili. But before Eusebius began to write, he wrote little works of authority not to be despised, of which I have found only: Against the Mathematicians, one book.

An Apology for Origen, one book.

He is also reported to have written certain letters full of faith and learning. At last, after blessed studies and many labors for the church of God, he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ at Caesarea in Palestine, under the persecution of Maximian, who ruled around the years of the Lord 240.

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures and second to none in secular letters in his own time, an eminent rhetorician, astronomer, and geometer, left many distinguished little works of his talent; yet very few of them have come to our notice. There survives his notable volume, entitled: On Easter, one book. On Arithmetic Instruction, ten books.

He flourished under the rulers Probus and Carus, in the year 285.

Three sermons by the same author, On Death, in Greek, are preserved in Italy, namely at Rome, as some will have it.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia in Syria, a learned man and a keen disputant, wrote some little works in the Syriac language, which among the Latins are rarely found. At the end of [Persia?] he disputed vigorously against Mani the heresiarch, and confounded all his arguments, although he could not call him back from error. He wrote that same disputation: Against Mani, one book.

Other works, however, are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Aurelian and Probus, in the year of the Lord 280.

Lucian, presbyter of the church of Antioch and afterwards bishop of Nicomedia, a learned and eloquent man, was of excellent talent in delivering homilies to the people, and venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. Under the persecution of Maximian he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, and was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. He wrote, among other things: On Our Faith, one book.

And various other treatises, sermons, homilies, and letters. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Pierius, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, a man of such learning and eloquence that he was called the younger Origen, was most excellent in delivering homilies to the people. Under Theonas, bishop of the Alexandrians, shining most brightly in life and doctrine, he was an eminent cultivator of voluntary poverty for the love of Christ, and an admirable teacher of the people. He wrote countless treatises, which, however, have not come to our notice. There survives his very long treatise, delivered to the people on the vigil of Easter: On the prophet Hosea, [unclear].

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, 22

[unclear]

Phileas, bishop of the city of [unclear] in Egypt, a noble and very learned man, distinguished no less for his character than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, after many labors and various treatises published for the benefit of the faithful, at last under the emperor Maximian was made a martyr for the faith of Christ and flew to the heavenly ones. Of his writings there is extant a disputation held Against an Unjust Judge, one book. On the Praise of Martyrs, one book.

Other things that he wrote are unknown to us, although many are reported by the fathers. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Arnobius the priest, an eminent philosopher and rhetorician, while he was still a pagan teaching rhetoric, was called by divine mercy and began to profess himself a Christian. And when, approaching them, he sought to be baptized, they did not believe him, fearing that a man swollen with worldly eloquence was trying to mock the sacraments of the faith; and therefore they postponed their decision. But Arnobius, seeing that no trust at all was being placed in him, as proof of his sincerity wrote and offered to the bishops an excellent volume: Against the Nations, seven books.

Also On the Psalter, one book.

On the Teaching of Rhetoric, one book.

He also published many other things, which have come to my knowledge. He taught rhetoric in Africa under the emperor Diocletian. He had many excellent and noble pupils, who became very learned men. He therefore flourished around the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 500.

He also wrote brief annotations on some passages of the evangelists.

John Climacus, which in Latin means Scholasticus, abbot of Mount Sinai, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellent in talent, gentle and humble, in life and conduct devout and most holy: when he was still sixteen years old, he left the world with its pleasures, and very earnestly sought, and obtained, to be made a monk in the said monastery. Then, after nineteen years, when he had already learned, according to the rule of monks, to fight and conquer as a solitary, with the permission of his abbot he sought a desert place, in which for many years he lived alone with God in all holiness. Finally, when his most holy life had become known to all, by the unanimous consent of all he was elected abbot, and, though reluctant, was recalled to the monastery. He wrote to John, abbot of Raythu, a very celebrated work, and one very suitable for the instruction of monks, containing thirty sermons, which he entitled On the Thirty Steps, one book.

From the good and supremely good to

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

To Pastor, *Sermons*, one book: “In the lower book indeed ...”
Several letters to monks, one book.
And certain other things.

In certain places, especially where he treats of the impassibility of the mortified spiritual man, he is censured by modern theologians, as is found in certain treatises in John Gerson. He flourished around the times of Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, brothers and emperors, who reigned in the year of the Lord 346.

Ildephonsus, bishop of the see of Toledo after St. Eugenius, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant either of secular literature, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and above all the bishops of his time fluent and eloquent, worthy of God and most holy in life and conduct. For he was endowed with constancy in the fear of God, devoted in religion, abundant in compunction, grave in gait, praiseworthy in honor, singular in patience, renowned for his talent in discourse, supreme in wisdom. When, while still a boy, he had been touched by the divine spirit, despising the guilty world and the affections of his parents, he sought the monastery of Agali, and there for many years fittingly showed himself a monk. He also built a convent of virgins in the little village of Deibia, which he endowed from the wealth of his parents. Then, made abbot of the monastery of Agali, he trained the manners of the monks, administered its property, and preserved its life. After this, by princely violence he was brought back to Toledo, and there, after the death of his predecessor, was appointed bishop in his place. He wrote many distinguished little works, of which the following are reported:

*On the Holy Trinity*, one book.
*On His Own Weakness*, one book.
*Various Hymns*, one book.
*Annotations on Sacred Matters*, one book.
*Many Epigrams*, one book.
*Annotations on the Sacraments*, one book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
And very many other things.

When this most blessed prelate Ildephonsus had completed to the end the book on the virginity of Mary, the most pure Mother of God, whom he was always accustomed to serve most devotedly with all the zeal he could, the most holy Lady of the world appeared to him, holding that book in her hands and giving him thanks for such service, which she affirmed was most pleasing to her. But he, desiring to honor her more deeply,

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

he decreed that its solemnity should be celebrated every year on the eighth day before the Nativity of the Lord; this solemnity has now prevailed, so that throughout the universal Church of the faithful it is celebrated in honor of her most pure Conception on the sixth day before the Ides of December. Hence the blessed Mother of God, appearing to him again, brought him a priestly garment, which we call an alb, and a chair; concerning these many wondrous and glorious things are related. He flourished * Firmianus Lactantius, once a hearer and disciple of Arnobius the rhetorician, a man abundantly learned in secular letters and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, so that in the art of speaking he easily held the first place after Cicero, taught rhetoric gloriously, first at Nicomedia, then at Rome under Diocletian, having been summoned by him. There, when through lack of pupils he had fallen into poverty, at last, already an old man, he became tutor in Gaul to Caesar Crispus, son of Constantine. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which these are reported: On the Divine Institutes, one book. “To the great and excellent...”
book 1. “Although in the first book...”
On the Origin of Error, book 1. “I should like it to be explained to me...”
On False Wisdom, book 1. “As I was reflecting and when...”
On True Wisdom, book 1. “There is no doubt with me...”
On Justice, to Constantine, book 1. “Because it was the duty undertaken...”
On True Worship, book 1. “It is well...”
On the Blessed Life, book 1. “I have often observed, Do...”
book 1. “How little I am one who...”
On the Wrath of God, to Donatus, book 1.
Letters to Probus, 4 books.
Letters to Severus, two books.
A Symposium in hexameter verse, one book.
An Epitome against the Gentiles, book 1.
The Grammarian, inscribed book 1.
On Paradise, in hexameters, book 1. “There is a happy place in the first...”
He says that he wrote not a few other things besides, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Constantine, to whom he was very dear, in the year of the Lord 320.

Eusebius, bishop of the church of Caesarea in Palestine, surnamed Pamphilus, once a disciple of Dorotheus the eunuch, a very learned man, most devoted to the divine Scriptures and, together with the martyr Pamphilus, a most diligent restorer of the ecclesiastical library: although he was an Arian, when he came to the first council of the Fathers held at Nicaea, he laid aside his error; and, following the opinion of the Fathers, by their command he composed the creed which is called Nicene and offered it to them to read and confirm as testimony of his own most pure faith. In it he vigorously crushed the errors of the Arians, and nothing has been either added to or subtracted from his edition, but to the present day it is publicly sung in the Church of God. Thereafter, persevering in the orthodox faith, he was most holily brought to his end. He wrote in Greek many excellent volumes, of which the following, that is, are current among the Latins: Against Porphyry, 30 books.
On Isaiah the Prophet, 10 books.
Books of Gospel Expositions, 20.
On Evangelical Preparation, 14 books. “Since what becomes Christians...”
Ecclesiastical History, 10 books. “The successions of the saints...”
Chronicle Epitome, book 1. “Moses of the Hebrew race...”
Theophanies, 5 books.
Topics, book 1.
On the Life of Pamphilus, 3 books.
Martyrology, book 1.
On the Disagreement of the Evangelists, one book.
Apology for Origen, 6 books.
On the whole Psalter, book 1.
He also composed many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Constantine the Great, to whom he was very dear because of his exceptional learning and holiness of life, in the year of the Lord 320.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

Rheticius, bishop of the Aedui at Autun, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and in his time a teacher of renowned reputation, is said to have written not a few little works, and especially commentaries on various books; but we remember that few have come to our knowledge, namely: On the Song of Songs, book 1.
Against Novatian, book 1.
Saint Jerome censures his exposition on the Song as inept. He flourished in Gaul under Constantine the Great, in the year of the Lord 320.

James, surnamed the Wise, bishop of Nisibis, a city of the Persians, a man of great learning and incomparable holiness, one of the number of the confessors victorious under the persecutor Maximian, attended the Council of Nicaea and condemned the most impious Arius by opposing the homoousion. This man of most holy conduct often delivered the city entrusted to him from many dangers by his prayers. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, not a few little works in the Syriac tongue, of which these are reported: On Faith, book 1.
On Love of Neighbor, book 1.
On General Charity, book 1.
On Prayer, book 1.
On Fasting, book 1.
On 26 *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

On the Resurrection, one book. On Life after Death, one book.
On Humility, one book. On Patience, one book.
On Penitence, one book. On Satisfaction, one book.
On Virginity, one book. On the Perception of the Soul, one book.
On Circumcision, one book. On the Blessing of Unleavened Bread, one book.
On Christ, that he is the Son of God, one book.
On Chastity, one book. Against the Gentiles, one book.
On the Conversion of the Tabernacle, one book.
On the Persecution of the Gentiles, one book. On the Kingdom of the Persians, one book.
Of Christians, one book.
On the Words of Isaiah, one book. A Chronicle of the Times, one book.
Thus the whole work already indicated is comprised in twenty-five books.
He flourished under the great prince Constantine, in the year of the Lord 350.

Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterwards of Tyre, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, an eminent confessor and defender of the Christian faith and a diligent emulator of evangelical perfection, after the publication of many volumes, was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ in Chalcis of Greece under the last persecution, or, as others affirm, under Decius and Valerian. He wrote not a few volumes in a polished and well-composed style, among which the following are reported: Against Porphyry, one book. On the Resurrection, one book.
On the Departure of the Soul, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book.
Also a Chronicle, one book. "For it must be known, brothers..."
On the Pythoness, one book. A Symposium on the Ten Virgins, one book.
He flourished under the great prince Constantine, or, as others prefer, under Decius and Valerian, in the year of the Lord 255.

Antony, monk and abbot, Egyptian by nation, a most holy man and distinguished inhabitant of the desert, whose praises the whole world proclaims, furnished many with a rule of religious and blessed life. Although he had not learned letters, yet he was so learned in the divine Scriptures that none of the teachers presumed to prefer himself to him. He had memory in place of books, understanding and sense in place of letters, grace in place of the study of reading. In the Egyptian language he dictated various letters, of apostolic meaning and speech, to diverse monasteries; among these there survives that distinguished one: To the Arsenoites, one letter. To other monasteries, six letters.

He wrote [unclear].

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

He also wrote a celebrated work in two books, entitled *Melissa* (that is, *The Little Bee*).

Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, described his life in Greek discourse in a notable volume.

He flourished under Constantine the Great, when his sons were reigning, in the year of the Lord 330, shining with many miracles.

Juvencus, a priest, a Spaniard by nation, a noble and most learned man, a philosopher, poet, rhetorician, and distinguished theologian, venerable to the Church no less in manner of life than in knowledge of the Scriptures, published for the edification of readers many excellent volumes, both in verse and in prose; but few of them have come to my knowledge. I have read the notable work that he composed in hexameter and pentameter verses:

*On the Four Gospels*, 4 books.

*On the Sacraments*, 2 books.

The other works that he is said to have composed have not come into our hands.

He flourished under Constantine the Great and his sons, in the year of the Lord 330.

Eustathius of Antioch, a Pamphylian by birth, first [bishop?] of Beroea in Syria, and then [unclear], learned and holy, endured many troubles from the Arians on behalf of the Catholic faith. For, having been banished into exile to Trajanopolis in Thrace, he died there; when the Arians invaded his church, they held it for many years. He wrote many small works, chiefly against the Arians, and various other diverse treatises, namely: *Against the Arians*, 5 books; *On the Soul*, 1 book; *Against Origen*, 2 books; Letters, almost innumerable, 2 books.

He flourished in the times of Constantine and his sons, in the year of the Lord 340.

Athanasius, the nineteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures, endured many persecutions from the Arians for the Catholic faith. Indeed, the whole world was narrow for him, with the Arians persecuting him everywhere, so that he seemed nowhere safe, nowhere secure. For a man’s enemies were those of his own household. Therefore, fleeing from the face of the Arian emperor, he came to Trier, a city of the Gauls, was honorably received by Saint Maximinus the archbishop, and for seven years [was hidden?] in a crypt at the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier. In this place, hiding for many years, as we have said, he did not see the sun, and there he composed the creed *Whoever wishes to be saved*, until at last, betrayed by a certain girl, by the will of God he escaped in flight. If anyone desires to know his deeds more fully, let him read the *Tripartite History*. He wrote in Greek discourse almost innumerable small works, of which I have found the following among the Latins:

*On the Unity of the Trinity*, 1 book.

*On the Proper Persons of the Trinity*, 1 book.

*On the Assumption of Man*, 1 book.

*On the Names of the Trinity*, 1 book.

*On the Single Substance of the Trinity*, 1 book.

*On the Blessedness of Faith*, 1 book.

*On the Profession of the Catholic Rule*, 1 book.

*On the Unity of Faith*, 1 book.

*On the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit*, 1 book.

*On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit*, 1 book.

*To Bishop Lucifer*, 1 book.

*Against the Objections of the Arians*, 1 book.

*A Disputation against Arius, etc.*, 1 book.

*Against Valens and Ursacius*, 1 book.

*On Virginity*, 1 book.

*To the Bishops of Egypt and Libya*, 1 book.

*On the Holy Spirit*, 1 book.

*Against the Gentiles*, 1 book.

*Against the Arians*, 1 book.

*Against the Same*, 1 book.

*On the Homoousion of the Father and the Son*, 1 book.

*A Dialogue with an Arian*, 1 book.

*An Exhortation to Monks*, 1 book.

*The Life of Saint Antony*, 1 book.

*The Creed of His Faith*, 1 book.

*On All the Epistles of Paul*, 1 book.

*On the Persecution by the Arians*, 1 book.

*On His Flight and Exile*, 1 book.

He published several letters to various persons, and also sermons and various treatises, which either have not yet been translated into Latin or have not come to my knowledge. He died in the time of the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 379, in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the seventh indiction.

There are extant at Rome, in the Vatican Library, thirty-two sermons in Greek, and

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

And a treatise to Antiochus, on very many necessary questions which are doubtful in the sacred writings and ought to be known by all Christians.

Theodore, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an excellent declaimer of well-composed speech, published commentaries of no contemptible reading on the sacred volumes, of which the following are reported: On the Psalter, one book. On the Gospel of John, one book.
On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.

He is said also to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Constantine II, in the year of the Lord 340.

Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, a man most learned in the divine writings, and in declaiming homilies to the people second to none in his time, a rhetorician and theologian most celebrated in the opinion of all, is said to have written many, almost innumerable, little works; but we have been able to find only the titles and numbers of a few, namely: Against the Gentiles, one book. Of many homilies, one book.
Against the Jews, one book. Sermons to the people.

He flourished while Constantine and his brothers were reigning, in the year of the Lord 550.

Triphyllius, bishop of Ledra or Leucotheon in Cyprus, a man most learned both in divine and in secular writings, and easily the most eloquent of all prelates in his age, is said to have written not a few volumes and to have expounded the divine writings in many ways; but I do not recall that anything of his works has come into our hands. His exposition is reported: On the Song of Songs, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 340.

Serapion, formerly a monk, bishop of Thmuis, and a very close friend of the blessed abbot Antony, a man of such great learning and eloquence that, on account of the excellence of his talent, he obtained the surname Scholasticus, is said to have written many little works, of which the following are extant: Against the Manichaean, one book. On the Titles of the Psalms, one book.
Several letters to various persons. He flourished under the prince Constantius, in the year of the Lord 540.

Acacius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a man indeed practiced in the divine Scriptures, but corrupted by Arian impiety, was held in such reverence by the emperor Constantius that he obtained the appointment of Felix, an Arian presbyter, as bishop at Rome in the place of Pope Liberius. This Acacius, because he was one-eyed, was called Monoculus. He wrote many varied treatises, which would truly have been useful if they had had a Catholic author. Of these, the more important are reported to be those which we set forth below: On Ecclesiastes, seventeen books. Sethematon, sixteen books.
Symicton, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 350.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, a man very venerable in morals, life, and doctrine, endured many wrongs from the Arians for the faith of Christ. For, through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, he was banished from the synod of Beziers into Phrygia, and for four years bore a hard exile with steadfast spirit; there, by his prayers, he is read to have called a dead man back to life. Since he was a man most learned in every respect, he composed many little works, of which the following are reported in number: Against Dioscorus, one book. Against Valens and Ursatius, one book.
On the Holy Trinity against the Arians, twelve books. “As I look about me”
A Defense of the Catholic Faith, one book. “God, who is everywhere”
Against the Arians, one book. “To the most beloved brothers”
On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. “The step which Matthew”
On the Synods, to the bishops of the Gauls, one book. “I had resolved”
On some Psalms, forty-two treatises.
On the Psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” twenty-two treatises.
To the emperor Constantius, fifteen books. “The time for speaking now”
Of Hymns, one book.
Of Mysteries, one book. On the Book of Job, one book.
Against Auxentius, one book. “To the most blessed and glorious”
On Heresies, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book.
Chronicles, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published some other works which have not come into our hands. At length, after returning to his city from his exile, he died under the emperor Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 371, in the fourteenth indiction; his feast is celebrated on the Ides of January.

Victorinus the African, a man of consular rank, the most celebrated rhetorician of all in his time, who in the city of Rome under the emperor Constantine taught rhetoric for a long time, where on account of the excellence of his learning he earned a bronze statue in the Forum of Trajan, having been converted to the faith of Christ in his old age, published many works on the sacred Scriptures, ..., in the dialectical manner quite obscure and scarcely accessible even to the most learned men; of these the following are extant: Against the Arians, one book.
On the Holy Trinity, one book. Its opening: “In the first discourse.”
Against Heretics, one book. Its opening: “Logos,” or [unclear].
On the homoousion also, one book. Its opening: “He lives, and life [is] one.”
On the Trinity, of hymns, one book. Its opening: “Be present, true light.”
On the Epistles of the apostle Paul, one book.
And certain other works.
He flourished at Rome under the emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 360.

*T*itus, bishop of Botra, otherwise Bostrinus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, sharp and forceful in talent, is said to have fashioned many little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of these, the following are given in number: Against the Manichaeans, [unclear] books.
A Commentary on the Gospel, one book.
And many others.
He flourished in the year of the Lord 340, and died under the emperor Valens.

Damasus the pope, Spanish by nation, sat after Liberius in the chair of Peter for eighteen years; a man most learned in divine matters and excellently instructed in secular letters, a very celebrated rhetorician and poet, and most skilled in composing verses; subtle in talent, devout in life and most holy, very dear to the priest Saint Jerome. He wrote various little works in both genres, of which the following are extant: Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs, one book. Its opening: “The blessed apostle Peter.”
On Faith against Heretics, one book. Its opening: “Since after the Nicene council.”
Letters to Various Persons, one book. Its opening: “Damasus the bishop.”
Various poems.
And other works.
He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

*Brocardium*, or Book of Brocards, on properties.

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and by far most learned in grammatical instruction, sharp and forceful in talent, clear in speech, wrote certain distinguished volumes in defense of the Catholic faith, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these there is extant a very celebrated work: Against the mad Porphyry, thirty books.
And certain other works.
He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

*He also wrote a work in verse, embracing the whole Scripture of the Hebrews.*

*On the Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

Didymus of Alexandria, blind from early childhood and on that account wholly ignorant even of the elements, furnished so great a marvel of himself that he learned perfectly dialectic and geometry, which especially require sight. In the divine Scriptures he was most learned, the teacher of blessed Jerome and very close friend of Saint Antony; sharp in talent and more distinguished in life. He wrote the following works in Greek: Against the Arians, seven books.
On Doctrines also, one book.
On the Canonical Epistles, seven books.
On the Holy Spirit, one book.
On the Book of Saint Job, one book.
On Hosea, to Jerome, three books.
On Isaiah the prophet, ten books.
On the Gospel of Matthew, one book.
On Zechariah, to the same, five books.
On the Psalter also, one book.
On the Gospel of John, one book.
And certain other works.
He flourished as an octogenarian under the emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 395.

[unclear]

Optatus, bishop of Milevis, African by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent, devout in life and Catholic, is said to have written certain distinguished little works in defense of our faith, in which he magnificently exercised his abundant talent. Of these there is said to be extant a large and notable volume, which he wrote: Against the Donatists, six books.
And several letters.
And many other works.
He flourished under the princes Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

[unclear]

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a most learned and most holy man, was of such authority among the Greeks that no one, however slightly learned, ever dared to contradict his teaching or writings in anything. He wrote many distinguished little works in Greek, but few of them have come into our hands: On the Holy Spirit, one book.
Against Eunomius, one book.
On the Hexaemeron, eleven homilies. Its opening: “In the beginning,” etc. [unclear]
Rule of Monks, one book. Its opening: “The human race.”
Exhortation of Monks, one book. Its opening: “Hear, my son, the admonition.”
On the Instruction of Boys, one book.
On Faith, one book.
On Hidden Speech, one book.
To a Fallen Virgin, one book.
[unclear]
Its opening: “Of God indeed without inter—.”
Its opening: “God [gave] the use of speech.”
Its opening: “All divine Scripture.”
Its opening: “It is time to cry out.”
Ho-

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

Many homilies, namely twenty-nine.

In addition he composed other treatises, sermons, and letters for various [unclear].

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 380.

He also wrote an Exposition on Isaiah; likewise On the Soul, On Natural Principles and Causes, Several Chapters on the Divine Nature, On Synods, and Origen’s Philocalia.

Ephrem, a monk and distinguished inhabitant of the desert, and deacon of the church of Edessa, ordained priest by blessed Basil, because of his humility never approached to perform the divine mysteries, although he was held worthy before God and men. Nevertheless, so far as pertained to his office, in admonishing the people he delivered countless homilies. He, as is read in the Lives of the Holy Fathers, was seen to have received from an angel a book written in golden letters; whence immediately on the next day, and thereafter, with the Holy Spirit speaking in him, he had such grace in declaiming that he found no one like himself in his time. He wrote in the Syrian tongue, for the instruction of readers, certain devout little works, of which the following are found among the Latins, namely: On the Holy Spirit, one book.
On Compunction of Heart, one book.
On Contrition of Heart, one book.
On Repentance, one book.
On the Struggles of the World, one book.
On the Day of Judgment, one book.
On the Resurrection, one book.
On the Blessedness of the Soul, one book.
On Thoughts, one homily.
On Severe Preaching, one homily.
On the Celebration of the Mysteries, one homily.
Lament over the City of Edessa, one book.

He also published not a few other works, especially sermons and homilies to the people, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, a very close friend of blessed Basil, as you may find in his Legend, in the year of the Lord 380.

Gregory, bishop of Emesa ([Nyssenus?]), brother of blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man very zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, stirred by his brother’s zeal, also himself wrote some little works in the Greek language, of which I have found among our writers only these:

*54 On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

On the Image and Creation of Man, one book. “Man from the soul [unclear].”
Against Eunomius, two books.

He flourished, younger than his brother, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, and composed various works, in the year of the Lord 380.

Gregory, from monk made bishop of Nazianzus, a man of such great learning, integrity, and eloquence that not even his adversaries dared in any way to contradict the things that were said by him, so that for the confirmation of authority it was enough that Gregory had merely said something. He, cultivator and lover of the monastic way of life, when on account of the excellence of his learning and the holiness of his life he was called to the episcopate, fled and hid himself, preferring to be abject in the house of the Lord rather than to be exalted among the crowd with perishable honors. But almighty God did not wish so bright a light to be hidden under the bushel of the aforesaid way of life, since it could be extended to the salvation of many. Found therefore by divine indication, he is led by the people to the episcopal see; and immediately, in excuse for his flight, a solemn homily is composed, in which he shows that the rule of souls is the art of arts. On account of his distinguished learning and holiness of life, he was called Gregory the Great before the blessed pope of the same name. He wrote many little works in the Greek language, of which the following are extant: On the Death of His Brother Caesarius, one book.
On the Praise of Maximus the Philosopher, one book.
On the Praise of Cyprian the Martyr, one book.
Against the Same, in Vituperation, one book.
On the Praise of Athanasius the Bishop, one book.
On Virginity, in hexameters, three books.
On the Holy Spirit, one book.
Apologetics, When He Had Fled, two books. “I have been conquered, and I confess.”
On the Nativity of the Lord, one book. “Christ is born; glorify...”
On the Second Epiphanies, one book. “Again my Jesus...”
On the Holy Spirit on the Day of Pentecost, one book. “On the solemnity of this...”
On Himself, Having Returned from the Field, one book. “I was longing for you...”
On Jeremiah, with the emperor present, one book. “My belly pains me...”
On the Reconciliation of a Monk, one book. “Our tongue [unclear].”
On the Devastation by Hail, one book. “What praiseworthy [unclear].”
Against Eunomius, two books.
Against Julian the Apostate, one book.

He published many sermons and homilies, and various treatises on diverse subjects, since they have not come to my knowledge. At last, worn out by old age, when he perceived that he could no longer be equal to the governance of the people, after another bishop had been ordained in his place, he returned to the pursuit of the solitude he had left behind.

He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.
