*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

Eutropius, monk and priest, a man of most religious manner of life, very zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, and fully instructed in secular letters, is said to have composed some little works, of which the following alone survive for us, known by their titles: To two virgins, sisters, 2 books. And a Chronicle down to his own times, 1 book.

He flourished under the rulers Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370. There are also some who write that he was a disciple of St. Augustine, and flourished in the year of the Lord 430.

Sychius, or perhaps more correctly Hesychius, priest and monk, once a hearer and disciple of the blessed bishop Gregory of Nazianzus, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, admonished by the example of his teacher, is said to have written many small works of explanation on the divine books; for he composed various volumes on both the New and the Old Testament, which have not yet come into our hands. I have read only that notable work of great size which he wrote to Eutychianus, the venerable deacon: On Leviticus, 1 book. Venerable deacon ...

I have seen nothing of the rest.

He flourished under the rulers Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, Roman by birth, a man most celebrated for faith and holiness, easily the most learned of all in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, fully instructed in the Greek and Latin tongue, whose merit the whole world proclaims, whose books holy mother Church confirms with a great commendation of authority. In expounding and explaining the divine scriptures he surpassed all teachers; no earthly power could ever break his faith, so that when many bishops were banished into exile for the faith, no one ever dared to touch Ambrose. For he was like a hammer of heretics, a most steadfast assailant, and while his tongue spoke in the faith of Christ, no human authority could ever impose silence on it. Always ready to undergo any dangers for the faith, with the Lord protecting him, he escaped everywhere free and unharmed. He wrote many very clear little works, of which I have found only those set down below: On Duties, 3 books. Not wishing to seem arrogant On the Calling of the Gentiles. Among the defenders, [unclear] book.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. Finally, he is said to have made Hegesippus and certain others Latin from the Greek. He flourished under the most merciful emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, known and familiar to blessed Ambrose of Milan, whom Saint Augustine mentions in a certain letter to Quodvultdeus, wrote for the common benefit certain excellent little works, of which I do not recall that any has come into our hands. There is said to be an outstanding work of his, as blessed Augustine, in the place cited above, attests, which he wrote: On 156 Heresies, one book. “The Simonians from Simon [unclear].”

The rest I have not seen. He flourished under the most Christian emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

Evagrius, monk, disciple of Saint Macarius the Egyptian, afterward bishop of Antioch, a man in every respect most learned, instructed in both secular and divine writings, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, even in the episcopate preserving the austerity of his former life, was of such abstinence that he was regarded as a marvel. He was the first to commit the life of the holy fathers to writing, and from his own vein he published many little works. Of these, however, very few have come to my knowledge. The following are reported as his: To the Anchorites, very useful, one book. On the Eight Principal Vices, one book.
Also to the Cenobites, [unclear], one book. Exhortations to a Virgin, [unclear] books.
He made the Life of Antony Latin, one book. “The presbyter Evagrius [unclear].”
On the Life of the Holy Fathers, one book. [unclear]
Commentaries on the Proverbs of Solomon.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He also wrote many other works, and translated from Greek into Latin works unknown to us. He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Maximus, bishop of Constantinople, an Alexandrian by nation, a distinguished philosopher and theologian, in whose praise Gregory Nazianzen published a book, having suffered many injuries from the Arians [unclear], and at last driven from his bishopric, wrote much against them. Of these there survives an excellent work addressed to Gratian: Against the Arians, one book. The rest are unknown to me. He flourished in Greece under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Ambrose, a priest, an Alexandrian by nation, formerly a hearer and disciple of Didymus the Blind, learned the divine Scriptures magnificently while he expounded them, and composed various explanations of them, which at that time were held in great esteem among the Greeks. Of these the following are current among us: Commentaries on Job, one book. Against Apollinaris of Laodicea, one book.

He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, in the year of the Lord [400?].

Petronius, bishop of Bologna, a monk in manner of life, very learned and eloquent in the divine Scriptures, and revered no less for holiness than for knowledge, because he shone with many miracles in life and after death, as is read in his history, wrote, among other works: On the Life of the Holy Fathers, one book. On the Ordination of a Bishop, one book.

And other works unknown to us. He died under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 383, in the thirteenth indiction.

Pachomius (Gennadius calls him Pachumius), abbot and a most magnificent founder of the monks of his time, founder of many monasteries, and a man of most holy manner of life, shining with many miracles in life and after death, since he was a learned man and instructed in the divine Scriptures, wrote many letters for the edification of the brothers; of these the following are reported: To Cornelius the abbot, a letter. To the provosts of the monasteries, a letter. To Syrus the abbot, a letter. To the brothers working outside, a letter.

Also a Rule for Monks, one book.

He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, a Christian poet, a man most learned in secular literature and sufficiently skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellent in meter and prose, having been held for fifty-seven years by the loves of the world, read and expounded many little works of the poets, and from his own vein wrote many profound poems.

*Of the Abbot of Spanheim*

John, monk and priest of Damascus, a learned and holy man, of whom marvelous things are told, held in great esteem because of the excellence of his doctrine and the purity of his life, appointed [unclear] of the monks at Constantinople, turned many away from iniquity. He wrote in the Greek language some little works of profound meaning, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read only that excellent work [unclear].

40 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* Four books of *The Tradition of the Orthodox Faith*. “No one has ever seen God.” One book of the *History of Barlaam and Josaphat*. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He also wrote one book *On Logic*; one book, *Introduction of Dignities*; one book *On the Two Wills and Operations in Christ*, etc.; an epistle or one book *On the Trisagion*; one book *On the Hundred Heresies*; one book *On the Dispute of a Christian and a Saracen*; one book of very compunctive hymns; one sermon *On Those Who Have Departed Hence in Christ, That They Are Greatly Helped by Sacred Offices and by the Good Deeds of the Living*. Of all these works, together with certain others, recently printed at Cologne by the Quentel presses, a good part had nowhere been printed before these days, so that you may readily believe the Abbot when he says that he had not seen them; but as to the time at which he asserts this author lived, and likewise as to the other Damascene placed below in his own place, you will not readily believe him.

He flourished under Theodosius, that most devout prince, in the year of the Lord 390.

Ticonius the African, whom blessed Augustine, in the first book *On Christian Doctrine*, records as having belonged to the Donatist party, although in certain matters he disagreed with them, was certainly a sharp-witted man and very much practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote not a few little works, of which these are reported, namely: one book *On Civil War*; one book, an exposition of diverse causes; one book *On the Apocalypse of John*; one book of rules for sacred Scripture; several letters to various persons; and many other things.

He flourished when Theodosius and his sons were ruling, in the year of the Lord 390.

Heraclides the monk, a man holy in conduct and distinguished in learning in the divine Scriptures, a most diligent investigator and imitator of the holy fathers, anchorites and monks, who, like a resourceful bee, gathering from the way of life of each one the flowers of virtues into the little hive of his breast, produced the honey of spiritual sweetness. Among other things, for the edification of readers, he wrote an outstanding work on the life and conduct of the holy fathers living in the desert or in a monastery under a rule, whose title is:

*Paradise*, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 580.

Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently imbued with secular letters, and worthy of the priesthood no less by his way of life than by his knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote, among other things, a useful work *On the Holy Spirit*.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

One book *On the Holy Spirit*.

Of the other things which he is said to have composed, nothing has come to my knowledge.

There are, however, extant in Italy sermons by the same author, which follow: *On the Life and Miracles of Basil the Great*; *On the Sinful Woman Who Anointed the Lord, Against the Pharisee*; *That One Must Not Despair*; certain orations and hymns, all in Greek.

He flourished in the times of the devout emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, a city of Cyprus, a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures, was of such sanctity that he deserved to be illumined by the spirit of prophecy and to become a worker of many miracles. He was a very close friend of blessed Jerome and wrote several letters to him. If anyone desires to know his deeds, let him read the *Tripartite History*. He composed some little works, of which these are reported: One book *On the Eighty Heresies*. “The Simonians, from Simon.” Two books *Against All Heresies*. One book *On the Errors of Origen*. One book *To Theophilus of Alexandria*. One book of letters to various persons. “To the lord, most beloved son.” And certain other things.

He flourished under Theodosius, that most religious prince, in the year 390.

There is extant by the same Epiphanius a Greek book, translated by Albanus Torinus, *On the Life of the Prophets and Evangelists*.

Theophilus, the twenty-first bishop of the church of Alexandria, a man devoted to the Scriptures, a very fierce opponent of the Origenists, who is said to have had great discord with Saint John Chrysostom and, after he had been driven from the episcopate by intrigues, to have compelled him to die in exile, as is contained more fully in the histories of the ancients. He is reported to have written certain little works, of which few have come to my knowledge. There is extant his one book of letters to various persons on various matters. “To the lord most beloved, a.” One book *On Easter*.

He also produced many other things, as is gathered from the letter of blessed Jerome directed to him, in which he asks that they be sent to him either to be read or to be translated. He flourished under the princes Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year 390.

Antiochus, bishop of a certain city, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular letters, whose conduct commended his teaching to his people, wr[ote]

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

...wrote for the edification of readers certain distinguished volumes, of which these are considered the more important: Against Avarice, 2 books. On the Illumination of the Man Born Blind, 1 book. Several Homilies to the People, 1 book. And other works unknown to us. He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, in the year 390.

Macarius, an Egyptian monk and formerly a disciple of the blessed father Antony, a devout man of most holy way of life, about whom many miracles are told, and how he even obtained the voices of the dead from tombs for the confirmation of the faith, sent to all religious men a useful letter, which is: To Monks, as one book. “In the first place indeed [unclear].” And other letters to others. He flourished in great holiness under the emperors Constantine and Constantius, in the year of the Lord 350. His deeds are contained in the Lives of the Fathers.

Faustinus, a priest, a man very learned in the sacred scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, of the Luciferian party, and for that reason deservedly blameworthy, wrote many excellent volumes, which are judged useful for the refutation of heretics; of these I have found only the titles of a few: Against the Arians and Macedonians, 7 books. An Apology to Valentinian, one book.

He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Jerome, priest and monk, born of his father Eusebius, from the town of Stridon, a man learned in secular literature and, among all the doctors, most learned in the divine scriptures, remarkable for his knowledge of many languages, interpreter of the sacred law, hammer of heretics and most powerful assailant: he is the true evangelical steward, faithful and prudent, who, bringing forth from his treasury things new and old, and giving to his fellow servants in due season the measure of spiritual wheat, despoiled the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins. He is the distinguished doctor of the Church of Christ, who, with his pious mother Rebecca, that is, the grace of God, brought forth the garments of Esau, wandering astray through the byways of errors, laid away idly at home, and clothed meek Jacob, faithful and serving Christ. He is Jerome, the sincere lover of Jesus Christ, who, passing no time idly, meditated day and night on the law of the Lord, and, scarcely allowing his body necessary sleep, always by day and night wrote, read, taught, or prayed, as the almost countless books that he published testify. This defender of truth, cultivator of virtue, most bitter enemy of vices,

*Abbot of Spanheim*

when he was a priest of the Roman Church and was steadfastly accusing the crimes of the clerics, withdrew from the city because of their envy; and coming into Judea, he visited the glorious sepulcher of the Lord, and, establishing for himself a dwelling-place beside the manger at Bethlehem, became known in glory to the whole world, divine providence arranging this, namely, that there the light of the world should rest where the true sun of righteousness had become known to human beings by being born. A holy and fitting inhabitant of the most holy place, firm in faith, kindled with charity, mature in conduct, who could not be led astray by prosperity, whom no adversity ever cast down from his holy purpose. But why do I, a foul praiser, touch the holy head of the man with impure lips? It would have been more humble for me to be silent than to speak insufficiently about so holy a man. Now therefore let us set down in order what we have found concerning his writings and little works; of these there are: On Faith, to Damasus, 1 book. “We believe in God the Father.”

These are the writings of the most blessed doctor Jerome which at present occurred to us to record. Nor do we doubt that he wrote more, which are not contained in this catalogue, chiefly for this reason: that they either remained unknown to us or dispersed among many things. For among all the doctors of the Church none was of more benefit than Jerome, who, besides innumerable small works, translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin, corrected the New according to the Greek truth, and faithfully offered it to the Church to be read. He also made many volumes of the Greeks Latin, namely those of Origen, Josephus the Jew, Eusebius of Caesarea, Didymus of Alexandria, Victorinus the martyr, and others.

At last, after many labors, full of days, he died under the rulers Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 422, in the fifth indiction, on the last day of the month of September, at the hour of Compline, in the ninety-ninth year of his age; he was buried at Bethlehem, shining with many miracles. Eusebius, his disciple, described his life.

47 *The Abbot of Spanheim* Audientius, a Spanish bishop, a man having a mind exercised in the divine Scriptures, wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, yet with his principal intention against the Photinians, who afterward were called Bonosians, an outstanding work, which is entitled *On the Faith against Heretics*, one book.

He also published certain other works, which have come to my knowledge.

Rufinus the monk, priest of the church of Aquileia, an eloquent man, very learned in the divine Scriptures, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, was of no small reputation among the ecclesiastical doctors. Although his writings are many, nevertheless they are counted among the apocrypha, distinction 15, *Sancta Romana*, because he wrote invective letters against the most holy man Jerome, as can be understood from the reading of them. But afterward, when they returned into the concord of brotherly love, the little works of Rufinus were made authentic, insofar as they were not contrary to the sayings of Jerome. Concerning the writings of Rufinus, therefore, the following are reported: On the prophet Hosea, one book. On the prophet Amos [unclear].
On the prophet Joel, one book. “To me indeed, most faithful...”
On his faith, to Bishop Laurentius, one book. “I have read your writings...”
Invectives against Jerome, one book. “I heard certain persons, when...”
On his faith, to Anastasius, one book. On the sacraments, one book.
On the blessings of the patriarchs, one book. Additions to the Ecclesiastical History, two books.
An exhortation to Proba, one book. [unclear]. He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius.
Letters to various persons, two books.

He is said to have composed many other things besides, but they have not come into our hands. He also translated into Latin the volumes of many Greeks, namely of Clement, Origen, Basil, Gregory the Great, bishop, Pamphilus the martyr, Eusebius of Caesarea, Evagrius, Sixtus the philosopher, and many others, all of which he marked with his own prefaces and prefixed letters. He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius; he wrote many and various works, in the year of the Lord 400.

John, bishop of Constantinople, once, while still a priest at Antioch, a hearer and disciple of Eusebius, bishop of Nyssa, who because of the charm of his speech is named Chrysostom, that is, “golden mouth,” a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, was of excellent ability in delivering homilies to the people, distinguished no less for holiness than for learning, and was held by the people in great reverence and love. This most blessed bishop endured many wrongs from Theophilus of Alexandria, and by his fraudulent and deceitful machinations [unclear].

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He is also said to have written many homilies, sermons, and innumerable letters, which have not come into our hands.

Letters, two books. Thirty-five homilies at the beginning of Lent. Ethics. Expositions on Isaiah. Two manuscript sermons on Jeremiah are extant at Bologna in the library of San Salvatore. At Rome, in the papal library, four Greek volumes are preserved. A homily on προστυχὴ, [unclear], from the third up to the thirty-eighth.

At length, after many labors and holy exercises, through the deceit of Theophilus of Alexandria and of the empress Eudoxia, he died in exile in Pontus, on the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 411, in the ninth indiction.

Severianus, bishop of Gabala, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, and an admirable teacher in delivering homilies to the people, was of incredible eloquence; whence he was frequently summoned by the emperor Arcadius to Constantinople by the aforesaid blessed bishop John, to preach. To him Saint John commended his people when he was being driven into exile, venerating not only his doctrine but the merit of his life. Severianus, however, commending himself to the people more than was fitting, supplied kindling for discord between him and John. But when the patriarch returned from exile, they returned to the bonds of brotherly love, as the homily delivered above in the church of Constantinople testifies. Of the writings of Severianus, a most learned man, few are possessed among the Latins; still fewer have come into our hands.

On the Epistle to the Galatians, one book. On baptism and Epiphany, one book. In the church of Constantinople, one homily. On the advent of the Lord, [unclear]. On the death of the innocents, one homily: “To what end zeal tends, to what [unclear].”

There are extant among us certain other homilies of his, brief indeed, but very useful. Concerning his other little works, though many are reported, I have as yet found nothing. He flourished under Arcadius and Honorius, at the time of John Chrysostom, in the year of the Lord 406.

Vitellius Afer, defending the Donatist schism, a man indeed well exercised in the divine Scriptures, would have composed doctrine useful enough if he had remained in ecclesiastical unity. But because he denounced true Catholics as persecutors and, as it were, betrayers, he was deservedly despised together with his volumes. The following volumes from his writings are extant: Against the nations, one book. That the servants of God are hated by the world, one book. A complaint against our own people, one book. He is said to have composed many other volumes besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Constans, son of Constantine the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 360.

Theodotus, presbyter of the church of Antioch, a learned and eloquent man, and practiced in the reading of the ancient authors, wrote against the Apollinarists and Eunomians a most elegant volume, in which by very clear reasoning and authority he refuted the depraved doctrines of the heretics. He entitled this magnificent and notable work: On the incarnation of the Lord, fifteen books.

He is said to have written many other things also, which have not come to my knowledge.

Acrobius, presbyter, and afterward hidden bishop of the Donatists in the city of Rome, while he was still a presbyter in the Church of God, wrote to the confessors and to the virgins of Christ a volume, moral indeed, but very necessary, of doctrine; in it he chiefly deals with and treats [unclear]. To show that there is one principle, and that nothing material was created from any other source than God, he wrote a sufficiently elegant and notable work, which he entitled On the natures of primordial things, one book.

He flourished first among our people at Rome, afterward among his own Donatists, the Montenses of Africa.

Heliodorus, once a presbyter, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, sufficiently sharp in disputation and of a vehement intellect in the scholastic manner, [unclear].

[Unclear], after the death of [unclear], provost of his monasteries, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, a vigorous governor of regular discipline, and venerable no less for sanctity than for doctrine, wrote lucid sermons on the holy Scriptures to the monasteries: Letters of exhortation, three.

He is said also to have written several other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Theodorus the monk, disciple of blessed Pachomius, and, after the death of that man, [unclear], distinguished both in life and in learning, wrote for the instruction of monks a work seasoned with divine salt and furnished with the instruments of the whole monastic discipline, which we may entitle [unclear].

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

*On the Instruction of Monks*, one book. If he wrote anything more, I do not know. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 420.

John Cassian, a Scythian by nation, formerly a hearer and disciple of blessed John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, and ordained deacon by him, after some years was expelled by the same man for I know not what cause. Consecrated priest at Marseilles, he founded two monasteries, one of men and one of women, in which a great fervor of regular discipline remained for many years. With experience as his teacher he wrote several little works, in which the grace of eloquence is apparent even in the translator. Among these are counted: at the request of Leo the archdeacon, afterward bishop of the city of Rome, he wrote against Nestorius the heretic:

*On the Incarnation of the Lord*, seven books.
*On the Institutes of Monks*, four books. “On the institutes and [unclear]”
*On the Eight Capital Vices*, eight books. “The fifth, with [unclear] helping us”
*Conferences of the Holy Fathers*, twenty-four books. “When in the desert of Scete” In these conferences of the saints there is useful and necessary instruction for monks; but because he is censured by blessed Prosper on certain points concerning freedom of the will, his little works are counted among the apocrypha. At length, after the publication of many books, he died at Marseilles, not without a reputation for sanctity, while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning, in the year of the Lord 455.

Lucian, priest of the church of Jerusalem, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and most holy in life and conduct, to whom in the times of Honorius and Theodosius almighty God revealed the place of the tomb and relics of the most holy protomartyr Stephen, is said to have written some little works. Of these there survives a lengthy letter:

*On the Discovery of Saint Stephen*, one book. “Lucian the priest” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He wrote that revelation itself in the Greek language; Avitus, a priest Spanish by birth, translated it into the Latin tongue and, with his own letter added, sent it through Orosius to the easterners to be read. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, around the year of the Lord 410.

Severus the priest, surnamed Sulpicius, born from the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and letters and distinguished by love of poverty and humility, dear also to the holy men Martin, bishop of Tours, and Paulinus, bishop of Nola, in his old age was deceived by the Pelagians; and recognizing the fault of loquacity, [he kept] silence until dea-

*ABBOT OF SPONHEIM.* [running head] …held [silence] until death, that the sin which he had contracted by speaking he might wholesomely amend by keeping silence. He wrote little works of no contemptible reading, of which the following are reported:
On the life of St Martin the bishop: 3 books. ["Very many of mortals…"]
The Conference of Postumianus and Gallus: 4 books. ["When into one place I…"]
Of letters to [his] Sister: 1 book. Of letters to various [persons]: 1 book.
To Paulinus, bishop of Nola: 2 books.
He is said to have written also some others, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished with Saint Martin, archbishop of Tours, under the princes Arcadius [and] Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Ausonius, bishop of Bordeaux, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, second to none of his time in secular letters, excelling in verse [and] prose, shone forth renowned no less for sanctity than for erudition; who at Trier, in a council under the prince Maximus, together with the saints Martin, Ambrose of Milan, [and] Jerome the presbyter, did many illustrious things. He wrote there, among other metrical [works], a distinguished little work, which is entitled:
The Moselle: 1 book. On the praise of the same homeland: 1 book.
But he is reported to have written many other little works, which have by no means come to us. He flourished under Maximus, in the year of the Lord 410.

Augustine, bishop of Hippo, a Carthaginian by nation, in Africa, a man most erudite of all the learned, both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, eloquent in speech, renowned in eloquence, profound in sense, most holy in life [and] conversation; he wrote so many little works that I should believe no one able either to read or to have them all. Whence without doubt he is convicted of lying who confesses that he has found the whole of Augustine. For he precedes all writers in the number [and] usefulness of [his] books, who composed more than a thousand distinguished treatises. No one so profoundly explained sacred Scripture as Augustine. No one so usefully instituted Christian morals, nor did anyone defend the catholic faith more ardently than he. The king led [him] into the wine-cellar, and clothed [him] with such fortitude that he strongly laid low all the adversaries of the faith with the sword of his mouth. If you have him as a teacher, even with the rest lacking, he himself suffices you. Now therefore, of the many books which he published, let us mark down even a few:
On the Holy Trinity: 15 books. ["[You who are] about to read these [things]…"]
On the City of God: 22 books. ["The most glorious city…"]
On the predestination of the saints: 2 books. ["[That] the Apostle indeed said…"]
[page 92:] On Genesis according to the letter: 12 books. On Genesis, unfinished: 1 book. On Genesis against the Manichees: 2 books. On the Academics: 3 books. On the blessed life: 1 book. On order: 3 books. Of Soliloquies: 2 books. On the morals of the catholic Church: 2 books. On the quantity of the soul: 1 book. On free will: 3 books. On the teacher: 1 book. On music: 6 books. On true religion: 1 book. On the usefulness of believing: 1 book. On the two souls: 1 book. Acts with Fortunatus the Manichee: 1 book. On faith and the creed: 1 book. On the Lord's sermon on the mount: 2 books. On eighty-three questions: 1 book. A Psalm against the party of Donatus: 1 book. Against the letter of Donatus: 1 book. Against Adamantius: 1 book. On lying: 1 book. Against lying: 1 book. To Simplicianus the bishop: 2 books. Against the letter of the Foundation: 1 book. On the Christian struggle: 1 book. On Christian doctrine: 4 books. Against the party of Donatus: 13 books. Of Confessions: 13 books. Against Faustus the Manichee: 2 books. Against Felix the Manichee: 1 book. On the nature of the good: 1 book. Against Secundinus: 1 book. Against Hilary: 1 book. Questions of the Gospels: 3 books. Of Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans: 1 book. On the Epistle to the Romans, an unfinished work: 1 book.

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*
