*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

On the Tabernacle, one book. On the Concupiscence of the Flesh, a treatise, or four books.

On the Unchangeable Essence of God, one book. On the Oath, one book.

On the Beautiful and the Fitting, three books. To Ambrose the Presbyter, one book.

On the Barbarian Time, one book. On the Words of the Apostle, treatises, or twenty books.

On the Samaritan Woman, one book. On the Instability of This Life, one book.

On the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, one book. Whence Evil Comes, two books.

On Jacob and Joseph, one book. On Blessed Jacob, brothers [unclear].

On the Fourth Feria, one book. On the Seven Liberal Arts, one book.

A Refutation of False Articles, one book. Against Porphyry, one book.

An Exhortation to the Faith, one book. On the Fear of God, a treatise, or one book.

On the Eclipse of the Sun, a treatise, or one book. On the Resurrection, two treatises.

Against the Jews, two treatises. These are extant in the library of Eberbach, B.

The Apostle Paul. On Unlawful Marriages, two books.

On the Eucharist, one treatise. On Saint Cyprian, four treatises.

On Jacob and Esau, one book. On Grammar, one book.

On Eternal Times, one treatise. On Restless Charity, one treatise.

To Victor, four books. On Chaste Fear, one treatise.

On the Eclipse of the Sun, one treatise. On the Sweet Yoke of the Lord, one treatise.

On Hope, one book. On the Two Blind Men, one treatise.

On Pleasing Men, or Not, one treatise. On the Rods of Jacob, one treatise.

On Abraham and Isaac, two treatises. On Goliath and David, one book.

On the Usefulness of Penitence, one treatise. On the Judgment of Solomon, one book.

On the Pilgrimage of Christians, one book. On the Song of Isaiah, one book.

On the Song of Exodus, one book. On the Deposition of the Bishop of Carthage, one book.

On the Calling of the Apostle Paul, one book. On Voice and Word, one treatise.

On the Last Day, one treatise. On the Woman with the Issue of Blood, one treatise.

On the Deposition of Bishop Restitutus, one treatise. On the Usefulness of Fasting, one treatise.

On the Drunkenness of Noah, one treatise. On the Works of the Six Days, six treatises.

On Jacob’s Wrestling with the Angel, one treatise. On Moses’ Rod Turned into a Serpent, one treatise.

On the Works of Mercy, one treatise. On the Strong Woman from Proverbs, one treatise.

On the Beatitudes, one treatise. On Fraternal Correction, one treatise.

On the Bush Which Moses Saw, one treatise. On Avarice Also, one treatise.

On the Love of God, a treatise, or one book. On the Ordination of a Cleric, one treatise.

On Electing a Bishop, one treatise. On the Wantonness of Young Men, one treatise.

On the Dead Raised by the Lord, one treatise. On Charity, two treatises.

On the Nativity of the Lord, seven treatises. On Epiphany Also, seven treatises.

On Lent, five treatises. On the Passion of the Lord, two treatises.

On the Vigil of Easter, twenty-three treatises. On the Creed, five treatises.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Of an exhortation to the candidates, one treatise. On the ascension of the Lord, two treatises. On Saint Perpetua and Felicity, one treatise. On Saint Vincent, two treatises. On spiritual almsgiving, one treatise. On bodily alms, one treatise. On Samson, one treatise. On Susanna and Joseph, one treatise. On the dedication of the temple, two treatises. Sermons on various subjects, 200, one book. Letters, more than 200, one book.

There is extant also a certain sermon on the mercy of God at Mount Saint John, a monastery of the Benedictines in the Rheingau.

He published many other works as well; if anyone desires to know them more fully, let him read the list of his books edited by Possidius, from which we have taken many items. Jacobus de Voragine, bishop of Genoa, writes in his treatise which he composed on the books of Augustine that the number of his books, treatises, sermons, and letters rises beyond one thousand thirty. And he concludes thus: And therefore no one has ever been found who was able to find all the books of Augustine. And Possidius says: He lies who declares that he has read you entire, Augustine.

But in this work I have deliberately omitted certain treatises which are ascribed by many to blessed Augustine. Among these is the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, in whose seventh chapter Boethius is cited, though he was born a long time after Augustine. But the style itself does not have the savor of Augustine. Likewise the book which has now been printed under Augustine’s name, *On True and False Penitence*, is falsely ascribed to him, since in the seventh chapter, toward the end, Augustine himself is cited. The book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*, which begins “The apostolic voice,” echoes the style of Pope Gregory, and agrees with the older copies. Likewise the book *On the Ladder of Paradise*, whose beginning is “When on a certain day,” is in the ancient copies inscribed to blessed Bernard, whose spirit and manner of speech it seems to express.

Why should I strive at length? So many treatises and sermons are falsely inscribed to blessed Augustine that a review of them would require its own volume. Nor is it my place to sit as judge and deprive of their titles things that belong to another. Let the prudent reader carefully consider what is to be done or held by him in these matters.

Saint doctor Augustine died in the city of Hippo when it was being besieged by the Vandals, in the year of the Lord 430, in the thirteenth indiction, in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the fortieth of his priesthood, according to Marianus Scotus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the third month of the city’s siege. While answering, amid the attacks of the besieging Vandals, the books of Julian the Manichaean at the very end of his days, he persevered gloriously in defense of the Christian faith. He made no testament, because there was nothing from which he might make one

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

He had nothing to leave, apart from the church library, which even at his death he most diligently commended to the brothers to be guarded. Poor in possessions, rich in merits and knowledge, Augustine the bishop rested in the Lord; Possidius, bishop of Calama, wrote his life.

Atticus, bishop of the city of Constantinople after blessed John Chrysostom, a man learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, was nevertheless blameworthy in this, that he allowed himself to be ordained in place of a living bishop who had been unjustly expelled; from this matter many scandals arose in the Church of God. He wrote little works not to be despised by us, among which there is an outstanding work to the queens, daughters of the emperors of Constantinople:

*On Faith and Virginity*, two books.

And not a few other things.

He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Paulinus the priest, disciple of Saint Augustine of Hippo, afterward bishop of Nola in Campania, to whom many letters and various treatises of Augustine and Jerome are said to have been addressed, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures and second to none in his own time in secular letters, shone forth no less in holiness than in learning. Concerning him blessed Pope Gregory writes in the third book of the *Dialogues* that he was of such piety and mercy that, after he had spent all his possessions for the use of the poor and the liberation of captives, he even handed himself over into slavery for the son of a certain widow; from that slavery he was finally released, together with many captives, on account of the merit of his life. He wrote many volumes, as much in merit as in number, of which the following are reported. First, at the request of Saint Augustine, he wrote:

*Life of Saint Ambrose of Milan*, one book. *Life of Saint Felix, bishop of Nola*, one book.

*On the Sacraments*, one book. *On the Death of a Baptized Infant*, one book.

*Panegyric of Theodosius*, one book. *Hymns in Various Metre*, one book.

*On Contempt of the World*, one book. *On Penitence*, one book.

*On the Blessings of the Patriarch*, one book. *On the Praise of the Martyrs*, one book.

*To Severus Sulpicius*, four letters. *Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He also published some other works which have come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 420.

Niceas, bishop of the city of Romaciana, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, acute in intellect, clear and polished in speech, wrote little works for the edification of readers, of reading not to be despised, among which the following are reported:

*To the Competentes who*

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

for those who are being prepared for baptism, *A Preparatory Work*, one book. *On the Errors of Paganism*, two books. *On the Faith of the One Majesty*, one book. *Against the Genealogy*, one book. *Also On the Creed*, one book. *On the Victim of the Paschal Lamb*, one book. *To a Fallen Virgin*, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Simplicianus, bishop of Milan after St. Ambrose, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and a lover of poverty, by many letters urged Augustine, while he was still a presbyter, to exercise his talent and devote himself to expositions of the Scriptures, so that he might seem like another Ambrose, a promoter of Origen’s work. Hence Augustine also resolved many questions and letters addressed to him. But he himself also wrote useful letters to Augustine and to various others, which are found partly here and there.

He flourished under the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Isidore the Elder, [unclear] of Corduba, a man very skilled in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent and sufficiently eloquent in speech, distinguished no less for the conduct of his character than for knowledge of the Scriptures, whose learning among the ancients was held at a great price, wrote no few little works on the divine volumes. Of these I have found only an excellent work which he published for St. Orosius, the Spanish presbyter: *On the Four Books of Kings*, four books.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under the rulers Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Orosius the presbyter, Spanish by nation, once a hearer of blessed Augustine, was a man learned in the divine writings and most skilled in secular letters, very renowned in life and conduct. Blessed Augustine had sent him, when he came to him from Spain to learn the question concerning the nature of the soul, to St. Jerome in Bethlehem of Judea. After staying there for a little while, he learned clearly the question for which he had come, and, returning to Hippo, carried with him the relics of Stephen the protomartyr. To this most studious man there are extant several little works of blessed Augustine and various resolutions of questions of the Scriptures. He himself also wrote the following volumes:

*An Apologetic against the Pelagians*, one book. *On the [unclear] of the World, a Chronicle*, seven books, “I have obeyed your instructions.” *On the Reason of the Soul*, one book, “When among you, heavenly [unclear].”

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

Several letters to Augustine, one book. Also letters to various persons, one book. *On the Song of Songs*, one book.

He flourished, illustrious in life and doctrine, with St. Augustine, in the year of the Lord 420.

John, bishop and patriarch of Jerusalem, studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, but too intent upon Origen’s teachings, stirred up against himself the writings of the fathers, namely of the most holy presbyter Jerome and of Bishop Epiphanius, as is found in their letters sent to him. But John himself, giving account of his study, says that he imitated not the faith of Origen, but his talent. For chiefly on this account he wrote a noteworthy work: *Against the Detractors of His Study*, one book; and certain letters to various persons, and certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Maximus, bishop of Turin, most learned in the holy Scriptures, second to none in his own time in delivering homilies to the people, was distinguished not only in doctrine but also in life. Holy mother Church has accepted his homilies to be read with great authority. Among these the following are reported:

*On Chapters of the Gospels*, one book. *In Praise of the Apostles*, two books, “Most glorious ones of Christ.” *On the Acts of the Apostles*, one book. *In Praise of John the Baptist*, two books, “Solemnities for us.” Three books. *On the Words of Isaiah*, one book. *On the Life of Eusebius of Vercelli*, two books, “Of the holy fathers [unclear].” *On Saint Cyprian the Martyr*, one book, “Of the feast of Saint Cyprian.” *On the Fast of Lent*, one book. *On the Grace of Baptism*, one book. *On Judas’s Betrayal*, one book. *On Hospitality*, one book. *On the Lord’s Sepulchre*, one book. *On Alms*, one book. *On the Accusation of the Lord*, one homily. Four homilies, “Not undeservedly, brothers [unclear].” *On the Passion of the Lord*, one book, “The reading of the Acts of the Apostles.” *On the Fast of Servants* [unclear]. *On the Nativity of the Lord*, five homilies. *On the Cross of the Lord*, one book. *On Easter*, five homilies. *On the Office of the Mass*, one homily. *On the Penitence of the Ninevites*, one homily. *On the Resurrection of the Lord*, three homilies. *On Saint Lawrence*, five homilies. *On Saint Stephen*, five homilies. *On the Kalends of January*, one homily. *On the Epiphany of the Lord*, two homilies. *On Pentecost*, three homilies. *On Not Fearing Bodily Enemies*, one homily. *On gra-*

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

One homily, *On Giving Thanks after Food*.

He also wrote many other things: sermons, treatises, letters, and homilies, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420. He died under Theodosius the Younger.

Julian, bishop of Campania, a man of sharp and vehement talent, learned in the holy Scriptures, trained in Greek and Latin speech, before he revealed in himself the impiety of Pelagius, was distinguished among the doctors of the Church. Afterwards, however, [embracing?] that man’s heresy, he wrote against the holy doctors little works suited to his own opinion, of which there are extant:

*Against St. Augustine*, 4 books. *Against the Same*, another 7 books.

*A Dialogue of the Disputation of the Parties*, 1 book.

And many other things, all of which, because of the author’s errors, have rightly been rejected from the ecclesiastical library. In a time of famine and distress, he distributed all his possessions in alms to the poor; he associated many noble religious men, deceived under the appearance of piety, with his heresy.

He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Innocent, the first pope of that name, a learned and most holy man, Alban by nation, the forty-second after blessed Peter, presided over the universal Church for fifteen years, and gloriously ordained many things for its benefit. To him, while he was still a priest, blessed Jerome composed the history of the woman struck seven times, as the prologue of that same work shows. Since he was most learned in the divine Scriptures, he wrote several excellent little works for the instruction of the faithful, of which I have found only these:

*A Decree against the Pelagians*, 1 book.

*Against the Bonosiaci*, 1 book. *We Have Long Wondered*.

Many letters to various persons, 1 book. *In Inquiring about These Things*.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He died in the year of the Lord 417, in the fifteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

Eusebius of Cremona, a monk and disciple of blessed Jerome the priest, a studious and learned man, venerable in life and conduct, continually intent on holy prayers and divine readings after the example of his most reverend master, attained a great reputation for holiness. He wrote to Damasus, bishop of Porto, and Theodosius, senator of the city of Rome, a sufficiently elegant and lengthy volume on the passing of St. Jerome, 1 book: *To the Most Reverend Damasus*. He flourished in the time of St. Jerome, in the year of the Lord 420.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Possidonius the African, bishop of Calama, once a hearer and disciple of blessed Augustine, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, having lived on familiar terms with St. Augustine for many years, shone forth brightly among ecclesiastical prelates in life and doctrine. Among other things, for the edification of the faithful, he wrote:

*The Life of Saint Augustine*, 1 book. *At the Inspiration of the Maker of All Things*.

*An Index of His Books*. *Against the Pagans Concerning* [unclear].

He flourished under the emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 430.

Siricius, pope, Roman by nation, sat after Damasus in the pontificate for fifteen years, a learned and holy man, a very keen defender of the Catholic faith. All the Manichaeans whom he found in the city he condemned to exile. Converts, however, for the doing of penance, he relegated to a monastery until the end of life. Among other things, he wrote to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona:

*A Decretal Work*, 1 book.

*Against Jovinian and Auxentius*, 1 book.

He died under the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 398, in the sixth indiction, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March.

Fastidius, bishop of the Britons, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, an excellent preacher of the word of God, illustrious also in life and conduct, distinguished in speech and talent, wrote several devout little works. Among them a certain volume of sound Christian doctrine is said to be addressed to Fatalis, 1 book. *On Preserving Widowhood*, 1 book.

He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Coelestine, the first pope of that name, Roman by nation, a learned and holy man, by whose order blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, held at Ephesus a synod of two hundred fathers, in which Nestorius and Pelagius were condemned with their wicked doctrines. There too it was decreed that the most blessed Virgin Mary should henceforth be called Mother of God. Blessed Coelestine wrote, among other things, a solemn decree:

*Against Nestorius*, 1 book. *Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book.

And certain other things.

He died under the emperor Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 435, in the tenth year of his pontificate, in the first indiction, on the Ides of April.

Theodoric, bishop of the city which, from its founder Cyrus, king of the Persians, was called Cyria, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, says

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear] to have composed little works on the sacred books, but they have not come into our hands. His distinguished work, however, is said to have been published after Jerome:

*Ecclesiastical History*, one book.
*On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Eutyches*, one book.

He flourished in the times of the most holy prince Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390. His history is now inserted in the *Tripartite History*.

Evodius, bishop in Africa, disciple of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to whom Augustine wrote the treatise *On the Soul of Christ among the Dead* and many letters, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and most upright in the conduct of his life, who deservedly ought to be placed in the catalogue of the saints, is said to have written certain devout little works. Of these there is extant a volume on the miracles done in Africa through the relics, brought by Orosius the priest, of Saint Stephen the martyr, [unclear book-count]. And several letters to various persons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Saint Augustine, in the year of the Lord 420.

Palladius, the first bishop ordained by Pope Celestine for the island of the Britons or Scots, Hibernia, Greek by birth, a learned and holy man, by his most sweet preaching converted to the faith of Christ the faith entrusted to him. After him Saint Patrick, a Briton by race, consecrated by Saint Celestine the pope as archbishop of Hibernia, shining for forty years with signs and miracles, converted the whole island to the faith. Palladius wrote:

*Life of Saint John Chrysostom*, [unclear book-count]. And certain other things.

He was sent into Scotland by Pope Celestine I in the year of the Lord 452, in the fifteenth indiction, according to Marianus Scotus.

Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, [unclear] by nation, once an outstanding [unclear] and cultivator of Carmel, a learned and holy man, by command of Pope Celestine I presided at the council of two hundred fathers at Ephesus, in which, condemning Nestorius and Pelagius together with their errors, he uttered many elegant opinions. Since he was most learned in the holy Scriptures, he wrote many little works, of which these are reported:

*On Faith against the Heretics*, one book. *Against Nestorius*, one book.
*On the Defection of the Synagogue*, one book. *On the Birth and Praise of Saint Mary*, one book.
*On the Paschal Cycle of Ninety-Five Years*, one book. *Commentary on the Gospel*, one book.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

Commentaries on Leviticus, arranged in sixteen books.
A work of treasures on the Trinity, extant in Greek in Italy.
Greek commentaries on several prophets, Isaiah, Hosea, Daniel, and certain very varied homilies, are preserved in Italy.
A Greek book on the fact that through all the books of Moses the mystery of Christ is signified enigmatically. Dogmatic solutions of questions which certain persons had put to him from the *Treasures*.
An exposition of the prayer of the prophet Habakkuk, in Greek.
A book *On Adoration and Worship in the Spirit of Truth*, and that the shadow is a type of life in Christ according to the Gospel, addressed to Palladius in dialogue form, with one interpreting and one responding, in Greek, in Italy.
Seven orations, in Greek. Certain Greek homilies on the sacred creed. A counsel on concord between Greeks and Latins, in Greek. Two letters of the same man to Successus, bishop of Diocaesarea in Isauria. One letter to Augustine on the miracles of Saint Jerome. A *Practica* collected by the same man before the third synod. A book entitled *Ta glaphyra*. A Greek vocabulary, and a little work on words which change their meaning by accent, with a Greek-Latin lexicon. All these are preserved in Italy.

Besides these he composed several letters, homilies, and sermons, and other diverse treatises, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished, presiding at the Council of Ephesus, under the emperor Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 432, in the fifteenth indiction.

Theodore of Ancyra, bishop of Galatia, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, especially strong in dialectic, eloquent in speech and a keen disputant, being quite distinguished in the Council of Ephesus, wrote there, in dialectical fashion and very obscurely:

*Against Nestorius*, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the prince Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

Sozomen, Greek by nation, an excellent cultivator of secular letters and sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures, is said to have written some little works for the edification of the Church. Of these there is extant a distinguished work addressed to the prince Theodosius the Younger, from the third consulship of the Caesars Crispus and Constantine down to the seventeenth consulship of the same Theodosius:

*Ecclesiastical History*, nine books. “The thought once came to me...”

The other things which he composed have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the aforesaid emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 450.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

A certain Socrates, Greek by nation, a learned and eloquent man, a distinguished historiographer, renowned for experience of great affairs, wrote, from the time of the first Constantine, the great emperor, down to the reign of Theodosius the Younger, a volume of *Ecclesiastical History*, one book.

He is also said to have written several other things, but they have not come into our hands. And it should be noted that three Greek authors, namely [Theodoret?], bishop of Cyrus, Sozomen, and this Socrates, each wrote histories of ecclesiastical affairs at almost the same time; Epiphanius Scholasticus translated these into Latin as they stood, and from them Cassiodorus Senator, a monk, made one continuous history, which he called the *Tripartite*.

Vigilius, a deacon and monk, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, a guardian and director of monastic discipline, is reported to have fashioned certain little works for the edification of monks, which distance of places and times has prevented from coming to our knowledge. The priest Gennadius says, however, that he wrote a very useful rule:

*On the Conduct of Monks*, one book. He says nothing about the rest. He flourished under the princes Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Osius, bishop of Corduba before Isidore, to whom Chalcidius the grammarian is recorded to have translated Plato’s *Timaeus*, a learned and eloquent man, presiding at the council of Sardica, uttered many excellent opinions, as is contained in the acts of that same synod. In his old age, however, greatly terrified by Constantius, the Arian prince, and fearing lest, as an old and wealthy man, he should suffer either exile or loss of property, he soon consented to Arian impiety. But not long afterward his life, as he deserved, was ended by a cruel death. For after his impious betrayal, when Saint Gregory, bishop of Eliberis, had come to Corduba by imperial decree and refused to communicate with Osius, the latter, moved with anger, asked Clementinus, Constantius’s prefect and vicar, to drive Gregory into exile. The vicar said to him: “I do not dare send a bishop into exile unless you first depose him from the episcopate.” Osius, tolerating no delay, mounted the chair as judge and summoned Gregory by royal edict. When Gregory appeared before the multitude, and Osius, proud in his arrogance, tried to pronounce the sentence of deposition, Gregory appealed with all his strength to Christ, that he should not allow so unjust a presumption of his to go unpunished. And behold, as the impious Osius sat there and wished to pronounce the sentence, his mouth twisted, and at the same time his neck was distorted; falling to the ground, he suddenly expired. Fear then seized everyone; thereafter no one dared touch Gregory. Osius, while still a Catholic, wrote:

*To His Sister, On the Praise of Virginity*, one book.

In the aforesaid council, eighteen opinions, one book.

And several letters. He flourished under Constantius as a very old man, by whom also he was deceived, and he died around the year of the Lord 590.

Ithacius, bishop of the city of [Lemica?] in Spain, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, renowned for his manner of speaking, who, together with Bishop [Ursacius?], because of the killing of Priscillian, whom he had accused at Trier, was separated from communion with the Church and driven into exile, and died there. He wrote works not to be despised, among which these are reported:

*Against Priscillian*, one book.

*Chronicles from the Time of Theodosius*, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the venerable emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Leporius, priest and monk, studious in the divine Scriptures, but presuming too much on the purity of his life, taught as doctrine that he lived religiously by his own judgment and effort, not by the grace of God, defending the Pelagian error. But after being admonished by the Gallic doctors and corrected in Africa by Saint Augustine, he abandoned his error; the heresy which he had formerly preached he afterward vigorously attacked. Therefore, giving thanks for his correction, he wrote:

*A Corrective against Heresy*, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished under the prince Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 450.

Sedulius, priest, a Scot by nation, from early youth a disciple of Hildebert, archbishop of the Scots, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, leaving Scotland out of love of learning, came into France, then traversed Italy and Asia; finally, departing from the borders of Achaia, he shone forth in the city of Rome, renowned for wondrous learning. He wrote many works in meter and in prose; of these I have found only the following: To Abbot Macedonius, a distinguished work according to the sequence of the whole Gospel, which he entitled *Paschal Song*, in meter, four books. “All you who [unclear] paschal [unclear].” On all the Epistles of Paul, in prose, fourteen books. “Before the apostolic words...” On

*70 On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On the miracles of Christ, one book, “From the quarter of the rising sun.”
To the emperor Theodosius, one book, “Leader of the Romulidae [unclear].”
On the larger volume of Priscian, one book, “Let us sing, companions, to the Lord.”
On the second edition of Donatus, one book, “Sedulius the Scotigene.”
An exhortation to the faithful, one book; book 2.
Several letters to various persons, one book, “Sedulius the Scotigene.”
On the miracles of Christ in prose, two books.
He also published a number of other things, which have not come to my knowledge. At length, as Sigebert writes, he was ordained bishop, but he does not state the church or city where. He flourished under Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 430.

Victorinus of Marseilles, rhetorician, a man most learned in secular letters and very devoted to the holy Scriptures, attempted to expound the holy Scriptures; but, being occupied with secular literature and having entered the field of the divine utterances without a teacher, he did not accomplish what he wished. Hence the little works that he wrote are indeed distinguished by Christian feeling and pious zeal, but are shaped with a lighter weight of opinions. He published, addressed to the person of his son Ethernius, commentaries from the beginning down to the death of the patriarch Abraham: On Genesis, four books.

And certain other things which are hidden from us. He flourished under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 430.

Philippus, monk and priest, once a hearer and disciple of blessed Jerome, a studious and learned man, an outstanding lover of voluntary poverty, who by word and example instructed many in piety, after the death of his master published certain commentaries on the divine Scriptures, among which there survives, as they say, an excellent work: On Job, one book.
A collection of letters, one book.

He flourished under the princes Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 430. And he died under Marcian.

Vincentius, monk and priest of the monastery of the island of Lerins, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in life and character. There survives an outstanding work of his, which he composed under the name Peregrinus, very famous among the ancient doctors and worthy of praise, on avoiding the errors and gatherings of heretics: Against all heretics, two books.

It is also read that he wrote a number of other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the reign of Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 429.

*Abbot of Spanheim*

Paulus, priest, a Pannonian by nation, which is now called Hungary, a man devoted to sacred letters and sufficiently learned, venerable no less for the cultivation of religion than for knowledge of the Scriptures, a zealous defender of the Christian faith, is said to have written not a few volumes, the reading of which is considered quite suitable for confounding heretics. There survive his works addressed to Constantia, a virgin dedicated to Christ: On virginity and contempt of the world, two books.

Concerning other works I have so far found nothing. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

Isaac, formerly a monk, priest of the church of Antioch, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, of very celebrated reputation for delivering homilies to the people, beloved by God in life and conduct, venerable to men, wrote in the Syriac tongue, in imitation of Saint Ephrem, several devout little works, the reading of which is judged very useful for religious men. Among these I have found the following among our materials: Against the Nestorians and Eutyches, two books.
An exhortation to the spiritual life, one book.
On the struggle against vices, one book.
On access to God, one book.
On the difficulty of the virtues, one book.
A dialogue on spiritual progress, one book.
On the order of the monastic life, one book.
On violent operation, one book.
On humility, one book.
On the three orders of those making progress, one book.
On the solitude of monks, one book.
On various temptations, one book.
On the instruction of novices, one book.
On penitence, one book.
A poem on the devastation of Antioch, one book.

He delivered several homilies to the people, but they have by no means come into our hands. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

Eucherius, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, a learned man, imbued from youth with monastic discipline, ready in talent, composed in speech, pleasing to God and men in life and conduct, since indeed he turned many away from iniquity by word and example, wrote several excellent volumes, but so far few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only these: On contempt of the world, one book.

Ex-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Expositions of the divine names, 1 book. Formulas of spiritual [unclear], To the sons Solon and Uranus, 1 book. An epitome of Cassian, 4 books. Certain letters to various persons, 1 book. To Bishop Hilary, On the praise of the desert, 1 book. The beginning of the commentaries on Genesis. Instructions, 2 books. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

Hilary, bishop of Arles, to whom Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, when he was seeking the wastes of the desert, published a book On the Praise of the Desert, was a man learned in the divine scriptures and sufficiently eloquent in speech. His merits of holiness the catholic Church proclaims. He showed such compassion toward the poor that, after all his possessions had been cheerfully distributed for their use, he was thereafter called, and was, the father of poverty. Among other things he wrote, in quite distinguished style, the Life of his predecessor, St. Honoratus the bishop, 1 book; almost countless homilies; and certain other works. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440. He died, however, under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.

Zosimus, pope, a Greek by nationality, sat in the pontificate after St. Innocent for one year and eight months. He was a learned, holy man, beloved by God, who by word and example governed the Church entrusted to him [unclear], and for whose edification he elegantly enacted many provisions, as is contained in his acts. He wrote for the ecclesiastical estate to various persons: Letters, 1 book. From the report of our brother [unclear]; On Easter, to Hilary, 1 book; On the priesthood, to Esychius, 1 book: “Your affection demands before...” He died under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 419, in the second indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January.

Boniface, the first pope of that name, succeeding blessed Zosimus, presided over the Church for three years and four months. He was a man of great learning and quite fit for the governance of souls, who enacted many provisions for ecclesiastical utility, which are found scattered in the canons of the holy fathers. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, as they say, some little works; of these I have found only: Decretal letters, 1 book: “To the Roman Church, which...” He died under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 422, in the fifth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

Proba, a most elegant woman, wife of Adelphius, Roman proconsul, a woman most learned in secular literature and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, burning with marvelous zeal, surpassed her sex by her learning. Perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin letters, and excelling both in meter and prose, since she held Virgil word for word in her mind, she conceived the idea of describing the New and Old Testament from his verses and of showing, by his own poems, that he had thought in this way. And so, courageously undertaking the work laid up in her mind, carefully going through all the books of Virgil, taking now this verse, now that one, sometimes half a verse, and sometimes smaller particles of verses, with marvelous industry, preserving everywhere the measure of the feet, she described the catholic volumes in the poet’s verses. This work, composed in almost seven hundred verses, she entitled with a Greek word, A Virgilian cento, 1 book: “Long since to have profaned...” If she wrote anything further, I do not know.

Nevertheless this work is counted among the apocrypha, since, although a devout woman undertook a pious study, Virgil nevertheless never intended that his little verses be referred to the honor of Christ or to our faith. For the interpretation of this matter is not proper but fictive, assumed by Proba. She flourished, however, as some think, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 430.

Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, a woman most devout in the Christian religion and most learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, returning from Jerusalem, brought with her the relics of the most holy protomartyr Stephen and placed them honorably in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lawrence. Since she was very learned and excellent in prose and verse, she is said, in imitation of Proba, wife of Adelphius, to have bent Homer’s poems back toward the Christian faith, likewise placing before the little work she published the following title: Homeric centos, 1 book. She also wrote certain other works. Since Saint Jerome, in a certain letter, declares that he had read Homeric centos and Virgilian centos, they must necessarily have been composed before his death. She flourished with her husband Theodosius, who took up the empire in the year of the Lord 423.

Primasius, an African bishop, as some will have it once a disciple of blessed Augustine, a man indeed learned in the holy scriptures, gloriously imbued with the disciplines of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, is said to have composed many little works, which among the ancients were held at a great price. Of these I have found only: Against heresies, to Bishop Fortunatus, 1 book. [unclear] In 74 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* On the Apocalypse of John, to Castorius, five books. But the book *Apocalyptica* which he composed has not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under the emperor Theodosius II, in the year of the Lord 440.

Vtilius, bishop of a certain city in Africa, though I have not been able to discover the name of the city, was certainly a man very learned in the sacred Scriptures and, in my judgment, sufficiently instructed in secular disciplines, profound in understanding, sweet and adorned in speech. He is said to have written many little works, but I have seen one notable work, which he wrote to the above-mentioned bishop Primasius, entitled:

*On the Parts of the Divine Law*, one book. “To the holy and most blessed bishop ...”

Of the rest I have seen none.

He flourished at the same time as Primasius, in the year of the Lord 440.

Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a distinguished theologian and computist: in the times of Leo Augustus, the successors of the heretic Dioscorus, after a sedition had been raised by Timothy, cruelly slew him on his journey, and set up that same Timothy in his place as an idol for the Alexandrian bishopric. He wrote, among other things, to Saint Leo the pope:

*On the Celebration of Easter*, three letters.

To Hilary, on the same matter, four letters. “Since your holiness ...”

Several letters to various persons. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

Paschasinus, Sicilian bishop, learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, reverend no less for his way of life than for his knowledge, is said to have presided in place of blessed Pope Leo the Great at the Council of Chalcedon, in which, together with the holy fathers to the number of two hundred, he condemned the heretics Eutyches and Dioscorus. Eutyches was a priest and abbot of a very celebrated monastery of Constantinople; he asserted that Christ the Lord was only God and not man, and wrote various things in support of his error, all of which were condemned together with their author. Paschasinus, however, wrote to Pope Leo:

*On the Question of Easter*, two letters. “The writings of your apostolate ...”

To the same, *On the Miracle of the Font*, one letter. “Not one day alone ...”

The acts of the Council of Chalcedon, [unclear] book[s]. “The rules of the saints ...”

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 450.

Leo, the first pope of that name, a Tuscan by nation, after Sixtus III sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and so celebrated and eloquent in declaiming homilies to the people that he had no superior in the Roman Church, as his most famous sermons will testify. He was the Cicero of ecclesiastical diction, the Homer of sacred theology, the Aristotle of the arguments of faith, the Peter of apostolic authority, the Paul in the Gallican pulpit. His sermons pierce the heart, clothe the soul, and confirm the catholic faith in sweet, brief speech. Nor is it any wonder: bearing the fire of divine love kindled in his breast, what else would he speak but burning words? He wrote many little works; of these I have found only the following, namely: Against Eutyches the priest, two books.

*On the Nicene Creed*, one book.

Testimonies to Leo Augustus, one book.

To the questions of Bishop Januarius, one book.

On the Passion of the Lord, twenty-four homilies, one book.

Many homilies to the people, one book.

To Bishop Flavian against Eutyches, one book.

To Leo Augustus against Eutyches, one book.

To Bishop Turibius against the Priscillianists, one book.

To Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, one book.

Many letters to various persons, one book.

Of the rest I have found nothing.

He died at last, after many labors for the benefit of the Church, under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 461, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

Peter, bishop of Ravenna, a learned and most holy man, shining in life with many miracles, was of excellent talent in declaiming homilies to the people, and by word as well as example converted many to the path of truth. He wrote many things for the edification of the faithful, among which are reported: Several sermons or homilies, one book.

Two copies of these sermons exist in the library of Eberbach.

To Eutyches the priest, one letter. “Sad, I read your sad letter ...”

He also wrote several other letters.

He flourished under Marcian Augustus, in the year of the Lord 450.

Pope Leo wrote many letters. He was indeed a learned man, an outstanding lover of catholic unity, who deposed and excommunicated Eutyches the priest and archimandrite, who held impious views concerning Christ’s humanity, as in a certain letter to the aforesaid Pa

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

...sent to Pope Leo testifies, he accomplished and endured many things for the extirpation of heresies. He wrote in the Greek language certain little works not to be despised; of these there are cited:

*Acts with Eutyches the Presbyter*, one book.
*Against the Errors of the Same*, one book.
*To Pope Leo on the Same Matter*, one letter. “No diabolical thing...”
*A Book of Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
And some other things which we do not know.
He flourished under Theodosius the Younger and Marcian, in the year of the Lord 454.

Hilarius the pope, a Sardinian by birth, after Leo the Great sat in the pontificate for six years and as many months. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and distinguished by the adornment of many virtues; constantly intent on alms and holy works, he shone with a great reputation for holiness [unclear]. At Rome, when a synod of fifty bishops had been held, he made a number of decrees for ecclesiastical propriety. He wrote certain necessary little works; of these I have found only:

*A Synodal Decree*, one book. “Since a religious [unclear]...”
*To the Bishops of the Province of Tarragona*, one letter. “After the letters of your...”
*To Ascanius, Bishop of Tarragona*, one letter. “Of divine grace toward us...”
*On the Council of Nicaea*, one letter.
*On the Council of Ephesus*, one letter.
*On the Council of Chalcedon*, one letter.
*A Book of Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
He died under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 468, in the sixth indiction, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March; Simplicius succeeded him.

Eusebius, bishop of Milan, very learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, both familiar and dear to the most blessed pontiff Leo, fighting and writing bravely for the holy Catholic faith against the heretics, is said to have published some little works for the edification of the faithful. Among the things he is said to have written in matters of faith is:

*To Saint Leo the Pope*, one letter. “Having returned [unclear]...”
He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

Asclepius the African, bishop of the territory of Vaga, a studious and learned man, an outstanding declaimer of homilies to the people, and a most vigorous assailant of heretics, wrote many volumes for the edification of the people. By their publication he was named glorious in every land, since he showed himself a useful teacher not only in words but also in works. For many most learned men made his age famous. Of his writings there are cited:

*Against the Donatists*, one book.
*Against the Arians*, one book.
*Countless Homilies to the People*, one book.
And many other things unknown to us.
He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 440.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

Prosper, bishop of Reggio after Faventius, an Aquitanian by birth, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, eloquent in speech, profound in sense, subtle in intellect, vigorous in assertion, and most holy in life and conduct. He was once notary of the blessed Pope Leo the Great, and composed many letters in his person. He also wrote from his own vein many splendid little works; of these I have found only the following: from the Sentences of the blessed bishop Augustine, in hexameter and pentameter verses, mixed with prose, a most beautiful work, which he wished to entitle:

*Epigrams*, one book. “When it pleases to direct the mind to sacred things...”
*On the Contemplative Life*, three books. “The contemplative life in...”
*On Free Will*, one book. “To the lord and most beloved brother Ru...”
*Responses to the Chapters of the Gauls*, one book. “The doctrine which the holy...”
*To the Objections of the Vincentians*, one book. “Certain Christian...”
*To the Extracts of the Genoese*, one book. “In the books of blessed memory...”
*A Great Sum of 350 Propositions*, one book. “True knowledge is that which...”
*Against Cassian on Free Will*, one book.
*A Chronicle of Histories*, one book.
*A Book of Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
*On Illustrious Men*, one book.
*On the Captivity of Rome*, one book.
He says that he wrote some other things besides, but they have not come into our hands.
He flourished in the times of the great emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460. His feast is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

Victor, bishop of Cartenna, a city of Mauretania, learned in the holy Scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, a notable persecutor of heretics, is said to have written many volumes, in which he both instructed the devout people and powerfully crushed those who erred concerning the faith. Of these the following are cited:

*Against the Arians*, one book.
*Against the Donatists*, one book.
*Consolatory Address to Basilius*, one book.
*On Penitence Also*, one book.
*Homilies to the People*, two books.
He published not a few other things as well, which have not come to my knowledge.
He flourished under Marcian Augustus, in the year of the Lord 450.

Vi-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

Victorinus, an Aquitanian by nation, a man very devoted to the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, is said to have left certain little works of his own genius, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge. At the command of Pope Hilarius he wrote, for finding the date of Easter, *The Great Cycle* of 532 years, in four books.

This is called the great cycle of 532 years; when these have run their course, all the computations of the heavenly bodies return to the same point. Dionysius the abbot afterwards corrected it, and down to this our own age it has endured, although in some matters it has failed. This Victorinus also wrote certain letters.

He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460, and wrote his cycle under Pope Hilarius, in the third year of his pontificate.

[unclear]

Peter, priest of the church of Edessa, learned and practiced in the holy Scriptures, endowed with an outstanding power and talent for declaiming homilies to the people, so that in his own times he had no equal, wrote in the Syriac language many very distinguished volumes, of which only very few have come to my knowledge: Commentaries on the Psalms, four books.

He also played in meter on the Psalms, five books.

He dictated, and delivered, almost countless homilies to the people, which are found among us rarely. But neither is the number of his treatises certain to us.

He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 300.

S[unclear], learned in [unclear] and sufficiently trained in secular letters, subtle and keen in intellect, often fought against the force of heretics, both by writing and by disputing. Hence, at the request of a certain Secunda, a virgin dedicated to Christ, he wrote a distinguished and memorable volume: Against Marcion and Valentinus, one book.

Against Eunomius and Aetius, six books.

He published some other things as well, but they have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, around the year of the Lord 440.

V[unclear]rsinus, a monk, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of humane letters, subtle in intellect and cautious in speech, is said to have composed many treatises for the benefit of the faithful, but I do not remember that any of them has ever come into our hands. There is, however, circulated a distinguished work of his against those who rebaptize persons once duly baptized, whose title is:

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

On not rebaptizing heretics, one book.
He flourished, as I have found, under Theodosius the Younger, in the year of the Lord 490.

Julianus, bishop of the church of Toledo in Spain, a Moor by nation, to whom Saint Prosper is said to have written three books On Contemplation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular studies, scholastic in speech, clear in understanding, wrote many notable volumes, of which the following are reported: On holy virginity, one book. On the nature of the soul, [8] books.
On the resolution of questions, one book. On contempt of the world, one book.
Prognosticon of the future age, three books. The faith of the nascent Church [unclear].
Letters to various persons, one book.
On vices and virtues, two books. Letters to various women, one book.

He is said to have composed some other works as well, which have not come to my knowledge.
He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

Victorianus Buconius, bishop of the city of Castelliana in Mauretania, a man trained by constant study in the divine writings and by no means moderately learned in the disciplines of secular letters, a most powerful hammer of heretics and an outstanding teacher of the faithful peoples, is said to have written many little works in defense of the Catholic faith, of which the principal ones are reported as follows: Against the Jews, one book. Against the Arians, one book.
Against all heretics, two books. On the sacraments also, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 460.

Museus, priest of the church of Marseille, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and polished by very subtle exercise in their meanings, scholastic and elegant in language, at the urging of Saint Venerius the bishop excerpted from the holy Scriptures lessons and responsories suited to the several festive days of the whole year, and arranged psalms suitable for singing in the church at the several times. He also wrote to Bishop Eustasius an excellent work: On the sacraments, seven books. Several homilies to the people.
And certain other things.

He flourished under the rulers Marcian and Leo, in the year of the Lord 440.

Vincentius, a priest, a Gaul by nation, much practiced in the divine writings, having a tongue polished by practice in speaking and by greater reading, and not ignorant of secular letters either, wrote, as our Gennadius reports, an excellent work, to be very greatly embraced by devout men: Commentaries on the Psalms, one book.
And certain other things.
He flourished under the emperor Marcian, in the year of the Lord 450.

*80 On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Cyrus, Alexandrian by birth, a physician by art, having from a philosopher become a monk for the love of Christ, a man very learned in secular letters, remarkable in skill of speaking, in his writings using syllogisms more than the authorities of the divine readings: while he inveighs too much against Nestorius, he is alleged to support the Timothean doctrine, and being uncertain of himself, he suspends his mind from agreement with the Council of Chalcedon, nor does he think one should assent that the Son of God after the incarnation is confessed in two natures. Of his writings, however, the following is reported: Against [unclear], one book. Against heretics, one book.

He flourished under Leo Augustus, in the year of the Lord 460.

Salvianus, priest of the church of Marseille, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, teacher of the bishops of his time, wrote in scholastic and clear speech many varied little works, of which the following are reported. To Claudius, bishop of Vienne, he wrote several letters, seasoned with the salt of wisdom. To Marcellus the priest: On the good of virginity, three books. Against avarice, four books.
To Claudius, bishop of Vienne, one book.
On the beginning of Genesis, the Hexameron, one book.
On the final part of Ecclesiastes, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.
Homilies made to bishops, one book. On the sacraments also, one book.

He also published many other works, which have by no means come to my knowledge.
He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

Samuel, priest of the church of Edessa, learned in the divine Scriptures by constant exercise, an outstanding declaimer of homilies to the people, skilled in the Greek and Syriac language, first flourished at Edessa; later, coming to Constantinople, and there held in high esteem, he closed his final day. He wrote, both in Greek and in Syriac, almost countless little works, of which very few have come to my knowledge. For I found only: Against the Nestorians, one book. Against the Eutychians, one book.

He flourished under Zeno Augustus, in the year of the Lord 480.

Gennadius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek language

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

some little works on the sacred volumes, but they have by no means come into our hands. For he was an outstanding preacher of homilies, and no less distinguished in life than in knowledge of the Scriptures. Among other things, a work of his commentaries is said to have been prepared: On Daniel the Prophet, one book; many homilies to the people, one book. He died under Emperor Leo I, who ruled in the year of the Lord 460.

Claudius (others call him Claudianus), bishop of Vienne, to whom Salvianus the presbyter composed one book, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly trained in secular letters, famous no less for holiness than for learning, shone in his times. Because of frequent earthquakes he was the first to institute litanies, which the Roman Church thereafter undertook to continue. He wrote On the State of the Soul, three books; also letters, and certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480. And lest the name Claudius trouble anyone, [unclear], let him know that the same man is called Mamertus.

Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, in the opinion of all men of his time most erudite, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote many distinguished little works both in meter and in prose. Of these I have been able to find only those which I set down below, namely: Panegyric to Anthemius Augustus, one book: ‘With auspice and number’; Panegyric to Julius Valerius, one book: ‘Conceive the former things, Phoebus, having traversed [unclear]’; Panegyric to his father-in-law, one book: ‘Speak, speak what I ask, [unclear]’; To Felix, one book: ‘Among the dark-blue [unclear]’; Epithalamium for Ruricius and Hiberia, one book: ‘By chance, stormy [unclear]’; Epithalamium for Polemius, one book: ‘Phoebus and the thrice three’; Eucharisticon to Faustus, one book: ‘Four days before’; also Epigrams, one book: ‘The stable of the Bistonian king’; To Pontius Leontius Burg[unclear], one book: ‘Hail, mighty Narbo’; Praise of the city of Narbonne, one book: ‘Long do you command, lord [unclear]’; Letters to various persons, nine books.

He also wrote many other works, short indeed, but sufficiently learned, whose titles I have passed over for love of brevity. He flourished in the times of Zeno Augustus, in the year of the Lord 480.

Pope Simplicius, a Tiburtine by nation, after St. Hilarius presided over the Roman and universal Church for fifteen years. He was a learned and holy man, who appeared not only simple according to his name, but also upright, departing from evil and fearing God; many churches 82 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he restored what had collapsed from excessive age, issued statutes necessary for the Christian commonwealth, and wrote some works for the edification of the faithful, of which I have read only: To John, bishop of Ravenna, one letter. “If anyone, being intent upon the church…”
To Florentius and Egistius, bishops, one letter. “Your report [unclear]…”
To Severus, bishop, one letter.

But he also wrote many other very useful letters, which I have not yet seen. He died under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 485, in the sixth indiction, on 6 Nones of March, and was enrolled among the saints.

*Servus Dei*, bishop of a certain church, whose city’s name I have not been able to find, a man learned through continual exercise in the divine Scriptures and rich in reading the ancients, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, is said to have fashioned some little works. Of these there survives a volume furnished with sacred Scriptures, against those who say that Christ, while living in this life, did not see the Father with his bodily eyes. The title of this work is: That the Son Saw the Father, one book.

In this work he shows that the Son of God, even from the hour of his conception in the womb of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, always saw God the Father with his bodily eyes, and thereafter, and now, clothed in human flesh.

He also wrote certain other things.

He is said to have flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 480.

*Victor*, bishop of Capua, learned in the holy Scriptures and sufficiently trained in secular letters, an excellent theologian and computist, sharp in intellect and renowned for eloquence; but very few of his works have come to my knowledge. He refuted the error of Victor of Aquitaine, who, at the order of Pope Hilary, while writing paschal cycles, taught that Easter was to be celebrated on 15 Kalends of May in the year of the Lord 455, although it should more correctly have been celebrated in that year on 7 Kalends of May. Therefore, when this occasion arose, he wrote: On Easter, one book. One Gospel from the Four, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

*Cerealis*, an African bishop, a man very skilled in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, was asked by Maximinus, bishop of the Arians, whether he could establish, with a few testimonies of divine Scripture and without, at least, the assertion of disputation, the consubstantiality of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. He replied not with a few, as the other had mockingly asked, but with many testimonies of both Testaments, composing a distinguished work: Against the Arians, four books.

He also wrote other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

*John*, priest of the church of Antioch, rich in reading the ancients in the holy Scriptures, after he had taught grammar at Antioch for some years, began to wish to profess himself a cleric. Made a priest by legitimate succession, he devoted himself to the divine readings; made more learned by these, he became so powerful in delivering homilies that he had no equal in his time. He wrote a sufficiently well-instructed volume: Against the Timotheans, one book. Several Homilies to the People, one book.

And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

*Theodolus*, priest, Italian by birth, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, coming from Italy into Coele-Syria, is recorded as having been ordained there as priest and finally as bishop; and by writing and composing many things he transmitted his name to posterity. Of his little works I have found only a metrical work on the miracles of the Old Testament and the fables of the poets, to which he gave the title: Eclogues, one book. “The lands of the Ethiopians…”
On the Harmony of the Scriptures, one book.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 480, under the emperor Zeno, under whom he also died.

*Eugenius*, bishop of Carthage in Africa, a learned and holy man, a public confessor of the undivided Trinity, suffered many injuries at the hands of the Arians while they were persecuting the Christians in Africa. For with many other bishops, their tongues cut out, he was sent into exile. He wrote some little works full of faith and learning, of which the following are reported: Exposition of the Catholic Faith, one book. Apology for the Faith, one book.
Disputation Held with the Arians, one book.
To His Church, when he was going into exile, one letter.

He is nevertheless said to have written other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of the emperor Zeno, in the year of the Lord 480.

*Felix*, the third pope, Roman by birth, after the holy pontiff Simplicius sat in the chair of Peter for eight years, a good, learned, and holy man, who, inflamed with zeal for the faith, Peter and Acacius 84 *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He condemned the Eutychian bishops, banishing them into exile. For this reason, holding a synod at Rome, he established many things for the benefit of the Church, and wrote: A synodal decree, one book. *To Flavius Boethius* [unclear].
Several decretal letters, one book.

He died under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 495, indiction 1.

*Gennadius*, priest of the church of Marseille, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, fully trained in both Greek and Latin eloquence, wrote many little works, and translated not a few volumes of the ancient fathers from Greek into Latin speech. Of his own writings he himself, at the end of *Illustrious Men*, listed the following: On his faith, to Pope Gelasius, one book.
Against Nestorius, six books.
Against Eutyches, nine books.
Against Pelagius, three books.
Against all heresies, eight books.
On illustrious men, one book. *James, surnamed* [unclear].
On the heresy of the thousand years, one book.

He wrote these and certain other works which have not yet come to me. He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 490.

*Gelasius*, the first pope of that name, an African by birth, sat after Felix in the pontificate for four [unclear], a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures. As soon as he entered upon the pontifical office, he sent into exile the Manichaeans whom he found in the city, and publicly burned their books at the basilica of Saint Mary Major. He established many things for the benefit of the Church, and wrote very many works against heretics. Of his little works the following are reported: A synodal decree, one book. *The necessity of things* [unclear].
Against the Arians, two books.
Hymns in the manner of Ambrose, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.
Several weighty prayers.

And certain other things. He arranged Graduals, Alleluias, and Tracts, with prefaces appropriate for the Mass, and separated the authentic books of the holy fathers from the apocryphal, as is found in distinction 15, *Sancta Romana*.

He died while Anastasius Augustus was emperor, in the year of the Lord 426.

*Faustus*, formerly abbot of the monastery of Lerins, bishop of Riez in Gaul, was indeed a learned and eloquent man, but stained by the Pelagian error; hence also his little works are counted among the apocrypha, just as

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

as is clear in distinction 15, *Sancta Romana*. At length, corrected and amended by blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, he abandoned his error and returned to the truth of the catholic faith. As proof of this, he published an excellent volume against his former errors, which he entitled *On the Grace of God*. Of his little works there are reported: The same volume, *On the Grace of God*, 1 book.
*Against the Arians*, 1 book.
*Against the Anthropomorphites*, 1 book.
*On the Holy Spirit*, 1 book. “The catholic faith in one...”
*To Gratus the Deacon, Against Nesto[rius]*, 1 book.
*To Felix the Prefect*, 1 book.
Several homilies to the people.

He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 490.

Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, deep in understanding, sweet, eloquent, and polished in speech, ready in teaching, sharp in argument, fit and very gentle in persuasion, shone out most brightly no less for the holiness of his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which the following are reported:

*On the Grace of God and Free Will*, 7 books.
*On the Holy Trinity*, 1 book.
*On the Truth of Predestination*, 2 books.
*On the Remission of Sins*, 2 books.
*Disputation with King Thrasamund*, 1 book.
*Rule of the True Life*, 1 book.
*On Predestination, to Monimus*, 3 books. “Your letters, dearest son...”
*To Ferrandus the Deacon*, 1 book. “Your letter, holy brother and [unclear]...”
*On Conjugal Continence*, 1 book. “Your letter, holy [unclear]...”
*On Virginity, to Proba*, 1 book. “With spiritual desire and...”
*On Prayer, to the Same*, 1 book. “The Lord in Christ [unclear]...”
*On Charity, to Eugippius the Abbot*, 1 book. “Would that, holy brother, such...”
*On the Sacrament of the Incarnation*, 1 book. “As the true light in no way...”
Of many sermons, 1 book.
“Adam without a, Abel without b,” etc., 1 book.
Of various questions, 1 book. “Although an ineffectual [unclear]...”
*Mythologies, to Catus the Presbyter*, 3 books. “Lest concerning your commands...”
*On Obscure Discourses*, 1 book. “Vir-”

86 *On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

*On the Moralized Meaning of Virgil*, one book. Incipit: “Indeed he was seeking [unclear].” *On the Immensity of the Son of God*, one book. *On the Passion of the Lord*, one book.

He is said also to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. For he was trained in both Greek and Latin speech. It should be noted that the title of the book *On Adam without a* is *The Book without Letters*, namely *On Adam without a*, *On Abel without b*, *On Cain without c*, and so with the rest according to the sequence of the letters. But in the book whose title is *Exposition of the Virgilian Content, according to the Moral Philosophers*, with marvelous industry he sought, and found, gold in the mud, so to speak, while he inclined the work of the poet toward physical reasoning. He wrote this work to a certain deacon. Another work, the *Mythologies*, he wrote to Catus, a priest of Carthage, and *On the Obscure Expressions of the Ancients* to Chalcidius the grammarian, already an old man, when he himself was still young and a teacher and rector in the school of humane letters. He flourished in the times of Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, persecutor of the Catholic churches, under Emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Ferrandus, deacon of the church of Carthage, to whom some little works of the above-mentioned Saint Fulgentius are extant, a man both devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and no less venerable for holiness of conduct than for doctrine, is said to have composed certain volumes of lively talent. Of these, only the following have come to my knowledge: To Count Reginus:

*On the Seven Rules of Innocence*, one book. Incipit: “For the labor of social life.” This book is extant among the [Ebirbacenses?].

To Saint Fulgentius, one letter. *Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He flourished with Fulgentius under Emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Anastasius II, pope, a Roman by birth, sat after the pontiff Saint Gelasius for one year and ten months. He was indeed an erudite man, but, seduced by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, not long afterward paid the due penalties for his error. For when he wished to obey the necessity of nature, struck by God, the wretched man poured out his intestines with his feces, as is clear in Distinction 19, *Anastasius*. And this was the second infamous pope. He wrote to Emperor Anastasius:

*On the Peace of the Church*, one letter. Incipit: “The beginning of the pontificate.”

He is said to have written other letters too, but they have not come into our hands. He died, struck by divine judgment, when he had secretly wished to recall from exile Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, condemned and cast out by the Church, under Anastasius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 498.

Ana-

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

The decretals of Pope [Anastasius?], and one letter, which is found in the second volume of the works of Saint Jerome.

Paschasius, deacon of the Roman church, a learned and holy man, father of the poor, wholly intent on the distribution of alms, was of such virtue and holiness that Pope Gregory writes, in the fourth book of the Dialogues, that after his death a demoniac was cured by the touch of his dalmatic. Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, saw his soul in the pains of purgatory, tormented for no other reason than that, in the election of Pope Symmachus, he had preferred Laurentius, and had persisted in this opinion, though peacefully, until death. He wrote, as Gregory attests, a notable volume against the errors of the Greeks: On the Holy Spirit, 3 books. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Symmachus, pope, a Sardinian by birth, a learned and holy man, obtained the pontificate after Anastasius, not without discord among the factions of Laurentius, and held it for fifteen years and six months. A man merciful and generous toward the poor, he loved the clergy, enriched the churches, and drove heretics out of the city. After holding a synod at Rome of one hundred and twenty bishops, he canonically cleared himself of the charges brought against him, and drove Peter, bishop of Ravenna, with his accomplices into exile. He wrote certain letters, works not to be despised, of which I have found: Decree of the first synod, 1 book. It begins: “Because frequent...”

Decree of the Roman synod, 1 book. It begins: “When in one place at blessed...”

Acts of another Roman synod, 1 book. It begins: “The fourth synod held...”

On the transgressions of clerics, 1 book. It begins: “Indeed well, brotherly...”

Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He died under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 515, in the eighth indiction, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August; Pope Hormisdas succeeded him.

Symmachus the patrician, senator and Roman consul, father-in-law of Boethius, a distinguished philosopher and rhetorician, and a magnificent worshipper of the Christian faith, was banished into exile at Pavia together with Boethius by Theoderic, king of Italy, on suspicion of having aimed at liberty; and not long afterward he had him cruelly slain. Since he was a learned and most eloquent man, he composed several works, of which I have been able to find only a certain short but elegant volume: Letters to various persons, 1 book. It begins: “Surely you laugh because...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He died in the reign of Anastasius, killed by Theoderic, king of Italy, at Ravenna, in the year of the Lord 524, in the eleventh indiction.

Aui-

*[page] 83. ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.*

Avitus, bishop of Vienne, a man erudite in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a theologian, rhetorician, and most renowned poet, who in his time was held in esteem no less for the sanctity of [his] life than for the erudition of the Scriptures, wrote, both in verse and in loose prose, not a few little works; but very few have come to my knowledge. Of these, the following, composed in heroic and elegant meter, are reported:
On the origin of the world: 1 book. On original sin: 1 book.
On the sentence of God: 1 book. On the flood of the world: 1 book.
On the passage of the Red Sea: 1 book.
On virginity, to his sister Fuscina: 1 book.
Of letters to various [persons]: 9 books. Of many homilies: 1 book.
And many others.
He flourished under the princes Zeno and Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 500.

Godelbert, presbyter, learned by continual exercise in the divine Scriptures and rich in old reading, and moreover most erudite in secular letters, a profound theologian, renowned orator, and distinguished poet, subtle in talent and adorned in eloquence, wrote in heroic meter a most renowned work, running most elegantly through histories and allegories from the beginning of the world up to the childbirth of the Virgin; the title of which work is:
Allegories of the Scriptures: 1 book.
But he wrote also several others.
He flourished, as they report, in the times of Anastasius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 500.

Eugypius, presbyter and abbot, erudite in the holy Scriptures, and singularly devoted to the reading of the books of Saint Augustine, and sufficiently instructed in the letters of the secular arts, illustrious also in life and in the conversation of monastic institution—to whom several letters of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe are reported [addressed]—wrote certain necessary little works, of which I have found only the following. He culled a great volume, having three hundred chapters, from the books of blessed Augustine the bishop, [dedicated] to Proba; which begins thus:
The Prologue (letter 1): "To the lady deservedly venerable…"
But the book thus (book 1): "What I wrote to you…"
The Life of Saint Severinus the monk: 1 book.
He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, according to Honorius the presbyter; but according to Sigebert, he flourished then under Tiberius Constantine, in the times of Pope Pelagius II, in the year of the Lord 580.

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

Benedict, the first abbot and founder of Monte Cassino, by country a man of Nursia, the foremost founder of the monks of the West, a man of most holy conduct, illuminated with a prophetic spirit, from whose order many very learned and most holy men thereafter shone forth, converted countless peoples from iniquity to Christ by word and example. From his order the Roman see has had eighteen pontiffs, more than two hundred cardinals, sixteen hundred archbishops in various churches, and almost four thousand bishops. Distinguished abbots who were famous for learning, writings, or life: fifteen thousand seven hundred. Those canonized or entered in the catalogue of saints, as we learn from ancient records: fifteen thousand six hundred, apart from those whose names in all these categories have not come down to us. And concerning these illustrious men of our order we have already written four special books, in which we have recorded the names of some, if not of all.

Saint Benedict wrote, in a clear style and with excellent discretion:

*The Rule of Monks*, 1 book.

It has seventy-three chapters.

Under this rule twenty orders serve, which we have set out one by one in the first book *On the Illustrious Men of Our Order*, of which some are rare among us. He flourished under Justin the Elder, in the year of the Lord 530. And he died, as some hold, in the year of the Lord 542, in the fifth indiction, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, when he was sixty-two years old, on the Saturday of Holy Easter. But Marianus Scotus, an excellent computist, writes otherwise, speaking thus: If the holy father Benedict the abbot, as some write, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, on the Saturday of Holy Easter, he is seen to have died in the year of the Lord 601. For unless [unclear] in the ninety-sixth year before that year, his death has no [unclear]; for if he was born then, he was very small.
