Therefore Saint Father Benedict died, according to this reckoning of Marianus, in the last year of the emperor Maurice, namely in the year of the Lord 601, at about the ninetieth year of his age, in the fourth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

Boethius, an orator and distinguished poet, learned in the divine Scriptures, in secular letters the most learned of all in his time, was the son-in-law of the patrician Symmachus; a man most abundantly imbued with Greek and Latin eloquence, since he translated many volumes, both of Aristotle and of other philosophers, from the Attic tongue into Latin; subtle in talent, ready in understanding, and Catholic, in speech not inferior even to Tully. It is certain that he had the friendship of Saint Benedict, and that on Monte Cassino he ate at his table with Tertullus, the senator father of the monk Placidus. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which I have found the following. To Symmachus, his father-in-law, patrician of the city of Rome:

*On the Holy Trinity*, 1 book. *Long investigated*.

1 book. *I ask whether the Father, Son*.

*Indeed anxiously and long*.

*I have known the Christian faith*.

*Unity is that by which one*.

*In the winter season of this year*.

*This second [unclear]*.

*When these matters have been dispatched, which belong to*.

*The great things indeed of the book*.

*Alexander in the commentaries*.

*How great things for the studious*.

*Of speaking and disputing*.

1 book. *Many ancient philosophers*.

*At your exhortation, father*.

*Every method of making distinctions*.

*Many ancient Greeks*.

*When all the philosophers*.

*You ask that from the hebdomads*.

*Among all the authors of antiquity*.

*Indeed the perception of all*.

*Songs which certain*.

*But since, my patrician*.

*Your [unclear] knows the intention*.

*On the Predication of Power*, 2 books.

*Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book.

Besides these, the common Latin translation into two books of Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics* is believed to be by Boethius.

He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He died in the same year as the patrician Symmachus and Pope John, under the emperor Anastasius, by order of King Theoderic at Ravenna, after a long exile, slain in prison, in the year of the Lord 524, in the second indiction. And under the name of Severinus he is said to have been entered in the catalogue of saints. Hor-

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

*Pope Hormisdas, a Campanian by birth, after Symmachus presided over the Church as pontiff for nine years, a good, learned, and vigorous man. When a synod had been assembled at Rome, he condemned the Eutychian heresy; and the Manichaeans, springing up again, he banished into exile after their books had been burned. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote:*

*A synodal decree, one book.*

*To the Emperor Justin, letter 1.* Among those things which pertain to unity

*To the clerics of Second Syria, letter 2.* Having read the letters of your affection

*Several letters to various persons, two books.*

He died under the elder Emperor Justin, in the year of the Lord 521, in the fourteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of August; John succeeded him.

*And certain other things.*

*On the Catholic Faith, one book.*

*Evodius, bishop of Ticinum, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of singular eloquence both in Greek and in Latin, was sent by Pope Hormisdas to Constantinople in matters of the faith to the heretical emperor Anastasius. After receiving many wrongs, he was driven from the city together with his companions, Anastasius saying: “Why do you deliver mandates to us, when we are under no one’s rule? The Roman pontiff ought to obey us, not also to command.” Evodius wrote to Pope Symmachus.*

*He flourished under the emperor Anastasius, in the year of the Lord 510.*

*And certain other things.*

*Jordanes, from a monk bishop of the Goths, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and suitably learned in secular letters, gentle in disposition and clear in speech, an investigator of times and an unworthy writer of deeds done, is said to have composed certain distinguished volumes, of which very few have come to my knowledge. For I have found only:*

*[unclear]*

*In the first of these he reviewed the deeds of the Romans, but in the second the origin and deeds of the Goths, down to the end of their kingdom.*

He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 530.

*Faustus, a monk and disciple of our most holy father Benedict, an Italian by nationality, a man venerable in [unclear] and morals, when he was seven years old was offered by his parents to the divine father Benedict. By him, at length, after the perfect instruction of the regular profession, he was sent with blessed Maurus into Gaul to build a monastery; there, having lived among many in great holiness, after Saint Maurus had died he returned to Monte Cassino. At the request of the brothers, however, he wrote in a very clear [unclear]*

*92 On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear] in eloquence, to Boniface, the second pontiff of the city of Rome,

The Life of Saint Maurus the Abbot, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Justinian the Great, emperor, nephew through his sister of the elder Justin, who reigned afterward for 38 years, a man of great and excellent talent, deservedly gained a place among the ecclesiastical writers. He both published a most distinguished volume against the heretics and, through the hands of John the patrician and the consuls Theophilus and Dorotheus, with marvelous brevity corrected the Roman laws, which lay in more than two thousand books. For, reducing to twelve books all the constitutions of the emperors that were contained in many volumes, he called it the Code. Again, reducing the laws of the individual magistrates and judges, which had extended to nearly two thousand books, as we have said, to the number of fifty books in three volumes: The Code of the Digests, or Pandects, 50 books.

The Institutes, 4 books. “The imperial majesty...”

Epitome of the Laws, one book. “O...”

On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Eutyches, 3 books.

Against the African Bishops, one book. “These things which necessarily...”

Who would doubt that he also wrote other works, especially many elegant letters, which have not come into our hands? At last, in his old age, having become mad and foolish, he died in the year of the Lord 565, in the thirteenth indiction. Justin the Younger succeeded him.

Dionysius, a Roman abbot, surnamed, as is said, Exiguus, a man certainly great and very renowned in talent and knowledge, learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly instructed in the discipline of secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, an outstanding computist and calculator of times, wrote some little works in the Latin tongue. Of these I have found only the following: The Great Paschal Cycle of 532 Years, one book. “O...”

On the Reckoning of the Paschal Feast, one book. “The reckoning of the Paschal feast...”

I have found nothing about the rest. He translated from Greek into Latin the life of Saint Pachomius the abbot, also the book of Gregory of Emesa on the condition of man, the writings of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo, and certain other things. He began his cycle in the year of the Lord 532, which was the last year of the great paschal cycle; once completed, it always returns to the same point.

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

He therefore flourished under Justinian the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 540.

Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, sufficiently learned in the holy Scriptures, is said to have written some volumes for the edification of readers. Of these there has come down to us only a great and excellent work, composed in an elegant style and furnished with great authorities of the ancients: In Defense of the Three Chapters, 12 books.

He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Justinian, bishop of Valencia, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of human letters, had from one mother three brothers who were bishops, namely Justus, Nebridius, and Elpidius, learned and erudite men who wrote various little works, which nevertheless have by no means come into our hands. He himself, among other things, composed for a certain man named Rusticus: On Five Questions, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in Spain under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Justus, bishop of the church of Urgell, brother of the aforesaid bishop Justinian, himself also a man practiced and learned in the holy Scriptures, of excellent talent in expounding the divine and canonical volumes, wrote a sufficiently elegant and commendable volume in a scholastic style: On the Song of Songs, one book. And many other things.

He flourished with his brother under the emperor Justin, in the year of the Lord 530.

Apringius, bishop of the church of Pax in Spain, learned in the divine Scriptures and most erudite in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, expounded the sacred Scriptures so gloriously and profoundly that, in comparison with him, the ancient writers seemed not to have expounded them. Of his little works there exists a notable volume, with subtle meaning and illustrious style: On the Apocalypse of John, one book.

On the Song of Songs, one book.

He also published many other works, which have not come into our hands.

He flourished in the times of Theodotus, king of the Goths, under Justinian the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 530. Cassio-

94 *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

Cassiodorus, monk and abbot of a monastery near the city of Ravenna, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, easily the most erudite of all in his time, shone forth most illustriously no less in holiness than in knowledge. He was first chancellor of Theoderic, king of Italy, and a senator of Ravenna, and later consul of the city of Rome; afterward, despising the vain honors of the world for the love of God, he became a monk. From then on, applying the study of humane letters to the exposition of the holy Scriptures, he composed many very elegant treatises. Of his works the following are reported: In the person both of himself and of King Theoderic, he wrote Letters to Various Persons, 28 books.

[unclear]

On the Nature of the Soul, 1 book. “When now the undertaking [unclear]” 1 book.

On the Whole Psalter, 1 book. “Blessed is the man,” etc. “Exceedingly” An Introduction to Divine Readings, 2 books. “When the pursuits of secular studies” On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “Solomon, inspired” An Introduction to Secular Letters, 9 books. “Our purpose is” He compiled the Tripartite History, 12 books. “Very usefully at the beginning” A Catalogue of the Roman Consuls, 1 book.

On Etymologies, 1 book.

The Priest Previously Noted, 1 book.

On Figures and Tropes, 1 book.

A Memorial of the Scriptures, 1 book.

On Orthography, 1 book.

A Summary on the Apocalypse, 1 book.

On the Canonical Epistles, 7 books.

[unclear]

He also composed many other works which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the times of Justin the Elder down almost to the end of the reign of Justin the Younger, being more than 58 years of age, in the year of the Lord 575.

Arator, subdeacon of the sacrosanct Roman Church, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in the letters of secular disciplines, powerful in verse and prose, subtle in intellect, clear and polished in speech, wrote a very notable volume, composed in meter, to a certain abbot Florianus: On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. “That Judea of its crime” To Abbot Florianus, 1 epistle. “They who flourish in merits” To Pope Vigilius, 1 epistle. “With wave-beaten walls” And certain other things which I have not seen.

This Arator, a very illustrious poet and notable theologian, offered to Pope Vigilius, before the confession of Saint Peter on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the presence of many bishops and learned men, the codex on the Acts of the Apostles which he had composed in elegant meter; and, at the pontiff’s command, [unclear] in great part

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

He recited it publicly before everyone. As the hour was passing, Pope Vigilius handed the volume to the venerable Surgentius, the primicerius, to be placed in the archive, so that he might read it through at a time of leisure. All the learned men earnestly begged His Holiness to order the book to be read before them in its entirety. When he had ordered this to be done in the church of Saint Peter in Chains, a great crowd of religious men and noble laymen assembled; and, as Arator himself recited in clear words, both books were heard four times, since on one day only half a book was read, because of the continual repetitions which the listeners requested with manifold favor. Where now, in these times, is such zeal for letters? Where is love of saving knowledge? Our religious and nobles, clerics also and pontiffs, heap up not books but revenues; not letters, but avarice do they cultivate. Now Antimachus reads many poems, and, as individuals withdraw, scarcely a single Plato is found and remains. But of these matters we are now speaking out of season. Arator flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Victor, bishop of the Cummenian church in Africa, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, was banished into exile in Egypt by the emperor Justinian and Eutychius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, for his defense of the Three Chapters. Summoned back again from there to Constantinople, when he resisted the emperor and the bishop, detractors of the same Chapters, he was sent to be guarded in a monastery of the same city; and, remaining under the same condemnation, as they say, he died. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote, from the beginning of the world down to the first year of Justin the Younger, a very useful history concerning deeds and ecclesiastical wars: *History*, one book. *For the Defense of the Three Chapters*, and certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord 540.

Gregory, the first pope from the monks of the order of Saint Benedict, a Roman by nation, sat after Pope Pelagius in the chair of Peter for thirteen years and six months. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and indeed most highly instructed in secular letters, prince of theologians, splendor of philosophers, and light of rhetoricians, whole and most holy in life and conduct. When he was explaining the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit several times appeared to him in visible form, and in visible teaching revealed to him the secrets of their mysteries. He, at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, held a synod of twenty-four bishops,

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

he established many things for the benefit of the Church, and promulgated the decree concerning the immunity of monasteries. He wrote, moreover, several necessary volumes, of which the following are reported: To Leander, bishop of Seville:

*Moralia* on the Book of Job, 35 books. “Among many often...”

On Pastoral Care, 2 books. “Pastoral care me...”

Dialogues on the miracles of the saints, 4 books. “One day, when too much...”

On the Song of Songs, 4 books. “After from paradise...”

On the prophet Ezekiel, 2 books. “Of almighty God...”

Brief homilies on the Gospels, 2 books. “The Lord and our Redeemer...”

A brief explanation of the four Gospels, 4 books. “Matthew, as in order...”

On the seven penitential psalms, 1 book. “If enticed...”

Letters to various persons, 10 books. “Gregory, bishop, servant...” or “Very necessary...”

Rationale of Divine Offices, 1 book.

Preface to the New and Old Testament, 1 book.

On the Sacraments, 1 book.

There is extant among the Eberbach books a brief and learned disputation of Gregory against the Arians, which begins: “For love of the Catholic faith.”

When he was still a levite, in the person of Pope Pelagius he composed a very distinguished letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, who refused to accept the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon; this letter is not found among his letters. It is reported also that he composed many other works, namely on the prophets, on the Books of Kings, also on the books of Moses, and on other holy scriptures. After his death, before these had yet been multiplied, his most wicked rivals, envying his glory and sanctity, burned them with fire, as John the Deacon complains in the book of his life. The most blessed Pope Gregory died in the second year of the emperor Phocas, which was the year of the Lord 605, in the eighth indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, shining with many miracles.

Leander, bishop of Seville, formerly a monk, by country from the province of Carthagena in Spain, born of his father Severianus, was a man most devoted to study and nobly learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, pleasing in speech, most excellent in talent, and also holy in life and conduct and beloved of God. By his preaching and industry Hermenegild, son of Leuvigild, the Arian king of the Goths, was brought back to the confession of the orthodox faith and, on the vigil of Easter, was killed by his heretical father and received the crown of martyrdom. His brother [Richardus?], as soon as he received the kingdom after his father’s death, at Leander’s urging and preaching renounced heresy and converted the whole people of the Visigoths subject to him to the Catholic faith. To this Leander blessed Gregory dedicated the volumes of his commentaries on Job. Leander himself wrote several little works, of which the following are reported. When, on account of the Catholic faith, he had been banished into exile by the Arians, he wrote: Against Heretics, 2 books.

Against the institutions of the Arians, 1 book.

On Virginity, to Florentina, 1 book.

Prayers in a double edition on the Psalms, 1 book.

On Contempt of Death, to his brother, 1 book.

On the praise of sacrifices, 1 book.

Letters to various persons, 1 book.

But he published some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the year of the Lord 590, under the emperor Maurice. He died under [Richardus?], the most devout prince of the Goths, renowned for miracles.

Priscian the grammarian, by country from Caesarea, a man most learned in secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, held in great esteem at the court of Chosroes, king of the Persians, wrote certain distinguished volumes in the grammatical art, which among the ancients were held in great authority. Of these the following are reported. To Julian the patrician: On the Parts of Speech, 2 books.

On Construction, 1 book.

On Accents, 1 book.

On Cosmography, 1 book.

On Natural Questions, to Chosroes, 1 book.

He is said to have written some other works also, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished, as some hold, in the times of Chosroes, king of the Persians, and of the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 610.

Marcus, a monk, disciple of the holy father Benedict and very dearly beloved by him, a man learned in the divine scriptures, most pious in secular letters, a distinguished orator and poet, eminent in morals and conduct, wrote after blessed Pope Gregory, adding certain things in a most elegant flowing heroic verse: The Life of Saint Benedict, 1 book. And certain other things.

He was illustrious down to the reign of the emperor Heraclius Augustus, in the year of the Lord 610.

Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, an Italian by nation, a man [unclear], subtle in talent, polished and eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, shone forth among all the teachers of his age no less clearly for the holiness of his conduct than for the knowledge of his learning. He, by the power of Saint Mar-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

...freed by [Martin?] from pain in his eyes, he came to Tours to his tomb to give thanks; and, proceeding to Poitiers, he was ordained there first priest and then bishop, and was distinguished for great learning and religion. He also wrote many useful and devout little works in elegant verse, of which I have seen only the following: To Saint Radegund, daughter of the last king of the Thuringians, captive of the king of the Franks, later abbess of the monastery of Poitiers, in hexameter verse: *The Destruction of the Kingdom of the Thuringians*, one book.

*To [Iuininius?] on Radegund*, one book.

*To Justin the Younger*, one book.

*To Sophia Augusta*, one book.

*In the Person of Radegund*, one book.

*In Praise of Bishop Martin*, one book.

*On Leontius, the Venerable Bishop*, one book.

*In Praise of the Same*, one book.

*Hymns*, seventy-seven, one book.

*On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, four books.

*The Life of Saint Hilary of Poitiers*, [unclear] book.

*To Oporicus, on His Life*, one book.

*The Life of Saint Maurilius, Bishop*, one book.

*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

*Poems to Friends*, one book. Incipit: “Rex regionis apex.”

He composed many other works also, but since they are brief, I did not wish to record them under the name of books. For he wrote many epitaphs and short verses, which I have seen. He flourished under Justin the Younger Augustus, in the year of the Lord 570.

Gregory, bishop of Tours, formerly a monk, once a disciple of Saint Avitus, bishop of Clermont, a learned and noble man, also gentle and humble, was of such sanctity and purity that even in life he shone with miracles. Visiting the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, he was received by the blessed Pope Gregory with the greatest reverence and charity, as truly a saint, and was loved by him as a singular and unique friend. He wrote several volumes in a simple and open style, of which there are extant:

*On the Praise of the Holy Martyrs*, one book. Incipit: “Hieronymus presbyter Statueram illa tantum scrib[ere?]”

*On the Miracles of Saint Julian the Martyr*, one book. Incipit: “Magnum in nobis quo Omnibus sanctis in Chri[sto?]”

*On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, one book.

[unclear]

*Abbot of Sponheim.*

*History of the Franks*, ten books. Incipit: “Scripturus bella regum.”

*Epicoma of the Same*, one book.

*Chronicle of Ecclesiastical History*, one book.

The other things which he composed have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the time of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

Martinus, bishop of Dumium, once also rector and abbot of a monastery, a man learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, coming from the regions of the East into Gaul, converted the people of the Sueves by teaching and miracles from Arian impiety to the right faith; he established rules of orthodox faith, founded monasteries, and reformed churches. He wrote to Mito, king of Galicia, an instructive volume on the four virtues which they call cardinal, which he wished to entitle:

*Formula of an Honorable Life*, one book. Incipit: “Gloriosissimo et tran[quillissimo?]”

*Moral Letters*, one book, and certain other things which I have not seen.

He flourished under Teudemir, king of the Sueves, while Justinian Augustus governed the empire of Constantinople, in the year of the Lord 540.

Paterius, of Rome, notary and secundicerius of the church, a man trained by constant study in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, collected all the testimonies of divine scripture by which the blessed Pope Gregory elucidated the obscure points of his exposition, and published three books: namely two on the testimonies of the Old Testament and one on the testimonies of the New Testament. He entitled this codex:

*Testimonies*, one book. Incipit: “Dum beatissimi atque apostolici.”

It exists among the Eberbach monks.

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished at Rome at the same time when Pope Gregory presided over the universal church; and at his urging he brought together the aforesaid volume, while Maurice Augustus held the empire, and afterward, with him, Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Columbanus, first founder and abbot of the monastery of Luxeuil, a Scot by nation, a man of distinguished sanctity, merit, and learning, father of many thousands of monks and founder of several monasteries, an outstanding sower of the divine word, coming from Ireland into Gaul and Germany, increased divine worship, monasteries, and servants, like once the chief of the Druids. When he was still rather young, he devoted great study to sacred letters, so that in an elegant style he wrote:

*Commentary on the Whole Psalter*, one book, and certain letters to the brethren.

He died under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 598, in the first indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

Jo 100 *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

John, bishop of Constantinople, a Cappadocian by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, of inestimable abstinence and holiness, so intent upon almsgiving and works of piety that he ordered all the begging poor to be expelled from the city of Constantinople. He wrote in Greek to St. Leander, bishop of Seville, of whom we spoke above: On the sacrament of baptism, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

Licinianus, bishop of Cartagena Spartaria, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, after many exercises in study, was killed at Constantinople by his rivals with a cup of poison, under the emperor Maurice. Nor did sudden death harm him, as Scripture says: “The just man, by whatever death he has been overtaken, shall be in refreshment.” For then he truly began to live, when, adorned with good works, he went through death to Christ, never to die. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, of which I have not yet deserved to see any. His little work is reported, however: On the sacrament of baptism, one book.
To Abbot Eutropius, one book of letters.
To various persons also, one book of letters.

And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 590.

Severus, bishop of the city of Malaga, sometime associate and colleague of the aforesaid bishop Licinianus, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, sharp in intellect, distinguished in speech, wrote against Vincentius, bishop of the city of Zaragoza, who had slipped from the Catholic faith into Arian depravity: A Correctory, one book.
On Virginity, to his sister, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 580, under the emperor Maurice, under whom he also died.

[unclear] Eutropius, bishop of the church of Valencia, formerly abbot of the monastery of Servitanum, of the order of St. Benedict, to whom Licinianus the bishop wrote many letters while he was still dwelling in the aforesaid monastery, a man magnificently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, and especially imbued with monastic disciplines, while he was still abbot wrote to Bishop Licinianus:

Why, after these things, the anointing of chrism is given to baptized infants, one book.
And several letters to various persons.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

He flourished in the times of the emperor Maurice, in the year of the Lord 600.

John, bishop of Girona, formerly a monk of our order, a Goth by nation, from the province of Lusitania, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and distinguished also in morals and conduct, was learned and renowned in the Greek and Latin tongues. When as a young man he sought Constantinople out of love of learning, after seven years had passed he returned to Spain. King Leovigild, when he wished to draw him over to Arian impiety and could not, condemned him to a very harsh exile for ten years. Then, recalled by the most Christian king Reccared, he founded a monastery, where by word and example he showed his brothers the path of regular discipline. He wrote: An Exhortatory to Monks, one book.
Additions to the Chronicle, one book.

He also composed many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Reccared, the most Christian king of the Visigoths in Spain, in the times of the emperors Maurice and Phocas, in the year of the Lord 600.

Maximus, bishop of the city of Zaragoza, learned in the divine Scriptures and not moderately instructed in secular letters, ready in intellect and polished in speech, excellent in verse and [unclear], published in both styles sufficiently distinguished volumes, which have not yet at all come to the knowledge of our reading. There is reported, however, his notable volume and pleasing work: On the Deeds of the Goths in Spain, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord [610].

Jonas, monk and disciple of St. Columbanus the abbot, and companion of his pilgrimage, a Scot by nation, a zealous man, learned and distinguished in knowledge, venerable no less for religion than for doctrine, at the brothers’ request and for the edification of many, wrote in composed discourse: The Life of Saint Columbanus, one book.
The Life of Saint Attala the Monk, one book.
The Life of Saint Eustasius the Abbot, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 630.

Leontius, bishop of the city of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, in life

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He, also most renowned in life and conduct, and a prelate worthy of God, wrote, among the other little works of his talent, a notable volume on the acts and conduct of that admirable patriarch of Alexandria who, because of his incredible piety and compassion toward the poor, was surnamed John the Almsgiver, one book. I have found nothing about the rest. He flourished in the time of the emperor Phocas, in the year of the Lord 610.

Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville after Leander, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular letters, subtle in intellect, clear in judgment, composed in speech, excellent in verse and prose, no less distinguished for holiness than for learning, shone forth. He is called the Younger to distinguish him from the elder, the bishop of Corduba, of whom we made mention above, or also from another bishop of Seville who preceded him. This Isidore the Younger wrote many distinguished little works, of which I have found only the following: To Bishop Braulio, one book of *Etymologies*: “Discipline from learning.”

On Genesis allegorically, one book: “The sacred history of the law.”

One book: “Certain mysteries.”

On Exodus, one book: “Therefore this one book.”

On Numbers, one book: “The following Leviticus [unclear].”

On Leviticus, one book: “The book of Deuteronomy.”

On Deuteronomy, one book: “After the death of Moses.”

On Joshua, one book.

On Judges, one book: “The history of the Judges.”

On Kings, four books: “After the book of Judgment follows.”

On Ruth, one book. On Chronicles, two books.

On Ezra and Nehemiah, one book. On Tobit, one book.

On Judith, one book. On Esther, one book.

On Job, one book. On the Psalter, one book.

On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book. On Ecclesiastes, one book.

On the Song of Songs, one book. On the Book of Wisdom, one book.

On Ecclesiasticus, one book. On the prophet Isaiah, one book.

On Jeremiah, one book. On Ezekiel, one book.

On the prophet Daniel, one book. On the Twelve Minor Prophets, one book.

On Maccabees, one book. Of Interpretation, seven books.

On the four Gospels, one book. On the Canonical Epistles, one book.

On the epistles of Paul, one book. On the Apocalypse, one book.

On the Acts of the Apostles, one book: “To my lord, the servant of God Pro-”

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

One book of proems: “The five books of Moses.”

One book of Differences: “Between God and the Lord.”

On the birth and death of the saints, one book: “Adam the first-formed [unclear].”

To his sister, against the Jews, two books: “Holy lady, flower [unclear].”

Of Synonyms or Soliloquies, two books: “Recently there came into my hands.”

On Illustrious Men, one book: “Osius, citizen of Corduba.”

On the Highest Good, of Sentences, three books: “The highest good is God.”

On the origin of offices, two books: “Those things which concerning the offices [unclear].”

On the Holy Trinity, one book. On the body and blood of the Lord, four books.

On the office of the Mass, one book. A decree of canons, one book.

On computus and the nature of things, one book. On the property of things, one book.

Of sermons, one book. Of ecclesiastical dogmas, one book.

The lament of a penitent, one book.

On astronomy.

A history or chronicle, [five?] books. On cosmography, [unclear] books.

On grammar and words.

Also one book of Allegories: “Mysteries of sacred Scripture.”

On heresies, one book. Of letters to various persons, [unclear] books.

He is said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Heraclonas, son of Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 630, in the time of Sisebut, king of the Goths in Spain. Because of his most holy life and conduct he was inserted into the catalogue of the saints; his feast is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Caesarius, from a monk of the monastery of Lerins bishop of Arles, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, gentle in intellect, sweet and adorned in speech, graced by a wonderful brevity of sentences, most holy in life and conduct, since from his youth he had been instructed in monastic disciplines and had been abbot of Lerins for a long time, wrote certain distinguished little works of reading not to be despised, which are very necessary and useful for monastic religious persons and persons dedicated to God. Of these there are extant: On grace and free will, one book.

Of sermons to monks, one book: “I fear in Christ [unclear].”

Some of these sermons are extant among the Eberbach monks.

A decree of three councils of Arles, three books. I have found nothing about the rest.

In the third sermon, which is on the struggle of the monk against the vices, he acknowledges that those to whom he is speaking are professed monks of the order of the rule of our most holy father Benedict.

Cla-

*104 On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantine, son of Heraclius, and of his sons, in the year of the Lord 670; under them he gloriously presided over the synod of Arles.

Audoenus, also called Dado, bishop of Rouen, a Gaul by nationality, brother of Saint Ado the monk, a learned and most holy man, founder of the monastery of Resbacum, since he was learned both in the sacred Scriptures and also in secular letters, wrote in a most elegant style to Rupert, bishop of Paris: The Life of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, 3 books.

And certain other works.

He flourished in much holiness, virtues, and signs, in the times of the aforesaid emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 660.

Theodorus, seventh archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated by Pope Vitalian, a Greek by nationality, from Tarsus of Cilicia, a monk of our order in the city of Rome, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in secular letters, very skilled in Greek and Latin speech, also excelling in verse and in prose, no less distinguished for holiness than for learning, held a synod in England and established many things for the advantage of the English church. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote an excellent work on the character of the penance to be imposed on those who had offended in many crimes; the title of this work is: The Penitential of Theodorus, 1 book.

Also some letters to various persons.

He died, not without a reputation for holiness, under Justinian the Younger as emperor, in the year of the Lord 690, in the third indiction, in the seventy-eighth year of his age and the twenty-second of his episcopate.

Leo, the second pope, a Sicilian by nationality, sat in the chair of Peter after Agatho for only eleven months, a man most learned in divine and secular writings, sufficiently instructed in the Greek and Latin language, subtle and eloquent, no less holy than learned. He translated from Greek into Latin the sixth synod, which in the time of Pope Agatho, his predecessor, had been celebrated in the city of Constantinople, in which Macarius, bishop of Antioch, was condemned with his accomplices, the bishops Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, who taught as doctrine that there was only one will and operation in our Lord Jesus Christ. He also wrote: Many letters to various persons, 1 book. And certain similar works.

Mo-

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

He died under the emperor Constantine, son of Constantine, in the year of the Lord 677, in the fifth indiction, on the fifth day before the Nones of July.

Adamannus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Hii, which Saint Columbanus once built on an island of Scotland, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, cautious in intellect and sweet in eloquence, distinguished in life and conduct, not without a reputation for holiness, was the father of many monks. Among other things, in a sufficiently well-composed style, he wrote a volume

*On the Places of the Holy Land*, one book.

There survives in the library of the abbey of Eberbach part of that book, on the location of Jerusalem, and certain letters.

He flourished under Justinian the younger, Augustus, in the year of the Lord 690.

Benedict, an abbot in Britain, a man both devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an outstanding preserver and extender of regular discipline, wrote a distinguished little work for monks, in which, comparing all the rules of the holy fathers with the Rule of our most blessed father Benedict, he shows that the rule of all the others agrees with it, and that it is at variance with none at all. For this reason he entitled his book

*The Concord of the Rules*, one book. He also wrote other things.

He flourished under the emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 670.

Aldhelm, bishop of the West Saxons, formerly abbot of the monastery of Malmesbury in Scotia, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a devout man and of exceptional holiness, devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and in secular letters the most learned of all in England in his time, excellent in verse and prose, a most fervent preacher of the divine word, wrote certain instructive volumes in both styles; of these I have found only the following. While he was still abbot, at the command of the synod of his people, he wrote against the error of the Britons a distinguished and useful work:

*On the Celebration of Easter*, one book. “Almighty begetter [unclear]” One book. “Most reverend man of Christ [unclear]” One book. Many letters to various persons.

He is also read to have written many other things, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. O Cla

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He flourished under Justinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 680.

Ceolfrid, after Benedict the second abbot of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in England, of the Order of Saint Benedict, teacher and fosterer of Bede the priest, a devout and learned man, and [unclear] governor of regular discipline, wrote to the king of the Picts, at his request, a quite lengthy letter in the form of a little book: On the Observance of Easter, one book.

He flourished in England in the times of the emperor Justinian the Younger, in the year of the Lord 680. At length, while returning after visiting the thresholds of the apostles, he died in the city of Langres, in the seventy-fourth year of his age.

Aegidius, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, Greek by nation, learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, an eminent physician, philosopher, and poet, venerable no less in manner of life than in knowledge, wrote certain little works of usefulness not to be despised, of which I have found only the following: An eminent work composed in meter, one book. “With modest powers of talent...”
On pulses. “With modest powers of talent...”
On veins also. “Hence it is called a vein, when it becomes...”
Of the others I have seen nothing.
On urines, one book. “It is called urine, because...”

He flourished under the emperor Tiberius, in the year of the Lord 700.

Bede, monk and priest of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which is in England, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and very skilled in secular letters, an eminent philosopher, astronomer, calculator, and poet. Not ignorant of the Greek language, outstanding in talent, not over-elaborate in speech, yet sweet and well ordered, he wrote many volumes, in which the keenness of his intellect is proved. When he was seven years old, by the care of his relatives he was given to be educated by Abbot Benedict, and then by Ceolfrid of the said monastery of [Wearmouth?]; and spending all the time of his life thereafter in residence in the same monastery, he devoted all his effort to meditation on the Scriptures, and, amid the observance of regular discipline and the daily care of singing in church, he always found it sweet either to learn, or to teach, or to write. In the nineteenth year of his age he received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the rank of priesthood, both through the ministry of Bishop John, at the command of Abbot Ceolfrid. From the time when he received the priesthood until the end of his life he composed the following little works:

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

On Genesis as far as Isaac, four books.
On Numbers, one book.
On Deuteronomy, two books.
On the Beginning of Kings, five books.
On Thirty Questions on Kings, one book.
On the Building of the Temple, two books.
On Joshua, one book.
On Chronicles, two books.
On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book.
On Ecclesiastes, one book.
On the Song of Songs, six books.
On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books.
On Tobit, one book.
On Isaiah the Prophet, two books.
On Ezekiel, one book.
On the Twelve Minor Prophets, twelve books.
On the Gospel of Mark, four books.
On the Gospel of Luke, six books.
Homilies on the Gospels, two books.
On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.
On the Canonical Epistles, seven books.
On the Acts of the Apostles, two books.
On the Apocalypse, three books.
On Times and the Nature of Things, two books.
Another smaller volume, two books.
Sparks from the Sentences of the Fathers, one book.
Deeds of the English, five books.
Flowers of Blessed Gregory on the Song of Songs, two books.
Deeds of Various Saints, one book.
On the Passion of Saint Felix, one book.
Life of Saint Albert the Bishop, two books.
Chronicle of his own monastery, two books.
Martyrology, one book.
Hymns in various meter, one book.
Epigrams in heroic meter, one book.
On the Holy Places, one book.
Readings on the Old Testament, one book.
Readings of the New Testament, one book.
On Exodus, two books.
On Leviticus, two books.
On the Tabernacle and Its Vessels, [unclear] books.
“To the most beloved brother no...” [unclear]
“He exhorts us, the chosen vessel...” On Judges, three books.
Parables in Greek, Latin...
“Scripture, with grace assisting...”
“Outstanding among the sacred...”
“The book of our holy father...”
On Jeremiah, two books.
On Daniel, one book.
Exposition of the Gospel. “Blessed Luke the evangelist...”
“But the Acts of the Apostles...”
“The Apocalypse of Saint John...” On the Nature of Things and the Reckoning [of Time]...
“[unclear] says in the Gospel...”
“Britain, an island of the Ocean...”
In the exposition of the Song...
“First God [created?] the globe...”

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Distinctions on Jeremiah, one book.
On Christ and the Church, two books.
On Metrical Art, one book.
On Figures, one book.
On Orthography, one book.
He also published many other works besides, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. His little works, even while he was still living and always writing new ones, were of such authority that, by ordinance of the prelates of England, they were read publicly in the churches. And when in the heading of the homilies they wrote, according to custom, the name of the author, “of the venerable priest Bede,” since they could not proclaim him otherwise while he was alive, the title once assigned from the beginning has endured down to the present day, so that Bede is called “venerable” rather than “saint.” For while he was alive it was not permitted to call him otherwise, even if he was holy. There are those who invent other reasons for this title “venerable”: some from the inscription of the epitaph, others dreaming that Bede was blind. But they are wrong, since Bede was not blind, nor do we know that such an epitaph was inscribed on his tomb. And indeed, if I were not consulting brevity, I would very easily refute these ravings. He died under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 732, in the fifteenth indiction, in the seventy-second year of his age, on the day before the Kalends of June.

Gregory, the second pope, a Roman by birth, sat in the chair of Peter after the pontiff Constantine for sixteen years and nine months, a man certainly learned and most holy; he ordained Boniface, a monk, English by nation, as bishop of Mainz. He wrote certain little works full of learning, of which the following are reported:
To the Questions of Justinian.
Against Leo Augustus, one book.
To John, bishop of Constantinople, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.
He died under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 734, in the fourteenth indiction, on the Ides of February; Gregory the Third succeeded him.

Boniface, the first archbishop of Mainz, a Scot by nation, a monk of the order of St. Benedict, when he was a boy of five years was offered by his parents to a monastery in England which is called Mischele. There, devoting himself to letters and morals, he became both a learned and most holy man. After he had been ordained priest, out of love of pilgrimage for Christ he came to Germany; and there, preaching the word of God, he was ordained bishop of Mainz by Pope Gregory the Second, and by his successor Gregory the Third he was raised to archbishop, primate of Germany. Since he was a learned man, he taught the people committed to him not only by word but by writings. Of his little works I have found only:
Letters to various persons, one book.
The Life of Certain Saints, [unclear] books.
He died in Frisia while preaching, crowned with martyrdom, in the times of the emperor Pippin, in the year of the Lord 755, in the eighth indiction, in the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate, on the Nones of June. His body blessed Lullus, whom he had ordained archbishop after himself, caused to be brought back to the monastery of Fulda, situated in Buchonia, and to be honorably buried.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Verus, bishop of Hispalis in the province of Baetica, where Isidore once held the episcopate, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, sharp in intellect, brilliant in speech, distinguished no less in life than in learning, wrote for the edification of the faithful, especially of the church of [Aransica?] in the Gauls, renowned for virtues and miracles:
The Life of Bishop Eutropius, one book. And certain other things.
He is said to have flourished in the times of the emperor Pippin, in the year of the Lord 760.

Walafrid, abbot of St. Gall, as is said, a German by nation, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, in secular letters the most learned of all in his time, renowned for eloquent talent, strong in verse and prose, a monarch of regular discipline, father of many monks, wrote for the edification of all the faithful who read devoutly:
The Life of St. Gall in prose, one book. The same afterward in meter, one book.
On the Divine Offices, [unclear] books. Many letters to various persons.
And he is said to have written some other things which have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Augustus Tiberius, around the years of the Lord 700.

Gregory, the third pope, presided over the universal Roman Church after Gregory the Second for [unclear] years, a pious, merciful, and most holy man, very learned both in secular letters and in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence. Having held a synod at Rome, he excommunicated the emperors Leo and Constantine, who despised the images of the saints, and deposed them from imperial rule. He also wrote, among other things, to the same emperors:
An Admonition, one book. To the same, one book.
Against the same, [unclear] books. Letters to various persons, one book.
And

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

And certain other things. He died under the emperors Leo and Constantine in the year of the Lord 742, in the tenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December.

John, monk and priest, surnamed Chrysorrhoas, a Damascene by birth from Syria, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, and no less renowned for his life than for his knowledge, encouraged and stirred by the writings of Pope Gregory III, in which he attacked the error of the emperor Leo, himself also wrote for his Greeks, in the Greek language: Against the emperor Leo, 2 books.

And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year 730.

Willibald, first bishop of Eichstatt, a Scot by birth, brother of Saint Walburga, virgin and abbess of Heidenheim, monk and disciple of Saint Boniface the martyr, of the order of Saint Benedict, a learned and most holy man, distinguished in talent and eloquence, wrote for the edification of the faithful, at the request of Saint Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, in a sufficiently distinguished style: The Life of Saint Boniface, bishop, 1 book. “Therefore the illustrious and truly...”

I do not know whether he published anything further. He flourished under Pippin, father of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 760.

Pope Zacharias, a Greek by birth, after Gregory III presided over the universal Church for ten years. He was a most learned man, who on account of his erudition and the holiness of his life is rightly judged comparable with the best pontiffs. He translated the four books of dialogues of blessed Pope Gregory the Great from Latin into Greek, and enlightened many ignorant of the Latin tongue by their reading. He also wrote from his own vein, in Latin speech, very elegant and useful: Letters to various persons, 1 book.

Among these several to Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, are extant. He died under Pippin, two years before the martyrdom of the same Saint Boniface, in the year of the Lord 752, in the fifth indiction, on the Ides of March.

Alcuin, or Albinus, monk and deacon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, an Englishman by birth, once a hearer of Saint Bede the priest, a man most learned in the divine writings, and in knowledge of secular letters second to none in his time, excelling in verse and prose, summoned from Britain by the emperor Charlemagne, was held in such intimacy by him that he was called the emperor’s beloved teacher; by his instruction the emperor himself strove to be initiated in all the disciplines of the liberal arts. He wrote many distinguished volumes, among which are reported: On the Holy Trinity and Faith, 3 books. “To the glorious lord Charles...”

To the Questions of Fredegisus, 1 book. “To the most desired son...”

To Eulalia on the Nature of the Soul, 1 book. “Most dear in Christ...”

To Count Guido on the Virtues, 1 book. “To the most beloved son Guido...”

Sentences, 1 book.

On Genesis, 1 book.

On the Song of Songs, 1 book.

On Ecclesiastes, 1 book.

On the Gospel of John, 7 books.

On the Epistles of Paul, 14 books.

On the Apocalypse of John, 2 books.

On the Adoption of the Sons of God, 1 book. “Venerable and in Christ...”

On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, 1 book. “We believe in one God...”

A Mirror for Little Ones, 1 book. “In divine Scripture...”

On the Property of the Names of God, 1 book.

A Dialogue to the Disciples, 1 book.

The Life of Saint Vedastus, bishop, 1 book.

An Enchiridion on Certain Psalms, 1 book.

Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

On the Liberal Arts, 1 book.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

The same man, by command of Charlemagne, collected the homilies on the Gospels of the Lord’s days, weekdays, and feasts of the whole year by the most excellent doctors of the catholic Church, and reduced them to order. They are these: Of Saint Augustine, 48; of Bede, 48; of Gregory, 39; of Jerome, 6; of Leo, 21; of Severinus or Severianus, 1; of Ambrose, 10; of Chrysostom, 2; of Haymo, 7; of Hilary, 1; of Maximus, 17; of Anselm, 14; of Fulgentius, 2; of Hericus, 37; of Isidore, 15; of Origen, 4. The sum of all: 254 homilies.

He says that he wrote many other things, which nevertheless have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the empire of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 770.

Stuartus, monk of the order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by birth, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, by command of the emperor Charlemagne, after Eusebius, Jerome, and Bede, gathered from the writings of the ancients the deeds and passions of the holy martyrs, confessors, and virgins into one volume of no small size, which we are accustomed to entitle: Martyrology, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the same emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 780.

Paul, monk of the Cassinese monastery, of the order of Saint Benedict, an Italian by birth, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, distinguished in speech, pro-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

because of his knowledge of letters, was held in great esteem by the emperor Charles. Formerly, before his conversion, he was a deacon of the church of Aquileia, and chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards; and, captured with him and brought by Charles into Gaul, he finally became a monk. He wrote not a few volumes, both in verse and in prose, of which I have found only the following: At the request of Aldeburga, daughter of King Desiderius, he added To the Chronicle of Eutropius, 2 books.
The Deeds of the Bishops of Metz, 1 book.
The Life of Pope Gregory the First, 1 book.
The Life of Saint Arnulf the Bishop, 1 book.
The Life of Saint Benedict, in verse, 1 book.
The Deeds of the Lombards, 6 books. “The northern region...”
Several hymns in various meters, 1 book.
Letters to various persons, 1 book.

By order of Charles he arranged histories and readings suitable for the individual feasts of the saints throughout the whole year. And he organized and wrote many other things. He flourished in the times of the same Charles the Great, in the year of the Lord 780.

Adrian, pope the first, a Roman by nation, after Stephen the Third sat in the pontificate for twenty-three years. A learned and most holy man, held in the highest honor by the emperor Charles, he established many things for the benefit of the Church, and condemned the Felician heresy in a synod of three hundred and fifty bishops, by order of the emperor Charles, at Frankfurt. Since he was studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, he abridged the thirteen books of letters of Saint Pope Gregory into two, selecting the more useful parts. He also wrote from his own inspiration to Leo the Younger and his son Constantine, emperors of Constantinople: On the Veneration of Images, 1 book.
To the Emperor Charles, 1 book.
Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He also wrote quodlibets.

He died while Charles the Great was emperor, in the year of the Lord 795, in the third indiction, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, the seventh day before the Kalends of January.

Ruggandus, bishop of Metz, grandson of King Pippin through his sister, noble in birth, made noble by holy manners and by study of the Scriptures, an outstanding venerator of the bodies of the holy martyrs, desiring to instruct the clergy and people committed to him in righteousness by word and example, wrote for the clergy of the church of Metz a sufficiently instructive and useful Rule:

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

The Rule of Canons, 1 book. And certain other things.

He transferred the bodies of the holy martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius from Rome into France; the body of Saint Nazarius was placed in the monastery of Lorsch, then of the order of divine Benedict, in the diocese of Worms.

He flourished under King Pippin, father of the emperor Charles, in the year of the Lord 760.

Leo, pope the third, a Roman by nation, after the pontiff Adrian sat for twenty years. He was a man very learned in both divine and secular writings, and also most renowned for the holiness of his life and conduct. He anointed Charles, surnamed the Great in deed, to the empire of the Romans, and transferred this dignity from the Greeks to the Franks. Among other things he wrote: Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He died under Charles on the Ides of June, in the year of the Lord 816, in the ninth indiction.

Haymo, the third bishop of the church of Halberstadt in Saxony, formerly abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, once a hearer of the monk Alcuin, for whom Rabanus, then abbot of Fulda, composed twenty-two books On the Universe, was certainly a most learned man in every respect, a most sagacious interpreter of the divine Scriptures, and of excellent talent in delivering homilies to the people. He was first a monk of the monastery of Fulda with Rabanus; afterward he became the third abbot of Hersfeld; later, consecrated the third bishop of Halberstadt, he vigorously governed that church by word and example for thirteen years. He wrote almost countless little works, of which these that we have set down are reported: On the Five Books of Moses, 1 book.
On Judges, 1 book. On Joshua, 1 book.
On Kings, 1 book. On Ruth, 1 book.
On Tobit, 1 book. On Chronicles, 1 book.
On Judith, 1 book. On Ezra and Nehemiah, 1 book.
On Job, 1 book. On Esther, 1 book.
On the prophet Isaiah, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book.
On Jeremiah, 1 book. “The prophet Isaiah, noble...”
On Ezekiel, 1 book. “And blessed [unclear] says that it was done...”
On Daniel, 1 book. “The word that was made...”
On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 1 book. “The Lord, considering human...”
Also on the Psalms, 1 book. “[unclear] on all...”

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On all the epistles of Paul, one book. “From Corinth, the metropolis ...”

On the canonical epistles, seven books. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. On the Apocalypse, one book. “We read in the Church [unclear] ...”

On the Variety of Books, one book. “Since you are the only and most holy ...”

On the Holy Trinity, one book.

On the Memory of Christian Affairs, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, letters, sermons, and various treatises, which have not come to my knowledge.

He died under the emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 854, in the twelfth indiction. He was buried in the church of St. Stephen at Halberstadt.

Claudius, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, once, as they say, a disciple of Bede in England, and a colleague of Albinus the deacon and abbot, a Scot by nation, a man very zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular learning, practiced in verse and prose, composed many short works on the sacred books, of which the following are reported: On the Five Books of Moses, five books. Also on Judges, one book.

On the Book of Ruth, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, [unclear] books.

And many other things.

Freculphus, bishop of Lisieux in the province of Rouen, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, for whom Hrabanus, while still abbot, exercised his talent in many volumes, a man most zealous and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, and well suited to teaching the people, distinguished no less by his way of life than by his knowledge, is said to have written certain excellent short works. Of these I have read only a large and notable volume, containing, from the beginning of the world down to the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, A History of Deeds, seven books. “While at some time ...”

I have seen nothing of the others.

He wrote the aforesaid work to Helisachar; in it he also explained the more difficult questions of the Scriptures, and set down in clear discourse the deeds of both the Jews and the gentiles, from the beginning of the world down to the Virgin’s childbearing.

He flourished under Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Theodulphus, bishop of Orléans, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fleury of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and instructed from youth in secular letters, excel-[unclear] in verse

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

[unclear] excellent also in prose, is said to have composed some little works in both styles; but they have not yet come into our hands. This man, having been innocently sent to prison by Emperor Louis (I know not on what suspicion), composed the hymn *Gloria laus*. When, on Palm Sunday, as the emperor was passing by near the prison, he sang it in a loud voice, it so pleased the emperor that he immediately permitted him to go away free. Among other things, he wrote in various meters:

One book of hymns.
One book of letters.

He flourished under the rule of Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

*Einardus* (otherwise Eginhartus), chancellor of the emperor Charles the Great, German by nation, and afterward a monk of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, wrote little works of reading not to be despised, of which the following are reported: Having imitated Bede, who abridged the Hebrew psalter by excerpting from it all verses containing words of prayer, he himself also abridged the Gallican psalter, excerpting from it all verses containing words of prayer. He also wrote, both in his own person and in that of the emperor: One book of letters to various persons.
One book on the life of the emperor Charles.
And certain other things.
One book of the history of the times.

He flourished under Charles and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 820.

*Johannes Scotus*, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, formerly a hearer and disciple of Bede, the most illustrious monk and doctor, a colleague of Albinus, coming with him from Britain into Gaul, was held in esteem by the emperor Charles the Great. Since he was a man most learned in all the scriptures, he published in clear language very distinguished little works, of which these are reported: Five books on the Gospel of Matthew.
One book on human duties.
One book on the division of nature.

He also composed many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles the Great, in the year of the Lord 800.

*Hilduinus*, abbot of the monastery of St. Denis of Paris, of the order of the divine father Benedict, archchaplain of the sacred palace, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, published commentaries on the four books of Kings, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and very [unclear] in secular letters, excellent both in meter and in prose, wrote to Emperor Louis in both styles: Two books on the life of St. Denis.
And certain other things, 116 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* He flourished under the emperor Louis, son of Charles, in the year of the Lord 840.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, formerly a monk of Saint-Denis of Paris, a man exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters second to none in his time, conspicuous for wisdom and uprightness of conduct and most eloquent, wrote several little works of authority not to be despised, of which I found only the following: In the person of the emperor Charlemagne, he wrote, very instructively, To the Church of Ravenna, one book.
The Life of Saint Remigius, bishop, two books.
To Walo, bishop of Metz, one book.
Many Letters, one book.
Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Charlemagne and Louis his son, emperors, in the year of the Lord's nativity 800. And he wrote many doctrines.

Amularius Fortunatus, archbishop of Trier, by nation [unclear], a learned and most eloquent man, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, was sent by the emperor Charlemagne to Constantinople to the emperor Michael, and with admirable industry and his eloquence confirmed peace and friendship between them, as is contained in the deeds of the people of Trier. Among other things he wrote: On the Ecclesiastical Offices, one book. Satis et nimium quidem.
To Louis on the same matter, four books.
On the Mysteries of the Mass, one book.
Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He died under the emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 813, in the sixth indiction, in about the sixteenth year of his episcopate.

Angelomus, monk of Luxeuil, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man endowed with a noble talent for expounding the divine Scriptures, so that, in comparison with him, the ancients seem not to have expounded those which he himself expounded; not ignorant of secular writings either, at the command of Drogo, bishop of Metz, who was the son of Charlemagne and brother of the emperor Louis, wrote a most excellent work, the like of which I do not remember ever having read elsewhere in the holy Scriptures: On the Books of Kings, four books. Igitur cum aquam pluribus.
To Lothar on the Song of Songs, one book. Priusquam augustale decus.
On the Divine Offices, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under Louis and his son Lothar, in the year 850.

Ra-

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

Rabanus Maurus, sixth archbishop of Mainz, formerly abbot of the monastery of Fulda of the Order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, from the city of Fulda in Buchonia, once a pupil of Albinus the Englishman, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, and most subtle poet, to whom, that I may speak without envy, Italy bore no equal, nor Germany his peer. For in the monastery of Fulda, while still a young man, he put on the monk, and advanced wonderfully both in morals and in knowledge; hence, consecrated fourth abbot of the same monastery, he presided for twenty-four years over the sheep entrusted to him, by word and example, and composed almost innumerable little works of Scripture. At last, offended by the wickedness of his monks, who, because they said he was too intent on the Scriptures and neglected temporal affairs, the devil working this in them, took displeasure against him, being scandalized in that in which they ought especially to have been edified. Therefore, giving place to wrath and not consenting to remain any longer with ungrateful sheep, he left the monastery and its inhabitants, and moved to Louis the emperor, son of Charles, with whom he also remained many days. But the monks, moved by repentance, sent an embassy to him and asked that he return to the monastery, but they did not obtain it. Therefore he remained with the emperor until the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz; appointed in his place, he presided over the aforesaid church of Mainz for nine years. Having also held a synod, he established many things for the benefit of the faithful. While still established in the monastery of Fulda he wrote many volumes, both in verse and in prose, especially on the holy Scriptures, all of which he explained from beginning to end. Of his writings the following are reported: To Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, of whom we made mention above, he wrote a distinguished work: On Genesis, four books. In the beginning etc.; [unclear].
On Exodus, four books. Exodus is said to be departure.
On Numbers, four books. The book of Numbers many [unclear].
On Leviticus, four books. Of the following book, that is, Leviticus [unclear].
On Deuteronomy, two books. The children of Israel set camps [unclear].
On Joshua, two books. To the most blessed and truly [unclear].
On Judges, one book. After the death of Joshua.
On the book of Ruth, four books. For those searching into the history.
On Kings, to Hilduin, [unclear]. There was a man, and [unclear]. Let us say [unclear].

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

On Chronicles, 4 books. Adam, and the tenth from...
On Ezra and Nehemiah, [unclear] books. On Tobit, 1 book.
On Judith, [1?] book. To the chosen lord and deservedly...
On Esther, [1?] book. The book of Esther which [unclear].
On Job, 1 book. On the Psalms, [unclear] books.
On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book. On Ecclesiastes, 1 book.
*On the Song of Songs*, 3 books. Love, etc. [unclear].
On the Book of Wisdom, 10 books. All [unclear], and [unclear], therefore...
On Ecclesiasticus, [unclear] books. To the most reverend lord and...
On Isaiah the prophet, [unclear] books. Among all things of divine history...
On Jeremiah, 20 books.
On Ezekiel, 5 books. And it came to pass, etc. [unclear].
On Daniel, 5 books. On the twelve minor prophets, 12 books.
On Maccabees, 3 books. And it came to pass after that, through...
On the Gospel of Matthew, 8 books. Therefore the expectation...
On the Gospel of Luke, 5 books. On the Gospel of Mark, 4 books.
On the Gospel of John, 4 books. The discussion of the whole...
On all the epistles of Paul, 23 books. To the venerable brother Lupus...
On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book.
On the praise of the Holy Cross, 2 books. The King of kings, the Lord, the world...
To Bishop Haimo on the universe, 1 book. First among the Hebrews...
On universal nature, [unclear] books. The discussion of the whole...
On the instruction of clerics, 1 book. To the reverend and religious lord [Haistulf?]...
On the divine offices, 1 book. Because you, venerable [unclear]...
A dialogue on computus, 1 book. On questions of the canons, 1 book.
To King Louis, 1 book. He also published many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.
He also wrote to King Louis another 12 books on the properties of words and the mystical signification of things, a work which may not undeservedly be called a Cornucopia.
To Bishop Reginbald, 1 book.
On the blessings of the patriarchs, 1 book.
Letters to various persons, 1 book.
Of almost innumerable sermons, 1 book.
There also exist some other little works of Rabanus, On Seeing God, On Purity of Heart, On Penance, in the library of Ebirbach.
He died under the rulers Louis and Lothar, in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the ninth year of his episcopate. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Alban near Mainz, not without a reputation for holiness; I have read his epitaph in about twenty ornate verses.

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

Ellator, a priest of a certain church, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, rich in reading the ancients, distinguished in talent and eloquence, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, is said to have expounded many volumes on the holy Scriptures, in which he splendidly displayed his ability. There survives, among other things, a notable volume of his, which he published at the request of friends:
On the Book of Wisdom, 7 books.
I have found nothing about the others.
He is said to have flourished in the times of Emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Strabus, a monk of Fulda, a German by nation, once a pupil and scribe of Abbot Rabanus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly trained in the studies of secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote not a few little works in exposition of the sacred volumes; in these, showing himself a learned man, he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Thus, imitating his master Abbot Rabanus, he wrote:
On Genesis, 1 book. On Exodus, 1 book.
On Leviticus, [unclear]. And many other works. This Strabus, finally, is remembered as the first to have assembled, from the sayings of the holy Fathers, the gloss on the whole Bible which is now called the Ordinary Gloss; others afterwards enlarged it by adding many sayings of the Fathers.
He flourished under Emperor Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Lupus Servatus, a priest, to whom Abbot Rabanus of Fulda is read to have written eight books on the epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Romans, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and, according to the age of his time, abundantly skilled in secular letters, wrote some little works of his own talent, of which very few have come to my knowledge. There survives a volume of his:
On Three Questions, 1 book.
And certain letters, as well as other works.
He flourished under Lothar, son of Louis, in the year of the Lord 850.

John, called Erigena, a monk, learned in the divine writings and very highly trained in the discipline of secular letters, fully instructed in Greek and Latin speech, subtle in intellect,

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

composed in discourse, at the command of Charles, son of Louis and brother of the emperor Lothar, he translated into Latin: The *Hierarchy* of Dionysius, 4 books.
He wrote on the same, 4 books.
And certain other things. He flourished under the emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 850.

Ansegisus, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of St. Benedict, later archbishop of Sens, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, distinguished in speech and talent, arranged and gathered together, for the use of the catholic Church, the laws of the emperors Charlemagne and Louis, which I have seen, as follows, namely: Ecclesiastical statutes of Charles, 2 books. “When our Lord Jesus was reigning.”
Secular laws of the same, 2 books. “Concerning peace we admonish.”
Ecclesiastical statutes of Louis, 2 books. “To all of you either by sight.”
Secular laws of the same, 2 books. “If servants through contumacy.”

He published besides not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Lothar, son of Louis, in the year of the Lord 840.

Amulus, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, learned by reading the ancients, and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, distinguished and eloquent, wrote little works of no contemptible reading, of which I have read only the notable work addressed to Charles: Against the Jews, 1 book. “The detestable things of the Jews.”

Of the rest I have as yet seen none. He flourished under Louis, son of Charlemagne, in the year 850.

Bertramus, priest and monk, very skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in the letters of the secular disciplines, subtle in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and no less notable in life than in doctrine, wrote many excellent little works, of which few have come to my knowledge. To King Charles, brother of the emperor Lothar, he wrote a commendable work: On Predestination, 1 book.
On the Body and Blood of the Lord, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 830.

Turpin, archbishop of Reims, friend and secretary of the great emperor Charles, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, having a talent exercised in verse and prose, advocate of the poor, beloved by God in life and conduct, who declares that he often fought the Saracens with Charles by his own hands and arms, wrote elegantly: The Deeds of Charlemagne, 2 books.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He flourished under the same Charles and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 850.

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

Anastasius, keeper and most sagacious restorer of the apostolic library, learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, very skilled in Greek and Latin speech, is said to have composed not a few little works, but none of them has come into our hands. He translated many volumes of the Greeks into Latin; for, at the command of Pope Nicholas I, he translated: The Life of John the Almsgiver, 1 book.
One Hierarchy of St. Dionysius, 1 book.
The Seventh Universal Synod, 1 book.
The Lives of Many Holy Fathers, 1 book.
And many other things.

He also wrote an Ecclesiastical History down to his own times, at the request of Charles II, to whom he was especially dear. He flourished under Louis II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 860.

Nicholas, the first pope of that name, a Roman by birth, sat in the pontificate after Benedict III for eight years; a man magnificently learned in the holy Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, who established many things for the use of the catholic Church. By his permission and authority, through the efforts of Notger, abbot of St. Gall, the use of sequences first began in the Gallican churches. He wrote, among other things, in the person of his pontificate, an excellent volume: Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He died under Lothar or Louis II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 869, in the second indiction, on the 8th day before the Ides of December.

John, deacon of the Roman Church, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, venerable in life and conduct no less than in doctrine, wrote for the edification of many, to Pope John VII, in a sufficiently illustrious style, a large volume, which contains: The Life of St. Gregory, Pope, the first of that name, 1 book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under Charles the Bald, emperor, in the year of the Lord 870.

Notger, bishop of Liege, formerly abbot of the monastery of St. Gall, of the Order of the holy father Benedict, a Teuton by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most learned of all men of his time, a philosopher, poet, and notable musician, and no less venerable in holiness than in knowledge

[He] wrote many little works, both in verse and in prose, of which few have come into our hands. For I have read only the volume which he entitled the *Sequentiarium*, which he wrote while he was still a monk in the monastery of Saint Gall, to Lutuardus, bishop of Vercelli, archchaplain of the emperor Charles the Great. This work begins thus: (Epistle 1) “Summe sanctitatis meri”; “Grates nunc omnes redd[amus?],” 1 book.

The *Sequentiarius* begins thus: “De musica symphonia,” 1 book.

*On the Expositors of Sacred Scripture*: “Cum prudentis sis prud[ens?],” 1 book.

Letters to various persons, 1 book.

Concerning the other things which he composed, nothing has come to the knowledge of our reading. Pope Nicholas I approved this most learned man’s *Sequentiarium* and ordered it to be sung at Masses. Because of the renown of his learning and life, he was first abbot and then, in his old age, was consecrated bishop; tenth in order, he presided over the government of the church of Liège, under the emperor Lothar, son of Louis, in the year of the Lord 850. Under him he died, not without a reputation for holiness.
