He also composed several chants in praise of the saints, with sweet and regular melody. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1115.

Franco, second abbot of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed in secular doctrine, strong in talent and renowned for eloquence, wrote certain commendable little works both in meter and in prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. When he was still a simple monk in the aforesaid monastery, at the command of his abbot Fulgentius, he began a notable work, which afterward, having been made abbot, he completed, adorned with knowledge and eloquence: On the Grace of God, 1 book.
On the State of Future Glory, in meter, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.
Sermons on the Blessed Virgin, 2 books.
And certain other things.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

He was elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Affligem under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1109, in the thirteenth indiction.

Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, formerly a Parisian scholastic, surnamed Porreta, a Frenchman by nation, a man much exercised in the divine Scriptures and magnificently learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and confused in speech by the novelty of his terms, was accused of heresy in certain matters by Blessed Bernard, and, convicted in the council of Reims celebrated by Eugenius, is said to have renounced his error. There are those who excuse him, saying that the authorities introduced in his expositions were understood by some in a less sound way. But we, agreeing with the Roman Church, confess that what has once been concluded by it may be infringed by no one. Gilbert wrote many little works, of which the following are reported: On the Whole Psalter, 1 book.
On All the Epistles of Paul, 14 books.
On the Gospel of John, 1 book.
On Boethius, On the Trinity, 1 book.
Books of Questions, etc., 1 book.
Several sermons.
And certain other things.

He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Lucas, abbot of Mount Saint-Corneille, of the order of the holy father Benedict, learned in the holy Scriptures by continual exercise, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters for his station, having obtained a noble talent in expounding the divine books, transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity by writing various treatises. But I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. There is reported a notable work of his addressed to Milo, bishop of the church of Therouanne, a man likewise most learned, which I have not yet seen: On the Song of Songs, 1 book.
Several sermons and letters.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Lothar, the last emperor, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Wilbert, bishop of Chartres, studious and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, and inferior to none of the learned men of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, acute in talent and sufficiently adorned with eloquence, distinguished in morals and life, and an especial lover and worshipper of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, wrote a notable little work on this prophecy: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah”: Against the Jews, 1 book.
On the Nativity of Saint Mary, 1 sermon. On the Approved Custom,

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

Various sermons, 2 books.

He is also said to have written several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. I believe he flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Odo, bishop of Cambrai, a man learned in the Holy Scriptures, nobly educated in humane letters, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, notably distinguished, in no slight degree, in composing and delivering homilies to the people after the manner of the ancients, wrote a disputation which he had had with a certain Jew concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, in dialogue form, marked with the first letter of his own name and of the Jew disputing with him: To Wilbodo the monk, 1 book.

On the Canon of the Mass, 1 book.

On the Unjust Steward, 1 book. “There was a certain rich man.”

Several homilies and letters.

And he composed not a few other things, which have come to my knowledge.

Eadmer, a monk of Canterbury in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, at one time a hearer and disciple of Archbishop Anselm, a man learned through long practice in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, wrote little works not unworthy of reading, by which he both benefited the edification of the faithful and made his name known to posterity. Among these there is a volume on the discord which existed between William, king of the English, and the aforesaid St. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: On Ecclesiastical Liberty, 1 book.

The Life of the same Anselm, 1 book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Gratian, a monk of Bologna or Classe, of the Order of St. Benedict, by nation, as some will have it, Etruscan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and burning with wondrous zeal, prompt in intellect and clear in eloquence, also distinguished in life and conduct, after Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote a notable volume of decrees, from the statutes, sanctions, and writings of the ancients, which teachers of canon law use in the schools down to the present, approved by Pope Eugene III. Its title is: The Concord of Discordant Canons, 1 book. “The human race by two.”

He also composed certain other things.

He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120. [unclear]

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

[unclear]

Hugh, a monk of Corbie, of the Order of St. Benedict, called de Folieto, a man rich and learned in the Holy Scriptures through reading of the ancients, clear in intellect and sweet in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, made his name known to posterity by his writings. For he wrote an excellent volume, for all religious and God-fearing people not so much useful as delightful, divided into four little books, headed as follows: On the Material Cloister, 1 book. “On the ordering of the cloister.”

On the Spiritual Cloister, 1 book. “The cloister of the soul contains.”

On the Cloister of the Soul, 1 book. “In the heavenly Jerusalem.”

On the Cloister of Paradise, 1 book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

[unclear]

Richard, a monk of St. Victor at Paris, of the Order of the Regular Canons of St. Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, exceptional in morals and conduct, wrote many and almost innumerable little works, by which he greatly benefited the usefulness of believers and consecrated his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported: On the Holy Trinity, 6 books. “My just man lives by faith.”

On Contemplation, 5 books. “Arise, Lord, into thy rest.”

On the Twelve Patriarchs, 1 book. “Benjamin a youth.”

On the Mystical Ark, 5 books. “That mystical ark of Moses.”

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “In the little bed, etc.; the soul which.”

On the Extermination of Evil, 1 book. “What is it to thee, O sea, that.”

On the Advancement of Good, 1 book. “Every head is sick.”

Against the Judaizers, 1 book. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and.”

On the Tabernacle of the Covenant, 1 book.

On the Forty-Two Stations, 1 book.

On the Four Degrees of Charity, 1 book.

On the Priesthood of Melchizedek, 1 book.

On the Twelve Attendants, 1 book.

On the Pursuit of Wisdom, 1 book.

On the Progress of Monks, 1 book.

On Mental Prayer, 1 book.

On the Threefold Holocaust, 1 book.

On the Authority of Peter, 1 book. “Whatsoever thou shalt bind.” On

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

On judicial power, one book.
On the difference of sins, [unclear] book(s).
On the instruction of novices, one book.
On the spirit of blasphemy, one book.
On the offices of the Church, one book.
On diverse affections, one book.
An epitome of the whole Bible, [unclear] book(s).
On the Apocalypse of John, one book.
On Daniel the prophet, one book.
A chronicle from the beginning of the world, one book.
On the double Passover, one book.
Of divisions or exceptions, twenty-four books.
On the vision of Nebuchadnezzar, one book.
On the sacrifice of Abraham, one book.
On the four winds, one book.
On the words of Isaiah, one book.
On the Acts of the Apostles, one book.
On violent charity, one book.
On newness of life, one book.
He also composed many other things besides: letters, sermons, and various treatises. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Guido, fifth prior of the Charterhouse, a man skilled by long study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, gentle in disposition and distinguished in speech, and venerable no less for his manner of life than for his learning, is said to have composed several little works, by which his name has been endowed with immortality. Of these there is extant an excellent work, written in lucid discourse: On the life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, one book.
On the institutions of the Carthusians, one book.
And certain other things.

He corrected with diligent study the letters of the most blessed father Jerome, which had been corrupted by the excessive fault of scribes, to the standard of truth, and brought them together into one. He died under Lothair the Younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1157, in the fifteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, formerly a scholastic, a man most studious in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech, transmitted his name to posterity by writing with such great glory that, down to the present day, the school of theologians, wherever it is practiced, names and regards him with singular veneration as the Master. For with discerning study he wrote, from the sayings of the holy fathers, a commendable work: Four books of Sentences. “Desiring something concerning…”
On the whole Psalter, one book. “Since all prophecies…”
“Seeking the beginnings of things…”
On all the epistles of Paul, four books. “Seeking the beginnings of things…”
Various sermons, one book.

He also composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Eckardus, first abbot of the monastery of St. Lawrence, which is called Vraugia, in the diocese of Würzburg in the Hercynian Forest, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, inferior to none among the learned Germans of his time, excelling in verse and prose, wrote little works not to be despised in reading, by which he showed the liveliness of his intellect. Of these I know only the excellent work, composed in a double style in imitation of Boethius, very useful and necessary for the instruction and consolation of monks and of all the faithful who fear God, which he entitled: The Lantern of Monks, one book.

He composed certain elegant sermons and various letters to different persons. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord [unclear]. He was buried in the middle of the church of the aforesaid monastery.

Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man very studious and learned in the divine writings, and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and speech, and no less worthy of reverence for his manner of life than for his knowledge, made his name known by writing and expounding various things, and both by word and by example did no slight service to the edification of his brothers. For he wrote: Elegant sermons, one book.
On vices and virtues, one book.

But he also published several other things, which have by no means come to my knowledge.

Peter, priest of the church of Troyes, surnamed Comestor or Manducator, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently trained in secular letters, practiced in verse and prose, wrote in both styles certain distinguished little works, whose authority has long since been approved by the Church through use. He was called Comestor or Manducator for this reason: because [unclear] the authorities of the Scriptures in

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

by very frequently citing them in his sermons and little works, as though he had eaten them into the belly of memory. Among the other volumes of his talent he wrote a distinguished work addressed to William, archbishop of Sens, expounding all the historical books of the Bible briefly and usefully, which now by usage is entitled The Scholastic History, 20 books. Incipit: “Imperatoriae maiestatis.”
On the Praises of Saint Mary, 1 book.
Sermons on the Season, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, and very many other things, 1 book.

He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Peter, the Parisian dialectician, called Abelard, a Gaul by birth, a man most learned in secular philosophy, attempting to investigate higher matters, overwhelmed by glory, fell into many errors; through the action of the holy abbot Bernard, he was condemned with his depraved doctrines in the council of Sens. From this time secular philosophy began to defile sacred theology with its useless curiosity. This Peter wrote some little works which, if he had not mixed errors into them, could have benefited posterity. Of these there survives a volume overshadowed by dialectical obscurity, varied with many opinions, which he wished to entitle His Theology, 1 book.
Know Thyself, 1 book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Adelphus, an abbot of the order of Saint Benedict, a man skilled in divine scriptures through long practice, not ignorant of secular letters, an indefatigable cultivator of regular observance, so that by word and example he might show himself a useful shepherd to the sheep of Christ entrusted to him, is said to have forged some little works for their benefit, in which a rich vein of talent commends an adorned eloquence. Of these there survive elegant Sermons to the Brethren, 1 book.
Against the Saracens, 1 book.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, afterward, as he says, a monk of Clairvaux under the divine father Bernard of the Cistercian order, a man studious and learned in divine scriptures, and also distinguished by the holiness of his life and conduct, and for that reason singularly beloved by him, published little works not to be despised in reading; of these few have come to my knowledge. He began to write, but, forestalled by death, did not complete, The Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot, 1 book. Incipit: “Scripturus vitam servitui.”
The Mirror of Faith, 1 book.
The Enigma of Faith, 1 book.
Sentences of Faith, 1 book.
To Theophila, on the Nature of the Soul, 1 book.
On Contemplating God, 1 book.
On the Nature and Dignity of Love, 1 book.
On the Sacrament of the Altar, 1 book.
Against Peter Abelard, 1 book.
On the Song of Songs, unfinished, 1 book.
On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, 1 book.
And certain other things.

There are some who say that this William, while he was still abbot of Saint-Thierry, wrote that well-known letter to the Carthusians whose beginning is “Fratribus de monte Dei orientale lumen,” which is ascribed by many to blessed Bernard. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140. And he died before Bernard, when he had completed one book on his life; Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, added four other books to it.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Conrad, a monk of the monastery of Hirsau on the borders of the Swabians, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in divine scriptures, very skilled in secular letters, an eminent philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and poet, composed many splendid little works under the name Peregrinus. In them the adorned arrangement of the thoughts and the charming cultivation of speech declare their author inferior to none of the ancients. Of these, only the following have come to my knowledge: A distinguished work of dialogues, under the name of Peregrinus the priest, addressed to Theodora, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled
The Mirror of Virgins, 1 book. Incipit: “Collaturus tecum, o Theo-.”
On the Gospels through the Year, 1 book. Incipit: “Quia in littera veteris te-.”
On the Life of the Spirit, the Fruit, and Death, 1 book. Incipit: “Cum omnis divinae paginae.”
The Matricularius, 1 book. Incipit: “Cum manifestum sit, mun-.”
On the Praises of Saint Benedict, in verse, 1 book. Incipit: “Luce velut solem.”
Didascalon, 1 book. Incipit: “Quia te video diu va-.”
On Music and the Tones, 1 book. Incipit: “Musica est secundum cui-.”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

There was another declaimer of the order of Preachers, who according to

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

...according to the custom of modern writers, he composed sermons to the people under the name of Peregrinus, much inferior to our man in eloquence, and also later in time. Whatever this Conrad wrote, however, echoes Ciceronian eloquence, which the other could not do.

He flourished under the emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian order, once the close friend of the blessed abbot Bernard, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, no less conspicuous in conduct than in doctrine, made his name known to posterity by writing. For after William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, had died, [he wrote] the work on the Life of Saint Bernard, 4 books; The Deeds of Illustrious Men; and certain letters.

He flourished under the emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Richard, monk of Cluny, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters reputed in his time the most learned of all, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, by writing and composing various treatises transmitted his name with great glory to the knowledge of posterity. Yet I do not recall that any of them has so far come into our hands. His distinguished and famous work is, however, reported to be: History and Times, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Ganfred of Auxerre, monk of the Cistercian order, once a hearer and disciple of Peter Abelard, but lest he should also become an imitator of his error, betook himself to the teaching of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. Under his discipleship he became distinguished in learning and religion, and composed little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known also to posterity.

Against Peter Abelard, 1 book.
On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180.

Peter, cleric of the church of Reims, called de Riga, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters the most learned among all the doctors of his time, an outstanding grammarian and philosopher, excellent in verse and prose, wrote not a few volumes in both styles, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable metrical work on the Bible, which he entitled Aurora, as follows: On Genesis, 1 book. It begins: “The beginning of the world, what sort...”
1 book. “These twelve of the fathers...”
1 book. “But the voice of the Lord [to] Moses...”
1 book. “God addresses Moses...”
1 book. “These are the words of God...”
1 book. “After Moses, Joshua...”
1 book. “The Hebrew sins, he says...”
1 book. “To Ruth hastens...”
3 books. “Dwelling on Mount Ephra...”
1 book. “Origen alone, with...”
1 book. “Solomon reigned...”
1 book. “After those subject to him...”
1 book. “You who read the history...”
2 books. “Certain people [assign] the book of Job to Moses...”
1 book. “To Eustochium and Paula...”
1 book. “As far as under the Ethiopians...”
1 book. “Great Alexander...”
1 book. “He shone under Herod...”
1 book. “In the nineteenth year of Tiberius...”
1 book. “These things concerning the new and old law...”
1 book. “[unclear].”

He also published many other things which have not come to my knowledge. In the aforesaid little works he expounded the historical books of the Bible with marvelous brevity, carefully observing the law of meter, and explained each item according to the historical and allegorical sense.

Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore, of the order of Saint Benedict, originally from Calabria, a man zealous and practiced in the divine Scriptures, who, being regarded in his time as a prophet, even attempted to foretell future things. But it seems to me, if I may speak without prejudice to his own opinion or that of his followers, that he spoke more from conjectures drawn from the Scriptures than that he was a prophet. For, to be silent meanwhile about the rest, he dreamed that the emperor Frederick would be an enemy of the Church, whereas we all know that he persevered until death as peaceable, and subject and faithful to the Roman pontiff.

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

[unclear]. He wrote, moreover, in plain language several little works, in nearly all of which, as though foreknowing the future, he was accustomed to mix predictions:

On Jeremiah the prophet, one book.
On Daniel the prophet, one book.
On the Gospel of John, one book.
On the Apocalypse of John, eight books.
To Henry VI, one book. “You piously ask something from...” “The first time of the synagogue...”
On the Seven Seals, one book.
The Psalter of Ten Strings, five books.
Concords, five books.
On the Fifteen Pontiffs, one book. “Go up, baldhead, that...”
On Future Times, one book. “Because the general [condition] of the world...”
Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published many other things, especially against the Jews and other adversaries of the Catholic faith, which have not come into our hands. But the treatise which he wrote against Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, was condemned in a general council, as is clear at the beginning of the Decretals, “We condemn.”

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Rupert, a monk of the monastery of St. Remigius in the diocese of Reims, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a Frenchman by nation, a man trained by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of the secular disciplines, distinguished in intellect and clear in speech, wrote several little works of his own ability, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the distinguished History of the deeds done in the Holy Land by the Christians in the time of Urban II against the infidels, one book. “Among all histories...” Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Roswitha, a noble woman, born in Saxony, a nun in the monastery of Gandersheim, which is not far from Hildesheim, was renowned for remarkable talent and learning, and admirable in both kinds of writing. For, exhorting consecrated virgins to chastity and continence, she wrote in Latin six Comedies.

A panegyric on the deeds of the Ottos, in hexameter verse.
In praise of the Blessed Virgin, in elegiac and hexameter verse, [unclear]. “Only hope...”
Likewise the Passion of St. Dionysius in elegiac verse.
Likewise on St. Gangolph and several other saints.
She also had knowledge of the Greek language.

She was contemporary with John the Englishman, who earned the papacy by his learning.

Udechinus, priest of the church in Logenstein, a German by nation, a man learned in the holy Scriptures through long practice, sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, went to Jerusalem with many others under the emperor Conrad III in hope of eternal reward. While they often fought with the Saracens in naval battle, he shone forth, beloved for his great devotion and constancy on behalf of the faith of Christ. After returning to his homeland, at the request of Cuno, abbot of the monastery of St. Disibod, then of our order, he wrote in a fairly elegant style, in the manner of a letter or little book, the History of that same pilgrimage, one book. “At your command, father...”
Letters to various persons, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Rupert, bishop of Lincoln, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, among all the learned men of his time most skilled in the disciplines of secular letters, a philosopher, astronomer, distinguished calculator, easily the foremost theologian of his time, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, transmitted his name with glory to posterity by writing many and various works. Of his little works few have come into our hands. These, however, are reported: A Summa of Theology, one book.
On the books of Dionysius, four books.
The Summa which is called Numerale, one book. “Those who rule well...”
On the Celestial Sphere, one book. “Our intention in this treatise...”
On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book. “Computus is the science of number...”
A beautiful Calendar, one book.

He published many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

John, bishop of Chartres, by homeland of Salisbury, formerly cleric and disciple of blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, a man learned in the divine writings, nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, composed with fine grace, excellent in poetry and prose, and no less venerable for religion than for knowledge, wrote many splendid volumes by which he made his name known to posterity, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read the distinguished work on the trifles of courtiers and philosophers, which he chose to title Polycraticon, eight books. “Most delightful then in many...”

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

A Penitential, one book. “When the mercies of the Lord ...”
The Life of St. Thomas the Archbishop, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.
He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, a close friend of the aforesaid prelate John of Chartres, to whom [unclear] some letters, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and also excellently instructed in secular letters, acute and forceful in talent, who knew how not to flatter the vices of princes and prelates but to rebuke them, held in esteem among kings, princes, and bishops because of his learning and the honesty of his life, wrote many little works, of which these are reported: On Christian Friendship, one book. “Since they have been diminished ...”
On Saving Penitence, one book. “You asked me that to you [unclear] ...”
On Hastening the Passage, one book. “Who will give water to my head ...”
On the Quality of Penitence, one book. “The excessive harshness of your severity ...”
On the Study of Wisdom, one book. “You are divided, and your heart ...”
Against a Depraver, one book. “Your little exhortation ...”
An Exhortation to an Abbot, two books. “He has been chosen by your ...”
On the Office of a Bishop, one book. “You ask very urgently, reverend father ...”
On the Danger of Prelates, one book. “As often as I recall the words ...”
On the Life of Court Clerics, one book. “I give thanks to your grace ...”
Letters, 194 in number, one book. “Asked by you, bishop ...”
On the Precipices of Fortune, one book. He wrote also many other things.
He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Alexander, the third pope, by homeland a Sienese, after Adrian IV sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years. He was a learned and vigorous man, who suffered many injuries from the emperor Frederick, while he forcefully crushed the three antipopes set up by him against himself; and at last, overcoming the emperor himself, as a sign of subjection he trampled his neck with his foot, saying: “It is written: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” He wrote elegant Letters to various persons, one book,
and On Ecclesiastical Power, one book,
and certain other things.

He died in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1181, in the fourteenth indiction. [unclear]

*168 On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

[unclear] Risolanus [perhaps Chrysolanus], archbishop of the church of Milan, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, produced certain works of great authority, but none of them has come into my hands. There is reported to be his On the Holy Spirit Against the Greeks, one book; On the Holy Trinity, one book; letters, sermons, and various other treatises, which are unknown to me.

Hugo Eterianus, by nation a Tuscan, easily the most learned of all the doctors of his time in the holy Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular letters, a most eloquent philosopher and rhetorician, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin speech, whom all Greece admired as a writer, very subtle in talent and second to none as a disputant, wrote many distinguished volumes both in Greek and in Latin, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only one work, short indeed, but not to be despised, on the heresies which the Greeks hurl against the Latins: To Cardinal Ardoinus, one book. “Diligent prudence ...”
On the Immortal God, one book.
Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, with whom he was of great authority, under Frederick, the first Roman Augustus, and Alexander, the fourth pope, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Christian, archchancellor of Frederick, the first emperor, by nation a German, a man very learned in secular literature, eloquent and industrious, whom the Italians admired when he spoke in his time, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, whom Leo the Tuscan, notary of Manuel, emperor of the Greeks, praises highly, wrote certain distinguished works of his talent, among which there are extant: The Deeds and Life of Frederick, the first emperor, one book;
with various letters,
speeches, and certain other things.

He flourished under the same Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1170.

Leo, by nation a Tuscan, chief interpreter of the imperial letters under Manuel, prince of the Greeks, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and an excellent cultivator of secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, whose office it was to translate letters sent to the emperor, or to be sent to others, from one language into another, produced

*Abbot of Sponheim.*

... certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name also to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have read only the excellent work which he entitled:

*On the Prevarications of the Greeks*, 2 books. “The intolerable [unclear] of the Greeks...”
*Against the Errors of the Greeks*, 1 book.

He flourished at Constantinople in the times of Emperor Frederick I and Pope Alexander III, in the year of the Lord 1170.

John, archdeacon of a certain church of [Horit?], a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, skilled in the Greek and Latin languages, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works not to be despised for the edification of the faithful, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists an excellent and distinguished work, addressed to Stephen, a certain royal notary, against the Greeks:

*On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, 1 book. “Many things in rounded Greek...”
Also various letters.

But he says that he wrote certain other things as well, which have not come into our hands.

Odefridus of Viterbo, priest, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and distinguished, practiced in verse and prose, wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of these there exists a large volume addressed to Pope Urban III, mixed in verse and prose, on the beginning of the world, on the whole Old and New Testament, and on the ages of the world, times, deeds, and all histories of kings, which he entitled:

*Pantheon*, 18 books. “On the beginning of the world and...”
I have seen nothing of the others.

Eckebert, the second abbot of the monastery of Saint Florin, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge, was the brother of blessed Elizabeth the virgin, abbess of Schonau. He had formerly been a canon of the church of Bonn; called to Schonau by his holy sister, he first became a monk and then abbot. He wrote little works of reading not to be disregarded, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found the following:

*Against Heresies*, 1 book. “The prophecy long ago...”
*On the Beginning of the Gospel of John*, 1 book. “The mysteries of the divine word...”
*On the Magnificat*, 1 book. “The spirit of the Lord upon you...”
*On ‘The Angel Was Sent’*, 1 book. “The evangelical sermon for every...”
*On the Death of His Sister*, 1 book. “To virgins consecrated to God...”
*Meditations*, 1 book. “I have a word for you...”
*Sermons Through the Year*, 2 books. “There shall be signs, etc., Advent...”
*Praises of the Savior*, 1 book.
*A Book of Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book.

He also published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. For he was an excellent declaimer, learned and eloquent, so much so that he overcame in a single disputation a certain heretic whom no one could refute. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Florin, which is called Schonau, in the diocese of Trier, under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160; and on account of his religion and learning he was held in esteem.

Elizabeth, nun and abbess of the sisters of the monastery of Schonau, of the order of Saint Benedict, for there are two monasteries, one of monks and the other of nuns, situated at the end of the diocese of Trier, not far from the Rhine in the Hercynian Forest, sister of the aforesaid abbot Eckebert, a virgin of most holy conduct, received many revelations from God, which she committed to writing for the edification of posterity. Of these I have read the following:

*The Ways of God*, a useful work, 1 book. “It happened at the beginning...”
*On the Eleven Thousand Virgins of Cologne*, 1 book. “To you who [unclear] pious affections...”
*Of Various Revelations*, 2 books. “All who are going to read...”
*To Her Brother Eckebert*, 1 book. “You ask of me, brother...”
*A Book of Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book. “From the bishopric of Metz...”
*To Saint Hildegard*, 1 book.
And certain other things.

She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1165, in the fourteenth indiction, in the thirty-sixth year of her age, the twenty-fourth of her conversion, and the thirteenth of the visitation of the heavenly splendor, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, and was buried in the church of the monks of Saint Florin, in the middle of the choir.

Hildegard, abbess of the monastery of Saint Rupert the confessor, opposite the town of Bingen, on the other side of the river Nahe, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of the divine father Benedict, German by nation, from the county of Sponheim, once a disciple of blessed Gutta, perhaps Jutta or Judith, the virgin, wife of Count Megenhard of Sponheim, our founder, a virgin of most holy conduct and from her childhood illuminated by divine revelations, whose life

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

proved by miracles, she spread the fragrance of her holiness into distant regions, so that Eugenius III, Anastasius IV, Hadrian IV, and Alexander III, Roman pontiffs, frequently visiting her by their writings, commended themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. Moreover, Eugenius III, in the council of Trier, with Saint Bernard present, publicly approved before all her writings and little works when they had been read aloud; and again strengthened her by letters, that she should persevere in the undertaking she had begun. All that she wrote, however, she learned by divine revelation. Among these are the following: On the Rule of St. Benedict, one book. “And I, a poor little [woman?]…”
Thirty Questions, one book. “Charity, which with abstin[unclear]…”
Life of St. Rupert the Confessor, one book. “For as in a true vision…”
Life of St. Disibod the Bishop, one book. “In a mystical vision,” etc.
Eight Homilies on the Gospel, one book. “A certain man who [unclear]…”
On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. “In the vision which of the soul…”
Scivias, a large volume, one book. “And it came to pass in the year [unclear]…”
Of the Merits of Life, one book.
Of Simple Medicine, one book.
Of Compound Medicine, one book. “And it came to pass in the sixth year…”
Of Divine Works, one book. “He who was, and who is, and…”
To the People of Cologne, one book. “I, a poor little [woman?], [unclear]…”
To the People of Trier, one book. “O crowds of men, born…”
An Exhortation of Secular Persons, one book. “O daughters, who [follow?] the footsteps…”
To Her Sisters, one book. “I, a poor little [woman?], in [unclear]…”
Various Poems, one book. “Who are these who, like a cloud…”
And to Saint Bernard, one epistle. “In the spirit of mysteries…”
Letters to Various Persons, 155, one book. “Father of all, I, poor…” She also wrote other things. In all her little works, however, Catholic doctrine shines forth, such as either confirms faith or instructs conduct; nor did she ever say or write anything that could be called into doubt. And although she was ignorant of the Latin language, nevertheless, through the revelation of the Spirit of God, she dictated everything in Latin and fittingly, while notaries took it down. We have seen many letters of Conrad III and Frederick I, emperors, and of the bishops of Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Bremen, Jerusalem, and of almost innumerable others, who, from different regions of the world, stirred by the fame of her holiness and revelations, commended themselves in writing to her prayers, and sought answers to various questions.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

They sought them. She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180, in the eighty-second year of her age, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, a learned and most holy man, who gave to the Carmelite brothers, while they were still living in the Holy Land, the rule which those same brothers, now settled in Europe, profess everywhere after it was modified and approved by the Apostolic See, at the urging of Pope Innocent III described, in a lucid and truthful style: The State of the Holy Land, one book.
The Rule of the Carmelites, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Innocent III, pope, a Campanian by nation, previously called Lotharius, presided over the Church after Pope Celestine III for eighteen years. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, since from his boyhood he had devoted himself to letters in the school of Paris, and he grew into a man no less upright than learned. He left not a few little works of his talent, of which, under the name of Lotharius the Levite, or also of Pope Innocent, the following are current: On the Usefulness of the Human Condition, two books. “Why from the womb of the mother…”
On the Seven Penitential Psalms, one book.
On the Office of the Mass, two books. “There are chiefly three things in which…”
On the Sacrament of Baptism, one book.
On the Cloister of the Soul, one book.
The Ancient Decretals, one book.
Several Sermons, one book.
Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He flourished at the time of the discord which existed between Philip, brother of Henry, and Otto, duke of Saxony, in the year of the Lord 1200.

G[unclear], most learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, having ascended the theological chair in the school of Paris, shone forth with distinction for a long time, and among all the doctors of that time was celebrated with the greatest fame and reputation. He wrote a very distinguished and useful volume, or: Summa of Theology, one book. “As the Apostle says, Faith…”
On the Divine Offices, one book.

He is said also to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Cy

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

Cyrillus, priest and monk of Mount Carmel, the third prior general of the same order, by nation, as they report, a Greek, a holy man illumined by a prophetic spirit, to whom almighty God is said to have disclosed his will through angelic ministry, while he is honored with silver tablets written by the finger of God, wrote, among the other little works of his talent, to an abbot, *On the Angelic Oracle*: The prologue begins thus, one epistle.
The oracle itself thus, one book.
*On the Course of His Order*.
Several letters to various persons.

He flourished under Philip and Otto, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Helinandus, a studious man learned by long practice, and nobly instructed in secular literature, acute in intellect, eloquent in speech, because of the excellence of his learning and the integrity of his life, appeared not the least among the ecclesiastical doctors of his time. For he wrote several little works, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these the following are reported: from the beginning of the world down to his own age, a great, distinguished volume:

*Histories*, 48 books.
*On the Restoration of the Fallen One*.
Several sermons, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.
And many other things.

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1209.

Gilbert, a monk of the Cistercian order, afterwards abbot of a certain monastery, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, excellently learned, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence, wrote after the death of Saint Bernard the abbot, where he had left off, namely from the place, “In my bed by night,” down to the end, forty-six subtle and most elegant sermons:

*On the Song of Songs*, one book. “Various are [the things] of lovers.”
And certain other things.

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Aelred, abbot of the same monastery, of the Cistercian order, a man exercised by constant study in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, gentle in intellect, sweet in speech, outstanding in devotion, wrote for the usefulness of his brothers a number of little works, by which he benefited them and transmitted the knowledge of his name to posterity.

174 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* Of these there is extant a little work of great usefulness for religious men, filled with spiritual maxims, which he entitled, one book:

*The Mirror of Charity*, one book. It begins: “When Jesus was [unclear]”

*On Luke*.

And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, around the year of the Lord 1200.

Maurice, bishop of Paris, very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, since before his episcopate he taught theology gloriously for many years at Paris, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, was of excellent zeal in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have composed certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there are said to be, throughout the cycle of the whole year, both on Sundays and on feast days:

*Sermons to the People*, one book.

*On the Care of Souls*, to priests, one book.

But the rest which he is said to have written have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Papias, a Lombard by nation, a man most learned in secular letters, the most renowned grammarian of all in his own time, fully instructed in Greek and Latin speech, and also not moderately exercised in the divine Scriptures, wrote in a twofold style, in both literatures, certain excellent little works, of which few have come to my knowledge:

*On the Order of Speaking*, two books.

*On the Words of the Latin Language*, three books. It begins: “All in this book [unclear]”

*Letters to Various Persons*, four books.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

John Beleth, once a distinguished theologian of the school of Paris, learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, not undistinguished among the doctors of his time, by writing and disputing brought his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. For he wrote the not useless

*Summa on the Divine Offices*, one book. It begins: “In the primitive church” Also various *Sermons*, one book.

In addition he is said to have written not a few other things, but they have not come to my knowledge.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

Theoderic, abbot of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished no less in manner of life than in knowledge, is said to have composed some little works, of which I have seen only, addressed to certain abbots:

*The Life of Saint Hildegard*, four books. It begins: “In the Roman commonwealth” And certain letters.

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Werner, otherwise Irnerius, an illustrious and notable man, a professor and most renowned interpreter of civil law, and an eminent cultivator of the other humane letters, who was deservedly called the lamp of the law, because he was the first to expound civil law with little glosses and, without example, gave to others an example of illuminating the law. And from this time the professors of both laws always shone in abundance, and they began to explain the volumes of their instruction down to the present day. He taught in both for a long time at Bologna, where he had many and excellent disciples, who by their learning spread the fame and glory of their master. His glosses and distinguished monuments on the laws are extant, which are very well known among the professors of this field.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, of the order of St. Benedict, a man learned through constant exercise in the divine Scriptures, gentle in intellect, sweet and well-composed in speech, and sufficiently fit for persuasion, devout and praiseworthy in manner of life, and a distinguished zealot for regular observance, making his name known to posterity by writing, composed certain devout little works for the usefulness of readers, of which these are reported:

*Revelations of Many Persons*, one book.

*On the Eremitic Way of Life*, one book. It begins: “I have received the letters of your affection”

*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He published some other things also, which have not come to my knowledge.

Peter, cantor of Paris, and afterwards, as they say, bishop, a man most learned in the divine writings and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, presided gloriously for many years over the theological school at Paris, and instructed many excellent disciples. He also wrote certain distinguished little works, of which I remember that few have come into our hands: a volume entitled,

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

*The Abbreviated Word*, 1 book. It begins: “The abbreviated word.”
Another work of *Distinctions*, 2 books. It begins: “Abel is called the beginning.”
*The Grammar of Theologians*, 3 books. It begins: “The soul, the spirit.”
Various sermons, 4 books. It begins: “On the soul and the spirit.”
*On Certain Miracles*, 5 books.
Also *On the Sacraments*, 6 books. It begins: “The people went about.”
He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Pilleus of Modena, professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished in learning and cautious in counsel, was held in the highest esteem among the older jurists. By writing and teaching various things in that faculty he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among his little works there is found a certain notable and not negligible *Summa*, which he entitled:

*On the Order of Trials*, 1 book. It begins: “The name of Christ having been invoked.”

Of the other things that he wrote, however, nothing has come to my knowledge.

John Bosianus, by country a Cremonese, a most famous expounder of laws, teacher of Azo of Bologna, the very distinguished jurisconsult, a man of great learning and reputation, who appeared first among the expositors of law and by his example gave many both spirit and form for study, is said to have written certain excellent little works in that faculty, by which he gave his name to immortality. Among these there is extant a brief *Summa* on the Pandects, which is entitled:

*Ventosa*. A lecture on the Code, 9 books.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 120[unclear].

Stephen the Englishman, once an ornament and rector of the school of Paris, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and in Aristotelian philosophy second to none in his time, taught theology gloriously for many years, and was the first to begin to expound Scripture scholastically and morally. And from this the custom took root that masters of theology should more clearly open the divine books to their students in their lectures in the schools. This Stephen wrote, as I have learned, the following little works: On the five books of Moses, 1 book.
On Joshua, 1 book.
Also on the book of Judges, 2 books.
Also on Kings, 4 books.
On the twelve minor prophets, 2 books.

He published many other things besides, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished around the times of the rule of Henry VI as king, but as the fifth emperor crowned by the pope, in the year of the Lord 120[unclear].

*Abbot of Sponheim*

Bagorotus, distinguished professor of both laws and a most celebrated interpreter, not ignorant also of other letters, whose authority among the ancient jurists was not small, on account of his excellent talent for teaching and his zeal for writing, also made his name known to posterity. Among his little works there is extant a notable *Summa*, which he entitled:

*Cavillations*, 1 book.
*On the Order of Trials*, 1 book. It begins: “By the prayers and insistence.”

He is said to have written very many other things besides, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Lacantinus, an Italian by nation, a most celebrated cultivator and expounder of both laws, won great glory by teaching and writing at Montpellier. He once held a place among the chief doctors among the professors of this art, because of certain highly commended volumes which he composed; among these, among others, there is said to be extant:

*A Summa of Trials*, 1 book.
Also on the Code, 9 books. It begins: “Since it is dangerous for me.”

Concerning the others I have found nothing. Mantua.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Rofredus, by country a Beneventan, a very distinguished doctor in both laws, subtle in intellect, composed in speech after the scholastic manner, and through long practice sufficiently suitable for resolving doubts and questions of law, wrote in that faculty little works not to be despised by students, by which he consecrated his name and reputation to immortality. Of these, however, we have been able to find only a few, which we have set down below: a very useful volume containing:

*Questions of Civil Law*, 1 book.
*Questions of Canon Law*, 1 book.
*A Summa of Law*, 1 book. It begins: “If I were to consider the intellect.”

On all actions. What more he published has as yet by no means come to my knowledge.

Peter, archbishop of Sens, learned in the divine Scriptures by constant study, rich in the reading of the ancients, and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote little works of no small usefulness, by which he both cultivated his own talent and prepared material for the edification of others. He wrote very subtly, with the opinions of the fathers appended: On all the epistles of Paul, 14 books.
Also various sermons, 1 book.

He also diligently expounded various books of the Bible, and is said to have written other treatises, varied and useful, which have not come to my knowledge.

Azo

*[page] 216. 178. ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.*

Azo, an Italian by nation, drawing the origin of [his] life from the city of Bologna, once hearer and disciple of John Bassiani of Cremona, a most learned man; a most famous interpreter of the civil law, a fountain of laws, an abundance of words, a lamp of law, who by his erudition and knowledge easily excels all the jurists who preceded him; he published many little works pertaining to the civil law, by which he acquired immortal praise and glory:
A notable Summa of law: 1 book.
On the Old Digest: 24 books.
On the Code also: 9 books.
Besides, he composed excellent apparatus on the laws, and appended additions to several Summas, and wrote various [things] which are not unknown to learned jurists.
He flourished in the times of Frederick II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1250, and left after him many distinguished disciples.

Giles de Fuscariis, a citizen of Bologna, a man most learned in canon law, and nobly erudite as much in the imperial laws as in the other disciplines of humanity, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence, a doctor of great authority among the ancient professors of this faculty, wrote certain illustrious volumes in that discipline, of which I have seen only:
On the office of the Notary: 1 book. ["It remains now that, concerning the office…"]
Various Questions of law.
The rest which he composed have as yet by no means come into our hands.

Francis, founder and prince of the order of Minors, an Italian by nation, sprung from Assisi, a city of Italy, a man of most holy conversation and a most ardent follower of evangelical poverty, who by word and example turned many from iniquity and directed [them] into the way of catholic justice; he was so great a lover of Christ that in contempt of the world and of transitory consolation he scarcely had an equal. In whose order many most learned men have thereafter become illustrious, who composed little works almost innumerable for the usefulness of the faithful. But Francis himself wrote, briefly:
The Rule of the Minors: 1 book. ["The Rule and life of the Minors…"]
A brief Testament: 1 book. ["The Lord gave to me, brother…"]
He flourished under Frederick II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Caesarius, monk at Heisterbach, of the Cistercian order, a Teuton by nation, of the diocese of Cologne, a devout man, outstanding in regular discipline, and studious in the divine Scriptures by long exercise, composed, for the instruction of novices, whose insti[tution]…

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

He was an instructor; in a simple and open style he composed some little works, the reading of which is not to be despised by devout and simpler brothers. Of these I have found only the following: A lengthy work on the miracles and various visions that occurred in his time in Germany, which, in imitation of Saint Pope Gregory, he entitled: Dialogues on Various Matters, 12 books. Incipit: “Gather up the fragments, lest...”

On the Sunday Gospels, 2 books. Incipit: “The cluster of Cyprus, beloved...”

Sermons to Novices, 4 books. Incipit: “Our Lord and Savior Jes...”

Besides these he published several others, which have not come to my knowledge.

William, a monk of the monastery of the blessed martyr Dionysius at Paris, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a Frenchman by nation, a man skilled in sacred Scripture through constant study, and outstandingly learned in the disciplines of secular letters, distinguished in talent and eloquence, and an eminent knower of the times, transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity by writing and teaching various things. Of these there is extant: A volume of Histories, 3 books.

And numerous letters to various persons, 4 books.

He is also reported to have published commentaries on sacred Scripture, which I have not yet seen.

James of Vitry, bishop of Acre, afterward cardinal of the holy Roman Church, bishop of Tusculum, a man learned in sacred Scripture and not ignorant of secular letters, notable in character and life, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. Gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, he marked many of the faithful against them by apostolic authority. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity, namely: Eastern History, 1 book.

Life of Mary of Oignies, 5 books.

Against the Saracens, 1 book.

On the Holy Women of Liège, 4 books.

Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

Besides these he composed some others, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Bonaguida of Arezzo, a man most learned in both laws above all others in his time, of great authority among the old professors of this faculty, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote for the benefit of students of law certain excellent volumes, by which he made himself useful to those present and known to those to come. Of these there is extant a noble summa, which he entitled: Introductory Work for Advocates, 2 books. Incipit: “Since of the office of advocacy...”

Pearl of Law, 1 book. Incipit: “When after the invasion...”

Declarations of Various Cases. But he is said to have composed certain other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Peter de Vineis, a German by nation, scribe and chancellor of Emperor Frederick II, a learned and eloquent man, but chiefly reprehensible in this: that, adhering to that Frederick, by his favor he foolishly barked against the Roman Church. At length, when he had offended him in certain matters, he was duly rewarded by him and lost the light together with his eyes. He wrote certain little works of his talent, of which I have found only: Letters in the Person of the Emperor, 6 books. Incipit: “The pontiffs have gathered...”

On Imperial Power, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the same Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Anthony, called of Padua, but Spanish by nation, born from the city of Lisbon, of the Order of Minors, disciple of Blessed Francis, a man most learned in sacred Scripture, since he taught gloriously for so long a time and left after him distinguished disciples; he was of such sanctity that, living and dead, he shone with many miracles. He was an exceedingly excellent preacher, so much so that the supreme pontiff was accustomed to call him the ark of the covenant. And Saint Francis was accustomed to call him his bishop. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote very elegant and most ardent: Sermons also on the Saints, 1 book. Incipit: “There shall be signs, he says...”

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. And because of the abundance of miracles after his death, he was immediately enrolled in the catalogue of the saints by Pope Gregory IX, together with Saints Dominic and Elizabeth, landgravine of the Thuringians.

Jordan of the Order of Preachers, after Saint Dominic, as they say, master general, a German by nation, a man practiced in sacred Scripture and sufficiently learned, an outstanding preacher of the word of God, venerable no less for sanctity than for learning, by his example and honey-sweet doctrine instructed many in piety. He is said to have written some little works, the reading of which is judged not useless for declaimers and devout brothers. Of these the following are reported: From the office of the priorate to the brothers of his order [unclear].

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

Several exhortatory letters, one book.
Sermons to the people, one book.
On the institution of the order, one book.
He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, at the same time also as Blessed Dominic, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Rupert of Bobbio, professor and expositor of both laws, most sagacious in interpretation, subtle in intellect, and brilliant in speech after the scholastic manner, who among the older professors of this science was held to be among its chief doctors, transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity by teaching and writing, as an example for others in learning and an aid to advancement. For he wrote a notable Summa, which he entitled: On the order of trials, *Because paternal piety*, one book.
Questions and determinations, one book.

And not a few other works, which nevertheless have by no means come into our hands.

Bernard Dorna, a Provençal by nation, once a hearer and disciple of the very famous man Azo of Bologna, a most learned professor and expositor of both laws, moved by the example of his most learned teacher, devoted himself wholly to letters and wrote various little works, by which he dedicated his name to immortality. Of these there is extant a distinguished volume: On the formulation of legal petitions, one book.

And other works which I have not seen.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Accursius, an Italian by nation, born in the city of Florence, once a hearer and disciple of Azo, a man most skilled in both laws and not least learned in the other disciplines of secular letters, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence. How great his authority is at this time among professors of law, no one even moderately learned is unaware. He wrote many excellent little works, and was the first to gloss the whole civil law: On the Old Digest. On the New Digest, twelve books.
On the Infortiatum, fourteen books. On the Code, twelve books.
On the Institutes, four books.

He also published not a few other works, which are very well known to students of law.

Johannes Fichardus relates in the Lives of the Jurists that he flourished in the year of the Lord 1226, at which time, as Accursius himself reports, he also composed glosses on the volume of the Authentics. He taught at Bologna, where, leaving behind his son Franciscus Accursius, himself also a jurist and professor, but far more obscure than his father, he died.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Upertus of Bonacurso, an Italian by nation, a man skilled in both laws, not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect and clear in speech, who among the older expositors of law was of no obscure reputation, composed in that faculty certain excellent little works, of which I do not remember any having come into our hands. There is reported to be his: On the preludes of cases, one book. *Since by imperial mandate*.
And certain works on trials.

We believe, however, that both those and his other works are not unknown to learned jurists.

John of Abbeville, archbishop of Besançon, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a Frenchman by nation, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, a very famous interpreter of those same sacred letters, who in the Parisian studium taught theology excellently for many years, and was most outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. For that reason especially, from a Parisian master he was made archbishop of Besançon. He wrote very useful and distinguished works: Sermons on the temporal cycle, two books.
Sermons on the saints, three books.

He also published many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He wrote the said sermons for the cycle of the year: first, to be sure, briefly expounding the short Gospel and apostolic readings; afterward, however, he published other sermons, both on Sundays and on feast days, so lengthy, introducing so many testimonies of the scriptures, that they could scarcely be committed to memory. Yet, with new ones now coming after them, they have in part fallen into little esteem.

Raymond of Penyafort, a Catalan or Provençal by nation, third master general of the Order of Preachers, a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect, distinguished in knowledge of canon law, made his name immortal by writing various works, and bound the Church to himself by his little works as a perpetual debtor, if I may so speak. For at the command of Pope Gregory IX he compiled: The Decretals of law, five books. *The peace-making king, with pious* [unclear].
A Summa on cases, six books. *Since, as Jerome says* [unclear].

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

Constitutions of his order, one book.
And certain other things.
He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Albertus Galeoti, by country a Parmese, a professor of canon and civil law and a famous interpreter, subtle in intellect, cautious in counsel, and scholastic in speech, who, because of his learning and experience in affairs, was counted among the chief doctors by the old jurists, wrote certain minor works in law not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with immortal praise. Of these there survives: The Summa Margarita of Questions, one book. “When I, Albertus Gal...”
And Declarations of Judgments, one book.
And certain other diverse works, unknown to us, are held by various persons.

Odofredus of Benevento, a hearer of Azo of Bologna and afterwards the teacher of Jacobus Balduini, a man most skilled in both laws, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, who left many distinguished disciples after him, was held in great authority among the ancients because of his teaching and erudition both in law and in the other humane letters. Many minor works of his are reported, by which he made his name known to posterity: On the Formation of Libels, one book. “After the work of the notary...”
On Judicial Order, one book. “As Christ...”
On the Art of the Notariate, one book.
And other works which I have not seen.
He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Johannes de Blanoso, Burgundian by nation, a man most learned in both laws and sufficiently instructed in the precepts of the secular philosophers, keen and ready in intellect, wrote in clear speech minor works not to be scorned by the professors of this faculty, by which the fame of his name became known far and wide both to those then present and to those who would come after. Of these there survives a volume of great utility, which he entitled: On the Actions of Advocates, one book. “I, Johannes de Blanoso...”
And Various Questions.
But the other works which he composed have not come to my knowledge.

Johannes, Teutonic by name and nation, born from the city of Freiburg, bishop of Bosnia in Hungary, of the Order of Preachers, a man much exercised in the divine Scriptures, learned in law, and excellently skilled in secular philosophy, who because of his learning and holiness of life had been taken from the order to the episcopate, which he later abandoned and returned to his order, and after Raymond was appointed master general of the order, did many good things. He wrote a notable Summa for Confessors, five books. “Since new matters of doubts...”
And certain other things.
He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1150. He was buried in his convent at Strasbourg, once shining, as they say, with many miracles.

Innocent, Pope IV, previously called Symbaldus, an Italian by nation, born from the city of Genoa, sat in the pontificate after Celestine IV for eleven years, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and in law, a lover of religious, who celebrated the general Council of Lyons, in which, with the consent of the fathers, he deposed Frederick from the empire and established many things for the utility of the Church. He nevertheless wrote certain excellent minor works, by whose publication he is worthily numbered among ecclesiastical writers, to be transmitted with them to the knowledge of posterity. Against Petrus de Vineis: On Ecclesiastical Power, one book.
An Apparatus on the Decretals, five books. “It is read in Ezekiel...”
The Rule of the Poor Clares, one book. “The form of life of the order...”
The Authentics also, one book.
Letters to Various Persons, one book.
And certain other things. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Rolandinus de Romanciis, a most celebrated professor and interpreter of both laws, and nobly learned in secular philosophy, who was not among the least with the old jurists, wrote in that faculty certain excellent minor works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I found only the Summa: On the Order of Crimes, one book. “The little book begins...”
Determinations and Questions.
The rest, which he is said to have composed, have not come to my knowledge.

Bernardus, priest of Compostela, intimate and chaplain of Pope Innocent IV, a man most learned in law, prompted by the zeal of that same pontiff, wrote certain excellent minor works in law, which are held in great authority in these times among jurists. Of these I have been able to find few, namely an eminent Apparatus: On the Decretals, five books. “At the beginning of this book...” Ca-

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

The Cases of the Decretals, 5 books. “The peaceful king, pious [unclear]…”
I have seen nothing of the rest.
He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

[Guido?] de Suzaria, a doctor most skilled in law and sufficiently instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, ready and cautious in counsel, among the ancients expert in these matters enjoyed great authority. He is said to have produced certain distinguished little works in law, among which there exists a notable Summa, which he entitled, in 4 books, On the Ordering of Cases.
Various Declarations also.
And many other works, which have not yet come into our hands.

Bartholomaeus Brixiensis, professor and interpreter of canon law, most [unclear] and excellently learned in the other disciplines of secular literature, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote various distinguished little works both in law and on other matters, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these the following are reported:
A Repertory of the Decretum, 3 books. “Since with favoring [unclear]…”
Disputations on the Decretals, 5 books.
A Chronicle of Italy, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.
And certain other works.
The same man wrote additions to the glosses of the Decretum.
Also Sunday and Friday Questions, 91 in number.
He also produced a history of times.

Johannes de Deo, professor and eminent expositor of both laws, and sufficiently learned in the disciplines of philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, who among the ancients was of great authority, wrote many various little works in both laws, through which the memory of his name came to the knowledge of many. Of these only a few have reached my knowledge. For I have found only the following:
A Summa of Cavillations, 7 books. “For the honor of the highest [unclear]…”
Another work entitled Judgment, 4 books. “At the beginning may [unclear] be present…”
A Table of the Decretum, 2 books. “The book of decretals [unclear]…”
A Concordance of the Decretum and the Decretals, 1 book. “For those willing, promptly…”
Various Questions.
He taught in the city of Bologna, where he composed the aforesaid works and others, from [unclear]

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Hugo Barchinonensis, of the Order of Preachers, cardinal priest of the title of Santa Sabina of the holy Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who before his entry into the order had been master of sacred theology and had had many distinguished pupils, wrote several excellent little works, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Shining no less brightly in conduct and religion than in knowledge, he remained the same in dignity as he had been before. Of his books these are reported:
On Genesis, 1 book. On Exodus, 1 book.
On Leviticus, 1 book. On Numbers, 1 book.
On Deuteronomy, 1 book. On Joshua, 1 book.
On Judges, 1 book. On the Books of Ruth, 1 book.
On Kings, 4 books. On Chronicles, 1 book.
On Ezra and Nehemiah, 5 books. On Tobit, 1 book.
On Judith, 1 book. On Esther, 1 book.
On the Books of Job, 1 book. On the Psalter, 1 book.
On Proverbs, 1 book. On Ecclesiastes, 1 book.
On the Song of Songs, 1 book. On the Book of Wisdom, 1 book.
On Ecclesiasticus, 1 book. On Isaiah the Prophet, 1 book.
On Jeremiah, 5 books. On Ezekiel, 1 book.
On Daniel, 1 book. On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 12 books.
On the Books of Maccabees, 2 books. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book.
On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book. On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book.
On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. On the Epistles of the Apostle Paul, 2 books.
On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. A Summa on Cases, 1 book.
He also composed several other works, which have not yet come to my knowledge.
He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Jacobus Baldeuini, formerly a hearer of Odofredus Beneventanus, a very distinguished man, professor and eminent interpreter of civil law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:
On the Code, 2 books. On the Old Digest, 11 books.
On the New Digest, 3 books. On the Infortiatum, 4 books.
And certain other works.
He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.
Da-

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

David, of the Order, as they say, of Minors, German by nation, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in life and conduct, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works in a plain style, the reading of which is not to be despised by devout brothers. Of these the following are extant: To novices.
On the composition of the outer man, one book.
On the composition of the inner man, one book.
Sermons on the season, one book.
Sermons on the Saints, one book.
And certain others.

He flourished not long after Blessed Francis; he is buried at Augsburg.

Humbert, of the Order of Preachers, the fifth master general, from his homeland a man of Vienne, formerly a pupil of Hugh of Barcelona the theologian, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding preacher, evangelical in life, pure in conscience, excellent in action, sweet in speech, fit for persuasion, who once drew Hugh, his own teacher of sacred theology, into the order: he wrote certain devout little works, by which his name came to the knowledge of posterity. Among them these are reported: On the Rule of Saint Augustine, one book.
A Summary for Preachers, one book.
The Deeds of the Friars Preachers, one book.
On the offices of his order, one book.
On the three substantial things of religion, one book.
Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Vincent the Gaul, Burgundian by nation, of the Order of Preachers, called of Beauvais, a man devoted to and practiced in the divine writings, and rich in ancient reading, subtle in intellect, ordered in speech, applied so much zeal to letters that he could never be called away from their cultivation by any labors, vigils, or occupations, since he was always either reading, writing, or preaching. Accordingly he was so great that after himself he necessarily had an equal, if we were to weigh with the others, in an even balance, the arduous little works that he wrote, laboriously collected from many sources. For, at his request and with the king of the Franks supplying the expenses, he brought together with the greatest labors a great and admirable work of Mirrors concerning everything, so to speak, knowable, in many volumes, which he entitled and divided thus:

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Historical Mirror, 32 books. God is a substance in
Natural Mirror, 53 books. Since the multitude in the book
Moral Mirror, 5 books. In all your things remember
Doctrinal Mirror, 4 books. Since the multitude in the book
Also On the Grace of God, 40 books. The book of the generation and [unclear]
On the Praises of Saint Mary, 7 books. If God with prophetic mouth [unclear]
On the Praises of Saint John the Evangelist. Blessed John the evangelist [unclear]
On the Education of Boys, 1 book. You have sons; instruct them [unclear]
A Consolation on the Dead, 1 book. First, therefore, attend
Letters to various persons, 1 book. He also published some other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Alexander of Hales, English by nation, of the Order of Minors, teacher of Cardinal Eustathius, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, when he was a doctor of sacred letters in the Parisian school, entered the order of the poor of Christ so that he might become a true disciple of heavenly philosophy; he wonderfully adorned it by his learning and holiness. At the command of Pope Innocent IV he wrote a distinguished work divided into four volumes, usefully embracing many things, which he entitled: Summa of Theology, 4 books. Since, as Boethius says. To the reverend in Christ [unclear]. The rest of his works I have not seen.

It is said, however, that he annotated both the Old and the New Testament for the most part, and discussed many matters subtly concerning the concord of divine and human law, and composed various other works, which have not come into our hands.

He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

John of La Rochelle, of the Order of the Friars Minor, master of sacred theology at Paris, learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently taught in Aristotelian philosophy, who, together with Alexander of Hales, subscribed himself in the declaration of the Rule of the Minors to the minister general: he published certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books.
A Summary of virtues and vices, 1 book.
Also On the Soul, 1 book.

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1250.
