Henry, archbishop of Embrun and cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, commonly called the Ostian, a man most skilled in both laws, who, on account of the excellence of his talent and learning, was held in esteem by Pope Alexander IV, wrote certain little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only the distinguished work known to all, *On the Titles of the Decretals*, in five books. “Alpha and omega, one in [unclear].” Also a concise *Summa*, in one book.

The other works that he composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1259.

[Unclear], a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in the disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, was of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported: for at the command of Pope Alexander IV he arranged, in a very useful style, through the cycle of the year, *Sermons*, in two books; *On the Sentences*, in four books; *Quodlibets*, in one book. “It is asked how virtue...”

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

[Unclear], a man exercised by long study in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and clear in eloquence, who in his own time, because of his learning and erudition, was of great reputation, wrote at the request of the provost and clerics of the church of Lille, *On the Psalter*, in one book, and certain letters.

He also published several other works, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Alexander, called de Villa Dei, of Dol as his native place, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Minor, a man certainly trained in every direction, a grammarian, philosopher, astronomer, and distinguished calculator, wrote not a few little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Of these I have so far found only the following: a volume written in leonine verse on grammar, whose use today is constant in boys’ schools, [unclear] so useful, because of the weakness of the younger age and the sloth of teachers. He prefaced this same work

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

The *Doctrinale puerorum*, [unclear]. “I prepare to write for little clerics...”
*On the ecclesiastical computus*, one book. “Although now at the end of time...”
*On the sphere*, one book.
*On the art of numbering*, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, sermons, letters, and various treatises, which have not yet come into our hands.

He flourished with great piety and learning under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Eustathius, who is Bonaventura, born at Bagnoregio, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, and afterwards bishop of Albano, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, formerly a hearer and disciple of Alexander of Hales, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, devout and most holy in life and conduct: when his teacher Alexander contemplated his intellect, his natural gift, and the purity of his life, he used to say: “In Brother Bonaventura Adam does not seem to have sinned.” He wrote many profound and most devout little works, in which, bringing forth burning words, he no less kindles the reader’s affection in the love of Christ than he enlightens the intellect with holy teachings. For he easily surpasses all the doctors of his time in the usefulness of his works, if you attend to the spirit of divine love and Christian devotion speaking in him. He is profound, not wordy; subtle, not curious; eloquent, not empty; bringing forth words that are flaming, not puffed up. Hence he is read more safely, understood more easily by one who loves, more sweetly retained the more often he is read, and more fruitfully. Many set forth doctrine; many, though few, preach devotion; by writing books they have taught both. But Bonaventura surpassed many, and few [equaled him], since his doctrine instructs devotion, and devotion instructs doctrine. Therefore, if you wish to be called devout, be attentive to his little works. These are:

*On the Sentences*, [unclear] books. “The depths of rivers...”
*Breviloquium*, one book. “Tell me, I ask, O man...”
*Soliloquium*, one book. “In the beginning, first...”
*Itinerary of the Mind into God*, one book. “I am fixed with Christ...”
*The Tree of Life*, one book. “Since, my beloved brother...”
*Exhortation to a Brother*, one book. “Every best gift...”
*On the Reduction of the Arts*, *The Rule of Those Making [unclear]: a small good*, one book. “Behold, I have described it to you...”

He also published some other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He died while the empire was vacant, under Pope Gregory X, in the Council of Lyons, in the year of the Lord 1285, in the first indiction, and was buried in the cathedral church of Lyons. At last, on account of his sanctity and miracles, he was canonized in our own days by Pope Sixtus IV, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1482, in the fifteenth indiction.

Philippus, chancellor of Paris, a man learned in the divine scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, since he was a famous master of sacred letters, presided gloriously for a long time over the theological school at Paris, where by lecturing to his students and preaching to the people he instructed them magnificently. He wrote two or three elegant sermons on each of the psalms, 1 book; a Summa of theology, 1 book.

He also published many other works, which by no means have come to our knowledge.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Albertus, bishop of Regensburg, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, a Swabian by homeland, originating from Lauingen, a man very studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and in secular philosophy second to none in his time; subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout and most holy in life and conduct. Because of his teaching and learning he was called Magnus. He taught sacred letters and Aristotelian philosophy for many years, first at Paris, later at Cologne, where among others he had Thomas Aquinas as an excellent pupil. Then, having been assumed to the episcopate of the church of Regensburg, after he had governed it for some years, he left it, and out of love for saving study returned to his convent at Cologne, where he continued teaching and writing until the end of his life. He wrote many and almost countless little works, of which the following are reported: Summa of Theology, 4 books.
On the Sentences, 4 books.
On the Four Coeval Things, 1 book.
On Man, 1 book.
On the Good, 1 book.
On the Spiritual Life, 1 book.
On the Office of the Mass, 1 book.

He wrote commentaries on the books of Aristotle, and composed many other works which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished at Paris in the year of the Lord 1257.
He died under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280, in the eighth indiction, in the eightieth year of his age, and was buried in the middle of the choir of his convent at Cologne. And after him there arose no man like him, who was so learned, educated, and expert in all letters, sciences, and matters. But as to his being accused of necromancy, this man beloved by God suffers injustice.

Simon of Tournai, priest, learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly instructed in secular philosophy, a very acute dialectician and most skilled in all the liberal arts, having been made master of the theological school, taught for many years in the university of Paris, where he instructed very many hearers. But while he follows Aristotle too much, he is found to have erred in certain matters. He wrote, however, a certain little work of his own talent:
On Athanasius, 1 book.
Various Questions, 1 book.
On the Creed, 1 book.
He also published some other works which have not come to my knowledge.

Thomas, of the counts of Aquino, of the Order of Preachers, hearer and disciple of Albert the Great in the convent at Cologne, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, notable in life and conduct, easily obtained primacy among all the doctors of his time. Like another Augustine, he gave himself wholly to the study of Scripture, spending day and night in its love and practice, and wrote so many and such great volumes that among the moderns he has few equals either in number or in usefulness 196 *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

On Time, 1 book. “Since it is holy, honor...”
On the Plurality of Forms, 1 book. “Since to know is the cause of a thing...”
On the Nature of Syllogisms, 1 book.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On sense and intellect, one book. It begins: Concerning consideration...

On the discovery of the middle term, one book. It begins: Since the principle of a syllogism...

On the nature of light, one book. It begins: It must be considered concerning [unclear].

On the nature of place, one book. It begins: For knowing the nature...

On universals, two books. It begins: Concerning universals much...

On intellect and the intelligible, one book. It begins: It must be known that of the nature...

The agreement of his own sayings, one book. It begins: Many shall pass through...

And many sermons, one book.

Against William of Saint-Amour, one book.

At the command of Pope Urban IV he composed the office for the feast of the Body of Christ. He commented on all the books of Aristotle and Porphyry. He also published many other works, both on divine scriptures and on secular philosophy, which have by no means come into our hands.

He died under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1274, in the second indiction. And he was canonized by Pope John XXII.

Thomas of Cantimpre, a Brabanter by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a certain disciple, as they say, of Albert the Great, a devout man, excellently learned both in divine scriptures and in secular letters, ready in talent, scholastic in eloquence, is said to have written certain distinguished volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant a work on mystical bees, which he entitled The Universal Good, one book. It begins: To the reverend in Christ...

On the nature of things, one book.

The life of Saint Christina, one book.

And other works which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270. And there are those who write that he had knowledge of the Greek language and translated the books of Aristotle that are now in use in the schools.

Alfonso, king of Castile and Leon, a philosopher and astronomer most excellent among all men of his time, subtle in talent and distinguished in speech, an outstanding lover and cultivator of letters, after a long vacancy of the Roman Empire, had been elected king of the Romans against Richard, brother of the king of England; and since he was a good and prudent man, when Richard died in the fifteenth year of his election, with a view to peace he voluntarily yielded before Pope Gregory X and freely renounced every right that he had had in his election. He wrote very useful and elegant works:

*Abbot of Spanheim*

Astronomical tables, one book.

Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished in the time of the vacant Empire, in the year of the Lord 1270.

[unclear]

Peter, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a Gaul by nation, and provincial prior in France of the same religious order, a man learned in divine scriptures by long study and not ignorant of secular philosophy, acute in talent and ready in speech, was apt in delivering sermons to the people. Hence, for the use of readers, he composed, through the cycle of the year, sermons not to be despised: Sermons for the season, one book.

Sermons also on the saints, one book.

But he is said also to have written some other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Peter of Tarentaise, of the Order of Preachers, and, after Gregory X, canonically consecrated pope under the name Innocent V, sat in the supreme pontificate for only five months. Certainly he was a man most learned in divine scriptures and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, who taught theology excellently for many years and acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote many distinguished little works, by which he made his name known both to those then present and to those who would come afterward. Of these there are extant: On the Sentences, one book. It begins: Do you know the order...

On all the epistles of Paul, one book. It begins: To inquire into the principles of things...

On the Psalms also, one book.

John of Ascoli, from Ascoli, of the Order of Friars Minor, minister general after Saint Bonaventure, a man learned in divine scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, was sent to Constantinople by Pope Gregory X. By his exhortations he brought the Greeks back to obedience to the Roman Church, and persuaded them to come with him to the Council of Lyons. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, works not to be despised: Sermons for the season, one book.

Sermons on the saints, one book.

Several letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished while the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1170.

Ru

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

Rupert of Rusia, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, inasmuch as he taught theology excellently for many years and left after him many distinguished disciples, wrote several excellent little works by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there is extant, addressed to Haymo the Englishman, minister general of his order, a man likewise most learned, a Declaration, one book.

On the Rule of St. Francis, four books.
Also on the Sentences, four books.
Various sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Udalric of Argentina, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, formerly a hearer and disciple of Albert the Great, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, composed little works not to be despised in reading, by which he became known to both present and future generations. Of these there are extant: A Summa of Theology, one book.

On the Sentences, four books.
Also On the Soul, one book. And many other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Haymo, an Englishman by nation, minister general of the order of friars, a man trained by long study in the holy Scriptures, who, having obtained the magisterial chair of the theological faculty, instructed many disciples in it, and who, by order of Pope Alexander IV, corrected and rubricated the Roman Breviary, is reported, among other things, to have written briefly: On the Sentences, one book. And certain sermons, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1279.

Otto, bishop of Freising in Bavaria in Germany, and, as some write, nephew of the emperor Frederick I, a German by nation, whom Pope Pius II, citing him in a certain oration, commends, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not meanly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, wrote certain little works not contemptible in reading, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a distinguished work, to be pursued with every praise: Histories, one book. And other things which I have not seen. He flo[unclear]

*Abbot of Spanheim*

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

Peter the Spaniard, a Portuguese, bishop of Tusculum and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, and finally supreme pontiff after Hadrian V, a man very learned in medicine and magnificently instructed in secular philosophy, sat in the pontificate for only eight months. He wrote little works not to be despised by physicians, of which the following are reported: Thesaurus pauperum, one book. On Problems, one book.
Canons of Medicine, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book.
And certain other things, namely several treatises in dialectic, already long very well known commonly.

He flourished in the pontificate under the name John XXI, in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1275.

William, a citizen of Piacenza, a learned doctor of the art of medicine and not ignorant of other humane letters, who, hired at a public salary at Verona, maintained a school in that faculty for many years and instructed several excellent disciples, wrote little works not to be despised by professors of this science, by which he made his name known to both present and future generations. Of these there is extant a distinguished volume which he wished to be entitled: On Universal Medicine, four books. Also On Surgery, one book.
Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William, bishop of Paris, by native land an Auvergnat, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent and open in eloquence, and venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge, composed not a few works of his learning, by which, showing himself both a learned and devout master, he rendered the memory of his name immortal. Of these the following are reported: a distinguished volume, entitled: On the Holy Trinity, one book. On the First Principle, one book.
On the Sacraments, one book. I shall add still four [unclear], one book.
Summa of Vices, one book.
Why God Became Man, one book. In the Order of Divine [unclear], one book.
On Good and Evil, one book.
Summa of Virtues, one book. On the Profession of Novices, one book.
On Faith and Laws, one book. On the Works of Virtues, one book.
On Human Souls, one book. [unclear] On the Tri[unclear]
On the Universe, one book. 401
On the Gift of Knowledge, one book. 203

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

*On the Thirty Remedies for Temptations*, 1 book.
*Against the Plurality of Benefices*, 1 book.
*On the Cloister of the Soul*, 1 book.
*On Divine Rhetoric*, 1 book.
*On Penance*, 1 book.
*On Demons*, 1 book.
*On the Psalter*, 1 book.
*On Ecclesiastes*, 1 book.
*On the Gospel of Matthew*, 1 book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, [unclear] books.
He also published certain other works which have by no means come to my knowledge.
He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

John Valeis, otherwise Galensis, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who for a long time taught theology with distinction in the school of Paris, was of such great learning and eloquence that he was called the Tree of Life. He wrote many excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But few of them have come into our hands. For I found a notable volume, which I judge very necessary and useful for preachers of the word of God, which most people call the *Communiloquium*, because it contains something concerning every estate; but he himself entitled it:
*Sum of Collations*, 7 books. "Since the doctor or preacher ..."
*On the Sentences*, 4 books.
*On the Ordering of Life*, 1 book. "Since in every undertaking ..."
*Handful of Flowers*, 1 book. "Abstinence is good in ..."
*On the Apocalypse of John*, 1 book.
*Various Sermons*, 1 book.
*On Diverse Subjects*, 1 book.
Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

And note that this book of John is called the *Handful of Flowers*, whose prologue begins, "Poor little Ruth"; he began it, but, prevented by death, did not finish it, but Brother Thomas of Ireland afterwards completed the same work. The book itself begins thus, according to alphabetical order: "Abstinence is good in food to receive with thanksgiving," etc. He flourished in the times of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William Durandus, bishop of Mende, once a hearer and disciple of Henry of Ostia, whom they call the Speculator, a most pious doctor in law and very zealous for ecclesiastical observance, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, wrote to Ottobono, cardinal of St. Hadrian, afterwards supreme pontiff, Hadrian V, an outstanding work divided into three volumes, which he entitled:
*Mirror of Law*, 3 books. "Reverend in Christ ..."
*Rationale of Divine Offices*, 8 books. "Whatever things in the ecclesiastical ..."
*Repertory of Law*, 1 book. "By the rust of the first-formed man ..."
And certain other works.
He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, and completed his work the *Rationale of Divine Offices*, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord 1286.

James of Belusio, a very distinguished doctor of both laws and a careful interpreter, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, profound in counsel and knowledge, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, is said to have written certain excellent little works in law, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity; of these I have not yet been able to see any. His works are said to be:
*On the Authentics*, 1 book.
*On the View of Fiefs*, 1 book.
*Additions on the Novels*, 1 book.
And many other works.
And various disputations.
He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William of Lyons, of the Order of Friars Preachers, as they say, bishop of the same church, a man much learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of sweet intellect and subtle speech, not over-curious, yet orderly, was quite outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have written certain little works, by which he magnificently instructed both those then present and those who would come afterwards; of these they report:
*On the Sentences*, 4 books.
*Sum of Virtues*, 5 books. "Since concerning individual useful things ..."
*Sum of Vices*, 8 books. "About to speak of individual vices ..."
*Sermons to the People*, 1 book.
He is said to have written many other works also, which have not come to my knowledge.

William of Ware, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, teacher of John Scotus of the same order, a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures and, through long study, very skilled in Aristotelian philosophy, in the manner of modern theologians, wrote certain works of his intellect not to be despised, by which he made himself known to posterity. Of these there are extant:
*On the Sentences*, 1 book. "Since, according to the testimony of Blessed Augustine ..."
Concerning the rest I have seen nothing.

204 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Gerard, a monk of the monastery of St Quentin in the Isle, a man devoted to the Holy Scriptures and skilled through continual exercise, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, by which he made his name known to those present and those to come. Among these is said to be a history of the translation of the crown and of part of the Lord's cross, which relics Louis, king of France, obtained from the emperor of Constantinople and transferred to Paris. He also wrote concerning blessed Elizabeth the Landgravine: Miracles after her death, four books.
Responsories and chants concerning the same, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280. And in both kinds of literature he composed various little works.

William Lamarensis, of the order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by long use and exercise, and also, according to the custom of that time, sufficiently skilled in secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, composed various little works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books.
Correctory of the works of Thomas, one book.
Additions on Bonaventure, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1289.

Richard, archbishop of Reims in Gaul, of the order of Friars Minor, excellently learned in the Holy Scriptures, inferior to none of the doctors of his time in delivering sermons to the people, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, is said to have written many excellent volumes, by which he rendered himself useful to those then present and known to those to come; but I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. The following are reported as his: Sermons for the season, one book.
Also sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William of Samuco, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary Ever-[unclear]

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

[unclear] learned in the Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, venerable no less in manner of life than in learning, published several little works of great usefulness, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported: a certain little work not useless to spiritual persons, which he entitled:

Decretals of religious, one book.
On the Sentences, one book.
On the rule of his order, one book.
Chronicle of his order, one book.
And many other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Aegidius of Rome, of the order of the Hermit Friars of St Augustine, prior general and afterward archbishop of Bourges, formerly a hearer of blessed Thomas Aquinas, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct, wrote almost innumerable little works, of which few have come into our hands. The following are reported as his:

[unclear], two books.
On the Hexaemeron, “Let your voice sound in my ears,” one book.
On the epistles of Paul, four books. “For it is the brightness of light,” one book.
“From the most sacred royal [unclear],” one book.
“Questions proposed,” one book.
[unclear], one book.
Exposition of the first decretal, Firmiter credimus, one book.
On the government of princes, one book.
Many quodlibets, one book.
[unclear], one book.
On the office of the Mass, one book.
On the possible intellect, one book.
Praises of divine wisdom, one book.
On divine wisdom in the blessed, one book.
On the subject of theology, one book.
On good fortune, one book.
On the body of Christ, one book.
On the measure of angels, “Because among the other things which,” one book.
“That concerning the measure of angels,” one book.
On the knowledge of angels. The question: “Whether angels,” one book.
[unclear], one book.
Distinction of the articles of faith, one book.
On the degrees of forms, one book. “It has been asked concerning God.”
[unclear] On pre-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On predestination, one book. “To the noble knight, lord ...”
The Theory of Being and Essence, one book. “Every being either is ...”
On the Soul, as the Philosopher attests ...
On generation and corruption, one book. “I am dust ...” In which are set forth ...
On original sin, one book. “Of theological truth ...”
On the formation of the human body, one book. “It will not please him when ...”
On ecclesiastical power, five books. “Why have you disparaged ...” [unclear]
[unclear], one book. And not a few other works.
A Compendium of Theology, six books.
On the Renunciation of the Pope, one book.
Against the Corrupter of Thomas, one book.
Various Sermons, two books.
On all the books of Aristotle.
Notable Letters.
He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

[unclear], chaplain of the pontiff, as they say, a man nobly learned in canon law and secular philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, who in his own time was considered not least among the doctors of this faculty, wrote some little works not to be despised in their reading, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a notable Summa, sufficiently widely circulated:

On the Titles of the Decretals, five books. “The diversity of glosses in ...”
Various Questions, one book.
Other works which he is said to have composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Guido de Baysio, archdeacon of Bologna, a man most skilled in both laws, acute in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, whose authority among the professors of this science has endured greatly down to the present day, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which, so to speak, he rendered the memory of his name immortal. Of these only a few have so far come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following: a very large and highly notable volume, which he entitled Rosarium: On the Decree, three books. “Reverend in Christ ...”
On the Decretals, five books.
He flourished under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Thaddaeus, a Florentine by nation, a most skilled doctor of the medical art, who taught that science excellently at Bologna for certain years, hired at a public salary, gathered an almost incredible treasure and acquired a great reputation for his experience. For when he was called by some prince, he wished to have no less than fifty gold coins as his daily wage. Once called by Pope Honorius IV, he refused to come until one hundred gold coins per day were appointed for him; when the pope had been cured of a most serious illness, he bestowed ten thousand gold coins on him. He wrote: On the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, one book.
On the Prognostics of the same, one book.
On the Work on Acute Diseases of the same, one book.
On Galen’s Techne, one book.
On the Isagoge of Johannitius, one book.
On Preserving Health, one book.
Various Counsels, one book.
And certain other works.
He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.
And at last, an octogenarian, he died at Bologna.

John of Parma, born from the territories of Bologna, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding lover of holy poverty, who from the Parisian school, where he had lectured on the Sentences, was elected general in his absence, is said to have written many and various treatises, by which his name has come down to our memory. Of these I have found only: On the Sentences, four books.
On the Conduct of Religious, two books.
He flourished while the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

John Christophori, of the Order of Friars Preachers, exercised in the scriptures by long and continual study and nobly learned in secular philosophy, ready in talent and scholastic in speech, is said to have fashioned many little works on the holy scriptures; their publication made him, useful to those then present, known to those to come. For over a long time he expounded the divine writings publicly by lecturing and explained them with subtle understanding. From his commentaries the following volumes are reported, namely: On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On Mark, one book.
On Luke, one book. On John, one book.
On all the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.
And many other works.

208 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

Hambaldus, a Roman by nationality, professor of sacred theology and an outstanding interpreter of the Scriptures, subtle and forceful in intellect, and quite capable in disputing and solving their difficult questions, is said to have written certain excellent little works for the instruction of his disciples, by which he made his name known. Among these there are extant: On the Sentences, one book. Quodlibets, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolph, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Henry of Ghent, archdeacon of Tournai, German by nationality, a man among all the doctors of his time most learned in the divine Scriptures, and very subtle in Aristotelian philosophy, was of such reputation and authority in the University of Paris that he was called the Solemn Doctor throughout the whole Christian world. For he was subtle in intellect and most acute in scholastic disputations, as his excellent works testify. Of these I have found only the following at present: Summa of Theology, one book. On the Sentences, two books. To the Sacred Virgins, beginning “Concerning virginity,” one book. On Penance, one book. On the Metaphysics, three books. On the books of the Physics, five books. On Metaphysics, four books. He indeed composed many other things, but they have not come to my knowledge.

He died under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1293, in the sixth indiction, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, and was buried at Tournai in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God.

Hugolinus, patriarch of Constantinople, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man trained by long study in the divine writings and sufficiently learned, subtle in intellect, almost scholastic, noteworthy in character and life, is said to have written certain excellent little works, of not contemptible reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following, among others, are reckoned the better ones: On the Sentences, three books. Quodlibets, six books. On the Difference of Idioms, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Arlotus, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, Tuscan by nationality, a man excellently learned in the divine writings and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, a subtle dialectician and a most acute disputant, who won great praise for his learning by writing variously, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people. He is said to have assembled the Concordances of the New and Old Testament into one volume, one book. Various Sermons, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Adolf, in the year 1290.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

James, bishop of Genoa, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man trained in the divine Scriptures, who because of his frequent citations of them was called Vorago, quick in intellect and clear in speech, was quite capable in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote not a few little works for the use of readers, by which he made his name known. Of these a few have come to my knowledge, which I have also set down below: A volume of great size on the life and deeds of many saints, which he entitled the Golden Legend or Mirror of Saints, but which is now commonly called the Legend or Lombardic History, one book. The whole present time [unclear]. “As I consider, the days [unclear].” On Saint Mary, one book.

Chronicle of the Genoese, one book.

On the Little Works of Saint Augustine, one book. “Sacred Scripture [unclear].” Sermons on the Season, one book.

“Following his footsteps [unclear] outstanding, in intellect [unclear] as I consider, the days [unclear].” Sermons on the Saints, one book.

An excellent preacher of the Word, distinguished in intellect and clear [unclear], he taught the people in truth, and, with the Holy Spirit working together, he brought the hearts of many to the love of Christ. He wrote sermons not to be despised, which he delivered to the people: Sermons on the Season, one book.

He is also said to have written a number of other things, which have not come into our hands.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Conrad of Halberstadt, German by nationality, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man nobly learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a philosopher and theologian not worthless, since by lecturing publicly in that faculty he taught many and acquired great praise for his learning, wrote certain things in both

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

... not to be despised in learning, by which he brought his name down to the memory of posterity. But few of them have become known to me. For I have found only: A *Summa for Students*, 3 books. “This little work into three ...”
Also *On the Trivium*, 1 book. “In three [unclear] ...”
A *Lecture on Job*, 1 book. “Until the time [unclear] ...”
Also *Sermons*, 1 book.

He is also said to have written commentaries on several books of the Bible, which, however, have not yet come into our hands. He is also said to have been the first to arrange concordances of the whole Bible of the New and Old Testament.

Richard of Middleton, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed both in philosophy and in canon law, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, subtle and ready in resolving questions and doubts concerning the Scriptures, is said to have written many very distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

*On the Sentences*, 4 books. “He brought forth hidden things ...”
*On the distinctions of the Decretum*, 1 book. “All our fathers under ...”
*On the Order of Judgments*, 1 book.
*On the Epistles of Paul*, 4 books.

It is said, moreover, that he issued elegant commentaries and lectures on several books of sacred Scripture, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Adolf and Pope Nicholas IV, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Nicholas of Bibra, German by nation, a man nobly learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher and distinguished poet, who at Erfurt in his time was held in esteem, acquired great glory for his learning and wrote not a few little works both in meter and in prose, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only a work whose title is hidden, which he composed at Erfurt in verse and in prose:

*On Avoiding Evil*, 1 book. “Hearer of the poem ...”
*Letters to Various Persons*, 1 book.

He flourished at Erfurt under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

John of Paris, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a theologian most learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, since, indeed, having ascended the magisterial chair in both branches of learning in the university of Paris, he taught publicly for a long time and left not a few disciples, is said to have written certain distinguished little works, by which he made himself useful to those then present and afterwards known to those to come. Of these I have found only a work not to be despised:

*On the Sentences*, 4 books.

Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

*Abbot of Spanheim*

Nicholas the Frenchman, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, seventh prior general, a learned and holy man, who, after he had ruled his order vigorously for almost twenty years, as far as he was able, yielded his office for love of Christ and returned to the quiet of the hermitage, where he persevered in holy conduct until death, wrote, among other things, a mournful work lamenting the state of his order, when the brothers had been expelled from the Holy Land, which he entitled:

*The Fiery Arrow*, 1 book.

He wrote other things also. He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Matthew of Aquasparta, otherwise Aquasputa, of the Order of Friars Minor, twelfth minister general, and afterwards bishop of Porto and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, a man most learned in these divine Scriptures and, according to the custom of this time, magnificently instructed in secular philosophy, composed certain distinguished little works of excellent talent, by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these the following are extant:

*On the Sentences*, 4 books.
*Inventory of Sentences*, 1 book.
*On the Epistle to the Romans*, 1 book.
*Several Sermons*, 1 book.

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1390.

William Peraldus, French by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and also sufficiently excellently instructed in secular letters, especially in Aristotelian philosophy, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, was of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He issued, in both faculties, several instructive volumes, by which he made his name known not only to those then present, but also to those to come. Of these there are extant:

*Summa of Virtues and Vices*, 2 books.
*On the Instruction of Religious*, 1 book.
*Sermons on the Season*, 1 book.
*Sermons on the Saints*, 1 book.

And very many other things, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

218 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* Garcias, Spanish by nation, a man most practiced in both laws, subtle in intellect, ready and cautious in counsel, acute in resolving questions of cases, held in esteem among the professors of this faculty in his time, extended his name by teaching and writing. For he is said to have written several small works both in the laws and in canon law, which have not come into our hands. There are extant by him:

*On the Decretals, five books.*

And several works in the laws.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

[Nicolaus?] IV, pope, of the order of the Friars Minor, [Hieronymus?] [unclear], sat after Honorius IV in the chair of Peter for four years: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not meanly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and venerable no less for goodness of life than for learning. He wrote a sufficiently excellent work:

*On the Sentences, four books.*

And certain sermons.

He is also said to have published useful commentaries on several books of the Bible. He died at Rome, the empire being vacant after Rudolf’s death, in the year of the Lord 1291, in the fourth indiction.

Boniface VIII, pope, Campanian by nation, previously called Benedict, sat after the renunciation of Celestine V in the chair of Peter for eight years and nine months; a man indeed learned, but excessively arrogant and ambitious. By what means he acquired the pontificate, the chronographers have not passed over in silence. Since he was very skilled in law and saw that new varieties of cases were daily arising in the contentious forum which could not be determined through the Decretals, he composed, through three men most learned in law, new constitutions, which he wished to be called:

*The Sixth of the Decretals of the Most Holy Roman [Church], one book.*

Letters, several, to various persons, one book.

He died under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1305, indiction 1. Concerning him it had previously been prophesied: “He entered like a fox, lived like a lion, died like a dog.”

Guilhelmus Mandagoti, archdeacon of Nimes, afterward archbishop of Embrun, and of the most holy church

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

... finally cardinal of the Roman Church, a man highly skilled in both laws, one of those who, by order of Pope Boniface VIII, issued the Sixth Book of the Decretals, as is clear at the beginning of that same volume. In that faculty he wrote works not to be despised, by which he preserved his name for immortality. Of these I have seen only the notable work which he wrote while he still held the office of archdeacon in the church of Nîmes, to Berengarius, succentor of the church of Béziers and afterwards bishop: On the election of prelates, book 1. “Because while elections in ...”
Exposition of the same, book 1. “Since I am not the author of that ...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Berengarius, succentor of the church of Béziers and afterwards bishop, and at last cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, to whom the aforesaid Guilhelmus Mandagoti, while both were still established in minor orders, composed the book On the Elections of Prelates, another of those who, at the command of Boniface VIII, compiled the Sixth Book of the Decretals, a man very learned in the same legal faculty, while he was still succentor, wrote to that same Guilhelmus, then archdeacon of Nîmes, a notable work on the Summa of Hostiensis according to alphabetical order; since it is, as it were, a clarifying glossary of that same Summa, he entitled it: The Eye, book 1.
On the sentence of excommunication, book 1.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1309.

Richardus de Senis, vice-chancellor of the Roman Church, and afterwards [unclear], in the praise of all [unclear] very celebrated in his time, the third of those who compiled the Sixth Book of the Decretals by order of Pope Boniface VIII, whose name is expressly contained at the beginning of that same volume, is reported to have written several works in law; but I do not remember that any of them have come into our hands. Let the studious reader inquire after them.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Dinus Mugelanus, professor of both laws and a notable expounder, subtle in intellect, and very ready and acute in disputing and resolving doubtful matters and questions of law, who by teaching and writing acquired great glory for himself among all the doctors of Italy, published many distinguished works in his faculty, among which the following are reported. By command of Lord Pope Boniface VIII he was the first after the archdeacon to write elegantly: On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, book 1.
On the Code, 10 books.
On the Old Digest, 24 books.
On the New Digest, 12 books.
On the Infortiatum, 14 books.
Many Consilia, book 1.

Besides these he also published not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He also wrote On Interest; On Prescriptions; On Successions from Intestacy; On the Method of Arguing; Contrary Glosses and their Agreements.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Johannes Duns, a Scot by birth, of the Order of Friars Minor, once a hearer of Alexander of Hales the Englishman at Paris, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and very learned in Aristotelian philosophy, and so profound that his writings are penetrable [unclear], and for that reason also less commonly used, published certain instructive volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant: On the Sentences, 4 books. “Desiring ... Around the prologue ...”
Quodlibets, book 1. “All difficult matters ...”
On the Knowledge of God, book 1. “Because the highest ... for us ...”
Questions on the Metaphysics, book 1.
Sermons on the season, book 1. “There shall be signs,” etc. “In this ...”
Sermons on the saints, book 1.

He is said to have written commentaries on the Gospel and the Apostle, and to have composed various other treatises, which have not come to my knowledge.

He died in the time of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1398, in the sixth indiction, and was buried at Cologne among the Friars Minor.

Simon, monk of Hasnon [unclear], of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, so put into practice the counsel of our divine lawgiver Benedict, by which the monk is commanded to love the divine Scriptures, that nothing in this life was sweeter to him than to read the sacred writings and to turn over with diligent study the works of the holy fathers. He abridged: The Moralia of Pope Gregory, 10 books.
On the Song of Songs he wrote sermons, book 1.
The vision of a certain convert, book 1.
Several sermons, book 1.

Epi...

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

Also letters to various persons, 1 book.
And many other things.

He also collected excerpts from the sermons of blessed Pope Gregory on Ezekiel; also from the Conferences of the holy fathers, from Richard of Saint Victor’s *On the Contemplation of the Twelve Patriarchs*, and various worthwhile things from various authors.

Peter de Bella Parthica, otherwise Pertica, a Burgundian by nation, a man most skilled in both civil and canon law, subtle and acute in intellect, and very ready in disputing and resolving doubtful questions of law, wrote many excellent volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, the following are reported: On the Code, 9 books.
On the Institutes, 4 books.
On the Old Digest, 24 books.
On the New Digest, 12 books.
On the Infortiatum, 14 books.
One Hundred Disputations, 1 book.
Several Opinions.
And certain other things.

He flourished at the same time as Dinus Mugelanus, under Emperor Albert and Pope Boniface VIII, in the year of the Lord 1300.

[Rainerus?] of Pisa, otherwise Rainerius, an Italian by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently skilled in canon law, quick in intellect, scholastic in speech, cautious in counsel, venerable no less for religion than for learning, in order to provide a path in hearing confessions for his brothers who were less experienced in law, wrote a great and distinguished *Summa* on cases, in two large volumes according to alphabetical order, which he entitled:

*Pantheologia*, 2 books. 'Absolution. Concerning abso[unclear]'
And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Gerard, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, lector of the convent of Liege, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding declaimer in making sermons to the people, distinguished in intellect and adorned with scholastic eloquence, wrote a very useful treatise for devout religious persons, teaching the seven dispositions to be made concerning the heart, and sagaciously gathering from the divine Scriptures on every side many things pertaining to edification, which he entitled:

*On the Teaching of the Heart*, 1 book. 'Prepare your hearts.'
Sermons for the Season, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.

In addition he published certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

James de Arena, a native of Parma, a very celebrated jurist in both laws, profound in intellect, scholastic in speech, whose opinions in explaining the laws, as Bartolus testifies, were so proper and fitting that [unclear] concerning civil understanding many excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name to the perpetual memory of posterity: On the Code, 9 books.
On the New Digest, 24 books.
On the Old Digest, 12 books.
On the Infortiatum, 14 books.
On Excuses, 1 book.
Various Disputations, 1 book.

But he also published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

John of San Gimignano, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man studious and especially learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in intellect and clear in speech, of excellent industry in declaiming sermons to the people, acquired great praise and fruit of doctrine in the salvation of souls. He wrote, among other things: On the Similitudes of Things, 1 book.
Sermons for the Season, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
Various Conferences, 1 book.

In addition he is said to have written certain other things, which have not come to me.

Peter of Dacia, a philosopher, calculator, and astronomer, the most excellent and celebrated among all men of his time, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures and of the Greek language, is said to have written many little works in astronomy and the art of calculation, which are judged not useless for ecclesiastical computation, by which he destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge.

On Calculation or Computation, 1 book.
Also a Calendar, 1 book.
And of his tables, 1 book.

The rest, although there are many things that he composed, have nevertheless not come to me.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Nicholas of Naples, a man skilled and very learned in civil law, nobly instructed also in other secular letters, whose authority among the professors of this faculty flourished in no small measure in his time, wrote several little works on the laws, of which

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

By the publication of books he entrusted his name to immortality. But I have been able to find only the titles of the following: On the Code, 9 books.
On the Infortiatum, 14 books.

Of the other things which he is said to have composed, I have so far been able to find nothing certain. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Hubertinus of Casale, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of Johannes of Parma, minister general, a devout man, sufficiently learned in the holy Scriptures, when he saw that his order was falling away from its first institution, began certain new separations under the appearance of reform, and obtained that they be confirmed by the supreme pontiff. Yet at the petitions of the custodians and ministers they were immediately revoked by the same pope, because they appeared to have been undertaken to the grave scandal and division of the order. Therefore Hubertinus, moved by this, entered the Order of the Carthusians. He wrote a very distinguished and notable volume, useful to religious and devout persons, which he entitled: The Tree of the Life of the Crucified, 5 books.
Sermons; Letters. To all true [servants?] of Christ. And certain other things.

Certain Catholic doctors warn us that Hubertinus, in the aforesaid volume, in certain places, especially where he takes up the Canticle of Simeon, must be read cautiously, because on certain articles he thinks otherwise than the Church, mother of us all. Yet the author himself is to be excused, because it had not yet been determined. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Jacobus of Ravenna, born in the province of Lorraine, a man most learned in civil law and the sacred canons, and easily the most skilled of all in his time both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, professor of sacred Scripture, a distinguished philosopher and dialectician, who, as Cinus says, converted what had been handed down by the elders in a simple sense into the dialectical mode of arguing. He wrote many small works in both laws, of which the following are reported: On the Code, 9 books.
On the Old Digest, 24 books.
On the New Digest, 12 books.
On the Infortiatum, 14 books.
Various Disputations, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Alanus de Insulis, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters second to none in his time, a very celebrated theologian, philosopher, and poet, who for a long time gloriously presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris, where, shining brightly in every divine and human science, he deserved to be called Universal, wrote in verse and prose almost innumerable little works, by which the memory of his name was made immortal among posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following under their titles: On the Sentences, 4 books.
Quodlibets also, 1 book.
The Eye of Sacred Scripture, 1 book.
On Doctrine also, 5 books.
On the Five Books of Moses, 5 books.
On the Song of Songs, 1 book.
On Penance, to the father of Bourges, 1 book.
On Mystical Equivocal Terms, 1 book.
On the Six Wings of the Cherubim, 1 book.
On the Complaint of Nature, 1 book.
A Summa of Virtues and Vices, 1 book.
On Parables, 1 book.
On the Art of Preaching, 1 book.
Anticlaudianus, 1 book.
On the Natures of Animals, 1 book.
Several Sermons, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

To the most reverend father and...
Every science rests upon its own rules.
Since many, for the adorning...
By the grace of God, to the father of Bourges [unclear]
From Phoebus, Phoebe [unclear] And he wrote some dialogues.

Finally, he is said to have produced notable commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, especially on the prophets, on the Gospel, and on the Apostle; concerning these I have so far been able to find nothing. Certain marvelous things are told about him, to which I neither lend credence nor rashly deny it. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Guilhelmus, a monk of the monastery of Hafligemen[unclear], of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, and for some time prior in the same monastery, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and learned by long practice, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, strong in verse and prose, published in both kinds of writing certain little works not to be scorned, by which he [perpetuated?] the memory of his name; among these are

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

Non-useless sermons, one book.
Visions of a certain nun, one book.
On the life of Saint Lutgardis, one book.
But other things which he composed have not yet come at all to my knowledge.

Franciscus Accursius, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, son of the most learned man Accursius, himself a man excellently learned in civil law and much instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, whose works survive with great authority among the professors of this faculty, made his own times illustrious by teaching and writing, and gave his name to immortality. Of his little works I have as yet been able to see nothing. Various works of his are reported: Disputations also, one book.
And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Martinus de Fano, a professor and interpreter of both laws, most celebrated among all in his own time, the teacher of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence, and most acute in pleading legal cases, wrote distinguished volumes in his faculty, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only: On actions, one book. “I indeed, Martinus...”
On judgment and cause, one book. “Since very many principal...”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Albertus Patavinus, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, once a hearer and disciple of Aegidius Romanus, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, and by his preaching converted many from iniquity to the path of justice. He wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made himself useful to those then present and memorable to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book.
On Leviticus, one book. On Numbers, one book.
On Deuteronomy, one book. On the Gospel, one book.
On the Epistles of Paul, one book. Sermons for the season, one book.
Sermons on the saints, one book.
Sermons throughout Lent, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Dinus de Garbo, Florentine by homeland, a most skilled doctor of the art of medicine, and nobly instructed in the institutions of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence, published in his faculty little works not to be despised by students, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported: Commentaries on Galen.
On the malice of varied complexion, one book.
On Hippocrates, On the nature of the fetus, one book.
A book of various questions, one book.
On Avicenna also, one book.
Various things also in philosophy.
And certain other things.

His father Brunus was a physician most skilled in the art of surgery; he entrusted this Dinus to the Florentine physician Thadaeus to be instructed in that science.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Guilielmus de Cumo, French by nation, a most learned interpreter of civil law, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence, who in that faculty had few more learned than himself in his own time, magnificently adorned the school of Orleans by teaching and writing. He published little works not to be scorned by professors of the laws, by which he made his name known to posterity: On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the Code also, 9 books.
And various other things.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Jacobus de Viterbio, archbishop of Naples, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, wrote little works not to be despised for the edification of readers, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity with glory. I have as yet deserved to see none of these. But the following work of his addressed to Pope Clement V is reported: On the government of Christians, one book. On the Sentences, 4 books.
Quodlibets also, one book.
And some other things.

He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh emperor, and of Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1316.

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

Henry of Brussels, a monk of the monastery of Affligem of the order of the blessed father Benedict, a man devoted to divine Scripture and skilled through continual practice, an excellent philosopher and computist, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote several commendable little works, by which in his own time he became known far and wide. Of these there are reported: On the Method of Computation, one book. A Calendar on Incensions, one book.

And certain other works, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge.

Alexander of Alexandria, the sixteenth minister general of the order of friars, a man most learned in the divine writings, and second to none in his own time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, profound in sense and understanding, composed certain little works in each science, by which, exercising his talent, he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are reported: On the Sentences, four books. Various Questions, one book.

On Aristotle's Metaphysics, twelve books. On the books On the Soul, three books.

He also commented on other books of Aristotle and wrote various works. He flourished under the emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Eckard, a German by nation, of the order, as some will have it, of Preachers, a man learned in the divine writings and, in Aristotelian philosophy, the most learned of all in his time, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence; but, while pursuing philosophy too much, he everywhere curiously mixed in novelty of terms contrary to the custom of theologians and introduced various errors, among which there survive seventeen articles condemned by the supreme pontiff and revoked at the end of his life by the same master Eckard. Many of these are contained in his exposition on the Gospel of John. Finally, the masters of the theological faculty of the school of Heidelberg, in the year of the Lord 1430, publicly declared the same errors, with certain others, condemned. Eleven articles, however, were left as suspect, all of which were customarily appended separately to his little works as a precaution. Nevertheless, where he wrote in Catholic fashion, he gave quite profound and useful teachings. Among his books I have found: On the Sentences, one book.

On Genesis, one book.

On Exodus, one book.

On the book of Wisdom, one book.

On the Song of Songs, one book.

The beginning of this writing: These are the names, etc.; because Love, etc.; The judge always [unclear] ij In

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

On the Gospel of John, one book. In the beginning, etc. [unclear] On the Lord's Prayer, one book. Our Father. Before Sunday A sermon in the chapter of the Preachers, one book. I as a fruitful vine Of his Positions, one book. Blessed be God the Father Sermons for the season, one book. The God of peace and love Sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished in his time especially in Austria, where he was held most famous in teaching and preaching; he wrote many other volumes.

Richard Malumbra, a native of Cremona, formerly a hearer and disciple of Jacobus de Arena, a man not moderately learned in imperial law, sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, who for many years publicly taught the laws in the school of Bologna, where he acquired no small praise for his learning. Although he was the most learned of all the doctors of his time, nevertheless he is read to have been condemned of heresy. He wrote many volumes in explanation of civil law: On the Code, nine books. On the Institutes, four books.

On the Digest, fifty books. Various Questions, one book.

And many other works.

He flourished under the emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Lampertinus de Ramponibus, a man most learned in both laws and nobly educated in the other arts of humanity, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, and notable for the practice of many virtues, wrote in that faculty many splendid volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great praise. Of these there are reported: On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

On the New Digest, twelve books. On the Infortiatum, fourteen books.

And certain other works.

He flourished under Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

William of Montlaudun, as they report, abbot of the monastery of Poitiers, of the order of the blessed father Benedict, a man excellently learned in divine Scripture, not ignorant of secular letters, especially Aristotelian philosophy and pontifical law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, published several little works of great authority, by which he made known to posterity the memory of his name. Of these the principal are reported: On the Sacraments, one book. A Summa on Cases, one book. On

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

Various *Declarations*. Moreover he published many other small works, especially in law, and arranged various glosses on the canons, about which I have nowhere been able to find anything.

Vido, priest of the church of Ferrara and afterwards, as they say, bishop, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures, rich in reading of the ancients, and nobly learned in secular letters, an eminent philosopher and poet, wrote several small works, both in verse and in prose, not to be despised in reading, by which he made his name known. Of these I have found only a volume written in verse to Pope Clement V, on the New and Old Testament, imitating Peter of Riga, which he entitled *The Pearl of the Bible*, one book. Its noble beginning [unclear]. I have seen nothing of the others.

He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh emperor, and Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Peter of Saxony, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, and nobly learned in canon law, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, an excellent preacher of the divine word, wrote certain excellent volumes of his own ability, which in his time were held in esteem. Of these there is extant a work useful for confessors: *A Summa of Cases*, one book; *Sermons on the Season*, one book; *Sermons on the Saints*, one book. The rest that he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Crufianus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, once a hearer and disciple of the physician Thadaeus, a man learned and instructed in philosophy and medicine, but by no means fortunate, and for that reason bidding farewell to the world and entering the Carthusian order, usefully exchanged the art of the flesh for the medicine of the spirit. He had previously written some small works in his own faculty, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a commentary *On the Techne of Galen*, one book, and certain others.

He flourished in the Carthusian order in the time of Albert, Roman emperor, in the year of the Lord 1300. And afterwards he is said to have written various treatises pertaining to spiritual edification.

Peter of Verberia, called Aureoli, of the Order of Friars Minor and archbishop of Aix, doctor of the Parisian school, very learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in Aristotelian philosophy according to the custom of this time, was subtle in intellect, an acute disputant, and excellent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote many excellent small works, by which he magnificently spread his name. Of these there are extant *On the Sentences*, four books; [unclear], *Come, let us go up*, one book; *The abysses were not yet*, one book; *Sermons on the Season*, one book; *Sermons on the Saints*, one book; and others that I have not seen.

He flourished before his pontificate, reading the Sentences at Paris, in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1317.

Gentilis of Foligno, an eminent professor of medicine and magnificently learned in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, whose skill in that faculty was not slight, wrote in medicine many excellent volumes, as they say, by which he made his name known with praise not only to those then present but also to posterity. But I have seen none of them. There are reported to be: commentaries *On Avicenna*, one book; *On the Degrees of Medicine*, one book; and certain others. *Counsels on All Diseases*, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Dantes Aligerus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, a man in his time most studious of all in both the divine Scriptures and secular letters, wrote many excellent volumes in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Driven from his homeland for all his days, he lived in exile in Gaul for some time; afterwards, at the court of the king of Aragon, he composed various works about his calamity. Of his small works these are reported: *Comedies*, one book; *On the Monarchy of the World*, one book; several letters; and certain others. Also by him, a disputation *On Water and Earth*.

At last he died in exile at Ravenna, under Louis the Bavarian, empe-

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

225 emperor IV, in the year of the Lord 1321, in the fourth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

Michael of Cesena, the seventeenth minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, and venerable no less for religion than for knowledge, produced in the holy writings works of exposition not to be despised, by which he became known far and wide both to those then living and now to posterity. Of these I have so far been able to find very few, namely: On the Sentences, 4 books.
On the prophet Ezekiel, 1 book.
Sermons for the season, 1 book.
Sermons on the saints, 1 book.
He produced readings and commentaries on many books of the Bible, which I have not yet seen.

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Bertrand, of the Order of Friars Minor, by country a Milanese, born of a noble family, and, as some think, cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, a man certainly exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures and not moderately instructed in secular philosophy, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote several works of great usefulness, among which I have found: On the Sentences, 1 book.
Sermons on the Gospels, 1 book. “They shall see the Son,” etc. [unclear]
Sermons on the saints, 1 book.

The rest that he composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1325.

Gerard of Bologna, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, the eleventh prior general, doctor of Paris, most learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, venerable no less for his way of life than for his knowledge, who governed his order vigorously for twenty years, wrote several volumes of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name also to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, 1 book.
Quodlibets, 1 book.
Ordinary Questions, 1 book.
Sermons for the season, 1 book.

226 *On Ecclesiastical Writers.* Sermons on the saints, 1 book. And many others.

He began a very distinguished Summa of theology, which, however, overtaken by death, he left unfinished.

He died under Louis the Bavarian, emperor IV, in the year of the Lord 1317, in the fifteenth indiction, and was buried at Avignon.

John of Colonna, by country a Roman, of the Order of Friars Preachers, archbishop of Messina, a man possessing a practiced intellect in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a very sagacious investigator of the histories of past time, wrote works of noble intellect not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these there survives the volume which he entitled: Sea of Histories, 10 books.
Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He also produced some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Martin, of the Order of Friars Preachers, penitentiary of the lord pope of the city of Rome, and afterwards, as they report, bishop of a certain city, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have seen only: A Table of the Decretum, 1 book. “Among any other things” [unclear]
A Brief Chronicle, 2 books. “Since to know the times is a very great” [unclear]
Sermons for the season, 1 book. “Knowing that it is the hour”
On Various Miracles, 1 book. “Confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

There are some who write that this Martin belonged to the order of our holy father Benedict. In my opinion the likeness of the name of Marianus Scotus, of our order, whom I mentioned above, has deceived them, for he too wrote a chronicle. There are likewise others who think that he should be assigned to the community of the Cistercian Order; these either ignorance of matters has darkened, or envy.

Gerard Odonis, of the Order of Friars Minor, the eighteenth minister general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in scholastic philosophy, subtle in intellect, apt in speech, and quite fit for disputation, is said to have composed certain works in the holy Scriptures, of which few have become known to me: On the Sentences, 4 books.
Also On Logic, 1 book.
Various Questions, 1 book.

On I

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

On the books of the Ethics, 10 books.

On moral philosophy, 1 book.

He also composed the office of the stigmata of Saint Francis, founder of the Order of Minors. Finally, he is said to have published commentaries on many books of the Bible, which have not yet come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Louis the Bavarian, the fourth, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Nicholas of Lyra, English by nation, of the Order of the Friars Minor, a man most devoted to the holy Scriptures and skilled through long practice, scholastic in speech, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, wrote many distinguished little works on the sacred volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. How useful and how necessary these are for all who desire to learn sacred Scripture no one knows better than one who has exercised himself in reading them. For there are some who think him to be despised because of the simplicity of his eloquence; they seem to me both vain and unlearned, and unworthy of the sacred knowledge of saving philosophy, since they disparage ecclesiastical simplicity and embrace words, not things.

Concerning the little works of this devout and learned man, the following are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books.

On Genesis according to the letter, book I.

On Exodus, book II.

On Leviticus, book III.

On Numbers, book IV.

On Deuteronomy, book V.

On Joshua, book IX.

On Judges, book X.

On Ruth, book [XI?].

On Kings, book [XII?].

On Chronicles, book [IIII].

On Ezra and Nehemiah, book [IIII].

On Tobit, book IV.

On Judith, book IV.

On Esther, book IV.

On Job, book IV.

On the Psalter, book IV.

On the Proverbs of Solomon, book IV. In the beginning, etc. Omitting. According to what Isidore says. But Moses called. And the Lord spoke, etc. A declaration of the words. He will bring them in and plant them. The Lord raised up judges. In the days, etc. Here [unclear]. By me kings reign. Gather up the fragments. They will be priests over [unclear]. These things ought to have been done. Arphaxad, etc. After these things. In the days, etc. After. Have patience with me. A great prophet [unclear]. Behold, I have described her to you.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

On Ecclesiastes, 1 book. The words of Ecclesiastes.

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Let him kiss me, etc. [unclear].

On the book of Wisdom, 1 book. After the historical books.

On Ecclesiasticus, 1 book. All wisdom, etc.

On Isaiah the prophet, 1 book. Jerusalem the evangelist.

On Jeremiah, 1 book. A prophet among the nations.

1 book. How she sits. In [unclear].

On the Lamentations of Jeremiah, 1 book. These words, etc. After.

1 book. The heavens were opened, etc.

On Ezekiel, 1 book. But to Daniel God gave.

On Daniel, 1 book. Of the twelve prophets.

On the twelve minor prophets, 1 book. And it came to pass, etc. After.

2 books. Four faces to one.

On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. The face of a lion on the right.

On Mark, 1 book. The face of an ox on the left.

On Luke, 1 book. The face of an eagle above.

On John, 1 book. Behold, I have described her to you [unclear].

On the epistles of Paul, 1 book. They were all filled with the Spirit.

On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. James, etc. This book.

On the canonical epistles, 7 books. You must prophesy again.

On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. I saw in the right hand a seat.

He expounded the following morally, 1 book. These names, etc. Through the sons.

Again on Genesis, 1 book. The Lord spoke.

On Exodus, 1 book. These are the words; it follows.

On Leviticus, 1 book. After the death, etc. Allegorically.

On Numbers, 1 book. There was a man, etc. [unclear].

On Deuteronomy, book [II?]. Adam, Seth, etc. In this.
