On Joshua, 1 book. In the days, etc. That order.

On Judges, 1 book. The vision of Isaiah. In this.

On Ruth, 1 book. The words of Jeremiah, etc. Through.

On Kings, 1 book. How she sat. Here begins.

On Chronicles, 1 book.

On Ezra and Nehemiah, 1 book.

On the book of Esther, 1 book.

On the book of Job, 1 book.

On the Psalter, 1 book.

On Isaiah the prophet, 1 book.

On Jeremiah, 1 book.

On the Lamentations of the same, 1 book. On Eze[kel]

*ABBOT OF SPONHEIM. 219.*

[A biblical-commentary works list:]
On Ezekiel: 1 book. ["And it came to pass, etc."]
On Daniel: 1 book. ["In the third year, etc."]
On the 12 minor prophets: 1 book. ["The word which, etc."]
On the Gospel of Matthew: 1 book. ["The book of the generation of Je[sus], etc."]
On Mark: 1 book. ["It was in the days, etc."]
On Luke: 1 book. ["In the beginning, etc."]
On John: 1 book. ["First, etc."]
On the Acts of the Apostles: 1 book. ["The first [account], etc."]
On the Apocalypse: 1 book. ["Tobias, of the tribe, etc."]
On Tobias also: 1 book. ["Arphaxad, etc."]
On the book of Judith: 1 book. ["And it came to pass, etc."]
On the Maccabees: [—] book[s]. ["First it is asked whether…"]
On the Song of Songs: 1 book.
On the body of Christ: 1 book.
Sermons on the saints: 1 book.
Sermons on the [seasons of the] year: 1 book.
Against the Jews: 1 book.
He published, besides, some others, which have not yet come into our hands.
He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, [and] John XXII, pope, in the year of the Lord 1320.

[Guido?], of [the order of] Mary ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, the twelfth Prior general, and afterward bishop of the churches of Mende and Elne, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent, sweet in eloquence, a keen disputant, distinguished no less in conversation than in knowledge: he wrote many illustrious little works, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: A tripartite work—polished [and] distinguished—on the perfection of the catholic life, to Pope John XXII: [—] book[s].
On the Sentences: 4 books.
Six Quodlibets: 1 book. ["In our first dispu[tation]…"]
Whether the Word in divine [matters]…
Ordinary Questions: 1 book.
On the concord of the evangelists: 3 books.
To the cardinal of Albano: 1 book.
On the books of the Physics: 8 books.
Questions on the soul: [—] book[s].
[page 268:] He composed also several others, which have not come to my knowledge.
He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and John XXII, pope, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Augustine of Ancona, of the order of the hermit-brothers of St Augustine, a man studious and erudite in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, prompt in talent, and scholastic in speech, wrote many volumes of no contemptible reading, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: To Pope John XXII, a work not small,
On ecclesiastical power: 4 books. ["To the most holy and reverend…"]
On the Sentences: 4 books.
Quodlibets also: 5 books.
On the Holy Spirit against the Greeks: 6 books.
On the ten strings: 7 books.
On the entrance into the promised land: 8 books.
On the powers of the soul: 9 books.
On the resurrection; On Matthew: 10 books.
On Mark; On Luke also: 11 books.
On John; On "Missus est" [the Annunciation]: 12 books.
On the Magnificat; On the Epistles of Paul: 13 books.
On the canonical Epistles; On the Acts of the Apostles: 14 books.
On the Apocalypse. And several others.
He began a distinguished volume from the writings of the divine father Augustine, which he entitled the Milleloquium; but, prevented by death, he left [it] unfinished; which afterward Bartholomew of Urbino, of the same order, completed.
He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, emperor, the fourth, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Peter of Abano, an Italian by nation, of Padua by country, a man studious [and] erudite in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, a physician of most celebrated repute, subtle in talent, renowned for [his] knowledge of many languages, is reported to have elaborated many little works, both in philosophy and in medicine, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. But there are [those] who write that he was a magician, [and] had shown many wonders through that superstitious art; whether [this be] true, [I know not]. For I recall having neither read nor anywhere seen anything of his little works. Of these, however, the following are reported: A distinguished work [of] a hundred and…

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

...divided into ten distinctions, which he entitled:

*On Medicine of Every Kind*, book I.
*To Pope John XXII*, book II.
*On the Book of John Mesue*, book III.
*On Aristotle's Problems*, book IV.
And certain other works.

He translated Galen *On Black Bile* and *On the Regimen of Health*, together with many others.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Sibertus de Beka, a German by nation, from Gelderland by homeland, of the Order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior provincial of Lower Germany, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained both in canon law and in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect and brilliant in eloquence, who shone in his time no less by his manner of life than by his learning, wrote certain commendable small works, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are reported:

*On the Sentences*, book II.
*A Summary of Censures of the New Law*, book III.
*On the Rule of His Order*, book IV.
And certain other works.

He also corrected the ordinal of his order with sagacious purpose.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Clement, the fifth pope, born in Gascony, formerly called Bernard, bishop of Bordeaux, sat after Benedict XI in the chair of Peter for eight years and ten months. He was a learned and energetic man; at his command the Order of Templars was destroyed throughout the whole world on one day. He celebrated the Council of Vienne, in which he established many things for the benefit of the Church. He composed the seventh book of the Decretals, which John XXII, his successor, published, as is stated at the beginning of the same. It is commonly called:

*The Code of the Clementines*, book I. *The foundations of the Catholic faith*...

He died while Henry VII was governing the Roman Empire, in the year of the Lord 1314, in the twelfth indiction.

Petrus de Perpiniano, called Rimi, a Catalan by nation, of the Order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures and a subtle expounder of scholastic philosophy, quick in intellect and an excellent declaimer, published many small works of reading not to be despised. By exercising in them the abundant vein of his talent, he made his name known even to posterity. Of these there are reported:

*Questions on the Sentences*, book I.
*On the Whole Psalter*, book I.
*Various Sermons*, book I.

But concerning other works that he composed, nothing has ever come to my knowledge.

Dericus, of the Order of Friars Minor, a holy and learned man, an excellent preacher of the divine word, because of his most fervent love for it took up a pilgrimage, penetrated Asia and India, where by preaching and teaching and proclaiming the faith of Christ, he converted many from iniquity to the path of justice. His most holy life was confirmed by many signs both in the flesh and after death. Among the other small works of his talent he wrote:

*A History of His Pilgrimage*, book I.
Also *Various Sermons*, book I.
And certain letters.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Franciscus Marionis, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of John Scotus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly trained in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, composed in style, constant in study, sufficiently acute and very fit for disputing and resolving questions of the Scriptures, wrote not a few distinguished volumes of his talent, in which he showed himself most learned and transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

*On the Sentences*, book I. *Concerning the proemium of the first*...
*On Formalities*, book I. *Various Questions*, book I.
*Sermons on the Season*, book I. *Sermons on the Saints*, book I.

He is also said to have composed certain commentaries on the divine volumes and some diverse treatises, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Bonaventura of Padua, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, formerly prior general, and thereafter cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Cecilia, a man in the divine [unclear]...

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

learned in the Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, no less reverend for his manner of life than for his knowledge, of great reputation in delivering sermons to the people; and, since he most vigorously defended the liberty of the Church against tyrants, he was at last pierced by an arrow by the lord of Carrara and was crowned with martyrdom. He wrote very useful and elegant works: Sermons for the season, one book. “The desired one will come [unclear]”
Sermons on the saints, one book. “But far be it from me to glory”
And certain other things.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

William Ockham, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a disciple of John Scotus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly taught in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain small works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Acting and writing against John XXII, who condemned the heresy of the Fraticelli, together with Peter of Piceno, whom Emperor Louis had set up as an idol and had caused to be called Nicholas V, and declaring him to be a heretic, he was excommunicated by him. Fleeing to Emperor Louis, likewise excommunicated, he said to him: “O Emperor, defend me with the sword, and I shall defend you with the word.” And so he remained excommunicated with the excommunicated man until the end of his life; at last, at his death, he was absolved. He was a most bitter assailant of Scotus, his master, and attacked almost all his sayings. He wrote: Against John XXII on the poverty of Christ and the apostles
An Apology, one book.
On the Sentences, four books.
Quodlibets, also one book.
On the Supporters of Heretics, seven books. “In all curious matters”
On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320. And he was buried in the convent of his order in the province of Noricum, which is now called Bavaria, of which Emperor Louis had previously been duke.

Alvarus, of the Order of Friars Minor, Spanish by nation, a hearer of John Scotus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, held in esteem by John XXIII, acted against William Ockham the Englishman in writings and in words. He published certain very distinguished volumes of his talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there survives a great and notable work, describing the defects of ecclesiastical persons, which he entitled: On the Lamentation of the Church, one book.
Likewise The Mirror of Kings, one book. “In the name of our Lord Jesus”
On the Sentences, four books.
An Apology, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished at the same time as Ockham, under Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Matthew Silvaticus, of Mantua by homeland, noble by birth, a physician by art and profession, in which faculty in his time he was held to be both learned and experienced before many others, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote in that science volumes not to be despised, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable work, addressed to Robert, king of Sicily and a physician, on all simple medicines and their properties, which he entitled: Pandects, one book. “Aaron in Greek, in Arabic”
I have seen nothing of the rest.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

A certain hearer and disciple of John Scotus in the schools of Paris, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly taught in secular philosophy, and also not ignorant of both pontifical and imperial law, is said to have composed certain distinguished little works, by which, exercising his talent, he also made his name known to posterity; but I have seen none of them. They are said to be: On the Sentences, one book.
Disputed Questions, one book.
And certain other things.

Durandus of Saint-Pourcain, of the Order of Friars Preachers, and afterward, as they say, bishop of Le Puy, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not meanly instructed in secular philosophy, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, first a defender of the writings of Saint Thomas Aquinas, but afterward their most bitter assailant. A certain shifting cause is reported for this change, to which I ought neither readily to give credence, nor

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

to deny rashly: he wrote certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books. “There is God in heaven [unclear]”
On the Instruction of the Clergy, 1 book. “Most beloved brothers and [unclear]”
A Notable Summary, 1 book.
Various Questions, 1 book.
Diverse Sermons, 1 book.
The rest which he is said to have composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

Erenus de Boyo, a Briton by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man in every respect most learned, an eminent professor of sacred scripture, of sharp and vigorous talent, quite capable in solving questions of the scriptures, is reported to have written some distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is found, as his people report, an excellent work: On the Sentences, 4 books.
And Various Questions.
But he is said to have composed certain other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Rupert, of the order of the Preaching Friars, a man learned through long practice in the divine scriptures, a subtle and profound interpreter of scholastic philosophy, an acute disputant, an outstanding declaimer, sharp in talent, scholastic in speech, published certain little works not to be despised; by exercising his talent fruitfully and usefully in them, he made his name known not only to the present but also to the future. Of these there survive: On the Sentences, 4 books.
Sermons on the Season, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
In addition, he adorned many books of Aristotle with most elegant commentaries.
He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Stephanus de Ast, of the order of the Friars Minor, a man nobly learned in the divine scriptures, an eminent philosopher and jurist, distinguished in knowledge, profound in talent, cautious in counsel, firm in judgment, composed in speech, is reported to have forged various little works of his excellent talent, by which he made his name known to those present as well as to those to come. Of these I have seen only the necessary work: A Summary on Cases, 8 books. “Therefore, about to speak in this first [unclear]”
Of the rest I have seen nothing.
He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1550.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

[unclear]

Johannes de Alerio, a Toulousain by nation, of the order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the thirteenth prior general, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, and venerable no less for fervor in religion than for learning, governed the Carmelite order vigorously for nine years. He published several distinguished volumes, by which he showed the abundant grace of his talent. Of these there survive: On the Sentences, 4 books.
A Reading on Ecclesiasticus, 1 book.
And several others.
He was elected general of his order at Montpellier in the general chapter, on the day of Pentecost, under Louis the fourth emperor and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1321, in the fourth indiction.

Johannes de Regno, a Frenchman by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the Toulouse convent, a man learned in the holy scriptures and not ignorant of secular learning, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, outstanding in delivering sermons to the people, published besides many volumes, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books.
On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book.
Sermons on the Season, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
A Lenten Work, 1 book.
The rest, however, which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Stephanus de Provincia, professor and excellent interpreter of both laws, and sufficiently instructed both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, distinguished in talent and eloquence, whose learning was approved among his contemporaries, wrote certain volumes [not?] to be neglected, by exercising his talent gloriously in which he also transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is an excellent work: On the Clementines, 1 book.
Various Questions, 1 book.
Of the rest I have found nothing.
He flourished around the times of Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Johannes Andreas, an Italian by nation, from Bologna by homeland, a jurist most celebrated to the admiration of all, a fountain of canons and a most cautious interpreter of doubts, distinguished in talent, profound in knowledge, composed in eloquence, who, contrary to the custom of the men of our

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

...of our time, although he was bound by the ties of a wife, nevertheless devoted incredible zeal to letters, so that nothing could have been sweeter to him than to write something for the edification of posterity. His distinguished volumes testify to this, by which he secured eternal remembrance for his name. Of these I have had the privilege of seeing a few: On the Decretals, 5 books.
On the Novellae in two forms, 1 book. “Because it is preposterous...”
Additions to the Speculum, 2 books.
The work entitled Mercuriale, 1 book. “I, Johannes And...”
A Summa on betrothals and marriage, 1 book.
On the Clementines, 4 books. “Since frequently in the forum...”
On the praises of Saint Jerome, 1 book. “Johannes Gratiosum...”
On the tree of consanguinity, 4 books. “Jerome continually...”
Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He died at last of the plague and was buried at Bologna, under Charles IV, emperor, and Clement VI, pope, in the year of the Lord 1348, in the first indiction.

[Unclear], formerly hearer and disciple of the most famous man Cinus of Mugello, and a close friend of Johannes Andreae, a man certainly most learned in civil law among all men of his time, subtle in intellect, ready and very abundant in knowledge, published many little works in that faculty, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Code, 9 books.
On the first part of the Old Digest, 1 book.
On the second part, 1 book.
Additions on the remaining parts, 2 books.
And many other things. He also wrote consilia.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Monaldus, of the Order of Friars Minor, a theologian and very learned jurist, subtle in intellect, cautious in knowledge, scholastic in speech, of excellent industry and virtue in delivering sermons to the people, published, for the benefit of the simple, little works not to be despised even by the learned, by which he usefully provided both for those then present and for those to come long afterward. Of these the following are reported: A necessary and very beautiful Summa of canon law, 4 books. “Since one ignorant...”
Questions on the Sentences, 4 books.
Various sermons, 1 book.
And many other things, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

[Unclear], an Italian by nation, formerly hearer of the very learned man Dinus of Mugello, and a very close friend of Johannes Andreae, a man very skilled in both laws, and also excellently imbued with the disciplines of philosophy, who for many years was a consistorial advocate and acquired great praise and glory for his learning, wrote some distinguished little works in both laws, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only: A volume of consilia, 1 book. “In the name of the Lord, Amen...”
Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He is said to have left after him many lectures in civil law, which I have not yet seen.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

[Unclear] Johannes de Blomendal, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence, was an eminent teacher in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have so far found only: Sermons on the temporal cycle, 1 book. “Take your weapons, your quiver...”
Sermons on the saints, 1 book.
Sermons for Lent, 1 book.

He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

[Unclear] Guido de Monte Rocherii, a man very studious in the sacred Scriptures and rich in reading of the ancients, clear in intellect, scholastic in speech, wrote little works of his talent not to be despised, by which he made the memory of his name known also among posterity. Of these I have seen only that well-known work circulated in print, which, composing it for the guidance of simple priests, he wished to be entitled: The Manipulus curatorum, 3 books. “Since, as the prophet says...”
I could not find other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

[Unclear] Johannes de Ligneriis, the most celebrated philosopher and astronomer of all men in his time, who magnificently restored this discipline, now almost erased from human memory, acquired immense praise for his learning in the school of Paris, where he had as collaborators and associates in this faculty men most learned in mathematical knowledge, Johannes de Muris and Ber-

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

[unclear], notable philosophers and astronomers, who also themselves wrote various short works. But of the works of this John of Lignières, although he wrote many excellent things, I have seen very few, namely:

Canons of the first movable sphere, one book. “Of any given arc ...”
Tables of the same, one book.
On the sphere also, one book.

Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Louis the Bavarian, the fourth, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

John Danck of Saxony, German by nation, contemporary of the aforesaid John of Lignières and his companion in studies, a man most learned in every respect, the most celebrated philosopher and astronomer among all men of his time, excellent in subtle intellect, published many excellent and admirable short works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. But thus far I have found very few: Eclipse Canons, one book. “The quantity of an eclipse of the sun ...”
Canons of the tables, one book. “The time of the fourth aspect ...”
On the astrolabe, one book.
On burnings, one book.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Peter de Palude, French by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law, an acute disputant and distinguished preacher, published certain excellent volumes on the holy Scriptures, by which he bestowed his name upon immortality. Among these are reported: On the Sentences, four books.
Various Questions, one book.
And various Sermons, one book.
And many other things.

He is also said to have adorned many books of the Bible with his commentaries, that is, to have expounded them.

John Calderini, Italian by nation, from Bologna, once a hearer and disciple of John Andreae, professor of canon law, a very celebrated interpreter, not ignorant of secular philosophy and of the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, apt in speech, wrote no few volumes in his faculty. By these, proving his intellect through diligent exercise, he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Among these I have found a great and notable work, divided into three not small volumes, which he entitled: Repertory of Law, one book. “A. This word a, sometimes ...”
On the Decretals, one book. “Although many doubtful matters ...”
On ecclesiastical interdict, one book.
Many opinions, one book.

Of the other things I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Paul de Liazariis, a hearer of John Andreae of Bologna and fellow student of John Calderini, a man most skilled in both laws, nobly instructed in the precepts of the philosophers, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, who among the doctors of law in his time was not [unclear], wrote, among the other short works of his intellect, a notable volume which is called: On the Clementines, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and of Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Lupold of Bebenburg, bishop of Bamberg, German by nation, as they report once a hearer of John Andreae of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist, nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published short works not to be despised in reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great glory. Among these there is extant a notable work: On the Zeal of the Christian Religion of the Old Princes of the Germans, one book.
On the Rights of the Roman Empire, one book.
And certain other volumes on diverse subjects, which have not come to me.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and of Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Nicholas of Modena, a man nobly learned in both laws, especially in the civil laws, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel, in order to leave to posterity monuments of his intellect, wrote certain excellent volumes in civil law, by which he had made himself useful to those then living, and known to those to come. Among these are reported: On the Code, nine books.
On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

*ABBOT OF SPANHEIM.*

On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books.
And certain other works.
He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Lapus de Castellione, abbot of San Miniato, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a jurist most learned among all men of his time, and imbued from early youth, as they say, with the disciplines of the philosophers, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, and an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions, whose authority among jurists is to be judged by no means slight, wrote several short works in his faculty, among which there is an excellent work: Of his Allegations, 1 book.
On the Clementines, 1 book.
And many other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Guerricus, abbot of Igny, a man by no means slightly learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, sweetly composed in speech, fit for persuading, distinguished no less by love of regular observance in his way of life than by knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote, for the edification of simple devout brothers, short works not to be despised; by these, showing himself a useful and faithful shepherd of Christ’s sheep, he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only the work of sermons on the temporal cycle and on the saints through the circuit of the year, which he delivered: To his brothers, 1 book. We await the Savior.

He also wrote letters.
Concerning the rest, however, which he is said to have composed, I have not been able to find anything anywhere.

Henry of Urimaria, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, by nation, as they report, a German, a man most devoted to the holy Scriptures from boyhood and very learned, second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, who for many years was an outstanding doctor in the Parisian academy, distinguished by celebrated doctrine, wrote many very famous volumes, among which the following are said to be: On the Sentences, 4 books.
Quodlibets, 1 book.
On the Ten Commandments, 1 book.
Flowers from the Collation of the Fathers, 2 books. Hear, Israel, the commandments.
On the Perfection of Man, 1 book. Because many [unclear].
On the Incarnation of the Word, 1 book.
On the Fourfold Instinct, 1 book.
On Exemption, 1 book.
Exposition on the Creed, on the celebration of Mass, 1 book.
Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
On the books of the Ethics, 10 books.
And many other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, surnamed Bavarian, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

[Unclear], studious [unclear], and excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and historiographer, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in speech, is said to have fashioned some volumes of excellent doctrine, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the distinguished work of Histories excels: 16 books.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Bartholomaeus Pisanus, of the Order of Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most skilled in both laws, and nobly learned in the knowledge of secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, open in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel, is said to have written certain very famous short works. Of these I have seen only the Summa, which he calls the Pisan, a work certainly not to be rejected, which a few years ago was in great use among confessors of the common people, which the author entitled: Summa magistrucia, 1 book.

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, and completed his Summa, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord [1338?].

Bartholomaeus Brixianus, of the Order of Preachers, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and by no means slightly learned in both laws, also an outstanding declaimer of sermons, and no less holy than learned, since he is said to have shone with miracles even in life, wrote, among the other monuments of his talent, a notable: Summa on Cases, 1 book.
Various Sermons, 1 book.
And certain other works.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

*Abbot of Sponheim.*

Ludolphus, of the Carthusian order, in the house of Strasbourg, a German by nation, sprung from Saxon land, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, gentle in disposition, sweet and composed in speech, and also distinguished in life and conduct, published certain excellent little works of great devotion and deep learning. By these, nobly exercising his talent, he bestowed his name upon immortality. Of these I have seen only the following: A large and distinguished volume on the Gospel, which he entitled *The Life of the Lord Jesus*, 2 books.

Also *On the Psalter*, 1 book. *Another foundation, lest...* [unclear] Other works of his are reported. *As once manna...* [unclear] He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

[Unclear], a man very zealous in the divine Scriptures, exceedingly skilled, eminent in ability, no less distinguished in life than in learning and knowledge, published many excellent volumes, in which he showed the abundant vein of his talent and transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great praise and glory. Of these the following are reported:

*On the First Book of the Sentences*, 1 book.

A lecture *On Genesis*, 1 book.

A twofold *Hexameron*, 2 books.

*On the Song of Songs*, 1 book.

*On the Matter of the Chaoticorum* [unclear], 1 book.

*On the Lord’s Prayer*, in two ways, 2 books.

*On the Ave Maria*, 1 book.

*Breviloquium*, 1 book.

*On the Four Senses of Scripture*, 1 book.

*Of the Exposition of the Mass*, 1 book.

*Manual for Priests*, 1 book.

*On the Capital Vices*, 1 book.

*The Cloister of the Soul*, 1 book.

*On the Conception of Saint Mary*, 1 book.

*On the Method of Study*, 1 book.

*Introduction to Law*, 1 book.

*On True and False Friendship*, 1 book.

*On the Canonical Hours*, 1 book.

*On the Five Senses*, 1 book.

*On the Forty-Two Mansions*, 1 book.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

*Against the Flagellants*, 1 book. *On the Comparison of the Mass*, 1 book.

*On the Division of Philosophy*, in verse, 1 book.

*On the chapter Omnis utriusque*, 1 book.

Various sermons, 1 book. Preachable conferences, 1 book.

Various questions, 1 book. *On Aristotle’s Rhetoric*, 1 book.

He published besides many other works which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Louis IV and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

William de Kaiotho, of the order of Friars Preachers, provincial prior in France, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, subtle in talent and clear in speech, of excellent ability in delivering sermons to the people, wrote certain little works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. He abbreviated the *Summa* of Johannes Teutonicus, which is called the *Summa of Confessors*, 1 book. *What is simony, say...* [unclear] Various sermons, 1 book.

The rest of what he composed has by no means come to my knowledge.

Peter de Casa, of Limoges, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the fourteenth prior general, and afterwards bishop of Vaison, and finally, as they report, patriarch of Jerusalem, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in talent and clear in speech, learned and eloquent in delivering sermons to the people, published certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported:

*On the Sentences*, 1 book. Sermons for the season, 1 book.

Sermons on the saints, 1 book.

And certain other works.

He flourished, and was elected prior general of his order from the convent of Limoges, under the emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1350, in the thirteenth indiction. He ruled his order energetically for twelve years.

Paulus of Perugia, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, published several little works of great authority. By exercising his brilliant talent in these, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity with great glory. Of these there exists a very celebrated and almost divine work, which he recited in the Parisian school:

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

On the Sentences, 4 books. "Concerning the first [unclear]"
Quodlibets also, 1 book.
And certain other things.

He flourished at Paris and completed his lecture under Emperor Louis the Bavarian, the fourth, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1344, in the twelfth indiction. And not long after that same lecture of his he died at Paris and was buried there in the convent.

Bernardus Parentinus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and skilled through long practice, and not moderately learned in the scholastic disciplines, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the instruction of simple priests certain volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there is extant: An Exposition of the Mass, 1 book. "Since the Wise Man cries out"
Various sermons, 1 book.
And several other things.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Osbertus, English by nation, of the Order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man certainly most learned in the holy Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, of acute and forceful intellect, scholastic in eloquence, subtle in debating and resolving questions of the Scriptures, wrote certain excellent little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there are extant: On the Sentences, 4 books. "One conclusion having been proposed"
Various determinations, 1 book. "It is asked whether [unclear]"
Various sermons also, 1 book.

The rest that he composed have not been able to come to the knowledge of our reading.

Johannes Estuidi, English by nation, a man easily the most learned of all his time in secular letters, a philosopher and astronomer second to none, outstanding in intellect and sweet in speech, wrote certain excellent little works of his intellect, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of a later age. Of these there is extant a notable work of judicial astrology, concerning the accidents of the world, which is commonly called: The English Summa, 2 books. "My intention in this book" Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished, and completed the same Summa, as he states at its beginning, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1347, in the fifteenth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

Bernardus, abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in life, and a notable cultivator and propagator of regular observance, wrote for the edification of monks certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are extant: The Mirror of Monks, 1 book.
On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book. "It is read in Proverbs"
On Regular Precepts, 1 book.
Sermons to the Brothers, 1 book.

He is also said to have composed many other things, which have by no means reached us.

Symon de Cremona, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in speech, quite excellent in delivering sermons to the people, since indeed at Venice he labored for a long time in this office, where by word and example he instructed very many, wrote for the instruction of simple preachers little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant. To Antonius, his brother, a priest, sermons: On the Gospels, 1 book. "Lift up your heads, because"
On the Epistles also, 1 book. "Let us cast away the works of darkness" The rest that he composed have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading.

Petrus Raimundi de Insula Grassa, French by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the fifteenth Prior General, who after Petrus de Casa, from Limoges, vigorously governed his order for fifteen years, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, wrote elegantly: On the Sentences, 1 book.
And certain other things.

He flourished and was elected general from the convent of Carcassonne in the province of Narbonne, under Emperor Louis IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1343, in the eleventh indiction.

Reinerus Foroliviensis, a jurist most celebrated of all in his time, the teacher of Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a man distinguished in intellect and speech, is said to have composed various little works in civil law

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

... little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. But I have not been able to find any of them anywhere.

He died under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1358, in the eleventh indiction.

*Simon of Cascia*, of the order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man [unclear], zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, who indeed is said to have been illumined by the spirit of prophecy in the Florentine convent, published several volumes of great usefulness, in which he showed himself a learned and devout man. Among these I found an outstanding work on the whole Gospel, which is commonly entitled:

*The Deeds of the Savior*, one book. “From the good and super-good...”

*On Christian Doctrine*, one book. “The imitation of God in men...”

*On Patience*, one book. [unclear]

*Exposition of the Creed*, one book. [unclear]

*On the Mirror of the Cross*, one book. [unclear]

*On the Discipline of Spiritual Men*, one book. [unclear]

*Letters to Various Persons*, one book. [unclear] And certain other works.

He ended his life under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 140[unclear].

*Simon of Speyer*, a German by nation, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, master of Paris, most learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse, taught theology for a long time with distinction in the school of Cologne, and won from all great praise for his learning. He wrote an outstanding volume:

*On the Sentences*, one book.

*Against the Jews*, also one book.

*A Postil Read at Cologne*, [unclear].

He published some other things recently, but they have by no means come to our knowledge.

*Sertorius*, whom some call Fortunerius, the nineteenth minister general of the order of Friars Minor, an Englishman by nation, from [Galenis?] by homeland, afterward archbishop of Ravenna, and finally patriarch of Grado and cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, published certain distinguished volumes by which he made his name known also to posterity. Among these there is extant an outstanding work:

*On Augustine’s City of God*, twenty-two books.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

De-

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Finally, he is also said to have composed various treatises on the books of the Bible. He flourished, and was elected minister general of his order in the chapter at Marseille, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1356, in the ninth indiction.

Albericus Roxiatus, otherwise de Rosate, a native of Bergamo, a distinguished professor of both laws and a very renowned interpreter, excellently learned also in the other secular letters, quick in intellect and polished in speech, produced many instructive volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity. Among these the following are reported: On the Code, 12 books.
On the Old Digest, 24 books.
On the New Digest, 13 books.
On the Infortiatum, 14 books.
On the Institutes, 4 books.
On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book.
On the comedies of Dante, 1 book.

He also composed some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Johannes de Saxonia, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, produced certain distinguished volumes of his intellect, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Among these there is extant: A Summa on cases, 1 book.

And other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Gerardus of Siena, Italian by nation, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man not moderately learned in the holy Scriptures and skilled in both laws by long practice, subtle and acute in intellect, whose learning his contemporary Johannes Andreas often praises and cites, wrote some excellent little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported as the more important: On the First Book of the Sentences, 1 book.
On contracts and usury, 1 book.
On prescriptions, 1 book.

I have found nothing about the rest. He flourished with Johannes Andreas, under Louis the Bavarian, Emperor IV, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Johannes de Rupe Scissa, of the Order of Friars Minor, very zealous in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, led astray by I do not know what spirit, not to say led on, began, as though a prophet, to predict the desolation of the Catholic Church and certain other terrible things; he was cast into prison by the ministers of his order, and a lying spirit was found in his mouth. In chains he wrote to a certain cardinal: His Revelations, 1 book. Most reverend in Christ...
Also on the Sentences, 4 books.
And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Gerardus, bishop of Savona, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a native of Bergamo, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in canon law, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, worthy no less in life than in doctrine, composed for the benefit of readers little works not to be despised; by usefully exercising his intellect in these, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books.
Two quodlibets, 1 book.
On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Two wings of the Cherubim...
On the Epistle to the Hebrews, 1 book.
On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, concerning religious houses, 1 book.

He says that he wrote many other little works, which have not come to my knowledge. In the Parisian school he ascended the magisterial chair. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Thomas de Garbo, a native of Florence, son of the former physician Dino, a man learned and skilled in medicine, nobly instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, adhering to the footsteps of his most learned father, produced in his faculty little works not to be scorned by physicians, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among these there is extant, very noteworthy: A Summa of Medicine, 1 book.
And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, fourth Emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Alphonsus, bishop of Seville, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man much learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, among ecclesiastical doctors in his time...

*Concerning Ecclesiastical Writers*

... most celebrated in [his] time, distinguished in talent and eloquence. He published several volumes of great authority, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have found only a subtle and notable work: On the Sentences, 4 books.

Of the rest I have learned nothing.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

John de Bachone, an Englishman, of the order of the friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed both in canon law and in secular philosophy, shone brilliantly in the Paris school no less for his conduct than for his learning; and afterwards, promoted to the provincialate of England, he energetically governed his order by word and example. He wrote many notable volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book.
On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book.
On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book.
On the Gospel of John, 1 book.
On the Epistles of Paul, 14 books.
On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book.
On the Canonical Epistles, 7 books.
On the Apocalypse, 1 book.
On the Sentences, 1 book.
Various Quodlibets, 1 book.
Mirror of His Order, 1 book.
Defense of His Order, 1 book.
Against the Jews, 1 book.
On the Poverty of Christ, 1 book.
On the Rule of His Order, 1 book.

He also published explanations on the books of blessed Augustine On the Holy Trinity and On the City of God, and on Anselm’s Why God Became Man and On the Incarnation of the Word; in all of these he exercised his talent splendidly.

He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John Eligerus de Gonderfluen, a German by nation, once a hearer of John of Saxony, the very famous astronomer, a man most learned in secular letters, the most celebrated philosopher and astronomer among all men of his time, and sufficiently imbued with the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote volumes in mathematical science not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Construction of the Astrolabe, 1 book.
On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe, 1 book.
On the Usefulness of the Quadrant, 1 book.
On the Magnet also, 2 books.
On the Astrogometer, 1 book.

King of the stars Ptolemy [unclear]
With principal zeal [unclear]
The uses of the new [unclear]
A treatise on the magnet [unclear]
The sum, with [unclear] bedewing us [unclear] And many other works. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

Rupert, a Frenchman by nation, of the order of the friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent, apt in speech, published various little works on the holy Scriptures; by splendidly exercising his talent in them, he made the memory of his name known also to posterity. He was an excellent preacher of the divine word, and wrote many things useful to composers of sermons. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, 2 books.
On the Epistles of Paul, 3 books.
Sermons on the Season, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.

He composed many other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Clement VI, pope, a Limousin by homeland, formerly called Peter Roger, abbot of Fécamp, of the order of Saint Benedict, sat in the chair of Peter after Benedict XII for ten years and six months. He was a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, a notable doctor of canon law, venerable no less for his conduct than for his learning; in declaiming sermons to the people he was of excellent talent. He published certain distinguished little works, by which he showed the liveliness of his talent. Of these are reported: Various Sermons, 1 book.
On the Canonization of Ivo, 2 books.
Rejoice and praise [unclear]
On the Approval of King Charles, 3 books.
Solomon will sit upon [unclear]
Many Collations, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He died and was buried at Avignon, under Charles IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1352, in the fifth indiction.

[unclear]
Gre

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

Gregory of Rimini, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, prior general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very well instructed in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent and eloquence, earned from everyone in the University of Paris great renown for his learning, since he shone forth as very celebrated in life and doctrine. He wrote some little works of no contemptible reading, of which the following are considered the more important: On the Sentences, 4 books.
On the Epistles of Paul the Apostle, 14 books.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Philip of Bergamo, prior of the monastery of Saint Mary of [Avantia?] in Padua, of the Order of our holy father Benedict, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote several little works of holy doctrine, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only a large volume On the Ethics of Cato, 1 book. He is also said to have written Sermons, To the glory and praise, 1 book.

The other things that he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of my reading.

John de Beka, German by nation, clerk of the church of Utrecht, a man very studious and learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, published certain little works of his talent not to be despised. Of these I have seen only a work written in a simple and clear style, addressed to lord John, bishop of the church of Utrecht, and William, duke of Holland, on the deeds of the bishops of Utrecht and the counts of Holland; carrying it down from the time of Saint Willibrord, the first bishop, as far as the year of the Lord 1346, he wished it to be entitled Chronicle of the Church of Utrecht, 1 book. Therefore from the year [unclear]. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV and likewise Charles IV, emperors, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Francis Petrarch, Tuscan by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, by far the most learned of all his time, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated poet, who after a long silence called back the letters of humanity, dead, so to speak, from the lower world to the upper, shone forth distinguished no less for holy conduct than for knowledge. For out of love of Christ and of saving philosophy he took up the solitary life, in which, persevering until death in meditation, prayer, and writing, his fame was carried through the whole world. Of his little works I have found: On the Solitary Life, 1 book. Few men have I known.
[unclear], 2 books. Since things and fortunes.
On the Remedies of Fortune, 1 book. Monica in tranquil [unclear].
What indeed are we doing now, 1 book.
On the Seven Penitential Psalms, 1 book.
On the Conflict of Cares, 1 book.
The Life of Scipio Africanus, 1 book.
Bucolics, in verse, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 8 books.
Africa, to King Robert, 1 book.
On the History of Griselda, 1 book.
1 book 254 *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]

Richard de Bury, bishop of Durham, chancellor of Edward III, king of the English, to whom there is extant a letter of Francis Petrarch asking about the island of Thule, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, a singular and very celebrated lover of books, founded, with much expense and labor, a notable library in the University of Oxford, which with incredible zeal he established there for the public benefit of students. He wrote a very fine treatise on the love of books and the establishment of the said library, which has now been printed, and which he entitled in Greek:

*Philobiblon*, one book.
Several letters, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

[unclear]

John Walsgram, an Englishman by nation, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly trained in secular philosophy, subtle and acute in intellect, adorned with the master's insignia in the Parisian school, was very celebrated in lecturing and disputation. He wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant the notable work: On the *Sentences*, four books.

The other things which he is said to have composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

Various questions, one book.

John de Saxo, of the order of Friars Minor, learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly trained both in canon law and in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, an excellent preacher in delivering sermons to the people, and very famous in his time, published certain little works of reading not to be despised, which are necessary for the instruction of simple priests. Of these I have found only: A summa of law, one book.
Sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1359.

[unclear]

Thomas of Argentina, a German by nation, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, after Gregory of Rimini prior general, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures and an outstanding cultivator of secular philosophy, distinguished by his life and the honesty of his conduct, who wonderfully raised up his order by word and example, wrote several distinguished volumes on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant the most brilliant work: On the *Sentences*, four books. “The abyss gave forth its voice.”
Constitutions of his order, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

John Brammart of Aachen, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior provincial of Lower Germany, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and, according to the custom of the scholastics of this time, a very celebrated expounder of secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect and speech, an excellent teacher in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the benefit of the faithful little works not to be despised; by exercising his talent in them, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there are extant: On the *Sentences*, four books.
Various sermons, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Henry of Erfurt, a German by nation, long exercised in the divine Scriptures and not moderately learned, and excellently trained in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote for the edification of the Church several volumes, by which he made his name and reputation known to many. Of these there is reported a work of histories: On memorable deeds, one book.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John of Erfurt, a German by nation, a Thuringian by homeland, of the order of Friars Minor, an enlightened and skilled doctor in the divine Scriptures, nobly and excellently trained both in both laws and in secular philosophy, published several little works of great authority, in which he also entrusted the force of his most excellent talent to posterity. Of these I have seen only a great volume, which he entitled: Table of law, one book. “As it is written,” two.
A summa on cases, one book. “Asked by the brothers that...”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

256 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* He is also said to have composed elegant sermons, but they have not come to me.

John Tacephale, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Brethren of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a doctor learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, the most celebrated preacher of sermons of all in his time, produced little works not to be despised in reading; by them, usefully exercising his talent, he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these, the following are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books.
On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book.
Sermons on the Season, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
And certain other things.

He flourished in his convent at Norwich, where, buried, he rests in peace.

Robert Holkoth, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of Preachers, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and also an excellent preacher of sermons, wrote many excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, 4 books. “Whether every wayfarer...”
On the Book of Wisdom, 1 book. “The Lord is my rock...”
On the Seven Mortal Sins, 1 book. “This is the way; walk...”
Moralizations, 1 book. “Theodosius concerning the life...”
On the Immortality of the Soul, 1 book.
On the Song of Songs, 1 book.
On Ecclesiasticus, unfinished, 1 book.
And many other things.

He died of the plague after he had begun a reading on the Book of Ecclesiasticus, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1349, in the second indiction.

Nicholas Dorhin, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Brethren of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine scriptures and excellently taught in secular philosophy, who in the University of Oxford, by reading and disputing, earned great praises from all, wrote little works not to be scorned in reading, by which he showed the rich, all-round grace of his very lively intellect. Of these there are extant: On the Sentences, [unclear], 4 books.
Determinations of Questions, 1 book.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the school of Oxford, and wrote many various volumes.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Paul of Perugia, professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, and excellently learned in other humane letters, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, was for a long time keeper and master of the library of Robert, king of Sicily, a most learned and studious prince. He wrote certain excellent little works by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a distinguished volume, in which there are many pleasant and useful things concerning the gods of the gentiles and of others, which he entitled: Collections, 1 book.
And certain other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Bonominus, by nation a [Permonensian?], born from the town of Clusone, a learned physician and easily the most skilled of all in his time, and not moderately learned in the other disciplines of philosophy, most experienced in healing human bodies, wrote in that faculty little works not to be scorned, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But I do not remember having seen any of them. The following, however, are said to be his: On Poisons, 1 book.
Of Various Questions, 1 book.
And certain other things.

Tilmannus of Aachen, a German by nation, of the Order of the Brethren of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, distinguished professor of sacred letters, outstanding in intellect and an excellent preacher, and also sufficiently learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, wrote, for the benefit of readers, compilations not to be despised, by which he sent the fame of his name to distant places. Of these there is reported one notably remarkable reading, which he read publicly at Cologne: On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book.
Also on the Sentences, 4 books.

He is also said to have composed sermons and various works on the Bible; since I am uncertain about them, I can make no judgment.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Bartholus of Sassoferrato, once a hearer and disciple of the doctors Cinus and Jacobus Butrigarius, a most celebrated jurist, one to whom earlier ages had had no equal in that faculty, subtle and keen in intellect, polished and eloquent in speech, published certain distinguished volumes, especially on the laws. How great an authority these have today among jurists, no one even lightly learned and experienced is ignorant. Among these are cited commentaries on civil law, as follows: On the Code, 9 books.
On the Old Digest, 24 books.
On the New Digest, 12 books.
On the Infortiatum, 14 books.
On the Institutes, 4 books.
Also the Tiberiadis, 1 book.
Also Councils, 1 book.
On the Guelphs and Ghibellines, 2 books.

And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1355, in the eighth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

Petrus Thomas, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, first bishop of Patti, then archbishop of Crete, and most recently patriarch of Constantinople, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, since he is read to have shone forth, living and dead, with many signs and miracles, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, of which these are cited: On the Sentences, 3 books.
Also various sermons, 2 books.

And certain similar things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350, and was buried in Cyprus.

Bartholomaeus, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, English by nation, a man most studious in the divine Scriptures and not meanly learned, and sufficiently imbued with secular letters, and distinguished no less by religious conduct than by knowledge, published little works of no negligible authority, the reading of which is judged necessary for simpler brothers. Of these I have found only the volume which he entitled: On the Properties of Things. When the properties of things ... [unclear] 19.

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

Various sermons, 1 book.

He says that he wrote many other things also, but they have by no means come into our hands.

Petrus Boherius, abbot of Saint Avianus, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a jurist and an outstanding cultivator of the sacred Scriptures, subtle in intellect, renowned in speech, a most celebrated governor of monastic discipline: for the edification of his brothers he published several little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these I have found only: On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book.
On the Mirror of Monks, 1 book.
On the Signs of Speech, 1 book.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

Since he was a most celebrated doctor of decrees, he commented on the Rule of the holy father Benedict in a new and unusual kind of exposition, comparing all its chapters, opinions, and teachings, and even, what belongs to greater diligence, its words, counsels, and precepts, with pontifical law; with admirable subtlety he approved them by the canons of the fathers.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Jacobus de Altavilla, a German by nation, from Rinaugia, of the diocese of Mainz, a most learned professor of sacred letters, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, most subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse: he published several distinguished little works on the divine Scriptures, by which he destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have hitherto been judged worthy to see only a distinguished volume: On the Sentences, 4 books.
Also Various Questions, 1 book.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Johannes de Imenhusen, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect, circumspect in knowledge, scholastic in speech, a distinguished teacher no less by example than by word: he wrote certain excellent volumes, of reading not to be despised, by which, exercising his magnificent intellect, he also made known to posterity the memory of his name. Of these I have found only: On the Sentences, 4 books.
Elegant Sermons, 1 book.

Of the others I have seen nothing.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Petrus Berthorius, otherwise Bercharius, a Frenchman by nation, from Poitiers, prior of the monastery of Saint Eligius at Paris, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and outstandingly learned in secular letters; in preaching sermons to the people, a philosopher of excellent intellect, a distinguished historian and cosmographer: he wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Johannes de Pratis, bishop of Palestrina and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, he wrote a great and outstanding work, which has now been printed in three volumes, not useless to the simpler preachers; they call it the Dictionary, but he himself wished it to be entitled: Moral Repertory, 5 books.
Also Moral Reductory, 4 books.
Moral Inductory, 3 books.
Breviary of the Histories of the Bible, 1 book.
He wrote a Cosmography, 1 book.
Various Sermons, 2 books.
And many other things.

Finally, at the request of John, king of France, he translated Titus Livius into the French language. And it should be noted that of the three moral works which we have set down in the first place, each consists of three large volumes; of these, one part of the Moral Reductory, embracing morally all the historical books of the Bible, has been printed, and it begins from Genesis thus: “God in the creation of the world,” etc. His letters to various persons are reported, and small but many treatises.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1369.

Johannes de Tambacho, a German by nation, of the order of Friars Preachers, a man much practiced and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also not ignorant of secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect and speech, and composed with scholastic refinement, published certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: a large work, and not to be rejected, against the missiles of adverse fortune for those [unclear], no less useful than pleasant, which he wished to be entitled: The Consolation of Theology, 15 books. Whatever has been written

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

On the sensible delights of paradise, one book, beginning: “In the delights of the paradise of God.”
He published Sermons, one book.
And certain other works.
He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord [1360].

Leonard of [Giffoni?], of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, the twenty-fourth minister general, and afterward cardinal priest of the Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence, is said to have left many monuments of his intellect, of which I have found very few: On the Sentences, four books.
On the Song of Songs, one book.
A Notable Summa, one book.
Various Sermons, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

John Balistarii, a Catalan by birth, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, the seventeenth prior general, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, who governed his order sternly in deed and speech for sixteen years, composed distinguished monuments of his intellect, among which are reported: On the Sentences, one book.
On the War of the Church Militant, one book.
Various Sermons, one book.
And certain other works.

The aforementioned notable work on the mighty war of the Church militant and of Antichrist attacking it he sent dedicated to Pope Gregory XI.

He died in the times of the emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord [1374], in the second indiction, in his convent of Majorca.

John Boccaccio of Certaldo, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, easily the most learned of all men of his time in secular literature and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated poet, philosopher, and astronomer, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, published many distinguished volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported. To Robert, king of Sicily: On the Genealogy of the Gods, one book, beginning: “If sufficiently from the things related, Lord...”
On Illustrious Men, one book, beginning: “When I was inquiring...”
On Famous Women, one book, beginning: “On the day before, of eminent women...”
On the Heresies of the Bohemians, one book.
On the Victories of Sigismund, one book.
On the Wars of the Emperors, one book.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

On Mountains, one book, beginning: “I had arisen, indeed weary...”
On Springs, one book, beginning: “After concerning mountains and...”
On Rivers, one book, beginning: “By poetic invention...”
On the Wars of the Florentines, one book.
On the Rebellion of the Lands of the Church, one book.
On the Victory of the Tartars, one book.
On Pools and Marshes, one book, beginning: “Although sometimes from pools...”
On the Names of the Sea, one book, beginning: “A modest amount of labor having been undertaken...”
Of Bucolics, one book, beginning: “Tyndarus, it was not enough...”
On the Capture of Constantinople, one book.
Letters to Various Persons, one book.
And many other works.

In the vernacular language, moreover, many books of his are extant, full of jests and vanities, such as the book of the Hundred Novels, Corbaccio, and Philostratus.

He died under the emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord 1375, in the thirteenth indiction, at the age of 62.

John of Hildesheim, German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, learned in the sacred Scriptures, nobly taught in secular literature, a theologian, philosopher, and distinguished poet, was of excellent intellect in declaiming sermons to the people. He was formerly at Avignon the familiar and devoted servant of Blessed Peter Thomas, the general and most holy man of whom we made mention above. He wrote many distinguished little works in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among these the following are reported. To Florentius, bishop of Münster, he published a lengthy volume: On the Three Holy Kings, one book, beginning: “When of the most venerable...”
A Chronicle of Histories, one book.
A Defense of His Order, one book.
On Monsters in the Church, one book.
On the Fountain of Life, one book.
On Antichrist, one book.
Against the Jews, one book.
Against One Painting Shameful Things, one book.
Eighty Letters, one book.
Various Sermons, one book.
And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Jo-

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

John Maronis, English by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in ability, and an excellent disputant of scholastic questions, composed certain distinguished little works commending his talent, by which he made his name known even to posterity. Among these there is said to be a notable work, which he entitled: Table of Originals, 1 book.
Against the Wycliffites, 1 book.
And certain others.

He flourished in the school at Oxford, where by teaching, disputing, and writing he earned great praise from all, at about the time when the errors of John Wycliffe were condemned by the archbishop of Canterbury.

John Golein, Norman by homeland, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of the convent of Rouen, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle in ability and clear in eloquence, wrote little works of no contemptible authority, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of later generations. Among these there survives a notable work: On the Sentences, 4 books.
On the Office of the Mass, 1 book. “Sing to the Lord a song.”
Various Questions.

He also published several other works besides, which have by no means come into our hands.

Henry of Dolendorp, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and perfectly instructed in the disciplines of worldly philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, acute in ability and very well suited for disputing and unraveling scholastic questions, wrote for the instruction of readers certain excellent volumes, of which I have found only: On the Sentences, 4 books.

Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Urban V, in the year of the Lord [1370?].

Gallus, abbot of the monastery of Aula Regia in Bohemia, of the order, as they say, of the Cistercians, German by nation, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and rich in the reading of the ancients, an excellent contemplator of divine things, subtle in ability, open and composed in eloquence, also distinguished in the conduct of regular life, published for the edification of his brothers certain excellent volumes, by which he sent his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there survives a great and notable dialogue between father and son, which he entitled: Pomegranate, 3 books. “Son, as you approach the service...”
Sermons to the Brothers, 1 book.

There is today great use of this volume, the Pomegranate, among the truly devout religious, because it is suitable for beginners, those advancing, and the perfect.

Richard, archbishop of Armagh, primate of Ireland, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law, distinguished in ability, scholastic in speech, of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people, wrote several little works of his talent, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. When at one time he was preaching to the people on the matter of mendicancy, he set forth nine conclusions; offended by these, the brothers of the mendicant orders appealed before the people to the Apostolic See. Therefore, when both the archbishop and the brothers appeared at Avignon before Pope Innocent VI and the cardinals, in the year of the Lord 1347, on the eighth day of the month of November, Archbishop Richard publicly set forth, read, and pronounced [unclear] of those propositions, 1 book. “Judge not according...”
He also wrote Sermons, 1 book.
Questions on the Sentences, 1 book.
And certain other things.
