*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Sermons on the saints, one book. Moral sermons, one book. And many other works.

He was personally prominent at the Council of Constance, having been sent by the University of Vienna, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Peter of Rosenheim, a monk of the monastery of Melk in Austria, of the Order of St. Benedict, German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and magnificently instructed in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher and poet, ready and distinguished in talent, produced both in verse and in prose little works not to be cast aside, in which he properly exercised his talent. Among these there is extant a metrical work which he wrote, at the urging and request of Nicholas [Dinkelsbuhl?], to Lord Branda, cardinal of St. Clement, apostolic legate in Austria, on the chapters of the whole Bible, which he entitled The Rosy Memorial of Divine Things, one book. The star-ruling [one], heaven, earth...

A Notable History of the Times, one book.

Various Sermons, one book.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420, and composed many and various works.

Raphael Fulgosius, from Piacenza by nation, a man most learned in both laws and well instructed in the precepts of secular philosophy, excellent in talent, cautious and steadfast in counsel, produced certain distinguished volumes in civil law, by which he displayed the force and liveliness of his talent even to posterity. Among these the following are reported: On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

On the New Digest, twelve books. Many Legal Opinions, one book.

And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1416.

John of Palomar, archdeacon of the church of Barcelona, an eminent doctor of the Decrees, and nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, produced little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a distinguished treatise to John, abbot of the monastery of the Scots of the Order of St. Benedict at Vienna: On Abstinence from Meat, one book. The sons will rise in judgment...

Sermons and Questions.

The rest that he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of my reading.

*The Abbot of Spanheim*

He flourished at the university of Vienna in Austria, and composed many works in the time of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Raphael Cumanus, eminent professor of civil law and a very celebrated interpreter, excellent in talent and outstanding in counsel, whose authority among jurists is by no means slight, wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported: On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

Also Legal Opinions, one book. And several other works.

He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1416.

John of Teneramunda, a man zealous and very learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, distinguished in talent, ordered in speech, produced very useful little works for the edification of religious brothers, by which he instructed not only those then present, but also those who would come after him, in the love of God. And they are these: On the Knowledge of God, one book. On the Nature and Fall of Man, one book.

On the Restoration of the Fallen, one book. On the Love of God, one book.

On the Joy of Man, one book. On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book.

On the Christian Faith, one book. On the Honor of God, one book.

On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book.

He also elegantly composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Gasparinus, a very celebrated grammarian, from Bergamo by native place, born in the little village of Barzizza, a man most learned in secular letters, a most outstanding philosopher and rhetorician, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, who called back from the dead the elegance of Latin speech, half-dead as it was: he wrote many distinguished little works in that faculty, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there are extant: On Orthography, one book.

Letters to Various Persons, one book. I rejoice very greatly and [am glad]...

Various Orations, one book.

On the Letters of Cicero, one book.

On the same author’s On Duties, one book.

On the same author’s On the Orator, one book.

On the same author’s On Old Age, one book.

And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Constance and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

298 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* Antonius of Genoa, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, and a professor and very celebrated interpreter of canon law, outstanding in ability and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain small works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with praise to posterity. But I have not had the privilege of seeing any of them, except that which is entitled: *Compendium of Moral Figures*, one book. The rest have not come to me. “To religious men [in Christ?]...”

He flourished in person at the general Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1418.

Johannes de Mola, by homeland a Bolognese, a very celebrated doctor of both laws, excellent in ability and distinguished in eloquence, whose learning and eloquence in his time splendidly illuminated all Italy, is said to have published many distinguished volumes in both laws, whose authority is extolled with the highest praises among the professors of this faculty. Among these the following are reported first:

*On the Three Books of the Decretals*, one book.

*On the Sixth Book of the Decretals*, one book.

*On the ff. Infortiatum*, fourteen books.

*On the ff. Novum*: “Before we come to...”

And certain others.

He died at Bologna in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1435, indiction 14.

Antonius of Parma, prior general of the Camaldolese Order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in ability, composed in speech, sufficiently fit in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the direction of preachers of the word of God several distinguished small works, by which he made his name known. Of these the chief are reported:

*Sermons on the Season*, one book. “When he had drawn near...”

*Sermons on the Saints*, one book.

*Sermons through Lent*, one book.

And certain others.

He was present in person at the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Leonardo Aretino, an eminent philosopher, orator, and historian, a man in every respect most learned, skilled in Greek and Latin speech,

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

[Leonardus Aretinus?], first secretary to Innocent VII, Gregory XII, Alexander V, and John XXIII, Roman pontiffs, down to the Council of Constance, and then summoned by the Florentine senate, was appointed general chancellor; in that office he remained until the end of his life with great fidelity and authority. Among other things he wrote an outstanding work of Dialogues, 1 book; A History of His Own Time; On the Good Deeds of the Florentines, 2 books; On the Praises of Florence; A History of the Goths, 4 books; A History of the Punic War, 2 books; The Life of Aristotle, 1 book; On the Life of Cicero, 1 book; A Volume of Letters, 1 book.

He also composed some other works most elegantly, which have not come to my knowledge. Moreover he translated many things from Greek into Latin: namely, the treatise of the blessed priest Basil On the Instruction of Pupils; also, from Plutarch, the lives of Tiberius and Gracchus among the Greeks, and of Paulus Aemilius, Cato the Younger, and Sertorius among the Romans. He likewise translated Xenophon’s little book On the Tyrant, Plato’s Gorgias and Phaedo, and certain letters, Aristotle’s Economics, and the books of the Ethics and Politics. And other things which have not come to me.

He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420. He died, however, under Frederick III as emperor and Eugene IV as pope, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction, on the seventh Ides of March, in about the seventy-fourth year of his age.

Poggio the Florentine, a philosopher and eloquent orator, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin speech, and for many years a most eloquent writer of apostolic letters, is said to have composed some little works of excellent talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Lorenzo Valla was this Poggio’s most bitter rival, and wrote various things against him. He himself published: On the Situation of the Region of India, 1 book; Against Lorenzo Valla, 2 books; Letters to Various Persons, 1 book; Various Orations, 1 book; and many other things.

He rendered Dionysius Siculus and many other Greek authors into Latin. Moreover, at the Council of Constance he delivered very many funeral orations. The filthy work which he entitled Facetiae I have judged rightly to be excluded from this catalogue of illustrious men, since the reading of it offends the devout, harms the unwary, and infects the carnal.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Lorenzo Valla, a Roman patrician, by far the foremost of the grammarians of this age, a most outstanding philosopher, orator, and theologian, subtle in intellect, sharp, and vehement, who, preferring Latin eloquence to Greek, composed many works for its adornment, and, being most skilled in Greek and Latin speech, published little works not to be despised in reading, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported: Elegances, 6 books; On the Reciprocity of sui and suus, 1 book; A Book of Many Letters, 1 book; also On Quintilian, 12 books; Dialectic, 1 book; Panegyric On the True Good, [unclear] books; On Free Will, 1 book; Apologue against Poggio, [unclear] book; Against Antonio da Rho, 1 book; and many other things.

“When often with me the elders,” 1 book. “You alone, Johannes,” 1 book. “When I was undertaking, Paul,” 1 book. “I would very much wish, Garzia,” 1 book. “I hear that Poggio another,” 1 book.

He translated into Latin Homer, Thucydides, and several others.

He flourished in person at the Council of Constance under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1429. Concerning him someone says as follows: What did that most biting censor of the Latin language, Lorenzo Valla, beget for himself by his dreadful and exacting reproof? What praise, I ask, did he obtain after death other than that, according to his merits, that fine epigram about him is read and proclaimed everywhere?

Now after Valla, dead, sought the shades,
Pluto does not dare to speak Latin words.
Jupiter would have deemed him worthy of heaven’s honor,
But he himself fears him as censor of his tongue.

What he thought about the Donation of Constantine, by which Constantine endowed the Roman church, his book beautifully shows; would that so great a man had never published it.

Giovanni Tortelli, by nation an Aretine, a very close friend of Lorenzo Valla, to whom Valla wrote the six books of the Elegances of the Latin Language; subdeacon and chamberlain of the Roman pontiff, and afterward companion of Pope Nicholas and an intimate associate of his studies,

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

a count, perfectly trained in Greek and Latin letters, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian. Among other little works of his talent he wrote a large and distinguished volume, which he entitled *Commentaries on Grammar*, one book.

Also *On Dialectic*, one book.

He published various letters, one book.

And many other things.

He translated the *Life of Athanasius of Alexandria* into Latin for Pope Eugenius, and rendered the historian Appian word for word. And other things.

He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Hermann Petra of Stutdorp, of the Carthusian order, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, vicar and rector of the house of nuns of his order, of Saint Anne near Bruges in Flanders, where for twenty-nine years he was distinguished by much religion and learning, wrote certain devout little works of his talent. Of these the following are reported: a notable work divided into six volumes over the cycle of the year, containing

*Sermons on the Season*, one book.

*Sermons on the Saints*, one book.

Fifty sermons *On the Lord’s Prayer*, one book.

*On the Governance of Nuns*, one book.

And very many other things.

He died under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth indiction.

[Guarinus Veronensis?], perfectly trained in Greek and Latin eloquence, the most celebrated philosopher and rhetorician of all in his time, once at Venice a pupil of Manuel Chrysoloras of Constantinople, who brought Greek letters back into Italy, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

*On Cicero’s Orator*, one book. “How much of Cicero’s ora-” [unclear] “In explaining this au-” [unclear]

*On the Poet Lucan*, one book.

*On Quintilian*, one book.

*In Praise of Eloquence*, one book. “How much admiration” [unclear] Many orations.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

And he published very many other things, which have not yet come into our hands.

He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Henry of Hesse the Younger, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of the monks of Mary, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published many very elegant volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity; and he publicly lectured on many of them in the universities before his entry into religion. Of these the following are reported:

*On the Sentences*, four books.

*On Genesis*, one book.

*On Exodus*, one book.

*On the Proverbs of Solomon*, one book.

*On the Apocalypse of John*, one book.

*A Dialogue between a Bishop and a Priest*, one book.

*Useful Sermons*, one book.

And certain other things.

He died under the emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1428, in the sixth indiction.

John Gerson, a Frenchman by nation, chancellor of Paris, formerly a disciple of Peter of Ailly, cardinal of Cambrai, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, sure and firm in judgment, cautious in counsel, and a very distinguished interpreter of doubtful matters, outstanding in life and conduct, by far the foremost of the theologians of his time, wrote in verse and prose many most excellent little works, through which his name will always possess immortality among posterity; the reading of them is no less useful than pleasant to devout and religious men. Of these there is extant:

*On the Praise of Scribes*, one book. “To search the Scriptures”

*On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, one book. “That the Gospel was brought”

*On Ecclesiastical Power*, one book. “Ecclesiastical power de-” [unclear]

*On the Removability of the Bridegroom*, one book. “But the days will come when”

*On the Manner of Conducting Oneself in Schism*, one book. “For the removal of certain” [unclear]

*On Ecclesiastical Unity*, one book. “Ecclesiastical unity” [unclear]

*On Ecclesiastical Estates*, one book. “The peace which all”

*On the Manner of Living of the Faithful*, one book. “The first rule which”

*On Ecclesiastical Defects*, one book. “Perhaps it is said to me, Ec-” [unclear]

*On schism-*

*The Abbot of Spanheim.*

On the schism, one book. “In the inquiry into truth.”
On the general council, one book. “About to provide an occasion.”
A trialogue on the schism, two books. “Very often the sublime.”
On the marriage of the Church, two books. “There was a marriage in.”
What things must necessarily be believed, one book. “A concise declaration.”
On various heresies, one book. “A protestation or revocation.”
On appeal from the pope, one book. “It is asked whether this.”
Against Peter de Luna, fifty articles, one book. “And first it is clear,” etc.
Against the same, eight articles, one book. “And first it must be noted.”
On the assumption of Christ’s humanity, one book. “Most reverend in Christ.”
Two readings on Mark, one book. “As it is written in.”
On the literal sense of Scripture, one book. “But he who blasphemes.”
Against the heresy of the Bohemians, one book. “About to offer according to himself.”
On the proving of spirits, one book. “Test the spirits, whether they are from God.”
On the examination of doctrines, one book. “Beware of false prophets.”
A trialogue against astrology, one book. “The wisdom which from the Lord God.”
On true and false visions, one book. “Lately, in one of the readings.”
On the literal sense of Scripture, one book. “The Apostle blames those who.”
Against Jacobus Angeli, one book. “Every work of God is [unclear].”
On the errors of magic, one book. “When I lately was praising.”
Against Matthew Grabon, one book. “To the most reverend in Christ.”
Against the flagellants, one book. “The law of Christ says, the law of love.”
Moral rules, one book. “Let us now meanwhile act.”
On the precepts of the Decalogue, one book. “To Christianity its own [unclear].”
On the difference of sins, one book. “He who considers well.”
On hearing confessions, one book. “And if the virtue which,” etc.
On confession of softness, one book. “A certain master in the [unclear].”
Remedies for those who relapse, one book. “Art has this as its own.”
On sacramental absolution, one book. “Grace to you and peace, brother.”
A dialogue on the power of binding, one book. “When Christ gave.”
On indulgences, one book. “Whatever you shall bind.”
On four questions, one book. “It is asked whether speaking ill.”

On contracts, two books. “Those who wish to become rich.”
On simony, one book. “On the matter of simony.”
On the solicitude of ecclesiastics, one book. “Do not be anxious what.”
The testament of the pilgrim, in verse, one book. “Blessed is that servant whom.”
One book. “Grace, whose name,” etc.
On [unclear].

*On Ecclesiastical Writers.*

On nocturnal pollution, one book. “It was doubted by me.”
On diurnal pollution, one book. “I wrote some things earlier.”
On the chastity of ecclesiastics, one book. “There are eunuchs who made themselves.”
On abstinence from meats, one book. “Great and wondrous is.”
On the temperance of prelates, one book. “Already in one earlier reading.”
On the life of clerics, one book. “Repent, believe.”
On humility, one book. “From God it came forth, to God.”
One book. “A certain noble man.”
On nobility, one book. “King of kings, kindly Jesus.”
On the consideration of a prince, one book. “Soldiers in the desert.”
A dialogue of two soldiers, one book. “Whatever things have been written.”
On the consolation of theology, one book. “A thing [unclear], O Monica.”
An apologetic dialogue, one book. “They have been accustomed [to seek] the source.”
Josephina, in verse, one book. “Conceived of a virgin.”
A centiloquy on concepts, one book. “I baptized you with water.”
One book. “He has put down the mighty from.”
A centiloquy on impulses, eight books. “Repent, believe.”
On mystical theology, one book. “Treating in the readings.”
On the same, practical, one book. “To you it has been given to know.”
An elucidation of the same, one book. “Grace to you, peace.”
On the perfection of religion, one book. “The meditation of my heart.”
On the meditation of the heart, one book. “In simplicity of heart.”
On simplicity of heart, one book.

On the Song of Songs, one book. “We have sung to you, and.”

*Abbot of Spanheim.*

On the Marriage of Wisdom, 4 books. “I sought a bride for myself.”
On the Twofold Logic, 2 books. “And John was clothed.”
To the Rectors of Boys, 1 book. “Allow the little children to come.”
Sermons in the Council of Constance, 1 book. “Walk while you have the light [unclear].”
Sermons to the Clergy, 1 book. [unclear]
Sermons to the People, 1 book.
Dialogue on Any Subject, 1 book.
Several Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.
He also published many other smaller works, indeed, but very useful, of which certain knowledge has not come down to us.

He was personally prominent in the Council of Constance, in which, laboring gloriously for the extirpation of heresies, at last, after it was dissolved, he was deprived of home, country, relatives, friends, dignities, and his own possessions for the defense of the truth, and was sought by many plots. Hence, compelled by necessity, he fled to the city of Lyons, and there after a few years he died, under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1429, in the seventh indiction, in the sixty-sixth year of his age, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, and was buried there with honor among the Celestines.

Vincent Ferrer of Valencia, of the Order of Friars Preachers, to whom some letters of John Gerson are extant, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, devout in morals and conduct, and the most celebrated preacher of sermons of all in his time, shining with miracles while alive and after death, wrote elegant works: Sermons on the Season, 1 book. “Blessed is he who comes in...”
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. “He is rich toward all who...”
Sermons throughout Lent, 1 book.
Certain Letters.

He was personally prominent in the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1418. After his death, because of his frequent miracles, he was canonized by Pope Callistus III, in the year of the Lord 1455, in the third indiction. His feast is in April [unclear].

Boniface Ferrer of Valencia, a Catalan by birth, twenty-fifth prior of the Carthusian Order, brother of the aforesaid Blessed Vincent the Preacher, a man learned in the divine scriptures and an outstanding doctor of canon law, not unlike his holy brother in life and conduct, governed the Grande Chartreuse vigorously by word and example. Among other things he wrote a noteworthy treatise on why few in the Carthusian Order have been canonized and why they do not publicly perform miracles: To Boniface of the Same Order, 1 book.
On the Approbation of the Order, 1 book.
Certain Letters. And many other things.

He was prominent in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Lupus of Oliveto, a Spaniard by birth, prior general of the Order of Hermit Monks of Saint Jerome, a man devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures, and an outstanding restorer of his order, wrote several excellent little works by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported: From the Sayings of Saint Jerome, The Rule of His Order, 1 book.
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
And certain other works.

This rule, newly compiled in thirty-three chapters, Martin V confirmed.

He was prominent at the time of the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Dominic of San Gimignano, a most excellent jurist, and nobly learned both in the divine writers and in the other secular disciplines, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain excellent volumes on canon law, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant a notable and very celebrated work, divided into two volumes: On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 2 books. “Because the first gloss at the end...”
And various declarations.

He also wrote a Repertory in law, and commentaries on the second and third books of the Decretals.
Counsels in law by the same author.

He flourished at the same time as Paulus de Castro and John of Imola.

The rest, however, which he is said to have composed, have not come to my knowledge.

Paul of Saint Mary, a Jew by birth, a Christian by faith, first bishop of Cartagena and afterward bishop of Burgos in Spain, archchancellor of the king of Castile and Leon, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine scriptures, and a master of sacred theology, having been converted to the Catholic faith in his mature age, advanced so far in life and doctrine that among all the doctors of Spain he had no equal in his time. He wrote to his son Alfonso de-

*THE ABBOT OF SPANHEIM.*

the dean of Compostela, doctor of laws, on the Postils of Nicholas of Lyra: Notable Additions, 1 book. “What do you want for yourself, as one living” Scrutiny of the Scriptures, 2 books. “Search the Scriptures” And certain other things.

He flourished, and completed this Scrutiny of his, under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1454, in the twelfth indiction, in the eighty-first year of his age.

Petrus Paulus Vergerius, by country a Justinopolitan, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, a philosopher and very celebrated rhetorician, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin speech, once a hearer of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher teaching Greek letters at Venice, wrote certain distinguished little works of excellent talent, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity. Among these there is extant a notable work, containing, concerning the deeds of the lords of Carrara: A very beautiful History, 1 book.

On Noble Manners, 1 book.

In Praise of Saint Jerome, 1 book.

And many other things.

He flourished at the Council of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Maphaeus Vegius, by country a man of Lodi, datary of Pope Martin V, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and outstandingly learned, and very learned in secular letters, a very celebrated orator and poet, and no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge; through whose care and expense the remains of Saint Monica, mother of Saint Augustine, were translated from Ostia Tiberina to Rome and were laid in a new chapel built at great cost by him, in which he himself also was buried: he wrote, both in meter and in prose, certain distinguished volumes, among which there is extant a very celebrated work, necessary for all religious persons, composed from divine and human literature, addressed to certain sisters, which he entitled: On Perseverance, 7 books. “Since grave matters often, as happens” On the Penitential Psalms, 1 book.

In Praise of Saint Monica, 1 book.

The Thirteenth Book of the Aeneid, in heroic verse, 1 book.

Many Epigrams, 1 book.

On Military Affairs, A Dialogue, which is called Philaletes, Many Letters.

And very many other things.

*ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.*

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Johannes Placth, a German by nation, ornament and pillar of the Heidelberg school, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct insofar as the secular estate permits, an outstanding teacher in delivering sermons to the people: among other things he wrote a great and notable volume, which he lectured on regularly and publicly in the aforesaid University of Heidelberg: On the first [unclear] of the Decretals, 1 book. “Venerable fathers” Against the Bohemians, 1 book. “As the wise man says” Questions on the Sentences, 1 book.

Several Sermons.

Various Questions.

And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1439.

Johannes Dieppurg, called de Franckfordia, a German by nation, a doctor of Heidelberg, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, a keen disputant and an outstanding expounder of sermons, formerly chaplain and secretary of Ludwig, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, and often an envoy in many difficult cases: he wrote little works of reading not to be scorned, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported: Against the Hussites, 1 book. “When recently in the year of the Lord” Against the Feymeros, 1 book. “The law of the Lord outwardly [unclear]” On Contracts, 1 book. “As in the forum of the soul where in” On Predestination, 1 book. “Glory to God in the highest” Many Sermons, 1 book.

An Oration before the King of England, 1 book.

An Oration before the Duke of Savoy, 1 book.

An Oration before the King of France, 1 book.

Various Questions, 1 book.

Several Letters, Diverse Orations.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

*Raymundus Sebeide, a Spaniard by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, and also exceptionally well taught in secular letters, a distinguished doctor of arts and medicine, who by teaching and writing in the university of Toulouse gave great proof of his erudition, is said to have written many excellent little works. Of these I have seen only a large volume, which he had read publicly in the aforesaid university; at its beginning he promises many glorious things, and some applaud themselves concerning the truth of them as though experienced, because he had noted beforehand:*

*Of Creatures, or On Man*, one book.

*Disputed Questions*, one book.

To the praise and glory [unclear] The rest are unknown to me.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1450.

Franciscus Barbarus, a Venetian by birth, a disciple in Greek letters of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, a clear philosopher and a supreme orator in both languages, while still a young man wrote certain little works not unworthy of reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there is extant a work which he entitled:

*On Marriage*, one book.

*Letters to Various Persons*, sixteen books.

And certain other things.

From Plutarch he translated into Latin, for his brother Zacharias, the life of Aristides and of Cato, and of many illustrious men. Likewise also other things.

He died in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Nicholas V, in the year of the Lord 1454, in the second indiction.

Thomas Walden, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, and prior general of the English province, a man most learned in the divine writings and nobly taught in Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect and quite fit for disputation, distinguished no less in conduct than in knowledge, also an excellent preacher of sermons, and formerly confessor and secretary of Henry V, king of the English, wrote, among the other monuments of his talent, a distinguished work divided into three great volumes against the infamous Wycliffites and Hussite heretics, which Pope Martin V, after examination, confirmed by apostolic authority. This work is entitled:

*The Doctrinal of the Church*, one book.

*Let God arise and let [his enemies] be scattered*, three

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Also on the Sentences, 4 books. On the Ethics, 10 books. On the Physics, 8 books. On the book On the Heaven and the World, 4 books. On Generation and Corruption, 2 books. On the Meteorology, 4 books. On the books On the Soul, 4 books.

He says besides that he wrote many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He died at Rouen, honorably buried in his own convent, under the emperor Sigismund, in the last year of Pope Martin V, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430, in the eighth indiction, on the third day of the month of November.

Paulus de Castro, a jurist, the most celebrated of all men of his time, a man of great learning and eloquence, who for many years taught civil law gloriously at Siena, Florence, and Padua, having been hired at a public salary, composed many little works on the laws, known and dear to the professors of this faculty; by these he left to posterity the memory of his most famous name. Among them the following are reported: On the Code, 9 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, [unclear] books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Institutes, 4 books. Most elegant Opinions, 1 book. And several other things.

He died in the times of the emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1437, in the fifteenth indiction.

Ambrosius Florentinus, general abbot of the Camaldolese order, once a pupil of Chrysoloras, the Byzantine philosopher, when he was teaching Greek literature at Venice, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular studies, a most lucid philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian, left to posterity many distinguished monuments of his talent. He was the nuncio and envoy of Pope Eugenius to the Council of Basel, where he delivered a solemn oration on his behalf before the fathers. He wrote a distinguished volume: Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. Various Orations. And several other things.

He also translated into Latin from Greek the four books of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, in a more elegant and easier style; also the original Life of Blessed John Chrysostom, addressed to the emperor Sigismund; likewise Basil On Virginity, addressed to Cardinal Gabriel, afterward Pope Eugenius IV; likewise Laertius On the Life of the Philosophers, addressed to Cosmas de’ Medici. But he also rendered the three books of Saint John Chrysostom to Stagirius, the afflicted monk, in lucid and adorned speech. And several other things still unknown to us.

He also translated Ephrem the Syrian. He himself wrote On the Sacraments; On [unclear] the Holy Spirit.

He flourished in the times of the Councils of Constance and Basel, both of which he adorned by his presence, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Caietanus, by country a Vicentine, a canon of Padua, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, notably instructed in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and physician, a most celebrated theologian, who publicly taught sacred scholastic letters in the school of Padua, acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote, in both branches of literature, as they report, several little works, by which he left to posterity the memory of his care. Among them these are reported: On the Physics, 8 books. On the books On the Soul, 4 books. On the book On the Heaven and the World, 4 books. And several other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1450.

Henricus Gulpen, abbot of the monastery of St. Giles in Nuremberg, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a German by nation, a distinguished jurist, exceptionally learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, and no less venerable for his religious way of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, whose readiness of talent and prudence in counsel Johannes Nider, having experienced them, commends in his little work On the Ants, wrote elegantly on the seven distinctions: On Penance, 1 book. On Consecration, 1 book. On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book. And certain other things.

He was personally present at the Council of Constance, when he was still a secular master of arts studying law, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Jacobus Forliviensis, a philosopher and physician of very celebrated reputation, who is considered by many to have far surpassed all professors of philosophy and medicine of his time, distinguished not only for learning but also for experience in curing human illnesses, wrote for those toiling in his faculty very useful little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. The chief of these are reported: On

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

On the extension of the degrees of forms, one book.
On the first [book of] Avicenna's Canon, one book.
On the aphorisms of the same, one book.
On the Techne also, one book. And certain other things.
He flourished in the times of Sigismund, the most Christian emperor, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1430.

Rudolphus of Bruxella, a village of Swabia, German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and notably learned also in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, an eminent professor of sacred theology, who in the Heidelberg school acquired great praises for his learning: in that faculty he wrote works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity, namely: Questions on the Sentences, one book.
Very useful sermons, one book.
Various questions, one book.
Several orations to the fathers, one book. Although holy mother
And many other things.
He flourished in the Heidelberg school at the time of the Council of Basel and thereafter, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Hugo of Siena, Italian by nation, a man very learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a distinguished philosopher and very celebrated physician, excellent in talent and outstanding in eloquence, wrote volumes in medicine not to be lightly esteemed by students, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Among these the following are reported: On the first [book] of Avicenna, one book.
On the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, one book.
On the Techne of Galen, one book. And many other things.
He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1450.

Henricus de Gauda, German by nation, magnificently learned in the holy Scriptures, subtle in talent and a very acute disputant of scholastic questions, in the Heidelberg school, both by reading, by teaching, and also by composing, easily held first place in his time. He wrote certain excellent works of his talent, of which only a few have so far come to my knowledge.

On the book of the Sentences, one book. A fountain of gardens, a well
On celebration, one book. Pray

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Various orations. Disputed questions. And certain other things.
He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1435.

Santes de Arduinis, born from the city of Pesaro, a man most learned in philosophy and medicine, and most experienced in healing human bodies, held in great esteem among the Venetians in his time, published certain excellent works of this faculty, by which he destined the memory of his most celebrated name for the knowledge of posterity. Among these there exists a notable work on all natural and artificial poisons, one book.
On smelling also, one book.
On procreation, one book.
And certain other things.
He flourished under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Nicolaus de Susato, German by nation, a very celebrated doctor of sacred theology, and most learned both in secular philosophy and in the divine Scriptures, held in esteem by Ludovicus, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, and in the Council of Constance joined with the other cardinals from the German nation for electing the supreme pontiff, as is found in the acts of the same council: he wrote several excellent works of his talent, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Among these are reported: Questions on the Sentences, one book.
Many sermons, one book.
Various questions. And many other things.
He flourished in the Council of Constance under Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1417.

Johannes de Marliano, a very celebrated philosopher and physician, excellent in talent, distinguished in experience of this art, and not among the lowest of the physicians of his age, published certain excellent and lucid works both in philosophy and in medicine, the reading and study of which are said to be of no little use to students of these subjects, namely: On reaction etc., one book.
On antiperistasis, one book.
And many other things.
He flourished in the times of Sigismund, the most Christian emperor, in the year of the Lord 1430.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear]
Johannes Gritsch, a German by nation, from Basel as his native city, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, sufficiently instructed both in canon law and in secular philosophy, outstanding in ability and distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote works not to be despised for preachers of the word of God, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book.
Sermons on the Saints, one book.
Sermons for Lent, one book. “When you fast,” etc., [unclear]
On the Passion of the Lord, one book.
And certain others.

He flourished, as his own people say, in the time of Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

[unclear]
Johannes Nider, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, sufficiently learned in scholastic philosophy, of excellent and distinguished ability in delivering sermons to the people, an inquisitor of heretical depravity and a very keen investigator of the little women whom the common people call witches, wrote in plain speech several volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Contracts of Merchants, one book. “Since the office of merchants”
On Moral Leprosy, one book. “Once, when we read in Le-”
The Law of the Decalogue, for consecrated [unclear]
On Ants Morally Treated, five books. “Often traversing those things which”
On the Consolation of a Fearful Conscience, one book. “Among the disciplines I found”
Mirror of Perfection, one book.
Sermons for the Temporal Cycle, one book. “Behold your king,” etc. “Three”
Sermons on the Saints. “Come after me,” etc.
Lenten Sermons, one book. “Be converted to,” etc. And many other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Sigismund, at the Councils of Constance and Basel, in the year of the Lord 1430.

[unclear]
Nicolaus Siculus, abbot of [Monacen?], of the Order of Saint Benedict, sprung from the city of Catania, called de Tudeschis, first auditor of the causes of the lord Pope in the Rota, afterward archbishop of Palermo, and finally cardinal of the holy Roman Church, the most celebrated jurist of all, subtle and acute in intellect, ready and firm in counsel, clear and composed in speech, who deservedly is called the lamp of the law, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity; of these the following are reported: On the Decretum, unfinished, one book.
On the Decretals, five books. “Since every reason of the supreme”
On the Clementines, one book.
For the Council of Basel, one book. “Since the truth of words”
Judicial Process, one book. “The peace-making king of all”
One Hundred and Four Opinions, one book. “The contingency of the fact is such”
Various Disputations, one book.
And many other things.

He flourished in person at the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1435. And on behalf of the authority of that council, before the princes at Frankfurt, he publicly read the aforementioned treatise and delivered an elegant oration there.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Ludovicus Pontanus of Rome, an Italian by nation, a very brilliant jurist, and no less devoted to the holy Scriptures than to secular philosophy, excellent in ability, concise and weighty in judgment, published volumes not to be despised for those wishing to make progress in the legal faculty, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number I have seen only the work entitled: Notable Singulars, one book. “The word is understood entirely” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the time of the most excellent Emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Johannes Noblet, of the Order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a Frenchman by nation, of the Paris convent and school, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, since before entering religion he had been, by art, practice, and profession, a salutary physician of sick bodies, wrote several distinguished little works, of which the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books.
On the Canonical Epistles, seven books. “Noble in the gates is her husband”
Centiloquy of Riddles, one book.
Various Sermons, one book.
And many other things.

In addition, on many books of the Bible he wrote marvelous and elegant commentaries [the text breaks off].

[unclear] are said to have been written, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Johannes de Ragusio, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, produced certain excellent little works of his ability, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have read a well-constructed work addressed to the fathers of the Council of Basel: *Against the Hussites*, one book, “Most reverend, venerable [fathers?] ...” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in person at the Council of Basel, where he publicly delivered the said treatise against the heretics before the fathers, under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1458.

B Londus Flavius of Forlì, secretary of Pope Eugene IV, a man skilled in every discipline of the liberal arts, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, and an eminent historiographer, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, and second to none in grace of expression, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

*Three Decades*, so entitled.

*On the Deeds of the Romans*, three books, “Of the Roman empire ...”

*On Rome Triumphant*, ten books.

*On Rome Restored*, five books.

*On Italy Illustrated*, eight books.

*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

*Various Orations*, one book.

And several other works.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund, under Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1435. He left five sons from a legitimate marriage, cultivators of the liberal arts.

H Heimericus de Campo, a German by nation, vice-chancellor of the University of Cologne, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent and an outstanding disputant of difficult questions, wrote many excellent little works; nevertheless, few of these have so far come into our hands. He was personally present at the Council of Basel, sent by the University of Cologne, where, at the urging of Master Nicholas of Cusa, later cardinal, he produced *Compendium of Questions*, one book. Afterward, on several occasions [unclear].

*The Abbot of Sponheim.*

*On the Sentences*, four books, “As Augustine says in the book ...”

*On Being and Essence*, one book, “Being and not-being are opposed ...”

*Compendium of Divine Things*, four books, “In this little work under ...”

*Various Questions*, one book.

*Many Sermons*, one book.

*On the Authority of the Council*, one book.

And several other works.

He flourished at the Council of Basel, where he wrote and disputed much, in the year of the Lord 1438, under Emperor Albert.

Georgius Trapezuntius, apostolic secretary, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and poet, who, having been put by Pope Eugene in charge of the public school at Rome, taught rhetoric and poetry for many years and left after him many disciples most skilled in every science, wrote certain excellent volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these are extant: A very beautiful *Rhetoric*, one book.

A singular *Dialectic*, one book.

*On the Orations of Cicero*, one book.

Various orations and letters.

And certain other works.

He flourished at Rome in the times of Pope Eugene IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1435.

Florianus de S. Petro, an Italian by nation, a native of Bologna, easily the most learned of all men of his time in civil law, and not ignorant of either the divine Scriptures or secular philosophy, sharp in talent, distinguished in eloquence, a subtle disputant and cautious counsellor, wrote in that faculty certain very excellent little works, by which he commended the memory of his very celebrated name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

*On the Code*, nine books.

*On the Old Digest*, twenty-four books.

*On the New Digest*, twelve books.

*On the Infortiatum*, fourteen books.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Sigismund and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1435.

Nicolaus Lackman, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor of St. Francis, minister of Saxony, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of Aristotelian philosophy, outstanding in talent and fit for disputation, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote not without [unclear].

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear] little works for reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these, the following are said to be the more important:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Various Questions, 1 book.
Sermons on the Temporale, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
And many other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Basel, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1440.

John of Schoonhoven, a German by nation, of the order of the Canons Regular of St Augustine, from the monastery in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, which is commonly called Groenendaal and in Latin Viridis Vallis, in which John Ruusbroec formerly held the office of prior, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, cautious in intellect, composed in speech, and no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge. He wrote to Simon, his nephew: A Spiritual Exhortation, 1 book. “Great joy to me”
On the Course of a Monk, 1 book. “That to you, dearest” [unclear]
On the Progress of a Monk, 1 book. “Fight the good fight”
A Defense of John Ruusbroec, 1 book. “When a certain doctor” [unclear]
Various Sermons, 1 book.
Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.
And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Constance, under Emperor Sigismund and Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1420.

Peter de Colle, of the order of the Friars Minor of St Francis, a German by nation, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, and eloquent and lucid in delivering sermons to the people. He published several volumes for the edification of readers, by which he transmitted the memory of his distinguished name to posterity. Among these there survives a well-arranged work, which he recited before the fathers at the Council of Basel: On the Authority of a Council, 1 book. “The Church fought many” [unclear]
Questions on the Sentences, 1 book.
Various Sermons, 1 book.
And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the same Council of Basel, at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1440.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Hermann, a monk in Campo, of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Münster, a German by nation and a Westphalian by homeland, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed both in canon law and in Aristotelian philosophy, ready in intellect and clear in speech. He wrote several little works of his practiced talent, by which he labored considerably in defense of the Council of Basel. Among these I found a little work that he entitled On Definitive Voices: In a General Council, 1 book. “Now after very often repeated” [unclear]
On the Power of the Pope and of a Council, 1 book. “Blessed Athanasius”
Also On Schism, 1 book.
On Neutrality, 1 book.
Of the rest which he composed, although many are reported, nothing has come down to me.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

John Gauer, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, lector of sacred Scripture, of the convent of Mainz, was a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently capable in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote little works of his practiced talent not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there survive: On the Sentences, 4 books. “To the praise of almighty God”
Also On Exodus, 1 book. “The law for the common utility”
A Harmony of the Evangelists, 1 book. “Because God sent his Son”
Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.
A Triple Lenten Work, 3 books. “When you fast, know” [unclear]
And many other works.

He flourished in the time of the Council of Basel, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1440.

Bernardino, of the order of the Friars Minor, an Italian by nation and from Siena by homeland, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures, the most celebrated preacher of all his time, most holy in life and conduct, inasmuch as both living and dead he shone with countless miracles. He wrote certain little works for the edification of the faithful, by which he also showed the power of his talent to posterity. Of these there survive: On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. “Blessed [unclear] threefold”
On the Eternal Gospel, 1 book. “For I did not come to dissolve the law”
On the Christian Religion, 1 book. “Now abide faith, hope”
On con-

320 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* On the conception of St. Mary, one book, “The depths were not yet,” and On the Passion of the Lord, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other works.

He died at Aquila, a city of Abruzzo, in the reign of the emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1443, in the sixth indiction, in the sixty-fifth year of his age. And because of frequent miracles he was entered by Pope Nicholas V in the catalogue of the saints, in the year of the Lord 1450, seven years after his death. His feast is celebrated on the twentieth day of the month of May.

Antonius Guainerius, an Italian by nation, from Pavia by homeland, a most celebrated doctor of the art of medicine, and nobly learned in the precepts of the philosophers, excellent in ability and notably distinguished by skill in his profession, wrote in that field of learning certain lucid little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On disease of the stomach, one book. On fever also, one book.
On diseases of the groin, one book. On pleurisy, one book.
On the womb, one book. On fluxes, one book.
On arthritis in the joints, one book. On the sufferings of stone, one book.
On the third book of Avicenna, one book. And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Gerardus Stredam, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of All the Apostles near Liege, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and excellently learned through long practice, also venerable in religion, prudence, and authority, wrote for the edification of simple brothers certain little works, of which the following are reported: To the abbot of Saint Adrian of Geraardsbergen, On pastoral care, one book. On the Ten Commandments, one book.
On the Seven Sacraments, one book. Mirror of religious, one book.
Dialogue on the virtues, one book. Dialogue on the vices, one book.
Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book.
And certain other works.

He died at the beginning of the reign of the emperor Frederick III, under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1445, in the sixth indiction.

Matthaeus Palmerius, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, a historian, philosopher, and most eloquent orator, who at the Council of Florence, which Pope Eugenius IV held against the synod of Basel, was counted among the distinguished men, wrote a book full of error concerning the angels; and, stubbornly defending it, he was condemned as a heretic and burned at the city of Corna. Carefully reviewing the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, he corrected it and, completing it down to the year of the Lord 1448, entitled it to Petrus Cosmas de’ Medici, one book, “Innate in our minds.”
Letters to various persons, one book.
Various orations also.
And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1440.

321 *The Abbot of Sponheim* Johannes Ernesti, a German by nation, once the ornament and rector of the school of Heidelberg, learned in the holy Scriptures and rich in his reading of the ancients, subtle in ability, eloquent with singular grace of speech, an outstanding disputant of questions, wrote, as they report, certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: Questions on the Sentences, one book.
A question in disputation, one book.
Many sermons, one book.
An oration on the Nativity of the Lord, one book, “Although of speaking concerning the greatest...”
On fasting, to the university, one book, “Most sacred desires...”
Many and various orations, one book.
And many other works.

He flourished at the time of the Council of Basel, at the beginning of the reign of the emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Bartholomaeus, of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of Bethlehem in the town of Roermond in Guelders, a German by nation, an acute, devout, and celebrated interpreter of sacred letters, wrote for the edification of his brothers certain distinguished little works, by which he magnificently exercised his ability and left to posterity the memory of his name. Of their number the following are reported: Exercise of devotion, one book.
Sum of vices, one book.
On abstinence from meats, one book.
On the proclamations of the brothers, one book. On an oath, one book. And certain other works.
On rash judgments, one book.

*On Ecclesiastical Writers*

He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1446, in the ninth indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of July.

Henry of Vuerlis, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, minister of the province of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in talent and scholastic eloquence, an acute disputant and an outstanding preacher of sermons, composed certain lucid volumes, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there is extant the notable work: On the Sentences, four books.
On Ecclesiastical Power, one book.
Various Sermons also, one book. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the Council of Basel and of Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1440.

Andreas of Traiectum, a German by nation, a monk of our monastery of Spanheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, which is situated within the bounds of the diocese of Mainz, between the Rhine and the Hercynian forest which, called Saonus, extends westward toward Trier, a man certainly studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant also of secular letters, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote, both in verse and in prose, not contemptible little works, of which the following are held: Soliloquies of a Man to God, one book. “When once the divine [unclear]...”
On the Progress of Virtues, one book. “Having gone out perhaps [unclear]...”
On the Use of [unclear], one book. “Your fraternity’s [unclear]...”
Letters to Various Persons, one book. “Reverend father, recently from...”
Various Conferences, one book. “Although among all who wrongly...”
Poems and rhythms. And certain other brief works.

He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Spanheim, before the introduction of the very recent Bursfeld reform, in the year of the Lord 1445.

Antoninus, of the Order of Friars Preacher, archbishop of Florence, an Italian by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, famous and of celebrated reputation in preaching sermons to the people, and no less venerable in life and conduct than in learning, wrote many splendid volumes, by which he labored magnificently for the edification of the Church militant. Of these there is extant a great and very celebrated work, divided into four not small volumes, which he entitled Sum[unclear].

Summa of Cases of Conscience, four books.
A Vast and Notable Chronicle, three books.
Manual for Confessors, one book.
On Ecclesiastical Censure, one book.
Sermons on the Season, one book.
Sermons on the Saints, one book.
And certain other works.

He died, after many labors in sacred study, not without a reputation for holiness, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1459, in the seventh indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, and was buried at Saint Mark’s, a convent of his order. He was inserted into the number of the saints by Pope Adrian VI; his feast is kept on the second day of May.

Leonard of Utino, of the Order of Friars Preacher, a man indeed studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, of excellent talent and outstanding reputation in preaching sermons to the people, wrote for the use of preachers certain splendid little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported: Sermons on the Season, one book.
Sermons on the Saints, one book. “Interpreter of divine things...”
On Laws through Lent, one book.
And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1445.

John of Capistrano, a town in Abruzzo not far from the city of L’Aquila, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a disciple of Saint Bernardino of Siena, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in canon law, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, and devout also in life and religious conduct, a very celebrated preacher of the divine word, who by word and example converted many from iniquity, wrote certain little works of no small usefulness, of which few have come down to me: On Covetousness, three books. “Do not lay up treasures for yourselves...”
Against the Hussites, one book.
Various Sermons, one book.
Some Letters. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1450, and not without a reputation for holiness.

Nicholas of Cusa, bishop of Brixen and cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church of the title of St. Peter ad Vincula, a German by nationality, from the diocese of Trier: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, easily the foremost of the theologians in his time, and outstandingly learned in secular letters; a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and mathematician; subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech; skilled in three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; most upright in life and conduct, and singularly devout; a sincere and fervent lover of the salvation of souls. When he was sent as legate into Germany, he did and established many things useful for the reformation of the Church, and especially of our order. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are extant: On the Vision of God, 1 book.

*The Abbot of Sponheim*

Near Cusa, the village of his birth, on the banks of the Moselle opposite Ürzig, he built a very famous hospital in honor of St. Nicholas the bishop; he richly endowed it with estates and revenues, and adorned it with many books in every branch of knowledge, Greek, Latin, and others.

He died under Emperor Frederick III in the year of the Lord 1464, in the twelfth indiction, on the eleventh day of the month of August, in the sixty-fifth year of his age. He was buried at Rome; his heart was sent to the aforesaid hospital and is buried there in the middle of the choir beneath marble.

Johannes Rode, abbot of the monastery of St. Matthias the Apostle outside the walls of Trier, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nationality, from Trier by homeland: a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstandingly learned in canon law, devout in morals and conduct, a very celebrated restorer of regular observance, from whose labor and foundation the most recent Bursfelde reform of our order in Germany began. He once devoted himself to letters in the school of Heidelberg, where, becoming a bachelor of sacred theology and a very learned licentiate of canon law, he seemed already in mind and body to despise the world. Then, having been made a canon of the church of Metz, dean of St. Simeon, and official of the court of Trier, he despised all things for love of Christ and, to everyone’s amazement, entered the Carthusian order outside Trier. After some years he undertook the office of prior, although unwilling and refusing it. But Otto, archbishop of Trier, seeing that this man was learned, experienced, and zealous, had him brought out of the charterhouse by authority of the supreme pontiff and appointed him abbot in the aforesaid monastery; through him he reformed many monasteries in his diocese. He himself also, by authority of the Council of Basel, magnificently extended the reform. He wrote, moreover, for the reformation of monks: Useful Constitutions, 1 book. Since the divine office which
On the Quality of an Abbot, 1 book. Since from on high proceeds every
And certain other works.

He died under Emperor Albert and Pope Eugene IV, in the year of the Lord 1439, in the twentieth year of his abbacy, in the second indiction, on the first day of the month of December. He was buried in the said monastery of St. Matthias the Apostle at Trier, before the altar of the protomartyr Stephen, in the right apse of the choir, beneath a stone inscribed with his name.

Varinus of Verona, once a pupil of Chrysoloras the Byzantine philosopher, a man in secular writings [unclear] of all in his time 326 *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

[unclear], by far most learned, and not ignorant of divine letters, most skilled in Greek and Latin speech; by whose efforts the studies of the liberal arts, which seemed weakened and now almost extinct, were stirred up and recalled into the light. He taught first at Venice, afterwards at Ferrara, and in both places had very celebrated pupils. He wrote to Prince Leonello the work entitled:

*On the Difference between a Flatterer and a Friend*, one book.
Also a brief *Grammar*, one book.
*A Comparison of Scipio and Gaius*, one book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
Several *Orations*, one book.
Many poems.
And not a few other things.

By order of Pope Nicholas V he translated into Latin Strabo’s *Geography*, a work no less useful than pleasant. From Plutarch he made Latin versions of the lives of many illustrious men. But he also translated Plutarch himself *On the Education of Children*, with many other works, most elegantly; these are partly extant.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460, in the eighth indiction, on the day before the Nones of December; buried at Ferrara in the convent of the Carmelites, honorably given a marble tomb.

Henry Kalteisen, archbishop of the churches of Nidaros and Caesarea, of the Order of Friars Preachers, German by nation, from Koblenz by homeland, where he also entered the order; first made lector of the sacred palace, preacher of the Holy Cross, and inquisitor of heretical depravity; and afterwards, as we have said, consecrated by apostolic authority as chief bishop of two provinces, he became known as renowned throughout the whole world for his learning and preaching. Since he was a very celebrated doctor of sacred theology, he wrote, among other things, notable works:

*Sermons on the Season*, one book.
*Sermons through Lent*, one book.
*On the Magnificat*, one book.
*Various Questions*, one book.
*Conferences to the Clergy*.
And several other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1465, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Nones of October; buried in his own convent at Koblenz.

Johannes Bertachinus of Fermo, a very celebrated legal scholar, and singularly devoted to that faculty, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain small works in law, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among them there is a most famous work, divided into three large volumes, which he compiled very diligently and in fine order with much labor, and entitled:

*Repertory of Both Laws*, five books. “Princes are wont [unclear] immortal...”
*Various Questions*.

He published besides several other things, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

Pope Pius II, Tuscan by nation, Sienese by homeland, previously called Aeneas Silvius, sat in the supreme pontificate after Callixtus III for six years. A man learned in every respect, an outstanding philosopher, orator, and poet, he left many monuments of his talent to posterity. He, poor, served a certain prelate in the Council of Basel for a time. Then, received into the chancery as a scribe, he was created first bishop of Trieste, afterwards of Siena, thereafter cardinal, and finally was elected pope by the votes of all. Johannes Kanneman, of the Order of Friars Minor, a German by nation, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent, renowned for eloquence, was outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. Thinking wrongly about ecclesiastical power, when he was sought by the minister of Saxony for prison, he escaped by flight and fled to the Observantines; thereafter he amended his error along with his life. Johannes de Hagen, the Carthusian, a very learned man, had already reproved him and recalled him to the paths of equity. He wrote: A defense of himself, one book. *Multi famosi viri... He was a profound interpreter and very keen defender of the sayings of John Scotus; expounding philosophy from his writings, and dividing this very work into three parts, mathematical, theological, and ethical, he named it the Compendium.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Callixtus III, in the year of the Lord 1455.

Johannes of Mechelen, a German by nation, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures, not moderately learned in scholastic philosophy, excellent in intellect, distinguished in knowledge, publicly taught theology for many years in the school of Cologne and acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: A notable work on the Sentences, one book;
On the Psalter, one book;

Dionysius Rykel, otherwise de Leuwis, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Bethlehem at Roermond, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled through continual exercise; *The Abbot of Sponheim* skilled also, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, singularly devout, so much so that he was even considered worthy of divine revelations, to whom there are extant several letters of Nicholas of Cusa, a most learned cardinal, wrote so many and such great works that, in number of little works, apart from Augustine, he had no equal among the Latins. He devoted himself to contemplation and prayer with such fervor that one would think he could never have written anything. Again, he was so diligent in writing and reading that one would suppose he could nowhere have been able to pray or contemplate. He slept very little, and his abstinence from food and drink was admirable; after the example of blessed Jerome, he judged it sweet to meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, always either writing something useful or reading, so that sacred reading frequently took its turn.

Bessarion, Greek by nation, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, commonly called the Nicaean, and patriarch of Constantinople, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher and orator second to none in either language, wrote certain very distinguished volumes of his genius, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with immense glory. Of these, the following are reported: against Mark, bishop of Ephesus, who held erroneous views on the Holy Spirit in the manner of the Greeks at the Council of Florence, he wrote an eminent and very distinguished work, which he entitled *Confutation*, one book.
In that work, “Thus when I wish to remain,” one book.
In praise of Plato’s philosophy, five books.
Praises of his fatherland, two books.
To the Greek emperor, of consolation, three books.
Several orations and letters.
And certain other things.
Against the calumniator of Plato, four books.
Whether nature and art act by design, one treatise.
On the Eucharist, one book.
He translated from Aristotle the fourteen books of the *Metaphysics*.

He also founded at Venice a notable library, very richly furnished with many books both Greek and Latin, over which Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, a most learned man, was placed at no small stipend; of him we shall speak later.

At length, full of days, he died while on an embassy to France, under Fre-

under Frederick, emperor the third, and Sixtus, pope the fourth, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1473, in the sixth indiction.

For, as I have learned from the writings of a certain devout father of the same order, he published more than three hundred treatises, among all of which the notable work that he entitled: On the Praise of Poverty, one book. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for...”

340 *On Ecclesiastical Writers* John, abbot of the monastery of Niuicella, devoted to and learned in the sacred Scriptures, nobly trained in canon law, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, wrote many different little works of his own, by which he transmitted the memory of his most celebrated name to posterity with glory. Of these the following are extant: an illustrious and distinguished work entitled *The Concordance of the Bible of the Canons*, one book: “In the beginning God created.”

*Sermons on the Temporale*, one book: “Look, lift up [your] head.”

*Sermons on the Saints*, one book: “Having left the nets, [unclear] Peter.”

*Letters, Various Questions*.

The rest which he composed have not come to the notice of our reading.

Jacob of Gruytrode, a German by nation, of the order of the Carthusians, prior of the house of All the Apostles near Liège, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in the conduct of his life, excellent in intellect, sweet in eloquence, wrote certain distinguished devout little works, the reading of which is not deemed unprofitable for religious persons, lovers of their own salvation. Of these the following are reported:

*On True Virtues*, three books.

*On the Seven Mortal Sins*, one book.

*On the Four Last Things*, one book.

*On the Life of the Lord Jesus*, one book.

*On Preparation before Mass*, one book.

*Colloquy of Jesus and the Old Man*, one book: “Do not be indignant, I pray.”

*Colloquy of Jesus and the Hermit*, one book.

*Colloquy of Jesus and the Disciple*, one book.

*Contemplation of Saint Mary*, one book.

*Little Crown of Saint Mary*: “You have wounded my heart, [unclear].”

*Abbot of Spanheim*

He died most devoutly under Emperor Frederick and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1472, in the fifth indiction, on the day before the Ides of February.

A man devoted to and learned in the sacred Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, ready and circumspect in counsel, and distinguished by experience in many matters, wrote certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity with glory. Of these there is extant the very elegant work *On the Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs*, one book.

And certain other things.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1477, in the ninth indiction.

William Forleon, a Breton by nation, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained in secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in eloquence, who in the Parisian school, by teaching, by disputing, and also by writing, won great praise for his learning, published certain distinguished little works on the Scriptures. Of these there is extant the very celebrated work *On the Sentences*, one book; *Various Questions*, one book.

A hearer and disciple of his was once that most learned man, and easily the foremost of the theologians of our age, Master Stephen called Brulefer, a Frenchman by nation, of the same order, who taught theology in the Paris convent; afterwards betaking himself to the observance of the order at Mainz in Germany, he there began to lecture on the *Sentences*, which he now continues with praise in the convent at Metz. This William flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Paul II, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Albertus de Eyb, a German by nation, canon of the church of Bamberg and chamberlain of Pope Pius II, a man zealous and learned in secular letters, not unacquainted with the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, an outstanding rhetorician and poet, wrote little works not unworthy of reading. Of these the following are extant: to lord Johann, duke of Bavaria, bishop of Munster and later primate of Magdeburg, a distinguished work entitled:

*The Poetic Pearl*, one book. “You have very often desired…”
*On the Married State also*, one book.
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.
And many other things.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Pius II, in the year of the Lord 1460.
